For the Respondent No.1: Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-record. (in both the appeals). 
For the Respondent No. 2: Ex-parte. (in both the appeals)
parties:
Kamrun Nahar Begum ------ Appellant (in both the appeals)
Versus

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Ruhul Amin, J: These appeals by leave are by the pre-emptee against the common judgment in Civil Revision Nos. 567 and 568 of 1990 of a single Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rules. The Civil Revisions were filed against the judgment and order dated January 24, 1990 in Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 120 and 121 of 1987 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge. Dhaka affirming the judgment and order dated April 23, 1987 of the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 189 and 190 of 1984 allowing the same. The Miscellaneous Cases were filed under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1949 seeking preemption in respect of the land in Dhanmondi Residential Area (Dhanmondi R/A).

2. The pre-emptor acquired ownership of the major part of the land of plot No. 543/A in Road No. 13 of Dhanmondi R/A by purchase in between 1975 and 1981 from some of the heirs of original allottee of the aforesaid plot and that he sought for pre-emption as regard the transfer made in February 1984 to the appellant (opposite party No. 1 in the miscellaneous cases) by the heirs of original allotted.

3. Late Kala Miah became owner of 10 Kathas of land of plot No. 543/A, Road No. 13 Dhanmondi R/A, upon obtaining lease from the Government. He died leaving 2 widows 8 sons and 10 daughters. Pre-emptor-Respondent No. 1 by purchase in between the ears 1975-1981 became co-sharer to the extent of 14 annas in the land of plot No. 543/A in Road No. 13. Dhanmondi, R.A. The appellant in February 1984 by 2 different deeds purchased shares of some or the heirs (4 daughters) of Kala Miah. Thereupon the respondent No. 1 tiled the aforesaid Miscellaneous Cases claiming to be the co-sharer of the land transferred to the appellant.

4. The Miscellaneous Cases were opposed by the appellant and another (Respondent  No. 2) by filing written objection contending inter alia, that in respect of the land transferred in the year 1984 there were agreements of the year 1977 between the vendor and the vendees and that the pre-emptor had knowledge about the sale long before 17.8.1984. It was also contended by the pre-emptee that miscellaneous cases were barred by limitation and that some were not maintainable because of the provision 01' section of 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

5. The trial Court allowed the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that Miscellaneous cases were not barred by limitation and that also not barred tinder the provision of section 85(2) of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act. 1949. The pre-emptee-Appellant went on appeal against the judgment and order of the Court of Assistant Judge before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. The Miscellaneous Appeal were heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka and he dismissed the appeals.

6. The preemptee-appellant thereafter moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rules in the Civil Revisions discharged the Rules on the finding "the land was acquired by the Government only to develop demarcate plots and lease out to interested persons retaining its superior right in respect of transfer correction of record, fixing of rent or subsequent enhancement of rent or any other terms on expiry of the lease of 99 years but by this Government does not create obstacle in the beneficial enjoyment of the property its transferability and inheritance by the descendants but the transferability will he always controlled on principle that the land as far as possible should he retained by the heirs of lessee under principles and policy of the pre-emption law. Therefore, I hold that preemption under section 24 of the Non-Agriculture Tenancy Act is very much applicable to the Dhanmondi Residential plot sold to others by the co-sharers".

7. Leave was granted to consider the contention of the appellant as in view of the provision of Sub-section 1(c) of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 as well as in view of the discussion in the of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 as well as in view of the discussion in the case of Md. Mosaddeque Hossain Vs. Dr. Esmat Mirza and others reported in 18 BID (AD) 57 pre-emption sought under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 was not maintainable the High Court Division was in error in discharging the Rule and not holding that pre-emption was not available under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as against the transfer to the pre-emptee-appellant by the co-sharers of the land of plot No. 543/A in Road No. 13 of Dhanmondi R/A .

8. The learned Counsel for the appellant primarily argued in the background of the decision of this court in the case reported in 18 BLD (AD) 57 as to the maintainability of the Miscellaneous cases tiled under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as regard non-agricultural land in Dhanmondi R/A.

9. The question similar to the question involved in the present appeals came up for consideration before this court in the case mentioned hereinabove This court upon considering the provisions of section 85(2) of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act,1949 which reads as:-

"Nothing in this Act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government:

Provided that the right vested in a tenant by the provisions of this Act shall not be divested by the acquisition of the superior right only in the land by the Government." and the provision of section 81 A (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which reads as" His rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants shall except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of the Property Act, 1882 (Act IV of 1882)" (provisio to the subsection is not relevant for the present purpose) has held   that the object of section 85(2) of the Act was to retain control over non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government unencumbered by the provisions of the NAT Act. Section 81A(2) stated positively how the rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants other that those who have become tenants under the Government by virtue of compulsory acquisition of land shall he determined. The NAT Act has not been mentioned to be a governing law in respect of such tenants of non-agricultural land under the Government. Hence on both accounts, under section 85(2) of the NAT Act and section 81A (2) of the SAT Act the ouster of NAT Act film) the categories mentioned therein are complete. Section 24 of the NAT Act has no manner of application to lands of Dhanmondi Residential Area".

<u>10. The learned Counsel for the Respondent No. 1 made submissions amongst other that prayer for pre-emption was very much maintainable since the land sought to be preempted was not acquired for the use of the Government directly or for any office or Department of the Government but for the use of the lessees of the Government which in no way can he considered that the land so acquired is being used by the Government or by any office or Department of the Government and that denying of right of pre-emption in respect of the land or Dhanmondi Residential Area which is non-agricultural land but exercise of right of pre-emption in respect of other non-agricultural land while available under the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy. Act would result in discrimination as regard the right of pre-emption amongst the non-agricultural tenants. This particular contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent in our view is not well funded in law in that in barring pre-emption in respect of the land of Dhanmondi Residential Area upon resorting to the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act no discrimination has been made in between the tenants of the said residential area. The tenants of the other non-agricultural land are being in the different category the bar of pre-emption as has been made as to land of Dhanmondi. R/A. cannot he said discrimination in any respect amongst the class of non-agricultural tenants in general The bar as to pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is limited amongst the tenants of Non- Agricultural land in Dhanmondi R/A and thereby no discrimination has been done amongst the non-agricultural tenants of the said particular area, rather the tenants of the said limited are has been treated equally. The bar so made as to pre-emption of the land of Dhanmondi, R.A. appears to be rational and does not offend the rule of non-discrimination amongst the same class of person placed in the same situation. The other contention that the land sought to be pre-empted as is not used by the Government or by any office or Department of the Government cannot he said immune iron being pre-empted under section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act also not well funded in law because of the fact that the land sought to be pre-empted is being held by the lessee-tenants under the Government in respect of acquisitioned land being same leased out. Provision of sub-section 2 of section 85 of NAT Act clearly shows that provision of section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act shall not he applicable in respect of non-agricultural land as mentioned in section 85(1) of NAT Act and that land of Dhanmondi R/A being the land of one of those categories as the same is held by special kind of tenant of the Government pre-emption is not available. There is no dispute that the lands in Dhanmondi Residential Area are non-agricultural land and the same are being held by the lessees as being the tenants under the Government. Proviso to sub-section (2) of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, and the sub-section (I) of section 81 A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 clearly show that non-agricultural tenants who have become tenants under the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior right in non-agricultural land by the provision of SAT Act the provisions of Nat Act, if so were application to such tenants at the time of acquisition would be regulated by the provision of NAT Act. The application by section 24 NAT Act has been excluded by the provision of section 85(2) of NAT Act in respect of the land mentioned in section 85 (1) (a,b,c,d,e) and land of Dhanmondi R.A being the land of one of the category of lands as in section 85(1) (a,b,c,d,e) application of provision of section 24 NAT Act has been excluded by section 85(2) NAT Act.</u>

11. The learned Counsel for the respondent in spite of best endeavour could not make out any distinction as to question of law involved in the present appeal and question of law considered and decoded in the case reported in 18 BLD (AD) 57. The Respondent could not make out any case to persuade us to take a different view as to the ratio of the reported case nor could the Respondent distinguish the reported case either on facts or law involved therein from the instant appeals.

12. Since the point involved in the appeals is as to whether lands in Dhanmondi Residential Area are or not subject to pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and as the said point is covered by the decision in the case reported in 18 BLD (AD) 57 and that as the decision in the reported case fully applicable to the facts as well as law involved in the appeals and that also to the points urged for consideration in the appeals we are of the view that in the afore state of the matter and also in the light of our discussions made herein over the judgment and decision of the High Court Division calls for interference.

13. Accordingly the appeals are allowed.

14. The judgment and the order Of the High Court Division in the Civil Revisions affirming the judgment and the order of the 2nd Court or Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in the Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 120 and 121 affirming the judgment and the order of the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 189 and 190 of 1984 are set aside and the Miscellaneous Case Nos. 189 and 190 of 1984 are dismissed.

15. There is no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
বিচারপতি জনাব এ, বি, এম খায়রুল হকঃ ইংরেজী বৎসরের ডিসেম্বর মাসে দেওয়ানী আদালতে অবকাশকালীন সময়ে প্রত্যেক জেলা সদরে অন্তত একজন ৰিচারককে বিচারিক দায়িত্ব প্রদান করিবার আবেদন করিয়া অত্র রীট মোকদ্দমাটি দায়ের করা হইয়াছে ৷

2. Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh নামক সংস্থার সভাপতি এ্যডভোকেট মনজিল মোরসেদ এবং আরও ৬ জন অত্র জনস্বার্থমূলক রীট মোকদ্দমাঢি দায়ের করিয়াছেন।

3. আর রীট মোকাদ্দমার দরখাস্তে বর্ণনা করা হইয়াছে যে, Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh একটি নিবন্ধিত সংস্থা ৷ ইহা বাংলাদেশের মানুষের ন্যায্য ও আইনগত অধিকার প্রতিষ্ঠার জন্য স্থাপন করা হইয়াছে ৷দরখাত্তে বর্ণনা করা হয় যে, ৭ নং দরখাস্তকারী ২০০8 ইংসনের ডিসেম্বর মাসে ঢাকা জেলা জজ আদালতে একটি দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করিতে গিয়া বিফল হন কারণ ঐ সময়ে সকল দেওয়ানী আদালতে বাৎসরিক অবকাশকালীন বিরতি চলিতেছিল ৷ ৭ নং দরখাস্তকারীর মোকদ্দমা দায়ের এবং অন্তর্বর্তীকালীন নিষেধাজ্ঞা আদেশের প্রয়োজন ছিল ৷জেলা জজ আদালতে মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করিতে বিফল হইয়া দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইনের ১০৭ ধারা ও ৩৯ আদেশের ১ও ২ নং বিধি এবং তৎসহ ১৫১ ধারায় সুপ্রীম কোর্টের হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে একটি আবেদনপত্র দাখিল করিলে বাংলাদেশের মাননীয় প্রধান বিচারপতি মহোদয় কর্তৃক উক্ত মোকদ্দমাটি শুনানীর জন্য হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে একটি দ্বৈত বেঞ্চ ১৩-১২-২০০৪ ইং তারিখে শুনানী অন্তে দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষে দায়েরকৃত সিভিল অর্ডার নং-৫৪৯৭/২০০৪ মোকদ্দমাঢি অরক্ষনীয় সূত্রে সরাসরি খারিজ করেন ৷ এই প্রেক্ষাপটে ডিসেম্বর মাসে দেওয়ানী আদালতের বাৎসরিক অবকাশকালীন সময়ে একটি অবকাশকালীন দেওয়ানী আদালত স্থাপন প্রার্থনা করিয়া অত্র রীট মোকদ্দমাটি দায়ের করা হইলে অত্র আদালত বাংলাদেশ সংবিধানের ১০২অনুচ্ছেদ অনুসারে ৩-৯-২০০৫ ইং তারিখে নিম্নলিখিত রুল জারী করেনঃ

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why a direction should not be given upon the respondents to constitute vacation Courts for civil cases during civil court vacation of the subordinate judiciary in every December order of orders that any be passed as this court may seem fit and proper.

The Rule is made returnable within 2(two) weeks from date”

4. জনাব মনজিল মোরসেদ, এ্যাডভোকেট, নিজ ও অন্য দরখাস্ত কারীগনের পক্ষে বক্তব্য উপস্থাপন করেন৷ অপরদিকে বেগম নাঈমা হায়দার, ডেপুটি এটর্নি জেনারেল ও তৎসঙ্গে জনাব মোঃ জাফর ইমাম ও জনাব মোঃ মঞ্জুর আলম, সহকারী এটর্নি জেনারেল মহোদয়গণ ১ নং প্রতিবাদী বাংলাদেশ সরকারের পক্ষে বক্তব্য উপস্থাপন করেন ৷

5. দরখাস্তকারীগনকে জনাব মনজিল মোরসেদ, এ্যাডভোকেট, নিবেদন করেন যে, বাংলাদেশ সংবিধান অনুসারে সকল নাগরিক আইনের দৃষ্টিতে সমান অধিকার সম্পন্ন।  বাংলাদেশের যে কোন নাগরিক সরকার এবং মাননীয় প্রধান বিচারপতি মহোদয় কর্তৃক নিদিষ্ট স্থানে ও সময়ে স্থাপিত ফৌজদারী ও দেওয়ানী উভয় আদালতে সাংবিধানিকভাবে বিচার প্রার্থী হইতে অধিকারী কিন্তু প্রতি বৎসর ডিসেম্বর মাসে একটি ফৌজদারী অবকাশকালীন আদালত জরুরী আবেদনপত্র শুনানীর জন্য নিয়োজিত থাকিলেও দেওয়ানী জরুরী আবেদনপত্র শুনানীর জন্য নিয়োজিত থাকিলে ও দেওয়ানী জরুরী আবেদনপত্র নিষ্পত্তির জন্য কোন দেওয়ানী আদালত কার্যকর না থাকায় সাধারণ নাগরিক দেওয়ানী আদালতে তাহাদের সাংবিধানিক অধিকার অনুসারে যথাবিহিত প্রতিকার প্রাপ্ত হইতে ব্যর্থ হয়েন ৷এমতাবস্থায়, তিনি নিবেদন করেন যে, ফৌজদারী অবকাশকালীন আদালতের ন্যায় দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমা দায়ের এবং জরুরী আবেদনপত্র শুনানী ও নিষ্পত্তির জন্য প্ৰতি জেলা সদরে অবকাশকালীন দেওয়ানী আদালত স্থাপন এবং কার্যকর করা ন্যায় বিচারের স্বার্থে একান্ত প্রয়োজন।

6. অপরদিকে সরকার পক্ষে উপস্থিত বেগম নাঈমা হায়দার, বিজ্ঞ ডেপুটি এটর্নি জেনারেল মহোদয় ডিসেম্বর মাসে অবকাশকালীন সময়ে ফৌজদারী আদালতে বিচার প্রার্থীগনের মত দেওয়ানী আদালতেও বিচার ও প্রতিকার প্রার্থনা করিবার অধিকার অস্বীকার করেন নাই ৷

7. উভয়পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ এ্যডভোকেট মহোদয়গণের বক্তব্য শ্রবণ করা হইল এবং দরখাস্তে সংযুক্ত কাগজাদি পরীক্ষানিরীক্ষাসহ পর্যালোচনা করা হইল ৷ উল্লেখ্য যে প্ৰতিবাদীপক্ষে কোন এফিডেভিট-ইন-অপোজিশন দাখিল করা হয় নাই।

8. ইহা অনস্বীকার্য যে দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইন ও কোর্টস এ্যাক্ট, ১৮৮৭, অনুসারে কোন মোকদ্দমা মূল দেওয়ানী আদালত ব্যতিত অন্য কোন আদালতে দায়ের করা যায় না। প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, ৭ নং প্রতিবাদী সরাসরি হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে একটি দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করিয়া বিফল হইয়াছিলেন (এ্যানেকচার-সি) ৷ কিন্তু বাংলাদেশের যে কোন নাগরিকের আইনের আশ্রয় লাভের অধিকার সাংবিধানিকভাবে স্বীকৃত। সেই কারণে বৎসরের যে কোন সময়েই বিচারপ্রার্থী মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করতঃ প্রতিকার পাইবার অধিকারী। ইহা স্বীকার্য যে সিভিল কোর্টস্ এ্যাকট্ ১৮৮৭, এর বিধান অনুসারে বৎসরে একমাস দেওয়ানী আদালত সমূহের বিচারক মহোদয়গন অবকাশ যাপন করিয়া থাকেন ৷ কিন্তু উক্ত অবকাশকালীন সময়েও ফৌজদারী অবকাশকালীন আদালতের ন্যায় দেওয়ানী অবকাশকালীন আদালত এর কার্যক্রম আরম্ভ করিতে আইনগত কোন বাধা নাই।  সিভিল কোর্টস্ এ্যাক্ট এর ৩৬ ধারা নিম্নরুপঃ

“36.(1) The government may invest with the powers of any civil court under this act, by name or in virtue of office,

-----

b) after consultation with the High Court Division any officer serving in any part of the territories to which this act extends and belonging to a class defined in this behalf by the Government.

2) Nothing in sections 4,5,6,8,10 or 11 applies to any officer so invested, but all the other provisions of this act shall, so far as those provisions can be made applicable, apply to him as if he were a judge of the court with the powers which he is invested.

……”

এমত অবস্থায় ডিসেম্বর মাসে বাৎসরিক দেওয়ানী অবকাশকালীন সময়ে কতিপয় জেলার জন্য একটি জয়েন্ট ডিষ্ট্রিক্ট জজ আদালত অথবা অবস্থাভেদে ও প্রয়োজন অনুসারে প্রত্যেক জেলায় একটি করিয়া অবকাশকালীন আদালত সংশ্লিষ্ট জেলা বা জেলা সমূহের জন্য দেওয়ানী মূল অধিক্ষেত্রের সকল মোকদ্দমাদায়ের এবং জরুরী আবেদনপত্র  শুনানী ও নিস্পত্তি করিবার ক্ষমতা অর্পন করা যাইতে পারে। ইহাতে আইনগত কোন বাধা নাই ৷ বরঞ্চ ইহাতে আইনের আশ্রয় লাভের জন্য যেকোন বিচারপ্রার্থীর আইনগত অধিকার সুরক্ষিত ও নিশ্চিত হইবে ৷

উল্লেখ্য যে বাৎসরিক অবকাশ সমাপ্ত হইবার পর দায়েরকৃত মোকদ্দমা এবং আবেদনপত্রগুলি সংশ্লিষ্ট এলাকা ও আর্থিক ক্ষমতা সম্পন্ন সংশ্লিষ্ট আদালতে স্থানান্তরিত হইবে ৷

এমতাবস্থায় দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ এ্যডভোকেট মহোদয়ের বক্তব্যের যৌক্তিকত আছে বলিয়া প্রতীয়মান হয় ৷

<u>9. অতএব, কয়েকটি জেলার জন্য একটি যুগ্ম জেলা জজ্ মর্যাদা সম্পন্ন আদালত অথবা প্রয়োজনে প্রতিটি জেলায় ঐরুপ একটি করিয়া দেওয়ানী অবকাশকালীন আদালত সপ্তাহের প্রতি কার্য দিবসে অথবা নির্দিষ্ট কয়েকটি দিবসে কার্যক্রম চালু করিবার নির্দেশ প্রদান করা হইল ৷ ঐ সকল দিবসে তাহারা জরুরী আবেদনপত্র গ্রহণ এবং নিস্পত্তি করিতে পারিবেন ৷ অবশ্য সপ্তাহের সকল কার্য দিবসে মূল মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করা যাইবে ৷</u>

<u>এই ব্যাপারে সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্তৃপক্ষ প্রয়োজন অনুসারে যথাবিহিত ব্যবস্থা অবিলম্বে গ্রহন করিবেন ৷</u>

10. এই  রায়ের কপি আইন, বিচার ও সংসদ  বিষয়ক মন্ত্রনালয়ের সচিব এবং সুপ্রীম কোর্টের রেজিষ্টার বরাবরে প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহনের জন্য অনতিবিলন্বে প্রেরন করা হউক।

অতএব অত্র রুলটি খরচা ব্যতিরেকে এ্যবসলিউট্ করা হইল।

End.

Mr. Md. Azizul Haq with Mr. Md. Anouroul Islam: For the Petitioner 
Mr. Hassan Foiz Siddiquee with Mr. Fazle Rabbi: For the Opposite Party No.1
parties:
Rafiqul Islam ------ Petitioner
Versus
Md. Abdul Jabbar Sarker & Ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Shahidul Islam, J.: This Rule arises from the judgment and order dated 10.02.05 passed by the learned District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal, Kurigram in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 2004, allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and order dated 25.4.04 passed by the learned Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal, Bhurungamari, Kurigram in Election Tribunal Case No 1 of 2003.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are that the election for the post of chairman of the Paikar Chhara Union Parishad under Bhurungamari Upazilla, Kurigram was held on 25.01.03. The petitioner Rafiqul Islam contested the said election for the post of Chairman having his symbol umbrella and the respondent No. 1 Abdul Jabbar and 4 others were his rival candidates. The symbol of Abdul Jabbar was pineapple. Election was duly held in all the 10(ten) polling centres. The unofficial result of all the poling Centres were declared and the final result was declared unofficially. As per unofficial final result, the petitioner got in total 2475 votes and the respondent Abdul Jabbar got in total 2517 votes. The other contesting candidate namely Abdur Rahkim got 1973 votes, Abdur Razzaque got 1470 votes, Mahmud Hassan got 2400 votes and Solaiman Ali got 49 votes. The opposite party No. 1 was declared elected by a margin of 42 votes. 

3. The petitioner submitted an Election Petition before the concerned election Tribunal on a number of grounds, such as, some of the ballot papers were torn and many of the them did not bear official mark or seal on the back, counting of votes were made after switching off the lights of the counting rooms, the election officer influenced the result of election in favour of A. Jabbar. He prayed, that he be declared elected in place of Abdul Jabbar, and in alternative, the election as a whole be set-aside.

4. The opposite party Abdul Jabbar denied those allegations by filing a written objection and Contested the election petition case contending inter-alia that the election was duly held and counting of votes in all the poling centers were lawfully done and the result was lawfully declared. 

5. The Tribunal recorded the evidence of PW1- PW13 and also recorded the evidence of DW 1-DW4. Exhibit 1, l(ka)- 1(Jha). 2, 2(ka)- 2(jha), 3, 4, 4(Ka), 5 and 6 were Marked in favour of the petitioner. Exhibit Ka, Kha, Kha(1)- Kha (9) and Ga were marked in favour of the opposite party NO. 1. 

6. Thereafter, on the prayer of the petitioner the gunny bags containing the ballot papers were called for. The petitioner made a prayer for recounting of ballot papers by the Tribunal but the Tribunal by order dated 26/2/04 requested the District Magistrate to depute a Magistrate 1st class for recounting of the ballot papers and to report to the Tribunal. 

7. That order was challenged by the opposite party before the learned District Judge Kurigram in Civil Revision Case NO. 8 of 04 and the learned District Judge by his order dated 24.3.04 rejected the said Civil Revision Case and upheld the order of recounting by a Magistrate 1st class. 
8. Thereafter the District Magistrate Kurigram appointed Mr. A. Jabbar, Magistrate 1st class for recounting of the ballot paper who after making recount submitted a report before the Tribunal alleging inter-alia that 102 ballot papers counted in favour of opposite party A. Jabbar were found without having any seal and signature of the presiding officer and further found as many as 320 ballot papers were counted in favour of the petitioner having double seal. 

9. The Election Tribunal on reciept of the said report declared the petitioner as elected by his judgment and order dated 25.4.04. 

10. The opposite party No. I took Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 2004 before the learned District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal, Kurigram and the learned District Judge by his judgment and order dated 10.2.05 allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and order of the election Tribunal.

11. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order the petitioner has obtained the instant Rule. 

12. Mr. Md. Azizul Haq with Mr. Md. Shaheen on appearing for the petitioner submitted that the election Appellate Tribunal being biased have passed the impugned judgment and order. He submitted that the recounting of votes were lawfully made by a Magistrate 1st class in presence of both the parties and the Magistrate found 102 ballot papers without having any official seal and signature of the presiding officer. He submitted that those ballot papers were counted in favour of the opposite party No. l. He further submitted that 320 ballot papers, having double seal were counted in favour of the opposite party. He further submitted that the Tribunal lawfully deducted 102 ballot papers from the total number of votes as against the opposite party NO. 1 and declared the petitioner to be elected. He lastly submitted, that the Appellate Tribunal without considering the evidences on record, most illegally reversed the finding of the Tribunal. He prayed for an interference by this Court. 

13. Mr. Hassan Foiz Siddique with Mr. Fazle Rabbi on appearing for the opposite party on the other has submitted that the entrustment made by the Tribunal upon the Magistrate for examine and recounting of ballot papers has vitiated the whole trial. He submitted that such entrustment was made illegally. He further submitted that only the Tribunal had the authority to re-open the gunny bags for inspecting and had the authority to recount the ballot papers. He further submitted that the Tribunal committed grave illegality on relying upon the report of the Magistrate blindly. He further submitted that the report of the Magistrate was not liable to be considered without examining the Magistrate. He submitted that the report itself cannot be considered to be an evidence without producing the Magistrate as an witness in the case and without giving any opportunity to the opposite party to cross examine the Magistrate. He submitted that the order dated 24.3.04 passed by the learned District Judge Kurigram in Civil Revision Case NO. 8 of 2004, affirming the order of recounting of ballot papers by the Magistrate will not extend the jurisdiction to the Magistrate for recounting of ballot papers and submitted that the judgment and order passed by the learned Appellate Tribunal is not liable to be disturbed. Mr. Siddidque relied upon the case law of Mohaprashad Singh V. S. Ramani Mohan Singh reported in A. I. R 1914 (P. C) at page 140. Mr. Siddique further submitted that the statutory power of recounting of ballot papers by the Tribunal cannot be delegated or assigned without having any statutory authority to do so. Mr. Siddique lastly submitted that the order of recounting of ballot papers by the Magistrate was although affirmed by the Appellate Tribunal but that affirmation did not give any jurisdiction to the Magistrate for recounting. He relied upon Maxwell on Interpretation of statute and submitted that consent cannot give jurisdiction. He submitted for discharge of the Rule. 

14. I have heard the learned advocates of both the parties at length and have gone through the evidence an record. I have perused the judgments of both the Courts below very carefully.

15. On perusal of the evidence on record and also on perusal of the entire lower Court's record it appears that the petitioner's evidence was closed on 5.11.03 and thereafter the opposite parties evidence was closed on 24.02.04. It further appears that thereafter by order dated 24.02.04 the Tribunal called for the gunny bags, containing ballot papers and other material and those were received by him on 26.02.04. It further appears that by order dated 26.02.04 the Tribunal requested the District Magistrate Kurigram for deputing a Magistrate, 1st Class for inspection and for recounting of ballot papers and for submitting report to him about the result of recounting. It further appears that the said order dated 26.02.04 was affirmed by the learned District Judge, Kurigram in Civil Revision Case No. 8 of 2004. It further appears from the order No. 35 dated 25.03.04 that Mr. Abdul Majid, Magistrate 1st Class was trusted to have an inspection and recounting of ballot papers who alleged to have submitted his report on 25.03.04. It further appears from the order sheets of the election Tribunal case that on receipt of the report from Mr. M. A. Majid, Magistrate, 1st Class, he fixed the date for hearing argument. It further appears from the order-sheet that neither the said Magistrate was examined as an witness nor the report of the Magistrate was admitted into an evidence.  It further appears from the order-sheet that the Tribunal neither inspected the election materials by himself nor formed any opinion by himself about the intactness of the Gunny bags. On perusal of the judgment and order of the Tribunal it appears that he allowed the election case and declared the petitioner to be a returned candidate not on consideration of the evidence of PW I -PW13 but on consideration of the report of the magistrate. It farther appears from the judgment of the Appellate Tribunal that before recounting of ballot papers, the Magistrate found the gunny bags without having any seal, that is to say that those gunny bags were found not in intact condition. 

16. It further appears that the learned Appellate Tribunal on considering the report of the Magistrate and also on considering the other evidence on record allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal. 

17. From the judgments of the Courts below and also on perusal of the evidence on record it is very much clear that the petitioner could not prove any of the grounds as taken in the election petition to nullify or to differ with the result of election. It further appears to me that after being unsuccessful to prove his specific grounds as taken in the election petition he lastly depended totally upon the result of recounting of ballot papers. 

18. From the facts and circumstances and from the evidences on record the following questions have to be decided by this court:-

1) As to whether the Tribunal was justified in disturbing the result of election only upon the report of the Magistrate. 
2) Whether the Tribunal was justified to deligate power of recounting of votes to a Magistrate. 

3) As to whether the order dated 24.3.04 passed by the learned District Judge, Kurigram in Civil Revision NO. 8 of 2004 authorised the Magistrate for recounting of ballot papers, lawfully. 

4) Whether the impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal is liable to be set-aside. 

All these issues are taken up together for disposal. 

19. The Union Parishad Election Rules do not provide any provision for recounting of votes on opening of ballot boxes. The recounting of votes by the Tribunal is the outcome of the judicial decision as clearly laid down from time to time. The principle stated in the judgments of the higher Courts of law for recounting of votes underlines certain conditions such as, the Tribunal felt the necessity of counting the votes to satisfy itself as to correct counting by the presiding officer or that the issue raised in the Election Petition cannot be determined without recounting. 

20. It the case law of Abdul Basher chowdhury reported in 31 DLR (A. D) at page 296, the Appellate Division observed as follows:-

"We have no manner of doubt that in an appropriate case the election Tribunal has authority to make a recounting of the votes in order to satisfy itself that the counting made by the presiding officer on the basis of which the result of the election has been declared was properly made". In the case of Azimuddin Ahmed V. S. Election Tribunal, Narayangonj and others reported in 21 DLR (H.D) at page 594, a division Bench of this Court observed as follows:- 

"The Election Rules do not provide for recounting of ballot papers by the Tribunal and the power to recount ballot papers has been given under Rule 41 to the presiding officer only. But if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal and the election petition cannot be determined without such recounting, only then the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot papers in presence of parties. Before doing so it must come to a finding by evidence on oath that this recounting is indispensably necessary. This view was endorsed by the appellate Division in case of Afjal Khan 1980 B. S. C. R. at page 96. It is by now well-settled that if recounting of ballot papers is material issue before the Tribunal then only the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes." 

21. In the instant case we do not find any such foundation available for recounting of votes. Moreover the judicial decisions authorises the Tribunal itself the power to recount votes in a proper case. in order to satisfy itself, that the counting made by the presiding officer on the basis of which the result of the election has been declared was property made. In view of the above it is my considered view that the Election Tribunal was not justified to delegate power to a Magistrate to recount votes and was not justified in interfering with the result of election upon consideration of the report submitted by the Magistrate. It is also my considered view that the order dated 24.03.04 lased by the learned District Judge in Civil Revision No. 8 of 2004 also did not give and authority to the concerned Magistrate for recounting of votes. 

22. It is further to be noted that the Tribunal itself having failed to feel necessity of counting the votes to satisfy itself as to correct counting by the presiding officer and no counting of votes having made by the Tribunal itself the result of election cannot be disturbed by him. Moreover the report of the Magistrate was not admitted into evidence. The so called report is also not  available on record too. The Tribunal was totally in an error of law in allowing the Election petition and declaring the petitioner as a returned candidate. The learned District Judge did not commit any error of law in setting aside the judgment and order dated 25.04.04 passed by the Election Tribunal, Bhurungamari in Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 2003. There is no merit in the Rule. 

23. In the result the Rule is discharged however, without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 10.02.05 passed by the learned District Judge and election Appellate Tribunal Kurigram in Miscellaneous Appeal No.8 of 2004 is hereby affirmed. The office is directed to send down the records.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Awlad Ali, J.: This Rule issued under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order dated 14.5.2005 passed by the District Judge, Chittagong was initially heard by a Division Bench comprising Mr. Justice A. B. M. Khairul Haque and Mr. Justice A. T. M. Fazle Kabir and a preliminary question of law arose as to the maintainability of Revisional application before the District Judge against an order passed by the Subordinate Judge in a suit the valuation of which is Tk. 3,77,61255/- and the said Bench in view of the conflicting decisions given by other Benches referred the case to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench and the Hon'ble Chief Justice constituted this full Bench in accordance with the revision of rule 4 of Chapter VII of the High Court Rules for final decision.

2. The questions as formulated by the Court referring the case at the time of hearing of the Rule are (1) "Whether the pecuniary jurisdiction of the District Judge under Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, is unlimited, if not, (2) Whether the High Court Division, under Section 115(1) of the Code can entertain revisional application hearing valuation of more than Tk. 5,000 Lac, in respect of orders passed by the Joint District Judge." 

3. The back ground and the facts from which the questions arose that the petitioner in the revision case instituted a suit being other Suit No. 96 of 2003 on 3.6.2003 in the second Court of Joint District Judge, Chittagong against the Opposite party Nos.l-8 praying for declaration of title in the suit properties. In the suit in pursuance of an application the defendant opposite party No. 9 was impleaded as defendant by an order dated 13.2.05 and the said defendant began to interfere with the possession of the plaintiffs and as such an application was filed on behalf of the plaintiffs praying for an order of temporary injunction and until hearing of the said application, prayed for ad interim order of injunction. The learned Joint District Judge by his order No. 56 dated 27.2.2005 issued notice upon the defendant opposite party No. 9 to show cause as to why injunction shall not be granted and since no ad interim order was passed another application under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was moved on 6.03.05 praying for an order restraining the said defendant from interfering with the possession or otherwise dispossessing the tenants of the plaintiff-petitioners from the disputed property, but the learned Joint District Judge after hearing the petitioner by his order dated 6.3.03 fixed the date of hearing of the said application on 12.3.05. Being aggrieved by the order dated 27.2.05 and 6.3.05 the plaintiff petitioners preferred a revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of District Judge, Chittagong, but the learned District Judge by his order dated 14.5.05 without entering into the merit of the revisional application rejected the application holding that since the valuation of the suit is above 5.00 Lac. Taka he does not have the pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain the revisional application under section 115(2) of the C. P. Code. The petitioners being aggrieved by the order dated 14.5.05 passed by the learned District Judge moved this court and obtained the Rule. 

4. The defendant opposite party No.9 filed a counter affidavit to oppose the Rule. 

5. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, at the very outset of the hearing of the Rule issued under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure brought to the notice of the referring court two judgments one passed in Civil Order No. 1105 of 2005 dated 5.4.2005 and the other one in Civil Order No.2345 of 2005 passed on 2.7.2005. In Civil Order No.1105, a Division Bench took the view that under the amended section 115(2) of the Code, a revisional application valued above 5,00 lac taka is not maintainable before the District Judge, rather the High Court is a proper forum under section 115(1) of the Code to dispose of such revisional application. A conflicting view was taken by another Division Bench presided over by Mr. Justice Md. Arayes Uddin and it was held by that Bench that since no valuation has been mentioned in any of the provision of section 115 of the Code, the revisional application with the valuation of any amount would lie before the District Judge under section 115(2) against an order passed by a Joint District Judge from which no appeal lies. In view of the above conflicting decisions Mr. Rafiqul Huq submitted that the matter should be referred to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for forming a Larger Bench to consider the question of pecuniary jurisdiction of the District Judge under section 115(2) of the Code. After hearing Mr. Huq the learned Counsel for the petitioners and Mr. Shafique Ahmed, who appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submitted that in view of the words "from which no appeal lies" the question of valuation is immaterial and relying on the decision in Civil Order No. 2345 of 2005 he concluded that all revisional applications irrespective of the valuation are maintainable before the District Judge and the reference to the Hon'ble Chief Justice to constitute a larger Bench will only cause delay in disposal of the revisional application. The concluding portion of the order dated 14.5.05 passed by the learned District Judge Chittagong is to the following effect "So since this Revisional application arose out of a suit which was valued for Tk. 3,77,61225/- and exceeds pecuniary jurisdiction of Tk. 5,00,000/- of the District Judge in which the District Judge has no appellate jurisdiction, this Civil Revision is not maintainable." 

6. The Bench referring the case observed that the question of jurisdiction of the Court has to be decided at the earliest opportunity and referred to section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is in the following terms:

"Save in so far as is otherwise expressly provided nothing herein contained shall operate to give any courts, jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject matter of which exceeds the pecuniary limits (if any) of its ordinary jurisdiction." Then observed that since the suit is valued at mud above Tk. 5 lac then the revisional application can only be disposed of by a Court which has got the necessary pecuniary Jurisdiction. It has been further observed by the referring Bench that sub-section (I) of Section 115 does not empower the High Court Division to call for the records in connection with an 'order' passed by the Joint District Judge, since the provision does not include an `order' passed by the Joint District Judge." 

7. We have noticed from the submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioners that two Division Benches, One Presided over by Mr. Justice Syed Amirul Islam and another presided over by Mr. Justice Md. Abdul Quddus took the view that, the District Judge cannot entertain any revisional application under Section 115(2) of the Code beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction which is fixed at 5 lac Taka being the appellate Jurisdiction. In the Judgment of Civil Revision No. 3318 of 2004, dated 31.7.2005 in the case of Joysna Ara Amin and others Vs. Sudhanghu Bimal Dhar and others Mr. Justice Syed Amirul Islam sitting with Mr. Justice Sheikh Abdul Awal considering the relevant provisions of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure observed that the court which is not invested with appellate power cannot also exercise revisional power. Only that court which has appellate jurisdiction can exercise revisional power as per law. It has further been observed that in view of the provision of Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure there is nothing in the sub-section expressly providing that a revision will lie against an order of a joint District Judge before the District Judge irrespective of the value of the subject matter of the suit or proceeding pending in the court of Joint District Judge where ordinarily suits or proceeding of unlimited valuation are tiled. It has been further observed that always revisional forum has been determined with reference to the pecuniary jurisdiction of the appellate court. The District Judge can exercise his power of revision under Section 115(2) of the Code where his pecuniary jurisdiction in revisional matter is co-expensive with that of his appellate jurisdiction. The conclusion drawn by their Lordships is that the learned District Judge cannot entertain an application under Section 115(2) of the Code beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction which is fixed for appellate jurisdiction. 

8. Another Division Bench Presided over by Mr. Justice Md. Abdul Quddus in Civil Order No. 1105 of 2005 by Judgment dated 5.4.2005 again considering the provision of section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 115(2) of the Code expressed the view that Civil Revision against an order of Joint District Judge in a suit or proceeding pending before it the value of the subject matter of which is above and beyond Tk. 5.00 lac being the pecuniary jurisdiction of District Judge can never be preferred in the court of District Judge without any express provision in that regard being provided in the amended section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

9. Conflicting decision was given by a Division Bench comprising Mr. Justice Md. Arayes Uddin and Mr. Justice S. M. Emdadul Haque in the Judgment dated 2.7.2005 in Civil Order No. 2345 of 2005 and their Lordships expressed the view that in view of the 3rd amendment of the Code of Civil Procedure (Act No. 40 of 2003) the learned District Judge under section 115(2) of the Code has been empowered to entertain revisional application against the order passed by the Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies. In this regard no pecuniary jurisdiction has been maintained in the aforesaid Act. 

10. For proper elucidation of section 115(1) and (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure as amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Third Amendment) Act 2003 and in determining the revisional jurisdiction of the District Judge with reference to other provision of law namely, Civil Courts Act, 1887 as amended, the Suit Valuation Act and the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code, we reproduce sub-section (1) & (2) of Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows: 

"115-Revision-(1) The High Court Division, any, Division may, on the application of any party aggrieved call for the record of any suit of proceeding, in which a decree or an order has been passed by a Court of District Judge or Additional-District Judge, or a decree has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies; and if much Court appear to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such decree or order occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division may, revise such decree or order and, make such order in the suit or proceeding as it thinks fit. 

(2) The court of District Judge may, on the application of any party aggrieved, call for the record of any suit of proceeding in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies; and if such Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning failure of Justice, the Court of District Judge may, revise such order and, make such order as it think fit." 

11. We need to discuss firstly certain provisions of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 as amended by the Civil Courts (Amendment) Act, 2001. 

Section 19, Extent of Jurisdiction of Senior Assistant Judge etc. save as other-wise provided by any enactment for the time being in force, the jurisdiction of a Senior Assistant Judge and Assistant Judge shall extend to all suits of which the value does not exceed four lac taka and two lac taka respectively. 

Section 21(1) save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a Joint District Judge shall lie-

(a) to the District Judge where the value of the original suit in which or in any proceeding arising 'out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed five lac Taka, and 

(b) to the High Court Division in any other case. 

(2) Save as aforesaid an appeal from a decree or order of Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge shall lie to the District Judge. 

12. Section 19 of the Civil Court Act provides for the pecuniary jurisdiction of Senior Assistant Judge and Assistant Judge in respect of suit, Sub-section 2 of Section 21 indicates that an appeal shall lie to the District Judge against a decree or order passed by the Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge Order as employed in Sub-section (2) implies appealable order as contemplated under Order XLIII Rule (I) of the Code of Civil Procedure of any order passed in any proceeding like pre-emption proceeding, Suits or proceedings of which the value exceeds four lac taka will lie to the Joint District Judge having unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction. but according to the provision of Sub-section (1) of section 21 appeal from a decree or order passed by the Joint District Judge will lie to the District Judge in which the value of the original suit or proceeding did not exceed -taka five lac. Therefore, in a suit filed before the Joint District Judge the value of which does not exceed five lac taka, if a decree or order as the case may be, is passed, appeal will lie to the District Judge. As per clause (b) of Sub-section (1) of Section 21 appeal will lie to the High Court Division in any other cases i.e. when the value does exceed taka five lac. 

Incidentally it may be mentioned that the District Judge and the Joint District Judge have equal pecuniary jurisdiction over all original suit cognizable by the Civil Courts, save as otherwise provided by any enactment, yet suits shall be instituted in the court of the lowest grade competent to try them as indicated in Section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

13. Section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure as we have already noted, indicates the pecuniary jurisdiction of any Court over suits. Therefore, the pecuniary value will determine the forum and the jurisdiction over the subject matter of the proceedings in the Civil Jurisdiction, Importantly, section 6 of the Civil Procedure Cc de is inextricably linked to Section 8 of the Suit Valuation Act, 1887 which is as under: 

"8, Court fee value and Jurisdictional value to be the same in certain suits—Where the suits other than those referred to the Court Fees Act 1870 (VII of 1870), Section 7, paragraph (v) (vi) and (ix) and paragraph (x) clause (d), Court Fees are payable advalorem under the Court-Fees Act, 1870 the value as determinable for the computation of court-fees and the value for purposes of jurisdiction shall be the same."

The above provision indicates that the value for the purpose of jurisdiction and Court-fees should be same. 

14. With advantage, we may also refer to Section 11 of the Suit valuation Act, 1887 where provisions have been made in respect of procedure where objection is taken on appeal or revision that a suit or appeal was not properly valued for jurisdictional purposes, And it is indicated there that the objection as to the valuation for jurisdictional purposes shall be taken at the first instance, and such objection as regards valuation for jurisdictional purpose can also be taken in revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

15. Reading Section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Section 8 and 11 of the Suit Valuation Act and the relevant provisions of the Civil Courts Act as stated above the conclusion would follow that the value of the suit or proceeding would follow that the value of the suit or proceeding would conclusively determine the forum where suits or proceeding will be filed and tried and the appeal will be heard and disposed of. Thus the forum of appeal is to be determined according to the value of the suit or proceeding and the value of appeal consequently will lead to the revisional forum and jurisdiction and that would be the basis for determining revisional forum. The provision of Sub-section (1) of Section 115 is not our concern as from the plain reading it would appear that the power is the revisional power of the High Court Division. But the question has arisen as to whether the High Court Division under Sub-section (1) is empowered to call for the records in connection with an "order" passed by the Joint District Judge, since the provision does not include the "order" passed by the Joint District Judge. 

16. Mr. Rafique-UI-Huq, has pointed out that under the original Section 115 and also in the amended Section 115(1) and (2) as introduced by the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978, the words "by any court subordinate to the High Court Division" were employed, which have been omitted in the newly enacted Sub-section (1) and (2) of Section 115 of the Code and thereby confusion has been created about the power of the High Court Division in calling for the records of any suit or proceeding in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Although some on the Courts including the Courts of Additional District Judge and Joint District Judge are subordinate to the District Judge but all the courts are undoubtedly subordinate to the High Court Division under the constitutional scheme, (Article 109 and 114 of the constitution) and in view of the provision of Section 9 of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 and some provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore in a proper case the High Court Division in exercise of the power of superintendence and control may call for the records of any suit or proceeding in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, particularly when the value of the suit or proceeding is above five lac taka, and that against an order passed by the Joint District Judge in a suit or proceeding the value of which exceeds taka four lac but does not exceed taka five lac revision will be to the District Judge. 

Section 115(2) was enacted by the Code of Civil Procedure (Third Amendment) Act, 2003 to prevent the overflowing effect or revision cases in the High Court Division in Civil Jurisdiction and to obviate the sufferings of the litigants But in enacting such provision the legislature has not expressly amended the other provisions of law such as Section 6 of the Code, the provisions of Civil Courts Act and the Suit Valuation Act and the effect of those provisions remained unaffected after the introduction of Sub-section (2) of Section 115. Therefore, unless specific rules to the contrary have been framed the revisional jurisdiction must be determined according to the value of the suit or proceeding. The courts having jurisdiction to entertain an appeal shall have jurisdiction on revisional application as per valuation of the original suit or proceeding. in the instant case the plaintiff valued the suit at Tk. 3,77,61,225.00 and the order proposed to be revised was passed by the Joint District Judge, and a revisional application was taken to the District Judge and the learned District Judge rejected the application summarily by his order dated 14.5.2005 on the ground of pecuniary jurisdiction. In view of our above discussion, the learned District Judge, rightly turned down the revisional application

17. Besides the order as aforesaid, which is revisable by the High Court Division, some other orders pssed by the Joint District Judge may be revised by the High Court Division, as for instance, an order of temporary injunction is or has been passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, or the Assistant Judge as the case may be, against that order an appeal will lie to the District Judge and if such appeal is transferred to the Joint District Judge and the appeal is heard and disposed of by the Joint District Judge, Judgment or order in such appeal is to be understood as judgment or order passed by the District Judge. Therefore, appeal arising of an order before the District Judge, transferred to the Joint District Judge for disposal, the Joint District Judge exercises the power of the District Judge in such appeal, District Judge and Joint District Judge in such case exercise concurrent jurisdiction. In this regard Section 22 of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 is relevant which is in the following terms: 

"22(1) A District Judge may transfer to any Joint District Judge under his administration Control any appeals pending before him from the decree or orders of Assistant Judges, 
(2) ……………………………………….   

(3) Appeals transferred under this section shall be disposed of subject to the rules applicable to like appears when disposed of by the District Judge. 

Similar power is exercised by the District Judge wider Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is provided under that Section that on the application of any of the parties or of its own motion the District Court may at any stage transfer any suit, appeal or other proceedings before it for trial or disposal to any court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same. 

18. Considering the above provision, the proposition has been settled in the case of Mohammad Eshaque Vs. Ruhum Amin and others reported in (4 DLR, 342 and 33 DLR 141) Abdus Salam Vs. Bangladesh. 

Ordinarily the forum choice is dependent on the pecuniary balue of the subject matter of suits or proceedings, unless there is contrary provision. Procedure for filing revisional application will require the petitioner to state the value of the suit from which it arises. 

19. In the "note" of Chapter 11 of part l of the High Court Rules it has been stated that "Every memorandum of appeal from orders and every application for revision should state the value of the suit from which it arises. 

In the absence of any prescribed rules or procedure for filing revisional 'application before the District Judge the aforesaid provision may be the guideline for presenting a revisional application before the District Judge, under section 115 (1) of the Code. 
20. In view our above discussions the question No. 1 as formulated by the court referring the case is answered in the negative i.e. the district Judge has not unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in entertain revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code. The second question is answered in the affirmative. The High Court Division under Section 115 (1) of the Code can entertain revisional application against the order passed by the Joint District Judges in a suit or proceeding the value of which is more than taka five lac in exercise of the power of superintendence and control over the subordinate courts

21. Therefore, the revisionsl application under section 115(2) against the orders dated 27.02.05 and 6.3.05 filed before the District Judge, Chittagong was not maintainable. The consequence would follow that the rile issue under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order dated 14.5.2005 passed by the learned District Judge will discharged. The petitioner may, however, bring an application under Section 115(1) of the Code before the High Court Division against the order of the Joint District Judge, if so advised. 

22. The reference is thus disposed of.

23. A copy of this judgment may be sent to the concerned ministries.

End.

parties:
Mahbub Alam ------ Petitioner
VS.
Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT, Sylhet and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Azizul Haque J: This Rule Nisi, on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the proceeding of Special Tribunal Case No.96 of 2003 pending in the Senior Special Tribunal, Sylhet, arising out of Kotwali PS Case No.5 dated 1-2-2003 corresponding to GR Case No.103 of 2003 under section 25B of the Special Power Act, 1974 in relation to seizure list made by the Customs Officials, should not be declared to have been continued unlawfully and without jurisdiction and/or such other or further order or orders passed as this court may deem fit and proper.

2. By the same Rule issuing order dated 17-8-2003, all further proceedings of the above mentioned Special Tribunal Case were stayed.

3. The facts found for disposal of the Rule are that on 1-2-2003 at 12-00 hours the petitioner Mahbub Alam landed at the Osmani International Airport, Sylhet by Bangladesh Biman bearing Flight No. BG-0052 and while he was going to make a declaration in declaration counter of the Airport, the Customs Officials took him to the office of the Deputy Commissioner of Customs and on interrogation, he confessed that he had 19 gold bars with him which were seized by the Customs Officials by a seizure list (Annexure-A to the writ petition). Thereafter, one Md Jahangir Hossain, Customs Inspector attached to the said Airport lodged first information report on 1-2-2003 with Kotwali Police Station, Sylhet (Annexure-B) alleging, inter alia, that on that day at about 1200 hours the Customs Officials on duty, on tip off, searched the body of the petitioner after his arrival from abroad and recovered 19 gold bars each weighing 10 tolas in hiding from within a belt alike bag, specially made for carrying the same, tied round his waist. They also recovered some drugs and cosmetics from his suit- case and carton. As the petitioner did not make any declaration as per provision laid down in Rule 3(5) of the Passenger (Non-tourist) Baggage (Import) Rules, 2000 (hereafter referred to as the Rules, 2000) and he brought the said gold etc. from abroad and evaded customs duties and taxes leviable there-on and thereby committed offence under sections 16/32/300/156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 and section 25B of the Special Powers Act, 1974 (hereafter referred to as the Act).

4. On the basis of this first information report, Sylhet Kotwali PS Case No.5 dated 1-2-2003 was started and the petitioner was arrested in connection with the said case. Thereafter, police investigated the case and submitted charge sheet (Annexure-E) against the petitioner under section 25B of the Act. The case record was transmitted to the Special Tribunal consisting of Sessions Judge, Sylhet and the case was registered as Special Tribunal Case No.96 of 2003 and formal charge was framed on 25-6-2003 against the petitioner under section 25B(1)(b) of the Act. The Customs Officials most illegally seized the gold which was lawfully brought by the petitioner under the Rule 2000.

5. The further case of the petitioner is that the act of searching the petitioner was illegal and beyond the jurisdiction of Customs Officials and the petitioner having felt aggrieved by the seizure of gold bars and in the initiation of the proceeding of the Special Tribunal Case preferred this writ petition and obtained the Rule and order of stay in the manner stated above.

6. Mr. Md Shahidul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the petitioner was entitled to bring 10 kg of gold under Rule 3(5) of the Rules, 2000 and as such, the seizure of the gold from the petitioner was illegal and consequently, the initiation of the proceeding of the Special Tribunal Case is also illegal. He further submits that the petitioner was about to give a declaration as regards the bringing of gold from abroad and he was ready to pay the customs duties and taxes, but he was not allowed to do so. He further submits that the petitioner did not evade customs duties and taxes in bringing the gold recovered and as such, no offence under Section 25B of the Act was disclosed .and constituted against him.

7. Mr. Islam further submits that the act of seizing the gold bars is illegal and beyond jurisdiction of the Customs Official and thus it is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. He further submits that the Customs Authority has also started a Seizure Case under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 1969 which must be disposed of in accordance with law and a direction may be given to that effect.

8. On the other hand, Mr. Abdur Rahman Howlader, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing of the respondents submits that this writ is not at all maintainable as the relief sought for clearly suggests that the proper forum of redress would be launching a quashment proceeding under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

9. He next submits that the Special Tribunal Case has been instituted on the specific allegations that the petitioner brought the gold bars, drugs and cosmetics recovered from abroad and after landing at the airport; he, without making any declaration of the possession of the articles recovered for payment of Customs duties-and taxes, evaded the said duties and taxes leviable thereon and thereby committed the offence punishable under section 25B of the Act. This, he submits that the allegations made in the FIR prima facie constitute the offence complained of and as such, it cannot be said that the proceeding of the Special Tribunal Case was initiated unlawfully.

10. Mr. Howlader further submits that though the petitioner has claimed that he was going to give a declaration in the counter of the airport, but this is a statement of his own. He further submits that whether or not the petitioner was going to give a declaration as claimed in not admitted by the prosecution or the respondents and as such, it is a disputed question of fact to be decided by the Special Tribunal wherein the Special Tribunal Case is pending. He further submits that this disputed question of fact cannot be resolved in this writ petition and as such, the writ petition is not maintainable in the eye of law.

11. The learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that since the allegation against the petitioner is of smuggling of the alleged gold and other articles, the same as property can be disposed of only by the Special Tribunal wherein the case is pending and as such, the respondent No.1 or the Customs Department has no authority to dispose of the articles and consequently, this Court has little scope to give a direction upon the respondents for disposal of the articles recovered.

12. We have considered the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the learned Assistant Attorney-General on behalf of the respondents and perused the writ petition along with the annexures.

13. On perusal of the Annexure A seizure list, Annexure B FIR, and Annexure F charge sheet, it appears that the smuggling case under section 25B of the Act has been started on a definite allegation that the petitioner smuggled the gold bars, drugs and cosmetics recovered by bringing the same from abroad by evading customs duties and taxes. It is true that gold is not a contraband item and it can be imported under the Rules, 2000 and that is why, it appears, the petitioner has claimed that he was going to give a declaration about his possession of the gold recovered and he was falsely implicated in this case. Thus, it is clear that whether or not the petitioner attempted to give a declaration about the possession of gold recovered is a disputed question of fact to be determined on evidence and as such, the same can- not be resolved in writ jurisdiction. Thus matter is well settled by our apex Court and this Court as well in plethora of cases. For proper appreciation, we would like to refer two decisions, one of which is the case of Khalilur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 2000 BLD (AD) 152= 52 DLR (AD) 115 wherein their Lordships have held that the dispute regarding variation of population cannot be resolved in a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution since it requires adjudication on facts and on evidence. The other one is in the case of Shamsunnahar Salam vs Md Wahidur Rahman 51 DLR (AD) 232 wherein, their Lordships have held that however extraordinary its powers, a writ Court cannot and should not decide any disputed question of fact which requires evidence to be taken for settlement.

14. It is claimed by the petitioner that the gold was seized illegally though the petitioner did not commit any offence. This question whether the petitioner committed the alleged offence or not will be determined by the Special Tribunal, where the case is now pending, on the basis of evidence to be adduced by the prosecution. Since the matter whether the petitioner committed the offence charged with is pending for decision in the Special Tribunal, the same cannot be adjudicated in writ jurisdiction. This view of us gets support from the decision held in the case of Md Idris vs EP Timber Merchants reported In 20 DLR 355. The decision runs as follows:

"The Court has already indicated in the case of Dr. MO Ghani vs Dr. ANM Mahmood 18 DLR (SC) 463 that where it is apparent from the facts of a particular case that the same questions are pending decision in a civil litigation the High Court should not during the pendency of that, litigation, take upon itself to decide the same questions under article 98 of the constitution. In such cases the parties concerned should be left to pursue their litigationin the ordinary courts and should not be allowed to short-circuit them by a petition under article 98 of the constitution. It was clearly laid down in that case that resort to the High Court's summary jurisdiction should not be personated if it amounts to circumvent in of the normal process of law'."

15. The relief sought for in this writ petition clearly shows that the proceeding of the Special Tribunal Case has been challenged the proceeding of a criminal case can hardly be challenged in writ jurisdiction. The proper remedy challenging the proceeding of a criminal case lies in the quashment proceeding under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure before this Court in its criminal jurisdiction. The power of this Court both under Article 102 of the Constitution and section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is extraordinary, but independent of each other and either proceeding is summary in nature. It is conceivable that we should not exercise our jurisdiction in an unwarranted manner as we feel that we must not transgress the bounds of decency also. Thus, we find that the petitioner ought to have approached this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in its extraordinary criminal jurisdiction which is meat and adequate for the purpose. Since there was parallel remedy for the petitioner under section 561A of Code of Criminal Procedure who did not avail of the same, this writ petitioner is not maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution. The petitioner, it appears to us, did not avail his redress under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the facts narrated in the first information report do constitute the offence complained of.

16. Mr. Shahidul Islam has tried to impress upon us that the Customs Authority has power to dispose of the gold recovered in accordance with the provisions laid down in the Customs Act, 1969. It may be mentioned that on behalf of the petitioner an application was filed on 18-5-2010 for a direction upon the respondent to dispose of the gold recovered as per the Customs Act, 1969. The application was kept in the record for disposal along with the Rule. This application therefore appears and requires our consideration and decision as well. For proper appreciation of the matter We need to examine the relevant provisions of law. Section 34B of the Act runs as under:

34B Act to override all other laws-The provisions of this Act shall have effect not withstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in the Code or in any other law for the time being in force."

<u>17. The quoted provisions of section 34B of the Act shows that it is then on-obstante clause of the Act on the strength of which the provisions of the Act shall over those of the Code of Criminal Procedure or any other law including the Customs Act, 1969. Since admittedly the smuggling case as Special Tribunal. Case is pending in the Special Tribunal, the articles recovered shall be disposed of by the said Special Tribunal alone. About disposal of property, there is no provision in the Act and therefore the Special Tribunal shall dispose of the property under section 516A or 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure being empowered to do so by section 29 of the Act which provides that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, so far only as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act, shall apply to the proceedings of Special Tribunals, and such Special Tribunals shall have all the powers conferred by the Code Criminal procedure on a Court of Section exercising original jurisdiction.</u>

18. To appreciate the provisions relating to disposal of property, sections 561A and 517 are reproduced below:

516A Order for custody and disposal of property pending trial in certain cases-When any property regarding which. any offence appears to have been committed, or which appears to have been used for the commission of any offence, is produced before any Criminal Court during any inquiry or trial, the Court may make such order as it thinks fit for the proper custody of such property pending the conclusion of the inquiry or trial, and, if the property is subject to speedy or natural decay, many, after recording such evidence as it thinks necessary, order it to be sold, or otherwise disposed of.

517. order for disposal of property regarding which offence committed-(l) When an inquiry or a trial in any Criminal Court is concluded, the Court may make such order as it thinks fit for the disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or otherwise of any property or document produced before it or in its custody or regarding which any offence appears to have been committed, or which has been used for the commission of any offence."

(2).......................

(3)...................

(4)...................

Explanation......................

19. Since the gold recovered is an offending article within the meaning of section 561A and 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Special Tribunal is seized with the trial of the smuggling case as Special Tribunal Case, no other department or authority but the Special Tribunal alone can dispose of the article recovered either under section 516A or 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In particular, we hold that the Customs Department has no authority to dispose of the gold and other articles recovered so long the smuggling case lies in the domain of the Special Tribunal.

20. Form what we have stated above considering the facts and relevant laws, we are of the view that this writ petition is not maintainable and the Rule is liable to be discharged.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The petition dated 18-5-2010 for direction is rejected. The stay order granted in connection with the Rule stands vacated. The Senior Special Tribunal consisting of Sessions Judge, Sylhet is directed to proceed with the Special Tribunal Case No.96 of 2003 in accordance with law.

Communicate this judgment and order to the Special Tribunal concerned for necessary action and the Respondent No.1 for information and necessary action.

End.
