full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, C.J- in this appeal a question of law of public importance is involved in that whether a monthly tenancy created under the provision of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is heritable upon the death of the tenant. The other question of law involved will be dealt with at its appropriate place.

2. Facts, in brief, are that the appellants as plaintiff landlords instituted a Small Cause Courts suit for ejectment of Respondents. Their case for ejectment is that Balaram, father of Respondents, was monthly tenant at the premises in 1968 and from April, 1969, Suresh, the first Respondent took the tenancy in his name, and he having defaulted in payment of rent was liable to ejectment. The second Respondent, brother of Suresh, was added as a party to the suit on the objection of Respondent as he was also residing in the premises and was said to be in permissive possession. Plaintiffs asserted that both were liable to ejectment. The defence, in substance, apart from other grounds not relevant for this appeal, was that the tenancy was in favour of Balaram, and on his death it has devolved upon both the respondents as his heirs and so the notice to quit u/s 106 of the first Respondent was insufficient.

3. The trial Court on consideration of evidence, both oral and documentary, accepted the plaint case that Balaram was the first tenant, thereafter from 1969 first Respondent became tenant as evidenced by Ext. 3 series and he did not make payment after October, 1969 and was a defaulter. The second Respondent was in possession as the brother of Suresh but not as a tenant. He, therefore, decreed the suit for ejectment. On revision by the Respondents, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division reversed the findings of the trial Court, and held that the tenancy was only in favour of Balaram and on his death it devolved on his sons, the Respondents and so the notice to quit on Suresh was insufficient. He made the rule absolute and set aside the decree of the trial Court.

4. Leave was granted to consider two questions, one of which has already been set out at the very beginning. Both the questions may be set out as follows:

1.	Whether the High Court Division was well founded in law in holding that a monthly tenancy under the Transfer of Property Act is heritable.

2.	Whether upon a correct principle of law the learned Single Judge reversed the finding of fact u/s 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act as to the creation of tenancy in favour of first Respondent.

<u>5. Consideration the importance of the questions, after hearing the learned Counsel, Mr. Khandker Mahbuddin Ahmed for the Appellants, and Mr. Salam for the Respondents, we thought it proper to call Mr. S.R. Pal as amicus curiae, to assist the Court. We have had the opportunity of hearing the learned Counsels and their learned arguments have helped us in coming to our conclusion in this, appeal. We, however, refrain from dealing separately with the submissions of each of the learned Counsels on the question.</u>

<u>6. Since the question will not take as long, we propose to deal with it first. It is now well settled that a revision under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act lies if there is an error of law involved in the decision or the trial Court. A revision is available with a wider scope than that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They are now well settled and require no further elaboration. What is to be seen is whether the learned Judge of the High Court provision has applied the correct principle in interfering with the decision of the trial Court under section 25 of the said Act. First of all, he is to come to a finding the decision of the Court below suffers from an error of law, and then to see whether the error of law has vitiated its decision, and on so finding, he can proceed to reverse the decision of the trial Court. Keeping this principle in view, we are to judge the finding of the learned Single Judge regarding the reversal of the finding of the trial Court on the question of creation of tenancy in favour of Respondent 1. It is to be remembered that both the Courts below have accepted the creation of tenancy in 1968 in favour of Balaram, the father of the Respondents. Where the two Courts differed is on the creation of tenancy in favour of Respondent 1. According to the trial Court, tenancy was created in his favour in 1969 and this he based on a reference to Ext. 3 series the rent receipts. This finding was reversed by the learned Single Judge making a bare observation that it was clear from the pleadings of the parties and the evidence that the tenancy of Balaram was created on 1.1.68 and that the tenancy devolved upon his death on his heirs. The question is whether this finding is in accordance with the provisions of section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act. Plainly it is not. The learned Judge has not shown what was the error in the appreciation of evidence by the trial Court in its finding which could be termed as an error of law.which would give the High Court Division an authority under the Act to interfere. The approach of the learned Judge was as if he was dealing with a first appeal on fact and not a revision under section 25 of the said Act. No error of law was pointed out by him, nor do we find any such error in the finding of the trial Court. The trial Court from evidence drew a conclusion of fact which the learned Judge reversed without pointing out any error of law. He merely drew a second conclusion of fact which section 25 of the said Act does not authorize him to do. In this view of the matter the reversal of finding of fact by the learned Judge on this point cannot be sustained and must be set aside. The finding of the trial Court that a tenancy was created in favour of Respondent 1 on the death of Balaram, his father, must be upheld. In view of this finding, the first question loses much of its importance but since a question of law of public importance is involved, we proceed to deal with it.</u>

<u>7. From the facts on record we find that there was no written contract between the plaintiff's on the one hand and Balaram or Respondent 1 on the other, and the tenancy was created on the mere payment of rent between the landlord and tenant. A tenancy of this nature is legal and valid in terms of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. It has been termed to be a lease or tenancy from month to month terminable on the part of either party by fifteen days notice expiring at the end of a month of the tenancy. The section also refers to certain agricultural and manufacturing leases, but we are not concerned with them in this appeal.</u>

8. It is further to be remembered that this monthly tenancy is also the subject of Bangladesh Premises Rent Control Ordinance, where, notwithstanding the provisions of Transfer of Property Act and Contract Act, wide-ranging provisions have been introduced encroaching upon the rights of the parties. But, in view of the question of law involved in this appeal, a detailed discussion of the Rent Control Ordinance need not be looked into as the Ordinance chiefly deals with the protection of the tenant from ejectment so long as he pays rent in terms of the Ordinance and with some other incidents of the tenancy but does not deal with the heritability of the tenancy. We only want to refer to the definition of 'tenant' given in the Ordinance. The Ordinance says, a tenant means a person by whom, or on whose account, rent is payable for any premises, and includes a legal representative as defined in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and a person continuing in possession after the termination of a tenancy in his favour. A glance at the definition along with the definition of 'landlord', which is noting but the counterpart of the tenant, indicates that the definition was inserted in the Ordinance only to emphasize the tenant's liability to pay rent and nothing more, and this meaning becomes clear when we advert to the second half of the definition of 'tenant,' which says that it also includes a person continuing in possession after the termination of his tenancy. In this view of the matter, we are not called upon to dilate on this Ordinance any further.

9. At the outset, it is to be observed that learned arguments have been advanced from the Bar on the English rule of the tenancy-at-will which is created where lands or tenements are let out by one man to another to have and to hold to him at the will of the lessor, by force of which lease, the lessee is in possession. A tenancy-at-will is determinable at the will of either landlord or tenant and is a personal relation between the original landlord and the tenant and is determined by the death of either of them. Whereas, the relationship between the landlord and tenant created under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act has been termed a lease from month to month, terminable on the part of either party by fifteen day's notice expiring at the end of a month of tenancy. The section, in a restricted sense, describes the tenancy as a lease. The difference between the two is also patently manifest that no fruitful purpose will be served in discussing the subject any further.

<u>10. In order to grasp the problem before us, we are to see the character of tenancy that created under the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. This section is specie of a rider to the principle section which is section 105, and which defines what a lease is, section 105 says that a lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property. made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, as hare of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically for or on specified occasions to the transferor by the transferee who accepts the transfer on such term. Now if we analyze the essential elements constituting a lease, we find the following elements : (a) the right must be one as to immovable property ; (b) the right must be that of enjoyment of immovable property ; (c) there must be a transfer of such right ; (d) the right of transfer is an interest in property ; (e) the transfer be made for a certain time express or implied, or in perpetuity ; (f) the transfer must be one for consideration : (g) the consideration must be of the particular kind mentioned in the section, namely, premium or rent, as defined by the section, either or both of them.</u>

11. The lease, as defined, no doubt creates an interest in immovable property and the Act also says that it is transferable, but the Act is silent on its heritability. I will depend of course upon the interest created by the lease and so, we are to see the true character of the lease created under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

12. Under section 106 of the Act, the lease contemplated, among others, is a lease or tenancy from month to month and is terminable by either party giving fifteen days notice expiring at the end of a month of the tenancy. A glance at the elements constituting lease under section 105 set out above reveals that all they are not present in a lease under section 106, nevertheless, it has been termed to be a lease under this section. An analysis of the elements constituting a lease along with a comparison of the two sections indicates that the lease coming under section 106 cannot be treated as a lease under section 105 having all its incidents.

13. Let us, therefore, consider what interest is created by the lease under section 106. The section says that the lease will be from month to month. No doubt this lease is for the occupation of the premises by the tenant which is terminable at the option of either party on giving fifteen days notice expiring at the end of a month of the tenancy. The termination of the tenancy, of course, cannot take effect unless the notice to quit under this section has been served by one or the other, and the statutory period had expired. Analyzing in this way, we find that a relationship is created under this section between the landlord and the Cannot which is of a personal nature. The right of occupation of the premises has been given and this right of occupation from month to month from its very nature cannot but be personal and so cannot create an interest in the land as a lease under section 105 does. The right of occupation remains personal with the tenant. The right being personal it ceases with the death of either party or so on the death of the tenant. the tenancy ceases and hence it is not heritable.

14. Since some interest is created, even though personal, by the monthly tenancy. This may not be, to borrow an English concept, an estate in favour of the tenant, nevertheless the heirs or successors-in-interest of a tenant in occupation of the premises on his death do not become trespassers, because neither their predecessor nor they entered the premises wrongfully, and so their continuance in the premises will be that of a tenant by sufferance. to borrow again another English concept. It is to be noted that tenancy by sufferance arises by implication of law and cannot be created by a contract between the parties. Such interest cannot be assigned or conveyed and is in fact a mere invention of law to prevent the continuance of possession acting as a trespass. Such a tenant may be ejected at any time without demand of possession. If, however, the landlord assents or receives rent, he becomes a tenant in terms of section 106, as his predecessor was, with all the incidents of a tenancy under that section.

15. In our view, the construction we have given on section 106 of the Act will obviate serious complications which would otherwise originate if we treat a monthly tenancy under section 106 as full fledged lease of property and so heritable. To illustrate, if it is heritable, then, according to the personal law of the tenant, it will be inherited by the whole group of heirs contemplated therein sons, daughters wife, other kinds etc. and all of them becoming tenants some of them may not be occupying the premises at all. Nonetheless, they will become liable to future rent and will be entitled to receive the notice to quit. Likewise, the landlord will be faced with an insurmountable problem of ejecting those innumerable "tenants by inheritance" many of whom might not be known to him. He would also be faced with the immense difficulty of serving the notice to quit on all of them.

16. Then again, under what principle this right is made available to the heirs? The original tenant himself did not enjoy more than a mere right of occupation on payment of rent was liable to be ejected on fifteen days notice. How this uncertain, if not precarious right of occupation, can become an estate to be inherited by persons who have never occupied the premises? It is a proposition which is untenable. In that event the tenant having the bare right of occupation will leave after his death a higher right to his heirs in the tenancy, which he never had. The heirs will become tenants without occupying or using the premises. This cannot be contemplated because in that event heirs will inherit a right higher than that of their predecessor.

17. The view we have taken is in accord with the true intent or section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this view, the decision in the case of Gouribala Pal vs Kunjalai Saha (1960) 12 DLR 37 where a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court has, relying on an earlier Calcutta decision in the case of Anwarali Bepari vs. Jamini Lal Ray Chowdhury 43 CWN 197, held that upon the death of an original tenant in respect of an immovable property, the tenancy being one from month to month, does not cease to exist and the heirs and legal representatives of the original tenant do not become trespassers but having continued in possession as heirs, they become tenants by holding over, cannot be sustained. The view taken in the Calcutta decision was that there was no reason why a tenant from month to month should not be heritable. For the reasons we have already given, we find it difficult to concur with the view expressed in this decision.

18. We therefore, conclude that on the death of the tenant a tenancy from month to month does not become heritable. The finding of the learned Judge of the High Court Division that upon the death of Balaram, the tenancy was inherited by his two son’s cannot, therefore, be sustained. For the reasons we set aside the decision of the High Court Division and restore that of the trial Court.

The appeal is allowed with costs.

End.

Vs.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 26.11.1971 passed by the Dacca High Court in S.A. No. 1381 of 1962)
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, C. J.:—In this appeal a preliminary objection has been raised by the learned Additional Attorney General that the appeal and the suit had abated in terms of President's Order No. 90 of 1972. The appellants instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge Dacca, being Title suit No. 12 of 1958 for declaration that the acquisition of the Hat at Shakherchar by the Government under Notification dated 2.4.56 issued under section 3(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was illegal and void and for injunction. The suit was dismissed. The appeal filed by the Appellants being Title Appeal No. 320 of 1960 was also dismissed. The Appellants thereafter filed a Second Appeal where it was recorded by a Division Bench that "Mr. A.W. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the Appellants, submits that the relevant compensation assessment roll has already been published and prepared and as such he does not press the appeal. The appeal is dismissed for non-prosecution,"

2. Leave was granted to consider whether non-retainable lands such as hat owned by non-rent receiver stood acquired by virtue of general notification dated 2.4.56 issued under section 3(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or by the notification issued under section 43 of the Act and further the Government is entitled to mesne profits from the plaintiffs with effect from 14.4.56 or from 1st day of the Bangali year following the notification under section 43. The last two questions do not directly arise from the appeal.

3. To revert back to the preliminary objection raised by the learned Additional Attorney General all that need be said, is that the plaintiff appellants in their suit made the following prayers:

“That the Court may be pleased to declare that the acquisition of the scheduled properties by the defendant No. 1 by the notification No. 4849 L.R-dated 2.4.66 and published in the Dacca Gazette Extraordinary dated 2.4.56 is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the Plaintiffs, and have in no way affected their right, title, interest and possession therein.

(b) That a permanent injunction res-training the defendants from taking possession of the scheduled properties and from interfering in any way with the plaintiff's rights to properties may be issued."

<u>4. There can be no denying the fact that the Plaintiffs sought to challenge the acquisition of their Hats and Bazars made under the general notification dated 2.4.56 issued under section 3(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and so it is directly hit by President's Order No. 90 of 1972, which gives a clear mandate of law that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of the Order, all suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (E.B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B. Ordinance No. III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedding shall cease to have any effect and no Court shall entertain and no person shall bring any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question.</u>

5. We had occasion, in Civil Appeal No. 46 of 1979. People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraha wherein the acquisition of debuttor estate by general notification dated 2-4-56 under section 3(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was challenged, to hold on a reference to President's Order No. 90 of 1972, that the directive in law is clear, that, on coming into operation of this Order, notwithstanding earlier view of the law on the subject, a pending proceeding seeking to challenge or call in question the acquisition of any property under any of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall abate and no proceedings shall be instituted in any Court.

As we have already mentioned that the plaint in clear language challenged the general notification whereby Hats and Bazars of the appellants were acquired and so the suit comes within the bar of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 and accordingly, the appeal and the suit have abated.

The appeal is accordingly dismissed it having abated but without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Abdul Hannan Khan (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman J : The petitioner Md. Abdul Hannan Khan obtained this Rule Nisi on 31.10.89 calling upon the respondent No.1, Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, respondent No. 3 Mr. Md. Abdul Hakim, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture (Inquiry Officer) and respondent No. 4 Mr. Ashraful Huda, Assistant Inspector General of Police, Headquarters, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka to show cause why the impugned charge (Annexure-D) dated 3.8.89 and the impugned notice (Annexure-G) dated 2.9.89 issued by respondent No. 3 asking the petitioner to appear before him and to remain present during the examination of witnesses on 16.9.89 in respect of the charge framed against the petitioner and the departmental proceedings pursuant thereto should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. The petitioner in his petition has stated that he joined the service under the Government of Bangladesh as Deputy Superintendent of Police Class-I on 21.8.73 in the Ministry of Home Affairs. He was finally promoted to the post of Superintendent of Police in 1983. He served as Superintendent of Police in Tangail from March, 1987 to April, 1989 and in Narayanganj from April 1989 to July 1989. On 1st August, 1989 the petitioner has been transferred to Bandarban where he is now serving. It is further stated that on 6.6.89 respondent No. 4 Ashraful Huda, Assistant Inspector General. of Police, Police Headquarter, Bangladesh Secretariat sent a telegram asking the petitioner to meet Mr. Ahbab Ahmed, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs on 7.6.89 at 10-00 AM. On 7.6.89 the petitioner appeared before Mr. Ahbab Ahmed and found respondent No. 4 sitting there as a member of the Committee. Mr. Ahmed informed him that a two-member Committee appointed by the Ministry of Home Affairs was conducting an enquiry against the petitioner. The petitioner then requested them to provide him with the name of the complainant, the charge-sheet, the names and addresses of the witnesses, the copy of the deposition made by the witnesses and the order of the Government, in respect of forming the Enquiry Committee against the petitioner. On 17.6.89 the petitioner made a representation (Annexure-C) to the Inspector General of Police, but received no reply. He also received no reply to the representation Annexure-B dated 7.6.89 made to Mr. Ahbab Ahmed, Joint Secretary. Respondent No. 4, Assistant Inspector General of Police by his letter dated 5.8.89 (Annexure-D) sent a charge (annexed at page 30 of the petition) framed on 3.8.89 by Mr. Mohammad Ali, the then Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs against him along with the statement of allegations (Annexed at page 33 of the petition) dated 2.8.89. The charge against the petitioner was framed by the respondent No. 1 Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. The said respondent No. 1 by his letter dated 10.8.89 (Annexure-E) omitted charge No. 3. The charge (Annexure-D) not only contained the allegations of misconduct and corruption against the petitioner but also contained the following paragraphs 10 and 11.

“১০। সেহেতু এক্ষণে আপনি জনাব মোঃ আব্দুল হান্নান খান, পুলিশ সুপার বান্দরবন (সাবেক পুলিশ সুপার, টাংগাইল) কে সরকারী কর্মচারী (শৃংখলা ও আপীল) বিধি মালা ১৯৮৫ এর বিধি নং ৩(ক) ও ৩(খ) এর অধীনে অদক্ষতা ও অসদাচরণের দায়ে অভিযুক্ত করা হইল এবং তজ্জন্য কেন আপনাকে উপরোক্ত বিধিমালার বিধি নং ৪ এর অধীনে চাকুরী হইতে বরখাস্ত করা যাইবে না অথবা অন্য কোন শাস্তিপ্রদান করা হইবে না তাহা উপযুক্ত কারণ দর্শাইয়া একটি লিখিত জবাব অত্র অভিযোগ নামা পাওয়ার ১০ দিনের মধ্যে উপরোক্ত বিধিমালার বিধি নং ১০(৯) এর অধীনে নিযুক্ত তদন্তকারী কর্মকর্তা জনাব আঃ হাকিম যুগ্ম সচিব, কৃষি মন্ত্রণালয় এর নিকট দাখিল করিতে এবং সেই সাথে আপনি ব্যক্তিগত শুনানী চাহেন কিনা তাহাও জানাইতে আপনাকে নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইল।

১১। যে সমস্ত অভিযোগের ভিত্তিতে অত্র অভিযোগনামা প্রনীত হইয়াছে তাহার একটি বিবরনী এতদসংগে প্রেরণ করা হইল।”

3. Allegations have also been brought against the petitioner that although three dangerous dacoits were caught red-handed in Nagarpun Ps Case No.2 (9)88, yet in lieu of illegal gratification he compelled his subordinate officer ASP Nazrul to submit final report in that case, that the supporters of Awami League killed Anju, Jinnah and Latif and hid their dead bodies regarding which deceased Jinnah's father informed the Gopalpur PS where GD Entry No. 486 dated 6.8.88 was noted, but the petitioner sided with the murderers and took no action in the matter and that the petitioner openly supported the Awami League and gave speeches as Chief Guest of the Mujibbadi Chhatra League at Bhuapur Collage, etc.

4. The petitioner submitted reply (Annexure-F at pages 38-45 of the petition) on 17.8.89 to the Enquiry Officer, (Respondent No. 3 Mr. Abdul Hakim, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture) who by his letter dated 2.9.89 (Annexure -G) asked the petitioner to remain present on 16.9.89 from 10.00 A.M. in his office in the Bangladesh Secretariat at the time of examination of the witnesses. At this stage on 13.9.89 the petitioner moved the present Writ Petition before a learned Single Judge of the Vacation Bench and obtained order staying further proceedings till the matter was placed before the regular Division Bench after re-opening of the Court. Thereafter on 31.10.89 the petitioner obtained the present Rule and the order of stay has been extended from time to time till 11.4.90.

5. Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate, submits that the petitioner is entitled to the protection of the fundamental rights as guaranteed under Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution. Article 27 of the Constitution provides that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law on the basis of which Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate, argues that petitioner cannot be treated differently from those who have been placed under similar circumstances i.e. those Government employees who are being proceeded against under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985.

6. Article 31 of the Constitution provides that to enjoy the protection of law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law.

7. In the instant case Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate, points out that the provision of Rule 27(2) of the said Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 has not been followed by the authority i.e. Respondent No. 1, the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, inasmuch as it is clearly provided in Rule 7 that when a Government Servant is to be proceeded against under any of the clauses of Rule 3 and the authority is of the opinion that the allegations, if established, would call for major penalty, the authority shall frame a charge, specifying therein the penalty proposed to be imposed and. communicate it to the Government servant together with a statement of allegations on which it is based and of any other circumstances which the authority proposes to take into consideration when passing orders on the case and require the accused Government servant to submit within ten to twenty working days, a written statement of his defence and to show cause at the same time why the penalty proposed to be imposed on him should not be imposed and also to state whether he desires to be heard in person and where the accused submits his .statement of defence within the specified or extended time, the authority shall consider such statement together with all materials relating to the charge and if after such consideration, the authority is of the opinion that

(a) there is no good ground (or proceeding against the accused, it shall withdraw the charge and the proceeding shall accordingly be disposed of.

(b) there is good ground for proceeding against the accused but the allegations, if established, would call for a minor penalty, it may, after giving him an opportunity of being heard in person, award any of the minor penalties within thirty working days from the date of submission of statement of defence or may follow the procedure laid down in Rule 6 for imposition of minor penalty by appointing an Inquiry Officer under that Rule.

(c) there is good ground for proceeding against the accused for imposition of major penalty, it shall appoint an Inquiry Officer who shall be an officer not below the rank of that of the accused or of Board of Inquiry to enquire into the allegations contained in the charge.

8. In the present case, Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the authority i.e. Respondent No.1 contravened the aforesaid provision of Rule 7(2) and without giving the petitioner any opportunity to submit his statement of defence to the authority directly, illegally appointed an Inquiry Officer namely, Respondent No. 3 in the same order by which the authority i.e. Respondent No. 1 framed the charge against the petitioner on 3.8.89. For this reason he submits that by contravention of the provision of Rule 7(2) by simultaneously appointing an Inquiry Officer, there has been a contravention of principle of natural justice inasmuch as the petitioner has been deprived of his initial right of submitting directly to the authority his statement of defence to be considered by the authority i.e. Respondent No. 1 who could consider the statement of the petitioner with all materials relating to the charge and could be of the opinion that there is no good ground for proceeding against the petitioner and dispose of the proceeding by withdrawing the charge.

9. Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that Rule 10(9) of the said Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 provides as follows:

"The authority may, in any case it deems fit, instead of appointing an Inquiry Officer under these rules, appoint a Board of Inquiry, consisting of three persons, and, where the Board of Inquiry is appointed references in this Rule to an Inquiry Officer shall be construed as reference to the Board."

The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the authority i.e. the Respondent No. 1 has stated in the charge that he was appointing Respondent No. 3 as the Inquiry Officer under Rule 10(9) although under the said Rule 10(9) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985, Respondent No. 1 is required in law to appoint a Board of Inquiry consisting of three persons and that consequently Respondent No. 3 being coram non judice has no jurisdiction to make inquiry under the said Rules. Mainly on these two grounds the learned Advocate for the petitioner argues that the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 31 of the Constitution to be treated in accordance with law has been violated and that his fundamental right under Article 27 of the Constitution not to be differently treated and discriminated against other person in similar circumstances has also been violated.

10. Mr. AF Hasan Ariff, the learned Deputy Attorney General draws our attention to Article 102 (5), Article 117 and Article 152(1) of the Constitution and submits that as the Parliament has enacted the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (Act VII of 1981) no Court including the Supreme Court can entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal set up under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 in view of the provision of sub-article (2) of Article 117 of the Constitution. He further submits that the fundamental rights of the petitioner as guaranteed under Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution to be dealt with in accordance with law and his right not to be discriminated from any person situated in similar circumstances are not at all attracted in this case because even if any violation or infringement of any law or rule having the force of law in respect of any provision of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 takes place, the remedy for the same is provided in the said Rules, 1985 as well under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980. He also refers to the decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of SP Sampath Kumar Vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1987 SC 386.

"102 Sub-article (5) of Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh reads as follows:

"102(5) In this article, unless the context otherwise required "person" included a statutory public authority and any Court or tribunal, other than a Court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force or a tribunal to which Article 117 applied."

But sub-article (5) of Article 102 cannot be read in isolation, it has to be read with Article 117 of the Constitution of Bangladesh as it is in the same Part VI (the Judiciary).

Article 117 of the Constitution reads as follows:

"117.( 1) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to and arising out of

(a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishment:

(b) the acquisition, administration, management and disposal of any property vested in or managed by the Government by or under any law, including the operation and management of, and service in, any nationalised enterprise or statutory public authority.

(c) any law to which clause (2) of Article 102 applied

(2) Where any administrative tribunal is established under this article, no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal.

Provided that Parliament may, by law, provide for appeals for, or the review of, decision of any such tribunal,"

11. Article 152(1) of the Constitution provides that the word 'Court" means any Court of law including Supreme Court.

12. Thus we find that Article 117 of the Constitution clearly provides that the Parliament, may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishment, and that where any such administrative tribunal is established under Article 117; no court including the Supreme Court can entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal. Therefore, in view of the provision of Article 117 of the Constitution read with Article 102 (5) of the Constitution this court has no jurisdiction to entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal. We have already expressed this view in our judgment in Writ Petition No. 309 of 1990 (Md. Serajul Islam Vs. Director General of Food) giving rise to CPSLA No. 64 of 1990.

<u>13. It is a general rule that no one is entitled to move the Court or the Administrative Tribunal for a supposed or threatened injury until all the available remedies at the hands of the administrative authorities have been exhausted (Myers Vs. Bethlehem Corporation (1938) 303 US 41), including appeal to an administrative superior or administrative appellate authority. The 'exhaustion rule' cannot be avoided on the ground of irreparable injury or expeditiousness of judicial remedy or remedy before the Administrative Tribunal set up under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980.</u>

<u>14. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner refers to the decision in the case of R Vs. Chief Constable of the Merseyside Police, ex parte Calveley and others reported in (1986) 1 All England Law Reports 257 wherein the Court of Appeal held in the particular facts and circumstances of that case that failure to notify the appellant in accordance with regulation 7 amounted to such a serious departure from the police discipline procedure that, even though the internal right of appeal had not been exhausted, the court would exercise its discretion to grant judicial review and accordingly the court of appeal granted the judicial review and made order of certiorari setting aside the decision of the Chief Constable. The aforesaid decision of the Court of Appeal of England has no application in Bangladesh in the matter of exercise of the extraordinary power in writ jurisdiction under section 102 of the Constitution in view of the provision of Article 117 read with Article 102(5) of the Constitution providing for alternative forum in matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic and barring the jurisdiction of any Court including the Supreme Court to entertain any proceeding or to make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of the administrative tribunal established by law.</u>

15. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also submits that on the grounds of malice in law malice in fact and coram non judice this Court should exercise its power of judicial review and make order of certiorari setting aside the illegally drawn up charge dated 3.8.89 framed against the petitioner by the Secretary. Ministry of Home Affairs. The petitioner has not alleged malice against the Secretary. Ministry of Home Affairs or any other official. The learned Advocate for the petitioner draws our attention to paragraphs 12. 13 and 20 of the petition wherein it is alleged that Major General (Rtd.) Mahmudul Hasan (at present Minister for Home Affairs), who hails from Tangail, told the petitioner at Tangail that if his candidate did not return in the Pourashava election. then the petitioner would face difficulties. As the petitioner told the said Minister that he cannot encourage unfair means in the election and as there was commotion and alarm among the public When the said Minister's wife entered the polling centre. the proceeding brought by the Secretary respondent No. 1 at the instance of the 'said Minster is mala fide. motivated and has been brought with the ulterior motive of maliciously victimising the petitioner. In the written reply (Annexure F) to the charge petitioner did not state any such thing. Petitioner even now can make his best to establish such allegations at the time of enquiry and can also make a representation to the President But in his reply Annexure-F he has stated.

“বর্তমানে স্বরাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের দায়িত্বে নিয়োজিত মাননীয় মন্ত্রী মহোদয়ের নিকট তাঁহার স্থানীয় এলাকা টাংগাইলের কোন disgruntled element আমার বিরুদ্ধে অপরাধ দিয়া থাকিবেন। কারণ, আমি টাংগাইল কর্তব্যরত থাকাকালীন সময় মাননীয় মন্ত্রী মহোদয় সর্বদা আমাকে সন্দেহ দেখাইয়াছেন। কখনও কোন প্রকার অভিযোগ করেন নাই।”

Malice in fact is to be established by evidence if it is alleged, The question of malice in fact is to be established by evidence. The petitioner is entitled to raise the question of malice in fact and malice in law under the aforesaid Disciplinary Rules of 1985 as well as before the Administrative Tribunal. Similarly the question of coram non judice can also be raised under the said Rules before the appropriate authority, appellate authority etc. and also before Administrative Tribunal. As already stated in view of the provision of Article 117(2) read with Article 102 (5) of the Constitution and in view of the enactment of the Administrative Tribunals. Act, 1980 the petition is not maintainable.

<u>16. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate refers to the decision in the case of Bangladesh and others Vs. AKM Zahangir 34 DLR (AD) 173 wherein it was observed by K Hossain, CJ as follows:</u>

<u>"As regards the person holding a civil post, he gets a constitutional guarantee under Article 135. His protection against his dismissal, or removal or reduction in rank is guaranteed, and no such action can be taken except by an authority not subordinate to one appointing him, and except by a procedure on giving him an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. Any statutory rule to the contrary, or any action contrary to other constitutional guarantee or statutory rules relating to these defined rights. can be redressed in a Civil Court and also in the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division. Any other service condition, even though provided by statute or statutory rules, will come within the ambit of Article 134, and if violated. unless the violation amounts to dismissal, removal or reduction in rank is remediable only by administrative process, but not in any court of law or in writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division. It is, however, to be remembered, that but for the exception contained in Article 45, protection available under the Fundamental Rights Chapter will, of course, be enforceable to the extent permitted by the Constitution."</u>

<u>We do not differ with this broad principle enunciated by K Hossain, CJ in 34 DLR (AD) 173. We have already stated that in this jurisdiction general rule. is that no one is entitled to relief in the Administrative Tribunal or in any court for a supposed or threatened injury until all the available remedies at the hands of the administrative authorities have been exhausted including appeal to an administrative superior or administrative appellate authority (which is known as the Rule of exhaustion of administrative remedies). We have also shown that the Legislature has enacted the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 (Act VII of 1981) which apparently ousts the jurisdiction of any court including in respect of matters relating to or arising out of terms and conditions of persons in service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishment in view of the provisions made in Article 117 read with Article 102(5) of the Constitution. In India in the case of SP Sampath Kumar Vs. Union of India AIR 1987 (SC) 393 vires of the (Indian) Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was challenged before the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution. It was argued in that case that Judicial Review is a fundamental aspect of the basic structure of the Constitution That, therefore the bar of the jurisdiction of the High Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Indian Constitution as contained in section 28 of the Indian Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 cannot be sustained. It was held by the Indian Supreme Court in the said decision that bar of jurisdiction of the High Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Indian Constitution does not affect the provision for a judicial review inasmuch as Article 32 of the Indian Constitution (which empowers the Supreme Court of India by appropriate proceeding for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights) has been left untouched. Under the Constitution of Bangladesh also similarly 10 order to protect the provision for judicial review, Article 44 of our Constitution (guaranteeing enforcement of the fundamental rights in accordance with Articles 102(1) of the Constitution) has been left untouched and unaffected by Article 117 and Article 102(5) of the Constitution and therefore in our view after exhausting all available remedies before the administrative authorities including administrative appellate authority, the Administrative Tribunal and the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, the petitioner can then alone attempt to move this Court for enforcement of the Fundamental Rights, if any, such as guaranteed under Articles 27; 31, etc. in accordance with the provisions of Article 44 read with Article 102(1) of the Constitution in spite of the provisions of Articles 117 and 102( 5) of the Constitution because of the clear and unequivocal guarantee given in Article 44 and also because Article 45 only relates to any provision of a disciplinary law relating to members of a disciplined force. Article 44 of the Constitution of Bangladesh reads as follows:</u>

<u>"44. (1) The right to move the High Court Division in accordance with clause (1) of Article 102 for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this part is guaranteed.</u>

<u>(2) Without prejudice to the powers of the High Court Division under Article 102, Parliament may by law empower any other Court; within the localities of its jurisdiction, to exercise all or any of these powers".</u>

17. As already stated, without exhausting all available remedies before the administrative authorities including administrative appellate authority, the Administrative Tribunal and. the Administrative Appellate Tribunal generally speaking the petitioner is not entitled to any relief before this Court for the enforcement of any Fundamental Right under Article 44 read with Article 102(1) of the Constitution. In the cases of State of UP Vs. Nooh, AIR 1985 '(SC) 86 and Abrahan vs. ITO AIR 1961 (SC) 609 it was held that the principle of exhaustion of statutory remedies is applied, as a general rule, in the matter of issuing certiorari, and the Superior Court will ordinarily decline to interfere until the aggrieved party has exhausted his statutory remedies.

18. On these grounds the Rule is liable to be discharged.

19. In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The learned Advocate for the petitioner prays for a certificate to appeal to the Appellate Division, but such certificate cannot be given as the question involved is well settled and, therefore, the case does not involve at this stage any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. The prayer is rejected.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazlay Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman, J.: These two writ petitions are disposed of by this judgment as they arise out of cognizance taken by the Special Tribunals under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and involve the same questions of law. Both the petitioners were Ministers of the Government of Bangladesh and Members of the Parliament till the fall of the Ershad Government on 6th December, 1990 due to the movement of the people and dissolution of the Parliament. 2. In Writ Petition No. 767 of 1991 at the instance of Anisul Islam Mahmood (a former Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Government of Bangladesh) Rule Nisi was issued on 9.7.1991 calling upon the respondents, Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh and the Special Tribunal No. 3-cum-2nd Court of Additional Sessions Judge, Dhaka to show cause why the proceeding in Special Tribunal Case No. 121 of 1991 arising out of Lalbagh PS Case No.17(2)91 under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act read with the Ministry of Home Affair's Gazelle Notification No. 500: Saw:Ma (Nira-3) dated 23.1.91 (Annexure-A) pending before the Special Tribunal No.3, Dhaka should not be declared to have been taken without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 3. In Writ Petition No. 947 of 1991 at the instance of Sardar Amjad Hossain (a former Minister for Agriculture of the Government of Bangladesh) Rule Nisi was issued on 14.8.1991 calling upon the respondents Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and the Additional District and Sessions Judge, 1st Court-Cum-Special Tribunal No. 2, Dhaka to show cause why the proceeding in the Special Tribunal Case No. 118 of 1991 arising out of Lalbagh PS case no 14(1)91 under section 7(b) of the special powers act read with the Ministry of Home Affairs Gazette Notification No. 499 Swa: Ma (Nira-3) dated 23.1.91 pending before the Special Tribunal No. 2, Dhaka shall not be declared to have been taken without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 4. In Writ Petition No. 767 of 1991 the facts of the case are that the respondent No. 1 Government of Bangladesh through its Senior Assistant Secretary (Security), Ministry of Home Affairs by order bearing memo no. 5697 Swa Ma (Nira-3) dated 11.12.90 passed an order of detention detaining detenu Anisul Islam Mahmood under section 3(1)(1) of the Special Powers Act 1974 stating as follows: যেহেতু সরকার এই মর্মে সন্তুষ্ট হইয়াছেন যে, জনাব আনিসুল ইসলাম মাহমুদ (সাবেক মন্ত্রী) পিতা/স্বামী-গ্রাম ৩৭ ইস্কাটন, গার্ডেন রোড, থানা-রমনা, জেলা-ঢাকা, বর্তমান ঠিকানা- জন নিরাপত্তা ও জন শৃঙ্খলা রক্ষার জন্য আটক রাখা প্রয়োজন। এক্ষনে সেহেতু সরকার The Special Powers Act, 1974 (Act XIV of 1974) Section 3(I)(a) ধারা অর্পিত ক্ষমতাবলে উপরোক্ত জনাব আনিসুল ইসলাম মাহমুদকে এতদউদ্দেশ্যে তার এই আদেশ জারীর দিন হইতে ১২০ (একশত বিশ দিন) দিনের জন্য কারাগারে আটক রাখার আদেশ প্রদান করিলেন।

রাষ্ট্রপতির আদেশক্রমে

স্বাঃ - আব্দুল মালেক, ১১/১২/৯০ ইং

সহকারী সচিব (নিরাপত্তা)

5. As the petitioner Anisul Islam Mahmood, in the opinion of the Government, was absconding and/or concealing himself so that the said order of detention passed against him cannot be executed, the Government in the Ministry of Home Affairs in exercise of its power under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act made the following notification on January 23, 1991 in the Bangladesh Gazette (Annexure 'A') dated 23.1.91. নং-৫০০-স্বঃমঃ (নিরা-৩), তারিখ ৯ই মাঘ, ১৩৯৭/২৩শে জানুয়ারী ১৯৯১ বিষয়ক ১৯৭৪ সালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের আওতায় জারীকৃত গ্রেফতারী পরোয়ানা মোতাবেক আত্মসমর্পণ করার আদেশ। যেহেতু আপনি জনাব আনিসুল ইসলাম মাহমুদ, সাবেক পররাষ্ট্রমন্ত্রী, গ্রাম-সাদেক নগর, ১৪ নং জামাল খান রোড, পাঁচলাইশ, থানা-হাটহাজারী, জেলা-চট্রগ্রাম সরকার কর্তৃক স্পেশাল পাওয়ারস এ্যাক্ট, ১৯৭৪ (XIV of 1974) এর সেকশন নং ৩(১)(এ) এর অধীনে ১১-১২-১৯৯০ তারিখে জারীকৃত আটকাদেশ নং ৬৫৯৭ - স্বঃমঃ (নিরা-৩) এড়ানোর উদ্দেশ্যে আত্মগোপন করিয়া আছেন এবং যেহেতু পুলিশ সূত্র মারফত জানা যায় যে, সংশ্লিষ্ট সকল মেট্রোপলিটন পুলিশ, জেলা পুলিশ এবং বিশেষ শাখার বিশেষ দল দেশের বিভিন্ন এলাকায় আপনার আত্মগোপনের সম্ভাব্য সকল স্থানে ব্যাপক তল্লাশী চালায়। এবং যেহেতু সরকারের বিশ্বাস করার যথেষ্ট কারন রহিয়াছে যে, আপনি জনাব আনিসুল ইসলাম মাহমুদ আপনার বিরুদ্ধে গৃহিত ব্যবস্থা সম্পর্কে অবহিত হইয়া অত্যন্ত সতর্কতামূলক ব্যবস্থাধীনে আত্মগোপন করিয়া আছেন এবং ইহার ফলে আপনাকে গ্রেফতার করা অত্যন্ত কঠিন হইয়া পড়িয়াছে। সেহেতু আপনি জনাব আনিসুল ইসলাম মাহমুদকে এই মর্মে নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইতেছে যে, এই আদেশ প্রকাশের ৭ (সাত) দিনের মধ্যে আপনি উপ-মহাকারা পরিদর্শক, ঢাকা কেন্দ্রীয় কারাগারে ঢাকা বিভাগ, ঢাকা এর নিকট হাজির হইবেন। অন্যথায় উক্ত স্পেশাল পাওয়ারস এর সেকশন ৭(বি) এর বিধান মোতাবেক আপনার বিরুদ্ধে ব্যবস্থা গ্রহন করা হইবে। 6. As the petitioner Anisul Islam Mahmood did not appear before the Deputy Inspector General, Prisons, Dhaka Central Jail within seven days from the aforesaid Gazette Notification dated 23.1.91 the informant Md. Anjum Ferdous, Inspector of Police, Officer-in-Charge, Lalbagh PS, Dhaka Metropolitan Police, Dhaka lodged the First Information Report in Lalbagh PS Case No.17 dated 14.2.91 as follows: আমি মোঃ আন্নজুম ফেরদৌস, পুলিশ পরিদর্শক ভারপ্রাপ্ত কর্মকর্তা, লালবাগ থানা ঢাকা মহানগর পুলিশ, ঢাকা, অদ্য ১৪/২/৯১ ইং তারিখে রাত্র ২২.৩০ মিঃ এর সময় স্বরাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রনালয়ের স্মারক নং ১৪০ স্বঃ মঃ (নিরা-৩) তারিখ ১/১১/৯৭ বাং ১৪/২/৯১ ইং তারিখ এর নির্দেশক্রমে সাবেক পররাষ্ট্রমন্ত্রী জনাব আনিসুল ইসলাম মাহমুদ, গ্রাম-সাদেক নগর, ১৪ নং জামাল খান রোড, পাঁচলাইশ হাটহাজারী, চট্রগ্রাম এর বিরুদ্ধে এই মর্মে এজাহার করিতেছি যে, গত ১১-১২-৯০ ইং মোতাবেক স্বরাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রনালয় এর স্মারক নং ৫৬৯৭ স্বঃ মঃ (নিরাঃ-৩) এর নির্দেশ অনুযায়ী তাহাকে ১৯৭৪ সনের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৩(১)(এ) ধারার বিধান মোতাবেক ১২০ (একশত বিশ) দিনের অন্তরীন রাখার আটক আদেশ দেওয়া হইয়াছিল। উক্ত অনুরীন রাখার আটক আদেশ ইস্যু হওয়ার পর হইতে তিনি ইচ্ছাকৃতভাবে গ্রেফতার এড়ানোর জন্য আত্মগোপন করিয়া থাকায় ঢাকা মহানগর পুলিশ, জেলা পুলিশ এবং বিশেষ শাখার বিশেষ দল তাহার আত্মগোপনের সম্ভাব্য সকল স্থানে তল্লাশী করিয়াও তাহাকে গ্রেফতার করিতে ব্যর্থ হন। এই কারনে স্বরাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রনালয়ের স্মারক নং ৪৯৩ স্বঃ মঃ (নিরা-৩) তারিখ ৯ই মাঘ ১২৯৭ বাং ২৩ শে জানুয়ারী ১৯৯১ ইং মোতাবেক বাংলাদেশ গেজেট বিজ্ঞপ্তির মাধ্যমে তাহাকে ৭ (সাত) দিনের মধ্যে উপ-মহাকারা পরিদর্শক, ঢাকা কেন্দ্রীয় কারাগার ঢাকা বিভাগ ঢাকা এর নিকট হাজির হওয়ার জন্য নির্দেশ দেয়া হইয়াছিল এই বিষয়টি যথারিতী টেলিভিশন, রেডিও, জাতীয় দৈনিক পত্রিকা সমূহে প্রচারের ব্যবস্থা নেয়া হয়। নির্দেশ মোতাবেক তাহার হাজির হওয়ার মেয়াদ গত ৩১-১-৯১ ইং তারিখ উত্তীর্ণ হইয়া যায়। গত ৩-২-৯১ ইং তারিখ উপ-মহাকারা পরিদর্শক, ঢাকা কেন্দ্রীয় কারাগার ঢাকা বিভাগ ঢাকার স্মারক নং ৪৩২। নিসা তাং ৩-২-৯১ ইং তারিখের মধ্যে ও উপ-মহাকারা পরিদর্শক, ঢাকা কেন্দ্রীয় কারাগার, ঢাকা বিভাগ, ঢাকার নিকট হাজির হন নাই। এমনকি তিনি অদ্যাবধি ও নির্দেশ মোতাবেক নির্ধারিত স্থানে উক্ত কর্মকর্তার নিকট হাজির হন নাই। উপরে বর্নিত পরিস্থিতিতে তিনি যথাযথ কর্তৃপক্ষের প্রদত্ত হাজির হওয়ার আদেশ পালনে ব্যর্থতার কারনে ১৯৭৪ সনের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৭ (বি) ধারায় অপরাধ করিয়াছেন। অতএব, তাহার বিরুদ্ধে বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের উল্লেখিত ধারায় মামলা রুজু করিলাম এবং তদন্তভার নিজেই গ্রহণ করি। 7. The Police investigated into the case and submitted charge sheet on 24.2.91 against accused petitioner Anisul Islam Mahmood under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act on the ground that in spite of notification (Annexure-A) dated 23.1.91 in the Bangladesh Gazette in view of the order dated 11.12.90 passed against him by the Government under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act detaining him for a period of 120 days with effect from the date of service of notice upon him, the petitioner failed to appear before the DIG, Prisons, Dhaka Central Jail within 7 days from the date of notification of the Gazette and till the date of filing of the charge-sheet. 8. It appears that the ex-officio Senior Special Tribunal, Dhaka (who is the Sessions Judge, Dhaka) took cognizance of the alleged offence against the petitioner under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 on 14.3.91 numbering it as Special Tribunal Case No. 121 of 1991. The Special Tribunal by its order dated 14.3.91 directed to publish in two national Bengali daily newspapers, namely, Sangbad and Dainik Bangla, to the effect that as accused Anisul Islam Mahmood is absconding and as there is no likelihood of his being arrested in the near future, he is directed to appear before the Senior Special Tribunal, Dhaka within 10 days from the publication in the said news papers. Accordingly, the notification (Annexure-B) was published in the Daily Sangbad and Dainik Bangla on 29th March, 1991 corresponding to 14th Chaitra, 1397 BS stating as follows:

গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার

সিনিয়র স্পেশাল ট্রাইবুনাল

ঢাকা।

বিজ্ঞপ্তিঃ যেহেতু নিম্ন তফছিলে বর্ণিত আসামীর বিরুদ্ধে পরওয়ানা জারি রহিয়াছে এবং যেহেতু ১৯৭৪ সনের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৭(এ) ধারার বিধান পালন করা হইয়াছে। এবং যেহেতু অত্র ট্রাইবুনালের বিশ্বাস করিবার কারন রহিয়াছে যে, অত্র ট্রাইবুনাল বিচারার্থে নিম্নবর্ণিত আসামী গ্রেফতার এড়াইবার জন্য পলাতক রহিয়াছেন বা আত্মগোপন করিয়াছেন এবং যেহেতু উক্ত আসামীকে শীঘ্রই গ্রেফতার করার সম্ভাবনা নাই। এক্ষনে বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ২৭(৬) সংশোধিত ধারায় প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতাবলে আসামীকে নিম্ন তফছিল বর্ণিত মামলার বিচারের জন্য অত্র বিজ্ঞপ্তি জারি হইবার ১০ দিনের মধ্যে অত্র ট্রাইবুনালে হাজির হইবার নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইল। অন্যথায় তাহার অনুপস্থিতিতে বিচার সমাধা করা হইবে।

(মোঃ হাবিবুল্লা)

সিনিয়র স্পেশাল ট্রাইবুনাল, ঢাকা

Inspite of the said notification published by the Special Tribunal, Dhaka, made in pursuance of section 27(b) of the special powers Act the accused petitioner failed to appear before the said Tribunal within the specified period. The senior special Tribunal thereafter by the order dated 20.4.91 transferred the case to the special Tribunal No.3-Cum Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court. On receipt of the case the Special Tribunal No. 3 decided to hold trial of the accused petitioner in his absence and accordingly on 7.5.91 framed the following charge against the accused petitioner: যেহেতু আপনি আনিসুর ইসলাম মাহমুদ, সাবেক পর-রাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রী এর বিরুদ্ধে এই মর্মে অভিযোগ আনয়ন করা যাইতেছে যে, আপনার বিরুদ্ধে বাংলাদেশ সরকার ৫৬৯৭ স্বঃ মঃ (নিরা-৩) স্মারক বিগত ১১-১২-৯০ ইং তারিখে ১৯৭৪ সনের বিশেষ স্মারক আইনের ৩(১) ধারা বিধান মতে আপনার বিরুদ্ধে ১২০ দিনের আটক আদেশ প্রদান করিয়াছেন। কিন্তু বাংলাদেশ সরকার আপনাকে খুজিয়া না পাওয়ায় এবং আপনি নিজেকে আত্মগোপন করিয়া থাকায় বাংলাদেশ সরকার বিগত ১৩-১২-৯১ তারিখে ৫০০ স্বঃ মঃ (নিরা-৩) নং সরকারী গেজেট প্রকাশিত মতে আপনাকে উপ-কারা-পরিদর্শক ঢাকা কেন্দ্রীয় কারাগার, ঢাকা বিভাগ এর নিকট ৭(সাত) দিনের মধ্যে হাজির হইবার জন্য নের্দেশ দেওয়া হইয়াছিল এবং উক্ত সরকারী আদেশ বিগত ২৫-১-৯১ ইং তারিখে দৈনিক সংবাদ সহ অন্যান্য পত্রিকার মাধ্যমে প্রচারিত হয়। কন্তু আপনি উক্ত আদেশ অমান্য করিয়া হাজির না হইয়া এবং কেন হাজির হইলেন না তাহার ও কোন কারণ দর্শান নাই। কাজেই আপনি ১৯৭৪ সনের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৭(বি) ধারার বিধান মতে অপরাধ করিয়াছেন। আসামীর অনুপস্থিতিতে অভিযোগ গঠন করা হইল। 9. Accused petitioner, however, on 19.5.91 went to the Dhaka Central Jail and volunteered to be detained if there was any order of detention or any proceeding pending against him. On that very day (i.e. on 19.5.91) the order of detention bearing No. 2167 Sea: Ma: (Nira-3) dated 28.4.91 passed by the Government of Bangladesh through the Senior Assistant Secretary (Security) of the Ministry of Home Affairs was served on him detaining him for a period of 120 days from that date on the ground “জন নিরাপত্তা এবং জন শৃংখলা স্বার্থে” (i.e. it is necessary to keep him under preventive detention for 120 days for public safety and in the interest of maintenance of public order). 10. In the Special Tribunal Case No. 121 of 1991 the detenu (Anisul Islam Mahmood) was produced before the said Special Tribunal on 22.5.91 when the Special Tribunal rejected the prayer for bail of the said accused petitioner. In the meantime in writ petition No.767 of 1991 this Court stayed the proceeding of the said Special Tribunal case No.121 of 1991 pending before the Special Tribunal No.3, Dhaka till 10th July, 1991. In Writ Petition No.318 of 1991 under Article 102(2)(b)(i) (Habeas Corpus) of the Constitution Mrs. Parveen Mahmood, wife of the petitioner obtained a Rule Nisi on 21st May, 1991 and after hearing of the said Rule it was declared by this Court on 4.7.1991 that the detenu Anisul Islam Mahmood was being held in custody without any lawful authority and in an unlawful manner and that he may be released only if he is not wanted in connection with any other case including I Special Tribunal Case No.121 of 1991 corresponding to Lalbagh PS Case No.17(2)91 pending in the Court of Special Tribunal No.3. Dhaka. In the present Writ Petition No.767 of 1991, as already stated, Rule Nisi was issued on July 9, 1991 and further proceeding in the Special Tribunal Case No.121 of 1991 (Dhaka) was stayed upto August 28,1991. 11. In Writ Petition No. 947 of 1991, all further proceedings in Special Tribunal Case No.118 of 1991 was stayed by two separate orders up to 21st November, 1991. 12. In Writ Petition No.947 of 1991 the facts of the case arc that the Government of Bangladesh through its Senior Assistant Secretary (Security) of the Ministry of Home Affairs by order bearing Memo No.5906 : Swa:Ma(Nira-3) dated 26.12.90 passed an order of detention detaining detenu Sardar Amjad Hossain under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act stating as follows : যেহেতু সরকার এই মর্মে সন্তুষ্ট হইয়াছেন যে, জনাব সরদার আমজাদ হোসেন (সাবেক কৃষি মন্ত্রী), সাবেক ঠিকানা-৩নং হেয়ার রোড, রমনা, ঢাকাকে জন নিরাপত্তা ও জনশৃংখলা রক্ষার জন্য আটক রাখা প্রয়োজন। এখানে, সেহেতু সরকার স্পেশাল পাওয়ারস এ্যাক্ট, ১৯৭৪ (এ্যাক্ট XIV অব ৭৪) সেকশন ৩(১)(এ) ধারা অর্পিত ক্ষমতাবলে উপরোক্ত জনাব সরদার আমজাদ হোসেনকে এতদ উদ্দেশ্যে তাহার এই আদেশ জারীর দিন হইতে ১২০ (একশত বিশ) দিনের জন্য কারাগারে আটক রাখার আদেশ প্রদান করিলেন।

As the said detenu Sardar Amjad Hossain, in the opinion of the Government, was absconding and or concealing himself so that the order of detention cannot be executed, the Government of Bangladesh in the Ministry of Home Affairs in exercise of its power under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 made the following notification dated 23 January, 1991 in the Bangladesh Gazette: নং-৪১৭-বঃমঃ (নিরা-৩) তারিখ ১ই মাঘ, ১৩৯৭/২৩শে জানুয়ারী ১৯৯১ বিষয়ঃ- ১৯৭৪ দালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের আওতায় জারীকৃত গ্রেফতারী পরোয়ানা মোতাবেক আত্ম সমর্পন করার আদেশ। যেহেতু, আপনি জনাব সরদার আমদাদ হোসেন , সবেক মন্ত্রী, পিতা সরদার মোহাম্মদ পিতা সরদার মোহাম্মদ আলী, গ্রাম-হামির কটসা , ডাকঘর-গোয়ালঘর, থানা-বাঘমারা, জেলা- রাজশাহী, ৪ ০/ই আজিমপূর ঢাকা সরকার কর্তৃক স্পেশাল পাওয়ারস এ্যাক্ট ১১৭৪ ( XIV অব ১৯৭৪) এর সেকশন ৩(১)(এ)এর অধীনে ২৬-১২-১৯৯০ তারিখে জারিকৃত আটকাদেশ নং ৫৯০৬-স্বঃমঃ (নিরা-৩) এড়ানোর উদ্দেশ্যে আত্মগোপন করিয়া আছেন। এবং এবং যেহেতু পুলিশ সূত্র মারফত জানায়া যায় যে, সংশ্লিষ্ট সকল মেট্রো পলিটন পুলিশ, জেনারেল পুলিশ এবং বিশেষ শাখার বিশেষ দল দেশের বিভিন্ন এলাকায় আপনার আত্মগোপনের সম্ভাব্য সকল স্থানে ব্যাপক তল্লাশী চালায়। এবং যেহেতু সরকারের বিশ্বাস করার যথেষ্ট কারণ রইিয়াছে যে আপনি জনাব সরদার আমজাদ হোসেন আপনার বিরুদ্ধে গৃহীত ব্যবস্থা সম্পর্কে অবহিত হইয়া অত্যন্ত সর্তকতা মূলক ব্যবস্থাধীনে আত্মগোপন করিয়াছেন এবং ইহার ফলে আপনাকে গ্রেফতার করা অত্যন্ত কঠিন হইয়া পড়িয়াছে। সেহেতু আপনি উক্ত জনাব সরদার আমজাদ হোসেনকে এই মর্মে নির্দেশ গেওয়া হইতেছে যে, এই আদেশ প্রকাশের ৭(সাত) দিনের মধ্যে আপনি উপ-মহাকারা পরিদর্শক, ঢাকা কেন্দ্রীয় কারাগার, ঢাকা বিভাগ, ঢাকা এর নিকট হাজির হইবেন। অন্যথায় উক্ত স্পেশাল পাওয়ারস এ্যক্ট এর সেকশন ৭ (বি) এর বিধান মোতাবেক আপনার বিরুদ্ধে ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করা হইবে। It further appears that in Lalbagh PS Case No.14 dated 14.2.91 informant Md.
