It appears from the records of the Special Tribunal Case No. 118 of 1991 that the accused petitioner Sardar Amjad Hossain surrendered before the Special Tribunal No. 2, Dhaka on 26.5.91 and prayed for bail which was not granted. Before the Special Tribunal Case No. 118 of 1991 was stayed on 9th June, 1991 by this Court, the Special Tribunal No. 1 had already recorded the evidence of two witnesses and since then continuance of further proceeding of the said Special Tribunal No. 118 of 1991 has remained stayed on the basis of this Court's order. As already stated the accused petitioner Sardar Amjad Hossain obtained this Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 947 of 1991 on 14.8.91. In Writ Petition No. 882 of 1991 under Article 102(2)(b)(i) (Habeas Corpus) of the Constitution, Ferdous Nigar Hossain, wife of the petitioner obtained a Rule Nisi on 3 June, 1991 and after hearing it was declared by this Court on 25.7.1991 that the detenu Sardar Amjad Hossain was being held in custody without any lawful authority and in an unlawful manner and that he may be released only if he is not required to be kept in custody in connection with any other case including Special Tribunal Case No. 118 of 1991 corresponding to Lalbagh PS Case No. 14(2)91 pending in the Court of Special Tribunal No. 2, Dhaka. 14. In both the Writ Petition Nos. 767 of 1991 and 947 of 1991 on behalf of the respondent No. 1, Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, affidavits-in-opposition have been filed. On behalf of respondent No. 1 supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 9.7.91, supplementary affidavit dated 18.7.91 and the supplementary affidavit dated 25.8.91 has been filed in Writ Petition No.767 of 1991. The learned Advocates for both the parties were heard at length. 15. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood with Mr. Murad Reza, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 767 of 1991. Mr. Md. Monsurul Huq, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 947 of 1991. Mr. Aminul Huq, Attorney-General with Mr. AF Hasan Ariff, Deputy Attorney-General along with Mr. QA Hossain and Mr. Obaidur Rahman Mustafa, Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the Government in both the petitions. 16. For appreciating the legal questions involved in this case it is necessary to quote provision of section 7 of the Special Powers Act which reads as follows: "7. Power in relation to absconding persons. If the Government or a District Magistrate or an Additional District Magistrate mentioned in section 3(2), as the case may be has reason to believe that a person in respect of whom a detention order has been made has absconded or is concealing himself so that the order cannot be executed, it or he may. (a) make a report in writing of the fact to a Magistrate of the first class having jurisdiction in the place where the said person ordinarily resides; and thereupon the provisions of sections 87, 88 and 89 of the Code shall apply in respect of the said person and his property as if the order directing that he be detained were a warrant issued by the Magistrate; (b) by order notified in the official Gazette direct the said person to appear before such officer, at such place, and within such period as may be specified in the order; and if the said person fails to comply with such direction he shall, unless he proves that it was not possible for him to comply therewith and that he had, within the period specified in the order, informed the officer of the reason which rendered compliance therewith impossible and of his whereabouts, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine, or with both". 17. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No.767 of 1991 cited the decision in the case of Union of India and others Vs. Haji Mastan Mirza, reported in AIR 1984 (SC) 681 and tried to argue that if an order of detention is subsequently set aside by a Court of competent jurisdiction, the proceeding under sub-sections (a) and (b) of section 7 of the Special Powers Act cannot legally continue and is to be declared to be without any lawful authority and of no legal effect in exercise of this Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) (Certiorari) of the Constitution. Mr. Aminul Huq, the learned Attorney-General, took us through the said judgment in the case of Haji Maston Mirza, AIR 1984(SC) 681 and the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 2 of the relevant Indian Law i.e. The Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulation (Forfeiture of Property), Act, 1976 (in short called SAFEMA) which clearly provides that legal consequences such' as are provided in sections 6 and 7 of the said Act shall not follow if such order of detention made under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 (COFEPOSA) has been set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction. In the Special Powers Act, 1974 there is no such provision that legal consequence such as are provided in sub-sections (a) and (b) of section 7 of the Special Powers Act will not follow if a court of competent jurisdiction sets aside the order of detention. Therefore Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood, the learned Advocate conceded that Haji Mastan's case, AIR 1984 (SC) 681 is not relevant in the present case. 18. Mr. Rokonnuddin Mahmood, the learned Advocate for petitioner in Writ Petition No.767 of 1991 thereafter referred to the decision in the case of Moazzem Hossain Chowdhury Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 43 DLR 186 to show that when the District Magistrate passed order of detention on the ground enumerated in section 2(1)(i) of the Special Powers Act, the order of detention is void ab initio. that the legislature in enacting the Special Powers Act has not empowered the District Magistrate and Additional District Magistrate (under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act) to make any order of preventive detention on the grounds mentioned in clauses (i) and (ii) of section 2(1) in respect of which the Government alone can make any order of preventive detention of any person. He thereafter, submits that if in the aforesaid case reported in 43 DLR /86 the District Magistrate who had passed the void order of detention, also notified in the official Gazette under section 7(b) of the said Act directing the detenu to appear before a specified officer, at a specified place and within a period specified in the order, if the said person failed to comply with such direction, if the police after investigation submitted charge sheet against such detenu and if the relevant Special Tribunal took cognizance of the said offence under section 7(b) of the said Act, this Court in exercise of its writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a)(ii)( certiorari) of the Constitution would have to declare the proceeding pending before the said Special Tribunal under section 7(b) of the said Act to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect (provided, of course, that the detenu did not remain fugitive from law and justice and surrendered to the jurisdiction of the Special Tribunal in question). Mr. Hasan Ariff, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government was candid enough to concede that by now it is well settled that in such circumstances where the initial order of detention is void ab initio. the proceeding under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act would also be without lawful authority and of no legal effect in view of the several decisions, such as, the cases of Sultan Ali Naghiana Vs. Nur Hussain, AIR 1949(Lahore) 13/ (Full Bench), Dr. MO Ghani Vs. ANM Mahmmod, PLD /966 Supreme Court 802, Director of Public Prosecutions Vs. Head (1958) 1 All ER 679 (686). In the case of Sultan Ali Naghiana, AIR /949 (Lahore) 131 (155) Munir, C] delivering judgment of the Full Bench observed: "There can be no disobedience of a void order, as such order in the sense of an order determining the parties' rights or liabilities, does not exist in law and unless the order is binding on a party, he is at liberty to ignore or disobey it .... .... ..... The crucial question in this case, therefore, is whether the stay order which the respondents are alleged to have disobeyed was with jurisdiction (or without jurisdiction)". The said decision in the case of Sultan Ali Nanghiana was referred to with approval and the same view was taken by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the decision of the case Dr M O Ghani Vs. Dr. ANM Mahmood, PLD 1966 (SC) 802. In the case of Director of Public Prosecutions Vs. Head, (1958)1 All ER 679 (686) by Lord Tucker delivering the majority judgment observed: "It think this is to be presumed. But the foundation for the presumption, in the case of a person under detention or on licence, is the legality of the detention, and the necessity for a licence to justify the patient's absence, and if it is shown and admitted, as in the present case, that, on the face of the documents produced and received in evidence without objection, the detention was illegal, the whole basis of the sub -section and the presumption of defectiveness goes and the prosecution must fail". '" In the case of Anisminic, Ltd. Vs. The Foreign Compensation and another, (1969) 1 All ER 208 Lord Reid delivering judgment of the House of Lords, inter alia, observed: "And there are no degree of nullity. There are a number of reasons why the law will hold a purported decision to be a nullity. I do not see how it could be said that such a provision protects some kinds of nullity but not others; if that were intended it would be easy to say so. It has sometimes been said that it is only where a tribunal acts without jurisdiction that its decision is a nullity. But in such cases the word "jurisdiction" has been used in a very wide sense and I have come to the conclusion that it is better not to use the term except in the narrow and original sense of the tribunal being entitled to enter on the enquiry in question. But there are many cases where, although tribunal had jurisdiction to enter on the enquiry it has done or failed to do something in the course of the enquiry which is of such a nature that its decision is a nullity or it may have given its decision in bad faith. It may have made a decision which it had no power to make. It may have failed in the course of the enquiry to comply with the requirements of natural justice. It may in perfect good faith have misconstrued the provisions giving it power to act so that it failed to deal with the question remitted to it and decided some question which was not remitted to it. It may have refused to take into account something which it was required to take into account. Or it may have based its decision on some matter which, under the provisions setting it up, it had no right to take into account. I do not intend this list to be exhaustive. But if it decides a question remitted to it for decision without committing any of these errors, it is as much entitled to decide that question wrongly as it is to decide it rightly. I understand that some confusion has been caused by my having said in Armah Vs. Government of Ghana, (1966) 3 All ER 177(178) that, if a tribunal has jurisdiction to go right, it has jurisdiction to go wrong. So it has if one uses "jurisdiction" in the narrow original sense. If it is entitled to enter on the enquiry and does not do any of those things which I have mentioned in the course of the proceedings, then its decision is equally valid whether it is right or wrong subject only to the power of the Court in certain circumstances to correct an error of law". In the case of F Hoffmann-La Roch & Co. AG and others Vs. Secretary of State for Trade and Industry, (1974) 2 All ER 1128 (1148) it has been observed by Lord Wilberforce, "This phrase "void ab initio" has engendered many learned distinctions and much confused thinking-unnecessarily, in my opinion. There can be no doubt in the first place that an ultra vires act is simply void: (see in confirmation Ridge Vs. Baldwin, (1963) 2 All ER 66". 19. Mr. Hasan Ariff, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government submits that the orders of detention dated 11.12.90 and 26.12.90 passed by the Government against the two petitioners on the grounds communicated to the petitioner under section 8 of Special Powers Act are not void ab initio but are voidable as in the instant cases the said orders of detention have admittedly been set aside by this court in exercise of its power under Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution, that, therefore, the proceedings in Special Tribunal Case No. 121 of 1991 and No. 118 of 1991 pending before the Special Tribunal, Dhaka are not without lawful authority and also not liable to be quashed and that as there is an alternative remedy under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the petitioners are not entitled to move this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution for declaring the proceedings to be without lawful authority. The learned Attorney-General appearing for the Government referred to the decision in the case of Wick Vs. Director of Public Prosecutions, (1947) 1 All ER 205 wherein it has been observed: "There is of course, no doubt that, when a statute like the Emergency Powers (Defence) Act, 1939, enable an authority to make regulations, a regulation which is validly made under the Act i.e. which is intra vires of the regulation making authority, should be regarded as though it were itself an enactment. As the court of Criminal Appeal has pointed out in its judgment that was decided by the Divisional Court in Willingdale Vs. Norris (1) and it appears to me that the decision is perfectly correct. Consequently, the charge against the appellant here was, in effect, that he had committed crimes defined or contained in the Act of Parliament." Neither the aforesaid observation nor any other part of this decision has any relevance in the present case. In the judgment of the High Court Division in Criminal Revision No. 723 of 1991 (Anwar Hossain Monju Vs. State) Anwarul Haque Chowdhury), delivering the- judgment of the Division Bench also observed that the decision in the case of Wick Vs. Director of Public Prosecutions, (1947) 1 All ER 205 is not relevant in the matter involving the question of validity of a proceeding under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act pending in the Special Tribunal. In the aforesaid criminal Revision No. 723 of 1991 (Anwar Hossain Monju Vs. State) under section 561 A CrPC it was only argued before the High Court Division that since the order of detention had been declared illegal by a Division Bench of this Court, the proceeding under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act against Anwar Hossain Monju is illegal, null and void and should be quashed. In the said criminal case (i.e. Criminal Revision No. 723 of 1991) before the Division Bench no question was raised as to whether the order of detention passed in that case is void ab initio because the grounds for detention communicated in that case to the detenu under section 8 of the Special Powers Act do not come within the mischief of the expression 'prejudicial Act' as defined in section 2(f) of the Special Powers Act or because the grounds are not at all based on reports and materials which are called 'jurisdictional facts'. So we find in the said judgment the Division Bench of the High Court Division nowhere dealt with the question whether the initial order of detention on the grounds communicated to the detenu under section 8 of the Special Powers Act was void ab initio and whether a proceeding under section 7(b) can continue in the Special Tribunal for noncompliance of an order which is void ab initio. 20. We will presently show that when the order of detention is nullity and void ab initio the subsequent notification in the Gazette under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 also becomes a nullity and void ab initio and the consequential proceeding before the Special Tribunal under the said section 7(b) of the said Act for non-compliance of such null and void order becomes illegal and without lawful authority and that in the instant case the order. of detention is void ab initio because the detaining authority did not at all have before it "the jurisdiction facts" i.e. any report or reports and materials to enable the detaining authority to form its opinion that the person concerned should be detained for preventing him from acting in prejudicial manner and also because the involvement grounds given for preventive detention do not come within the meaning of the expression "prejudicial act" as defined in section 2(1) of the Special Powers 10 Act. In this context in those two Habeas Corpus Writ Petitions we relied upon the following portions of the celebrated decision in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Bangladesh, 31 DLR(AD) 1 (which are based on several other important decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan referred to by the Appellate Division in that decision) : (1) "In construing section 3 of the Special Powers Act we have held that there must be some materials before the detaining authority to form its opinion that a person should be detained for preventing him from acting in a prejudicial manner. The sufficiency of the materials will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case and is incapable of precise formulation. What is essential is that there must be some materials before the detaining authority to form an opinion as to the necessity for detaining a person so that he might be prevented from acting in a prejudicial manner. If this order is challenged, the detaining authority is required to disclose the materials to satisfy the High Court Division on the basis of which it based its decision to detain a person. If this condition is not satisfied the order of detention would not be sustained." "(In the instant two cases admittedly there were no materials before the detaining authority to form its opinion that the persons in question should be detained for preventing them from acting in a prejudicial manner. (2) "We like to observe here that the validity of the order of detention and the facts of detention on the score of vagueness of grounds stands on a different footing. The order of detention for its validity is to be tested on the basis whether the detaining authority had before it materials which give a rational probative value to the order and are not extraneous to the purpose of the Act and beyond which, the order of detention is immune from challenge, except on the ground of malafide. But in judging the grounds served on the detenu to enable him to make a representation so that the fact of detention as distinguished from order of detention, is valid, the Court is to consider whether the grounds arc vague, or indefinite or irrelevant or are co-extensive with facts and on pain of the detention being invalid." 21. Before entering into a discussion of the said question, we may state regarding the question of alternative statutory remedy that in a recent decision of the Appellate Division in CA Nos. 85, 86, 87 and 88 of 1990 in the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd. and others Vs. Assistant Collector of Customs and others, the Appellate Division after quoting the decision in the case of Shafiqur Rahman Vs. Certificate Officer, 29 MR (SC) 232 observed: "In principle, where an alternative statutory remedy is available, an application under Article 102 may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory procedure. There are, however, exceptions to the rule. Without attempting an exhaustive enumeration of all possible extraordinary situations we may note a few of them. Inspite of an alternative statutory remedy an aggrieved person may take recourse to Article 102 of the Constitution where the vires of a statute or a statutory provision is challenged; where the alternative remedy is not efficacious or adequate; and where the wrong complained of is so inextricably mixed up that High Court Division may, for the prevention of public injury and the vindication of public justice, examine that complaint. It is needless to add that the High Court Division is to see that the aggrieved person must have good reason for by-passing an alternative remedy." If there was any statutory provision of appeal or revision in this case for setting aside the proceedings, then the question whether any equally efficacious adequate alternative remedy is available to the petitioner would act as a bar to move this Court under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. In the instant case the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot he said to be an alternative remedy to this court's writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. In the case of Nagina Silk Mills, Lyallpur Vs. Income Tax Officer, A Ward, Lyallpur, 15 DLR (SC) 181 it was observed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan: "It was laid down that the general rule undoubtedly is that it is wrong on principle to entertain petitions for writs except in very exceptional circumstances when the law provides a remedy by appeal to another tribunal, fully competent to award the requisite relief. At the same time it was held that in cases of absence or excess of jurisdiction or where the impugned order suffers from illegality on the face of the record, a certiorari may be granted even though the right of statutory appeal had been availed of." In the case of A V Venkateswaram, Collector of Customs, Bombay Vs. Ramchand Sobhraj Wadhvani and another AIR 1961 (SC) 1506 it has been observed in paragraph 9 that in the case of Union of India Vs. TR Varman AIR 1957 (SC) 882 (884) the Supreme Court of India observed that it is well settled that when an alternative and equally efficacious remedy is open to a litigant, he should be required to pursue the remedy and (should) not invoke the special jurisdiction of the High Court to issue a prerogative writ. It is true that the existence of another remedy does not affect the jurisdiction of the Court to issue a writ. The existence of an adequate legal remedy is a thing to be taken into consideration in dealing with a writ petition because where such alternative statutory remedy exists, it will be a sound exercise of discretion to refuse to interfere in a petition unless there are good grounds thereof; that it must be borne in mind that there is no rule, with regard to certiorari as there is with mandamus that it will be effective remedy. It has already been stated that in the instant case no appeal or revision lies. In the case of Isha Bee vi and others Vs. Tax Recovery Officer and others, AIR 1975 (SC) 2145 has been stated in paragraph 5 that in order to substantiate a right to obtain a writ prohibition from a High Court (or from the Supreme Court), an applicant has to demonstrate total absence of jurisdiction to proceed on the part of the officer or authority complained against. 22. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmood, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has taken us through the grounds taken by him in the petition dated 21.5.91 on the basis of which this rule was issued and also the grounds taken by him subsequently and as an illustration of an order void ab initio he referred to the decision of Indian Supreme Court in the case of Nawabkhan Abbas Khan, AIR 1974(SC) 1471. 23. In the case of Nawabkhan Abbaskhan Vs. State of Gujrat, AIR 1974 (SC) 1471 the facts were that the externment order was made against Nawabkhan Abbas Khan under section 56 of the Bombay Police Act, 1951 by the Police Commissioner without giving him an opportunity to tender explanation under section 59 of the said Act; subsequently when he re-entered the area in contravention of the order of externment he was prosecuted under section 142 of the said Act for violating the order of externment. The Indian Supreme Court upon a finding that the order of externment being in violation of audi alteram partem rule is a nullity (void ab in intio) held: "In the present case, a fundamental right of the petitioner has been encroached upon by the Police Commissioner without due hearing. So, the court quashed it not killed it then but performed the formal obsequies of the order which had died at birth. The legal result is that the accused was never guilty of flouting an order which never legally existed. Beyond doubt, an order which infringes a fundamental freedom passed in violation of the audi alteram partem rule is a nullity. When a competent court holds such official act or order invalid, or sets it aside, it operates from nativity i.e. the impugned act or order was never valid". The learned Attorney-General was under the impression that the case of Nawabkhan Abbaskhan Vs. State of Gujrat, AIR 1974 (SC) 1471 was a ordinary criminal appeal as in the said decision the court has observed that on the aforesaid limited ratio the appellant is entitled to an acquittal and that the appeal is allowed. But it will appear from the paragraph 2 of the said Judgment that the petitioner Nawabkhan as petitioner moved the High Court of Bombay under Article 226 (Writ) of the Indian Constitution whereupon the High Court refused to interfere and against the said order of the High Court of Bombay the appellant Nawabkhan preferred appeal to the Supreme Court of India which allowed the appeal and granted relief under the writ of certiorari. 24. বিরোধীতা করেন, আপনি কিছুদিন পর নিজ দলের অস্তিত্ব বিলুপ্ত ঘোষনা করিয়া নিজ স্বার্থ হাসিলের উদ্দেশ্যে জাতীয় পার্টিতে যোগদান করেন এবং জাতীয় পার্টির সরকারের মন্ত্রীত্ব গ্রহন করেন, আপনি এরশাদ পদত্যাগের ঘোষনা প্রদানের পর পরই জনতার পুঞ্জীভুত ক্ষোভ ও রোষানল হইতে নিজেকে রক্ষা করিবার নিমিত্তে আত্মগোপন করেন, আপনি আইন শৃঙ্খলা বিঘ্নিত হইতে পারে এমন কাজে নিয়োজিত থাকার পর ইচ্ছাকৃত ভাবে অত্যন্ত সতর্কতার সহিত আত্মগোপন করিয়া থাকেন, আপনি পলাতক অবস্থায় জাতীয় সংসদের নির্বাচনে প্রতিদ্বন্দিতা করিয়া সদস্য নির্বাচিত হওয়া সত্ত্বেও যথারীতি শপথ গ্রহন না করিয়া আত্মগোপন অবস্থায় থাকিয়া দেশের আইন শৃঙ্খলা ব্যহত করার চেষ্টায় লিপ্ত থাকেন। আপনার দলীয় জাতীয় পার্টির সমর্থক বৃন্দ পুলিশের সহিত প্রায়শঃ সংঘর্ষে লিপ্ত হইত এবং ইহাতে দেশের সার্বিক আইন শৃঙ্খলা পরিস্থিতির মারাত্মক অবনতি ঘটিয়াছিল, এই প্রসঙ্গে বিশেষ ভাবে উল্লেখযোগ্য যে গত ৫ই ফেব্রুয়ারী ১৯৯১ ইং জাতীয় পার্টি ঢাকা শহরে লাঠি মিছিল বাহির করিয়া বোমাবাজি করতঃ একটি সন্ত্রাসী ভাব সৃষ্টি করে এবং ইহাতে ১০ জন আহত হয় এবং ২৫ টি গাড়ী ভাংচুর করা হয়, গত ২৮ শে মার্চ ১৯৯১ ইং জাতীয় পার্টি একটি মিছিল বাহির করিয়া বঙ্গভবনের দিকে অগ্রসর হওয়ার চেষ্টা করিলে পুলিশ বাধা প্রদান করাতে জাতীয় পার্টির সমর্থক বৃন্দ পুলিশের সহিত সংঘর্ষে লিপ্ত হয় এবং মিছিল হইতে পুলিশ একটি পিস্তল ও ১০ রাউন্ড গুলি সহ একজন জাতীয় পার্টির সমর্থককে গ্রেফতার করিতে সমর্থ হয়, আপনি এইভাবে দেশের আইন শৃঙ্খলা পরিস্থিতির অবনতি ঘটাইয়া রাজনৈতিক বিশৃঙ্খলা সৃষ্টি করতঃ ক্ষমতা দখলের প্রয়াসে লিপ্ত থাকেন। আপনার মত একজন রাজনীতিবিদ বাহিরে থাকা দেশের সার্বিক আইনে ও শৃঙ্খলার প্রতি হুমকি স্বরুপ এবং আইন ও শৃঙ্খলা পরিপন্থী। উপরোক্ত অনুচ্ছেদে বর্ণিত অবস্থা এবং দেশের সার্বিক আইন শৃঙ্খলা পরিস্থিতির সামগ্রিক বিবেচনায় সরকারের নিকট সন্তোষজনক ভাবে প্রতীয়মান হইয়াছে যে, জন নিরাপত্তা এবং জন শৃঙ্খলা রক্ষার স্বার্থে আপনাকে ১৯৭৪ সালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৩(১) (এ) ধারার বিধান অনুসারে জনস্বার্থে অনুরীন রাখা প্রয়োজন। ২। উপরে প্রদত্ত ঘটনা বা তথ্য ব্যতীত অন্য কোন ঘটনা বা তথ্য প্রদান জনস্বার্থের পরিপন্থী হইবে বলিয়া প্রদান করা হইল নাঃ ৩। মন্তব্য যে, আপনি এই অন্তরীনাদেশ এর বিরুদ্ধে নিবেদন পেশ করার অধিকার সংরক্ষন করেন। We have found in the judgments of the said two writ petitions that the orders of detention made against the two detenus under section 3 of the Special Powers Act read with the grounds of detention communicated to the detenus under section 8(1) of the Special Powers Act were made arbitrarily for collateral purpose in colourable exercise of power and that none of the grounds of detention communicated to the accused petitioners comes within the mischief of the expression "prejudicial act" as defined in section 2(f) of the Special Powers Act. These grounds of detention were undisputedly and admittedly not based on any report or material whatsoever to enable the detaining authority to make the order of detention within the meaning of section 3 of the Special Powers Act. Since the detaining authority is curtailing the liberty of person of a citizen by detaining him on the preventive detention, it is undisputedly exercising quasi judicial authority. To curtail fundamental right of personal liberty of a citizen which is enshrined in Article 32 read with Article 33 of the Constitution, it is essential that the detaining authority must have reports and materials, that is 'jurisdictional facts' for exercising of its power to detain the detenu under section 3 read with section 8 of the Special Powers Act (see Abdul Latif Mirza, 31 DLR (AD) 1). The question of "jurisdictional facts" giving power to an authority or tribunal to exercise statutory power has been dealt with by HKR Wade in his book "Administrative Law" (4th Edition) (2nd impression) (1979) at page 238-243. In the book "Principles of Administrative Law". by MP Jain and SN Jain (4th Edition) at page 538 it has been observed. "There are two types of facts: facts which an authority has to determine to dispose of a dispute before it, and facts which must exist before an authority could exercise jurisdiction in a matter. The latter are known as "jurisdictional" or "collateral" facts. The existence of these facts is a condition precedent for the application of a statutory standard or the assumption of jurisdiction on a body over a dispute and to decide it on merit. Thus, where an authority has power to requisition a vacant house, it is a condition precedent for requisitioning the house, that it must be vacant which is a "jurisdictional" or a "collateral" fact." In the instant case the detaining authority did not have before it the jurisdiction fact i.e. any report or material whatsoever to bring the activities of detenu within the definition of the expression "prejudicial act" as defined in section 2(1) of the Special Powers Act. Therefore, the orders of detention of the detenus which were passed against the two petitioners in the writ petitions were nullity and void ab initio. The impugned notifications made in the official Gazette dated 23.1.1991 under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act directing the petitioners to appear before the DIG Prisons, Dhaka Central Jail, Dhaka within a specified period being based on an order which was nullity and void ab initio. the impugned notifications in question are also consequently null and void and, therefore, the two impugned proceedings in Special Tribunal Case No. 118 of 1991 pending in the Court of Special Tribunal No. 2 and the Special Tribunal Case No. 121 of 1991 pending in the Court of Special Tribunal No. 3, Dhaka arc declared to be without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. In the result these two rules are made absolute without any order as to costs (the consequence of which is that the said two proceedings are quashed). End.

case_source: On appeal from the Judgment and order dated 15.4.76 passed by the High Court Division in F.M. A. No. 15 of 1975
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, J.—This appeal arises from the judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division passed in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 15 of 1975 on April 15, 1975, reversing the judgment of the Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Dacca, in Miscellaneous Case No. 247 1973.

2. Appellant Abdur Rouf filed an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the Third Court of the Sub-ordinate Judge Dacca. His case was that the 'A' schedule property originally belonged to one Samru Goala in whose name C.S. record stood on February 28, 1927. The property was sold by him to Snehalata and Jiban Ranjan Nath on December 23, 1936. Jiban Ranjan Nath sold a portion of his share to Anukul Chandra Majumder. Subsequently, Snehalata, Anukul and Jiban sold the entire plot to Abdus Sultan Wali Bhai who, in his turn, sold the entire 'A' schedule property with standing structures thereon to Mrs. Fatema Begum on January 8, 1955. Since then she was in possession of the property until she transferred 1½ kathas of land along with standing structures as shown in schedule, 'B' to one Sakina Bai by a sale deed dated May 11, 1966.

3. Subsequently, Fatema Begum sold the remaining portion of 'A' schedule property and structures to the appellant by three registered sale deeds dated September 1, 1972. Since then the appellants have been living in that home-stead while Sakina Bai possessed the 'B' schedule land and structures. Thus, while the appellants were possessing the said land in Ejmali with Sakina Bai the latter sold the 'B' schedule land and structures for the sum of Tk. 25,000/- to one Keramat Ali, predecessor in-interest of the respondents Nos. 1-6 by a sale deed dated October 30, 1972 and delivered possession to him after registration of the deed on the same day. No notice of this transfer was served on the appellants who were co-sharers. After his purchase, Karamat Ali shifted to schedule homestead land in the latter part of January, 1973. On making enquiries the appellants came to know about the transfer in February, 1973. As the schedule properties are non-agricultural homestead which existed for over twenty years prior to the appellants purchase, they sled the aforesaid petition for preemption of schedule property after depositing the consideration money along with the statutory compensation.

4. The application for pre-emption was resisted by Keramat Ali on the ground, among others, that the 'B' schedule lands, buildings, and structures which bear Municipal holding No. 49/2, Purana Paltan Line, Dacca, was previously held by Sakina Bai on her purchase from Fatema Begum. She possessed the same on amicable partition with Fatema and mutated her name in the records of the Municipality. On receiving the consideration of Tk. 25,000/- from Keramat Ali, Sakina Bai executed the same deed in his favour on October 30, 1972. The appellants are not entitled to pre-emption as they are not co-sharers in respect of schedule property. Furthermore, the application under section 24 of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable and the same is barred under section 8 (2) of the same Act. The appellants should have filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Moreover, he has, since his purchase improved the schedule property by additions and alterations in the existing structures at a cost of Tk. 15,600/- without depositing which amount the appellants were not entitled to any relief.

<u>5. The application for pre-emption being miscellaneous case No. 247 of 1973 was allowed by the Trial Court on September 30, 1974. The respondents preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 15 of 1975 in the High Court Division which considered the following questions, namely,</u>

<u>1. Whether, in view of the provision of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, application for pre-emption of non-agricultural land under section 24 of the Act was maintainable.</u>

<u>2. Whether, having regard to the amended provisions of section 81 and insertion of section 81(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the application for pre-emption, whether of agricultural land or non-agricultural land was to be made under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>3. Whether the non-consideration exhibits, F & G, which showed the splitting up of the Jama and extinguishment of the appellants right as co-sharer in the disputed land has led to an error and as such whether the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was wrong in allowing the application.</u>

6. Since, as the learned Judge of the High Court found that the case of Akhtaruzzaman vs. Jadu Nath Pal, (1965) 17 DLR 384 (FB) PLD 1967 Dacca 546, decided by a Full Bench of the High Court has already settled the point involved in the first question they application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was competent.

7. As regards the second question, the learned Judges after consideration the diver-gent views of the different Benches held that the provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act would apply to agricultural land lying outside the municipal areas and section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act would be applicable to all classes of land, whether agricultural or non-agricultural within the municipal areas.

In deciding the third question the learned Judges held that since during the pendency of the pre-emption proceeding the record of right was changed in the name of Sakina Bai by mutation, the appellants ceased to be co-sharer tenant and, accordingly, pre-emption was not available to them.

<u>8. The High Court Division accordingly allowed the aforesaid Miscellaneous appeal on April 15, 1976. Being aggrieved the appellants moved this Court and obtained leave to appeal to consider only the last two among the three questions raised before the High Court. As the decisions by the serveral benches of the High Court on the second question were found conflicting the issues involved therein required to be finally resolved by this Court. So far as the third question is concerned, the contention of the learned Counsel of the appellants was that the learned Judges were wrong in dismissing the application for pre-emption since they ignored the doctrine of lis pendens.</u>

<u>The first question mentioned above required no further consideration as the point involved therein was already settled by the aforesaid Full Bench decision.</u>

9. The second question regarding which conflicting decisions exist requires the consideration of the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as well as section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act both which confer the right of pre-emption. Their application in a particular case would depend on the nature of land, the person who holds such land and the relationship between him and the person who claims to pre-empt the land transferred by the former. Since the two laws, namely, Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the State Acquisition Act dealt with two kinds of land, i. e., non-agricultural land and agricultural land, the right of pre-emption in respect of the former could be claimed under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in respect of agricultural land right of pre-emption could be claimed under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This position is stated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in deciding the question whether in respect of non-agricultural land pre-emption could be claimed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The dispute before the Supreme Court related to non-agricultural homestead, land within the municipality. The Supreme Court observed as follows:—

"Because section 96 occurs in Chapter XIII the trial Court held that the right of pre-emption can be claimed in respect of non-agricultural land. The court, however, overlooked the fact that this Chapter, which regulates the right and liabilities of a raiyat was made applicable to tenants of non-agricultural land but it does not enlarge the content of the right as given in section 96 or introduce any change in the incidents  of the right. In other words, it does not materially affect the character of the land in respect of which the right of pre-emption can be claimed. Section 96 in clear terms lays down that this right of pre-emption will be available only in respect of a 'holding'. In view of the definition of 'holding' as given in section 2(13) of the Act it cannot be said that the right of pre-emption can be exercised in respect of non-agricultural land. Here it may be mentioned that there is specific provision for pre-emption of non-agricultural land in the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (XXIII) of 1949. Under that Act a contiguous owner cannot claim a right of pre-emption. After review of relevant provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act we think that section 96 is confined to agricultural land and, therefore, a right of pre-emption under this section cannot be claimed in respect of homestead land within a municipality'.

This conclusion has been followed in Abdul Khaleque v. Jadav Chandra, (1968) 20 DLR 562 and Mst. Lutfun Nahar v. Syeeda Hashmatar Begum, (1969) 21 DLR 633.

10. Had there been no amendment of certain provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the law stated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan would perhaps have remained unquestioned, but the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 and the insertion of section 81-A by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967 were claimed to have changed this otherwise unassailable position. The provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the aforesaid amendment were as follows:

"2. The provisions of this Part except those in Chapters and XIX shall not apply to tenants of land in so far as the are tenants of non agricultural lands.

3. The provisions of Chapters XIII, XVI, XVII, XVIII and XIX shall apply to the tenants of non-agricultural lands so far as such provisions are applicable to such tenants."

11. The newly inserted section 81-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides as follows :-

"81-A(I) Except as otherwise provided in this part, the right and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the Provincial Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act shall, where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such Acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act.

(2) The rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants shall, except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 :

Provided that, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms and conditions whatsoever, and if any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sublet in contravention of this provision, the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be, shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Provincial Government from the date of such subletting free from all encumbrances".

12. The effect of these amendments on the applicability of the provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act to non-agricultural land was considered in Mst. Noor Jahan Begum vs. Md. Tobarak Ali decided by a Single Bench of the High Court Division (Civil Revision No. 639 of 1969). Referring to the aforesaid amendments and their effect on the question the learned Judge observed as follows:

"By the new provisions, the entire Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has been made applicable to a holder of non-agricultural land. The simple test is as to whether the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant under the Provincial Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior rights in such land. If the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant directly under the Provincial Government his rights and liabilities will be governed by the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act subject to the provisions contained in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It comes to this that for the purpose of pre-emption relating to non-agricultural land if the holder of the holding has be, come tenant directly under the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior rights in such land, section 96 of the State Acquisition Act will be applicable in preference to section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 81-A(2) makes provision for other non-agricultural tenants."

13. After considering the provisions of law contained in the two Acts. the amendments to the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and other provisions defining the expressions 'holding', 'raiyat', 'land' agricultural land', 'non, agricultural tenancy' and the decisions quoted above, the learned Judges of the High Court Division in this instant case expressed their agreement with the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. They observed as follows:

Under section 24, only the co-sharer tenants of non-agricultural land, which is the subject of the transfer, can make an application. This distinction has been maintained in the two Acts even after the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) from section 81 and insertion of section 81-A to the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus, we find that insofar as an application for pre-emption is concerned section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and section 24 or the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will have their applications in their respective areas, namely, section 96 shall be applicable to agricultural lands beyond the Municipal area whereas section 25 will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal area and this view that we have taken is supported by the said un-reported decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Appeal No. 47-D of 1963."

This is evidently contrary to what had been decided by the learned Single Judge in Civil Revision No. 639 of 1969 which has been referred to above.

<u>14. The views expressed above are no doubt correct, since even after the insertion of section 81-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which proceeded to regulate certain rights and liabilities of a bolder of non-agricultural land who has become a tenant under the Government as a result of the acquisition of the superior right in such land, the distinction between the rights of a holder of non-agricultural land and those holding agricultural land was not entirely done away with. For, as it appears from the very provisions of sub-section (1) of section 81-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, insofar as they were sought to be not affected by this section, were to be still governed by the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. There is no ambiguity in this respect and the relative positions of the holders of non-agricultural land and agricultural land concerning the right of pre-emption exercisable by them under the, two different Acts have not been disturbed by any express provision in that part of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which contains the aforesaid section 'as might have been supposed by the opening words of sub-section (1) of section 81-A, "except as otherwise provided in this part".</u>

<u>Neither in sub-section (2) of this section which deals with the rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants, that is, those who did not come under sub-section (1), nor in any other provision in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is there any provision which has obliterated the distinction. Moreover, the ingredients of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and of Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are different. Some of these distinctions are that while section 96 confers right of pre-emption on the holder of land contiguous to the land transferred, no such holder of land can exercise the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which merely confers the right of pre-emption on a non-agricultural tenant in respect of non-agricultural land. Moreover, as observed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan which has been referred to above, the use of the expression 'holding' in section 96 which is not to be found in section 24 also makes for a meaningful distinction.</u>

<u>15. We, therefore, hold that in spite of the omission of section 81A, section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has not been rendered ineffective nor impliedly repealed so as to compel the owner of any land falling within the municipal area to prefer an application under section 96 of that State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>16. Now, turning to the second contention it appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division had, in relying upon exhibits F & G, dakhila and a certified copy of khatian respectively, came to the conclusion that the appellants ceased to have any subsisting interest in the holding during the pendency of the preemption proceeding and could not, therefore, claim the right of pre-emption. In support of this conclusion the case of Chandra Kutner Maladas v. Abdul Matalbed, (1967) 19 DLR SC 36, was referred to. According to the Supreme Court of Pakistan, a co-sharer means a person whose interest subsists throughout the course of the application to pre-empt and not a person who held such interest in the beginning but lost it before its disposal. It was, therefore, held that a pre-emptor must not only have a subsisting interest in the holding when he files an application for pre-emption but must continue to hold the self-same interest till the date when the case is finally disposed of. Without disputing the proposition of law laid down in this case, the question that has to be resolved is whether the appellants ceased to be co-sharers if it is established that the jama in question was split up behind the back of the appellants. In other words, whether exhibits F & G produced a legal effect on the subsistence of the appellants interest so as to defeat their right to pre-empt the sale in question, if these exhibits are shown to have been obtained unilaterally without serving notice upon the appellants. The learned Judges do not seem to have been prepared to consider this aspect of the question, as would appear from the following observations made by them:</u>

<u>"We do not see how in such a proceeding we can adjudicate or for that matter the learned Subordinate Judge was within his jurisdiction to adjudicate merits of the mutation case. Whether notice was served or not is a question that is involved in the mutation case itself. There is nothing on record to show that the respondent-petitioner has taken any action against the preparation of records of right in the name of Sakina Bai. In a proceeding under section 24 all that the Court is to see is, whether application under section 24 is filed by co-sharer tenant and whether he continued to be so throughout till the disposal of the case."</u>

17. The position does not seem to be what has been stated here. If the mutation itself has not been according to the provisions of law the co-sharers cannot be said to have loft their interest in the tenancy. The provisions for subdivision of tenancy which are contained in section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are as follows:

"117. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue-Officer may,—

a) for the purpose of amalgamation of tenancies under section 116, either on his own motion or on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, in that behalf or

b) for the purpose of consolidation of holdings of a malik, under section 119 either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf, Or

c) for the purpose of subdivision of joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent if any as he may consider fair and equitable : Provided that no such order shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter : Provided further that where an order under clause (c) is passed, and distribution of rent, by reason thereof, results in bringing the rent of a portion of the tenancy below one, a fraction of one shall be rounded off into one

(3) When an order under sub-section

(1) has been passed subdividing a joint holding such subdividing he demarcated on the ground and also shown on the cadastral survey map,"

18. These provisions correspond-roughly with those contained in section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act. From the first provision to clause (c) of section 117 it will appear that no order for the sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants shall be passed unless reasonable notice has been served upon all of them to appear and are heard in the matter. Mr. M.H. Khondker, Counsel for the respondents, submitted that the word 'shall' used in the, proviso is directory and not mandatory. Therefore, even if no notice has been given to the appellants of the application of the respondents to sub-divide the tenancy who did not, therefore, appear before the Revenue Officer when he passed the order for splitting up of the jama, such order cannot be said to have been vitiated by such non-service of notice upon the appellants. Furthermore, even though no such notice has been served upon him, it was open to the appellants to take recourse to the remedy provided in the Act to rectify their grievances with the time provided therein. Since they have not done so, the matter is concluded and the Court cannot while hearing the application for pre-emption entertain an objection regarding the non-service of notice during the mutation proceedings. In support of his submission that the word 'shall' is mandatory and not directory, he quoted the decisions re-ported in (1895) 1 QB 724 at 729 and 47 CWN 323.

19. On the other hand, Mr. T.H. Khan, Counsel for the appellants, submitted that the word 'shall' is mandatory and not directory in the absence of notice, as provided in section 117(1)(c), upon the co-sharer tenants, the order of sub-division of the tenancy will be bad and not be binding on the non-notified co-sharer tenants. In support, Mr. Khan, relied on Begum Asia Rahman Vs. Abdul Basir Bhuiyan (1974) 26 DLR (SC) 58. Here, the provisions of section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act which corresponds to section 117 (1)(c) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, were being considered. In saying that the sub-division of the holding could not create a bar for the exercise of, the right of pre-emption by the respondent when no service of notice under section 88A was served upon him, the Court observed as follows:

"A non-notified co-sharer of the holding which was divided would remain co-sharer of the holding as if there was no sub-division of holding relating to the claim of respondent or, in other words the respondent would not take cognizance of such sub-division of holding obtained by the appellant when he wanted to exercise his right to pre-empt the co-sharer of the holding. We are of the view that the right of pre-emption which accrued to the respondent on the sale of a portion of the holding remains un-affected by the sub-division of the holding under the order of Revenue Officer, vide exhibit 'B' as the respondent who was not a party to proceeding before a Revenue Officer is not bound by such order and is not required to get it set aside."

<u>20. In the present case before us the respondents produced exhibits F & G, the record of right and rent receipts respectively, in order to establish that during the pendency of the application for pre-emption the record of right was changed in the name of Sakina Bai. As a result of the mutation so effected by the respondents the appellants ceased to have any subsisting interest in the disputed land. Had this mutation been effected with a notice to the appellants, it might be argued that the mutation was binding upon the appellants but the non-service of notice of the mutation case has not only resulted in the violation of the principles of natural justice so far as the appellants are concerned but is in direct violation of the statutory requirement laid down in section 117 (1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The words used therein are both positive and clear and the requirement of notice being in respect of rights to property the word 'shall' used therein in mandatory and not directory. There is no vagueness or ambiguity about the intention of the legislature in imposing the duty of serving notice upon the co-sharers when one of them wants to divide the holding. The respondents have failed to show the fulfillment of the requirement provided under the aforesaid section. They have no doubt been able to produce the order of sub-division of the holding but such sub-division which is an exparte order in substance having been obtained without notifying the appellants cannot be binding on them. As a consequence their interest in the holding subsisted and the intended effect of the document contained in exhibits F & G which might have otherwise taken away such interest has not been produced. The principles laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the decision reported in (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 36 is not, therefore, applicable to the facts of the present case and right of pre-emption claimed by the appellants is not accordingly affected by the order of sub-division of the holding.</u>

<u>21. Apart from the failure to fulfill the requirement of notice laid down by the aforesaid provisions of law which has not, therefore, made the order of sub-division binding upon the appellants, it is also hit by the doctrine of lis pendens inasmuch as the petition for mutation was filed on July 18, 1974 which is long after the pre-emption proceedings initiated by the appellants. The principles of lis pendens as contained in section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act is as follows:</u>

<u>"During the pendency in any court of any suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the court and such terms as it may impose."</u>

<u>22. Mr. Khondker, Counsel for the, respondents, vehemently argued that the mutation which had been affected by the respondents under the provisions of section 117 (1) (c) does neither come under the word 'transferred' or the word 'otherwise dealt with' and cannot therefore, be questioned by the respondents as affecting his rights to property. What the word 'transferred' means is not vague or unclear. It means such transfers as are contemplated by the Transfer of Property Act, such as, sales, gifts, mortgages, leases and exchanges but there is some scope for doubt as the meaning of the word 'otherwise dealt with'. Whatever other transactions may be included by them the questions is, as has been raised by the learned Counsel for the respondents, whether they include mutation as a result of an order of sub-division of a tenancy effected under section 117 (1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He submitted that the expression 'otherwise dealt with' ejusdem generis with the word 'transfer' and therefore, the transaction which may be included under former expression must partake of the same nature as that of a 'transfer. Since the order of sub-division under section 117 (1) (c) cannot be viewed as 'transfer' mutation effected thereunder is not hit by the principle of lis pendens. On the other hand, the learned Counsel for the appellant made contrary submissions. According to him, the expression 'otherwise dealt with' does not bring ejusdem generis rule into play. In support, he relied upon the decision reported in AIR 1958 SC 838; 1943 AC 166.</u>

<u>23. It seems difficult for us to accept the contention that transaction which may be included as a dealing with property otherwise must also have the same characteristics as that of transfer between two living persons such as sale, mortgage, lease or exchange. A dealing with property otherwise may include any transaction which is not a transfer of any one of the kinds just mentioned above but such dealing must actively involve anyone of the parties to a pendine suit which may have some consequence on their rights upon which the Court was to adjudicate. In the present case the respondents initiated the mutation proceeding during the pendency of the pre-emption case and the order obtained by them has affected the appellants' right of pre-emption which accrued earlier than the proceedings for mutation initiated by the respondents. We are, therefore, of the view that the respondents dealing with the disputed property which resulted in the sub-division of the holding is hit by the doctrine of lis pendens. Such sub-division of the holding does not constitute a bar for the exercise of the right of pre-emption by the appellant.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment and order of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the Trial Court are restored.</u>

End.
