full_judgment:
K. Hossain, C.J:—I concur with the decision of my learned brother Fazle Munim, J.

Fazle Munim, J:—This appeal arises from the judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 507 of 1976 on December 6, 1977. The respondent who joined the police service in 1962 as a Sub-Inspector of Police was promoted as an Inspector of Police in 1972. When he was Inspector of Police, he was posted in Mohammadpur Police Station, Dacca as the Officer-in-Charge. While holding this office he went on leave in November, 1975. He was served with a notice dated December 23, 1975 issued by the Chairman, Second Screening Board, Dacca, which has since been abolished, asking him to show cause why a recommendation will not be made against him under the Government of Bangladesh (Service Screening) Ordinance, 1972 (the President's Order No. 67 of 1972).

Charges against him were as follows:-

1) That the respondent had abused his power of office by utilising the police force for some personal purpose and with its help assaulted the members of the family of Abdur Rashid and Jainal Abedin on May 4 and 5, 1975 and drove them out from house No. 7 and 7 Ka, Mohammadpur Colony.

2) These two houses which have been allotted by the Government to Abdur Rashid and Jainal Abedin were secretly purchased by the respondent in the name of his wife and father.

3) The price paid in purchasing the house in his wife's name on March 13, 1975 is Tk. 20,000/00 and the price of the other house purchased in the names of his wife and father is Tk. 30,000/00. Besides this, he had a bank balance of Tk. 8,719/00. He had also a TV set, a Three-in-One set and a Honda Motor Cycle. The possession and ownership of these recently purchased houses and other assets indicated that he could not have acquired them with the income he derived from his meager salary, they being disproportionate to the known source of his income.

2. On January 5, 1976 the respondent submitted his explanation to the Screening Board wherein it was stated that there was no incident on May 4 and 5, 1975. No occasion, therefore, arose for misusing his official power. As a result of an information lodged by one Abul Kashem who claimed to be a resident of the aforesaid houses. P.S. Case No. 40 was started under sections 323 and 448 of the Penal Code on April 11, 1975. A Sub-Inspector of Police of the Mohammadpur Police Station took up investigation and arrested Abdur Rashid and Jainal Abedin on April 14, 1975 who were produced before the Court on the next day. The charge-sheet was eventually submitted against them.

3. As regards the houses and other assets, his explanation was that his father-in-law whose two sons had been earning abroad purchased the aforesaid houses with the money sent by them. He denied to have beaten up Abdur Rashid and Jainal Abedin nor did he drive them out from the houses. The houses were not allotted to them or any of them, he asserted. As regards the other assets, the respondent claimed that they were not purchased by him. His father-in law who is a wealthy person of Bogra district made a gift of the 'Honda' Motor Cycle to him in 1966. The three-in-one set was sent to him in 1977 from London by his brother who owns a restaurant there. The TV set was presented to his children in 1975 by his mother-in-law.

Documents in support of the facts stated by the respondent in his explanation were also put in. He also prayed for examination of certain witnesses for proving his innocence.

4. The respondent's grievances were that the Screening Board did not examine any witness excepting his father, nor was he supplied with any copy of the evidence recorded by it. Further, the Board directed an enquiry by the District Anti-Corruption Department and on its receipt which was obtained behind the back and without the knowledge of the respondent; the recommendation was made by the Board. As a result thereof he received an order on July 1, 1976 dismissing him from service.

5. His contentions were that the findings of the Screening Board violated the provisions of Articles 5 and 7 of the aforesaid President's Order and Rule 7 framed thereunder and also that the Board violated the principles of natural Justice in not disclosing the content of the report to him. He was, therefore, denied the right to put up proper defence.

6. On behalf of the Government it was asserted that there was no proof as to the purchase of the aforesaid houses with the money of his father-in-law. It was submitted, that the respondent purchased the houses by using the names of his father and wife with his ill-gotten money. Further, the respondent had set up Abul Kashem to institute a false case against Abdur Rashid and Jainal Abedin in order to drive them out from the above mentioned houses and to take vacant possession. The Board was not convinced by the explanation submitted by respondent which, therefore, recommended his removal from service.

7. The Writ Petition was allowed by the High Court Division. Being aggrieved by the decision the Government moved this Court and obtained special leave on the following points:—

(1) Whether the respondent, who was Inspector of Police could maintain a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution, he being a member of the Disciplined Force.

(2) Whether the finding of the High Court Division, that there was no evidence supporting the conclusion of the Enquiry Committee, is sustainable in view of the materials on record.

(3) Whether the learned Judges were well founded in law in observing that the Screening Board based its decision on extraneous circumstances in coining to its conclusion.

8. Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellant, made submissions on the first point, that is, regarding the locus stands of the respondent to present an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. He reasoned that in view of the provision of Clause (5) of the aforesaid Article which debars a member of the disciplined force from maintaining an application under the Article, the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. He submitted that having regard to the definition of the disciplined force as given in the Constitution, the respondent who is a member of the disciplined force cannot be permitted to seek any remedy by invoking the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division.

Clause (5) of Article 102 of the Constitution is as follows:

"In this article, unless the context otherwise   requires, 'person' includes a statutory public authority and any court or tribunal other than a court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force or a tribunal to which article 117 applies.

9. The definition of what constitutes a disciplined force, as appears in the interpretation clause of the Constitution, which is contained in Article 152, is as follows:

"disciplined force" means—

(a) the army, navy or air force ;

(b) the police force ;

(c) any other force declared by law to be a disciplined force within the meaning of this definition ;

<u>10. The two definitions set out in the Constitution require analysis. The word person in Clause (5) of Article 102, gives an inclusive definition first and then it excludes something from the inclusive meaning. It, therefore, envisages within its definition all entities called 'Person' in law and includes something more as given in Clause (5). But then this clause again excludes some entity already included in the inclusive meaning, one is Court or Tribunal established under a law relating to the defence service and the other is a tribunal to which article 117 applies. From this definition it would thus appear that it includes the respondent within its scope. Being an Inspector of Police, the respondent is and must be held to be a member of the disciplined force. Next, on referring to the provision of Clause (5) of Article 102 quoted above, we can see that a plain reading of its provisions would show that a court or tribunal set up under law to deal with any matter relating to a disciplined force cannot be directed under this Article to do or be refrained from doing any act mentioned in this Article, nor can any act done or proceeding taken by such a court or tribunal be declared to have been taken without lawful authority and of no legal effect.</u>

<u>11. In view of the express provisions excluding such a tribunal as dealt with the case of the respondent from the connotation and meaning of the expression "person" as used in this Article, it suffices to say that such exclusion is a bar to the maintainability of the respondent's application under Article 102, though he might have otherwise claimed to have come under the expression "any person aggrieved". There may not be doubt as to his being an "aggrieved person", but, even so, his locus standi is gone due to the ouster clause in clause (5) of Article 102 as mentioned above. The very fact of one's being a member of the disciplined force furnished the reason which impelled the Constitution makers to provide the ouster of the jurisdiction of the High Court Division from entertaining any application against the decision of any tribunal which deals with anything or matter relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force. Howsoever the respondent may wish for welcome interference by the High Court Division with the decision of such a tribunal as referred to in clause (5), the wisdom of the Constitution-makers in providing against such interference is more welcome and significant.</u>

<u>13. Quite understandably, a member of the disciplined force cannot, for the very reason that has assumed a kind of responsibility which is not expected of any other person in the service of Bangladesh, hope to have all the rights which the Constitution has conferred on the latter. One of such rights being the power to invoke the special jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 for the redress of any grievance against the administration. Needless to say, extension of such right to a member of the defence services of Bangladesh or to a member of any disciplined force would militate against the very essence and reality of the special role which he is called upon to discharge. One of the most elementary assumptions upon which a person proceeds to join the armed or police force is that if he is punished by the authority under whose command he has been placed for any infraction of duty or responsibility, he cannot seek remedy from any ordinary civil authority. Any interference by such authority other than in a case where lack of jurisdiction of the military or police authority is challenged would undermine its discipline and efficiency. No ordinary court can give protection to a member of the defence services or of any disciplined force in case he challenges the decision of the authority under which he serves.</u>

<u>14. Mr. S.R. Pal, counsel for the respondent, submitted that as the Screening Board cannot be termed a court or a tribunal set up under a law relating to any disciplined force, it does not come under the expression ‘person’ used in clause (5) of Article 102. Its decision can, therefore, be challenged before the High Court Division under the aforesaid Article. Though apparently plausible, his contention, as it issues from a very narrow and literal construction of the word "a court or tribunal established under a law relating to ... any disciplined force", would seem to have no sound basis. Among the seven grounds taken by the respondent in his Writ Petition challenging the legality of the order of his removal from service, none appears to have questioned the jurisdiction of the Screening Board to try him. What Mr. Pal wanted to say is, as I understood it that as the Screening Board had not been set up under a law relating exclusively to the police force, it could not be viewed as a court or a tribunal, envisaged in clause (5). Its decision could, therefore, be challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution. The acceptance of his argument would not only be contrary to what has been intended by the makers of the Constitution, but would tantamount to denying the authority of the Screening Board to try the respondent. Nowhere has the respondent challenged the vires of the law which set up the Screening Board nor its jurisdiction to try him. As the law which has set up the Screening Board permits it to exercise jurisdiction in relation to a member of any disciplined force, it must be considered a court or tribunal under a law in relation to a disciplined force, though such law is not meant exclusively for it.</u>

<u>15. In interpreting the Constitution this Court has always avoided to attribute any such meaning to the words used therein as has not been intended by the framers of the Constitution. Besides, it will never put any narrow and literal construction upon any word or expression used in the Constitution. The view we have expressed as regards the meaning of the expression "a court or tribunal established under a law relating to any disciplined force", apply equally to the meaning of similar expression used in the corresponding Bengali text of clause (5). The Bengali text cannot, therefore, be interpreted to mean either the exclusiveness of the law or of court or tribunal. Considering the two texts, English and Bengali, of clause (5), side by side, the meaning appears to be the same as we have indicated above. What is of essence is whether the law which set up the tribunal has empowered it to deal with any member of the defence services or of any disciplined force. If the connection or the link between the law, the court or tribunal and the member of the defence services or of any disciplined force is established, no remedy against the decision of such court or tribunal is available by invoking the writ jurisdiction. More so when the alleged grievance concerns matter relating to discipline.</u>

16. In view of our conclusions as to the incompetence of the High Court Division to entertain an application under Article 102 of the Constitution against the Screening Board dealing with the respondent who belongs to the disciplined force as defined in the Constitution, and the resulting lack of his competence to present such an application, it is no longer necessary for us to determine the other two points on which leave was granted.

I would, therefore, allow the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court Division and recall the writ.

Ruhul Islam; J: I also concur with the judgment of my learned brother Fazle Munim, J.

Sd/- R. Islam

K.M. Subhan, J.—This appeal by the Government by way of special leave arises from the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ petition No. 507 of 1976 making the Rule absolute. The learned Judges declared that the recommendation of the Screening Board and the impugned order dated 24.7.76/30.7.76 removing the respondent above named from service, has been made without, any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

18. Having disagreed with the majority view taken by my lords in the matter I give my reasons for disagreement. For the avoidance of repetition I am not covering the facts of the case which have been amply given in the judgment of my lord, Mr. Justice Fazle Munim.

The appeal merited consideration on the following questions:

(1) Whether the respondent, who was Inspector of Police, could maintain a Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution, he being a member of the Disciplined Force.

(2) Whether the finding of the High Court Division, that there was no evidence supporting conclusion of the Enquiry Committee, is sustainable in view of the materials on record.

(3) Whether the learned Judges were well founded in law in observing that the Screening Board based its decision on extraneous circumstances in coming to its conclusion. Before the High Court Division no objection was taken by the Government regarding the maintainability of a Writ Petition by a Police Officer, under Article 102 of the Constitution and as such we are deprived of the observations of the learned Judges of the High Court Division on the subject.

19. On the first ground in which leave has been granted, the learned Assistant Attorney-General submitted that the petition is not maintainable in view of the petitioner being in the police service which comes within the meaning of Disciplined Force.

20. There cannot be any controversy regarding the 'police force' coming within the meaning of the 'disciplined force' because in Article 152, the interpretation of sub-Article (6) does include the 'Police force' within the meaning of ...disciplined force. It has been argued by the appellant that Article 102 (5) creates a bar. Art. 102 (5) is reproduced below:

"In this Article, unless the context otherwise requires, "person" includes a statutory public authority and any Court or tribunal, other than a court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force or a Tribunal to which Article 117 applies."

<u>21. In the writ petition the petitioner prayed for declaring the recommendation of the Second Screening Board and the impugned order passed in pursuance thereof to be illegal and without lawful authority in terms of Art. 102 (2)(a)(ii). The word 'person' has been mentioned in this Art, 102(2) (a) (ii) twice. First, the application is competent only when it is made by a 'person aggrieved' and secondly, the High Court Division may, if satisfied, make an order declaring that the act of a `person' has been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

<u>22. The bar created under sub-Article (5) is of that 'person' and the makers of the Constitution have sought to give a comprehensive meaning to the word by including "a statutory public authority and any court or tribunal other than a court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services or a tribunal to which Article 117 applies." From the plain language the exclusion applies to a court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or a court or tribunal established under a law relating to any disciplined force. I have taken the view that the exclusion is applicable only to a Court or a tribunal as the language indicates. The governing inclusive clause is any "Court or tribunal" and the legislature while including "Court or Tribunal" excludes , "Court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh" or "a tribunal to which Article 117 applies". A reading of Article 117 would show that it is in the contemplation of the Constitution-makers that "administration tribunals" would be set up which would exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters referred to in clauses (a) and (b) of that Article 117. Sub-Article (2) seeks to oust the jurisdiction of the Courts from entertaining any proceedings or making any order in respect of matters with the jurisdiction of the administrative tribunal.</u>

23. The learned Counsel Mr. Pal's contention in that "any disciplined force". in Sub-Article (5) of Article 102 has not to be read in violation of the language of the sub article but in conformity with meaning of "disciplined force" given in Article 152. His contention is that "disciplined force" used in sub-article (5) has to be read along with the words" a court or tribunal established under a law relating to any disciplined force".

24. The contention of the learned Assistant Attorney-General that the exclusion of the words "disciplined force" from the meaning of "person" creates a bar for a member of the "disciplined force" of being a "person aggrieved" occurring in sub-article (1) of Art. 102 and a writ cannot be issued because of the language of sub-article (5).

<u>25. This contention of the learned Assist-ant Attorney-General does not stand to reason neither from the grammatical construction of the exclusion clause nor from the democratic spirit of the Constitution. Article 117 contemplates setting up of "administrative tribunal" which would exercise exclusive jurisdiction over matters referred to in clauses (a) and (b) of Article 117. The administrative tribunal shall have jurisdiction to examine the terms and conditions of person 'in the service of the Republic". The words "in the service of the Republic" have been interpreted in Article 152 to mean any service, post or office whether in a civil or military capacity, in respect of the Government of Bangladesh and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic." The words "civil or military" have not been interpreted in Article 152. Reference may be made in this connection to Article 135 which lays down provisions for dismissal, etc. of the civilian public officers and occurs in Part IX of the Constitution, which relates to the Service of Bangladesh, has no reference to any "service, post or office in a military capacity." The Constitution makes it clear that although service, post or office in the military capacity comes within the service of the Republic but under Article 133 appointments and conditions of service for the service, post or office in the military capacity are to be regulated by separate laws made by the Parliament. This is clearer because of the provisions of Article 135. The dismissal, etc. of military officers are not articulated in the Constitution and they would have their own laws made fox them by Parliament. The word "military" has to be given the dictionary meaning of that word. In Article 152 also clauses (a) and (b) are separate clauses.</u>

<u>26. It is interesting also to note that Sub-article (5) also separates "defence services" from disciplined force which otherwise also under Article 152 includes "defence services" for the simple reason that while there are under military law "military court or tribunal" there is none so far as "the police force" of the disciplined force is concerned. If, however, any court or tribunal is set up for "the police force' in future on amending the Constitution the embargo created under sub-Article (5) shall be attracted.</u>

<u>27. I am, in the premises, of the view that there being no comma after the words, "defence services of Bangladesh," "any disciplined force" is not to be read in isolation but is to be read as a "court or tribunal established under a law relating to any disciplined force".</u>

<u>The view that I have taken is further strengthened if the Bengali text of sub-article (5) is read which is thus:</u>

<u>(৫) প্রসঙ্গের প্রয়োজনে অন্যরূপ না হইলে এই অনুচ্ছেদ “ব্যক্তি” বলিতে সংবিধিবদ্ধ সরকারী কর্তৃপক্ষ ও বাংলাদেশের প্রতিরক্ষা কর্মবিভাগসমূহ বা কোন শৃংখলা বাহিনী সংক্রান্ত আইনের অধীনে প্রতিষ্ঠিত কোন আদালত বা ট্রাইবুনাল ব্যতিত কিংবা এই সংবিধানের ১১৭ অনুচ্ছেদে প্রযোজ্য হয়, এই রুপ কোন ট্রাইবুনাল ব্যতিত যে কোন আদালত বা ট্রাইবুনাল অন্তর্ভূক্ত হইবে।</u>

<u>The words “কোন শৃখংলা বাহিনী সংক্রান্ত আইনের অধীনে প্রতিষ্ঠিত কোন আদালত বা ট্রাইবুন্যাল” clearly speaks of "any disciplined force" to be preceded by the words "a court or tribunal established under a law relating to" in the English text of the Constitution.</u>

28. There is superficially a conflict between the English and the Bengali texts and in the event of a conflict between the language of the English and Bengali texts, the language of the Bengali text is to prevail.

Reference, in this connection may be made to proviso to Article 153(3); which Is quoted below:—

"Provided that In the event of conflict between the Bengal and the English Text, the Bengali text shall prevail."

It is pertinent at this stage to refer to Article 18B of the second Proclamation (Fifteenth Amendment) Order 1978 being second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1978 which substituted sub-paragraphs (9) and is a part of the Proclamation of 8th November, 1975 and is as follows:

"In the event of the conflict, contradiction, discrepancy or inconsistency between the Bengali and English Text of the Constitution insofar as it relates to any amendment, addition, modification, substitution or omission made in any of the texts or In both the texts by the said Proclamation the English Text shall prevail."

Article 102 was amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975 but after amendment Sub Article (3) of Article 102 Is in the same language as it was before the Fourth Amendment of 1973 and by the Second Proclamation (Seventh Amendment) Order 1976 being Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1976 Sub-Article (5) in the same language was incorporated in the Constitution. It is sufficient to mention that Sub-paragraph (9) of Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1978 is not available In this case because the relevant Sub-Article (5) only was subjected to numerical change only and it did not suffer "any amendment, addition, modification, substitution or omission" in its text.

31. The Bengali text of Sub-Article (5), apart from anything else, makes it abundantly clear that relief cannot be sought against a court or tribunal established under a law relating to any "disciplined force".

32. Insofar as the actual aspect of the decision of the High Court Division, the learned Assistant Attorney General has not taken any exception and in that view I find no reason to lake a view on it different from the High Court Division. The appeal, therefore, fails, and it is dismissed without any order as to costs.

ORDER OF THE COURT

In view of the decision of the majority, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The order of the High Court Division is set aside and the writ re-called.

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: —These eighteen Rules under Article 102 of the Constitution were obtained by persons owning various plots of land in Mouza Ramchandrapur under P.S. Mohammadpur, district Dacca, challenging requisition notices under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, for the purpose of acquisition for Mohammadpur Housing Pisciculture and Farming Co-operative Society Ltd. in L.A. Case No. 54/77-78.

2. For the purpose of convenience the writ petitions may be divided into three groups. The first group comprises of Writ Petition Nos. 5/80, 30/80, 31/80, 32/80, 33/80, 39/80, 40/80, 86/80, 87/80,90/80, 91/80, 112/80, 133/80, 134/80 and 135/80. The second group comprises of Writ Petition Nos. 65/80 and 96/80. The third group comprises of Writ Petition No. 155/80.

3. These three groups of writ petitions were heard consecutively and, as common questions of facts and law are involved in all of them, they will be disposed of by this single judgment.

4. The petitioners of the first group and the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 96/80 of the second group received the notices of requisition under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency), Requisition of Property Act, 1948 hereinafter referred to as the Act, simultaneously with notices under section 5(3) of the Act bearing the same date. They filed written objection to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.), Dacca respondent No. 3 without any result. They then moved the respondent No. 1, Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms in revision. The Joint Secretary of the Ministry, who heard their petitions, rejected the same on the ground that as notices under section 5 of The Act have already been served there is no scope for filing the revisional applications.

5. The petitioners of Writ Petition No. 65 of 1980 the second group allege that notices under section 3 of the Act have not been served on them, They collected copies of the notices from the Office or the Authorised Officer and Land Acquisition Officer, Dacca, respondent No. 3. They preferred separate appeals before the Commissioner, Dacca Division. The Additional Commissioner, Dacca Division rejected their appeals by a composite order. They preferred revisional applications before the Minister, Land Administration and Land Reforms who rejected the same with the observation that there is no substance in the petitions.

6. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 96 of the second group is Dacca Housing Corporation Limited, a public limited company registered under the Companies Act. The purpose of the Company is to purchase lands at market price, develop them and allot the same to their share-holders to mitigate the acute housing problem in the Dacca city. They purchased two acres of land in two C.S. plots, and went ahead with sub-division and allotment of the plots to their share-holders when they received the notice of requisition which covered their purchased land. The requiring body, the petitioner alleges, has been floated by a handful of high Government officials and businessmen who had no earlier experience or performance to their credit. Their object is to earn profits by allotting small plots to people.

7. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 155 of 1980 of the third group is a Co-operative Society registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1940. Its name is Panthoshala Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. It has acquired by private purchase 8'62 acres of land of several plots in the Mouza in question, and applied to the requisitioning authority for acquisition of 50'80 acres of land around the purchased lands of the Society for a housing scheme. But the requisitioning authority requisitioned the said land including the purchased lands of the Society for acquisition for Mohammadpur Housing Pisci culture and Farthing Co-operative Society Ltd.

8. Respondent Nos. 2 to 4 are the requisitioning authority in the first group. The requisitioning authority features as respondent Nos. 3 to 5 in writ petition No. 96 of 1980 of the second group, as respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in Writ Petition No. 65 of 1980 of the second group and as respondent Nos. 3 and 4 in the third group. The requisitioning authority has filed affidavit-in-opposition in each writ petition.

9. The requiring body Mohammadpur Housing Pisciculture and Farming Co-operative Society Ltd., which will henceforth be referred to as the respondent-Society, is added respondent No. 6 in the first group, respondent No. 4 in Writ Petition No. 65 of 1980 of the second group, added respondent No. 7 in Writ Petition No. 96 of 1980 of the second group and respondent No. 6 in the third group. The respondent-Society has filed separate affidavits-in-opposition in each writ petition.

10. Besides, Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms also features as a respondent in all the writ petitions. But it has neither entered appearance nor filed any affidavit-in-opposition.

11. The petitioners have filed affidavits-in-reply in all the writ petitions. During the course of hearing it was found that the two sets of contesting respondents did not bring out some relevant materials and information concerning the requisition in question in their respective affidavits-in-opposition. They were, therefore, given a chance to file supplementary affidavits-in-opposition which they did. The petitioners in their turn filed supplementary affidavits-in-reply.

12. The case made out by the requisitioning authority in their affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits-in-opposition is that the Dacca Improvement Trust prepared a Master Plan for Dacca City under the Town Improvement Act, 1953 with the approval of the Government. In the master plan some areas are shown as low lying areas which are called "unzoned area". The area under the instant L.A. Case No. 54/77-78 falls within the "unzoned area" as shown in the master plan. In this area buildings can be constructed with the permission from the authority. The respondent-Society, which is a Co-operative Society registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1940 adopted a housing scheme for acquisition and development of lands and sub-division of the said land into plots for construction of residential houses for those of its members who have no house in the city of Dacca. The Board of Trustees of the Dacca Improvement Trust in its 226th General Meeting held on 23.8.79 gave no objection for requisition and acquisition of the area in question. The requisitioning authority admitted the petitioners allegation that acquisition of the private property of individuals for Co-operative Housing Societies has been prohibited by the Government in the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives by Memo No. S-XIII/1-15/ 78/681(21) dated 5.7.78 (vide Annexure to the petitions of the first group), but justified the present requisition and acquisition on the ground that the Government in the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms accorded permission to start requisition and acquisition proceedings by Memo dated 28.8.79 on condition that persons having no land in the area will be allotted plot if they agree to be members of the Society and abide by its bye-laws. Earlier the scheme was approved by the District Land Allocation Committee on 20.10.78. The scheme was forwarded by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.) to the Government on 30.4.79. Hence the embargo placed by Memo dated 5.7.79 is not applicable to the present scheme, All legal formalities have been observed in requisition proceeding and the lands have been acquired for public purpose: Vacant possession of the land in question has already been delivered to the requiring body on 7.12.79. Before delivery of possession an Agreement was executed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.), Dacca, with the requiring body on 6.12.79. embodying the condition on which the allotment of the lands was made, and further stipulating that if on examination it was decided by the Government that the lands would not be required for the purpose mentioned in the Agreement, the requiring body would surrender the lands to the Government.

13. With respect to writ petition No. 155 of 1980 of the third group, the requisitioning authority submitted that the petition is not maintainable. It was denied that Panthoshala Co-operative Housing Society was the owner by purchase of different C.S. plots measuring an area of 8.26 acres of land. Notices under sections 3 and 5(3) of the Act in respect of those plots were served upon other persons as per information gathered from the locality and available records.

14. The case of the respondent-Society is that it adopted a housing scheme for which acquisition of lands was necessary, and accordingly, it applied to the District authority for the same. The District Land Allocation Committee passed a resolution on 19.5.78 approving requisition and acquisition of 44.23 acres of land for the housing scheme of the respondent-Society. As the respondent-Society required an area of 45.10 acres of land, the District Land Allocation Committee passed a further resolution on 20.10.78 approving the requisition and acquisition of 45.10 acres of land. The Member-Society of the said Committee thereafter sought approval of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms for the allocation by a Memo dated 9.12.78 Similar approval was sought for by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.) from the same Ministry by a Memo dated 30.4.79. The said Ministry accorded approval to the requisition and acquisition of 45.10 acres of land for the housing scheme of the respondent-Society by a Memo dated 28.8.79 Annexure  'X3'). Earlier the respondent-Society applied on 11.1.79 to the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operative for an administrative approval of its aforesaid housing scheme. The Registrar of Co-operative Societies forwarded the said application to the said Ministry which accorded its administrative approval by a Memo dated 18.1.79 (Annexure 'X5'). In view of the administrative approval dated 18.1.79 subsequent embargo on the acquisition of lands for Co-operative Housing Societies by Memo dated 5.7.79 issued by the said Ministry is not applicable in respect of the impugned requisition and acquisition. The Dacca Improvement Trust by a Memo dated 31.3.79 gave no-objection certificate to the respondent-Society (Annexure 'X6'). Director Urban Development Directorate by a Memo dated 14.1.79 also accorded consent to the housing scheme (Annexure 'X7'). Thereafter the actual order of requisition was passed by the Authorised Officer and Land Acquisition Officer, Dacca by his order dated 7.9.79. The respondent-Society has deposited a sum of Tk. 66.57,924/88 on 8.11.78 as provisional estimated compensation of 45.10 acres of land. In its supplementary affidavit-in-opposition the respondent-Society stated that its housing scheme is not a commercial venture and has not been taken on profit-making motive. It is essentially a Co-operative venture for the benefit of its members who have no land or house in the city of Dacca. The ownership of the land covered by the housing scheme will not be transferred to anybody, and shall remain with the respondent-Society and the members of the respondent-Society who have no land or house in the city of Dacca will be allotted residential plots of three kathas each. In the Agreement dated 6.12.79 between the Additional Deputy Commissioner ( L. A. ) and the respondent-Society ( Annexure 'X9' ), the respondent-Society has also undertaken that after the land is acquired by the Government the said la, d shall be held by the respondent-Society for the purpose for which it has been acquired and for no other purpose whatsoever without the previous permission from the Government in writing. When the respondent-Society applied to the District Authority for acquisition of land it had 1064 members vast majority of whom have no land or house at Dacca. At present the number of members of the respondent-Society has increased to 1847. When the respondent-Society invited applications from the members who have no land or house in the city of Dacca, 613 members applied for allotment. The respondent-Society will also have to make allotment in favour of persons affected by the acquisition of land if they become members of the society and apply for allotment. Out of 45.10 acres of land, 30 per cent of the same will have to be set apart for common facilities and thus 600 plots of 3 kathas each will be available for allotment as residential plots. The costs will be at actuals without keeping any profit for the respondent-society which will levy some extra charge for the purpose of providing and maintaining the common facilities. When the Additional Deputy Commissioner (L.A.) by Memo dated 28.8.78 asked the respondent-Society to deposit the provisional amount of 66,57,924/88 for the acquisition of the lands in question, the respondent-Society took advance at the rate of Tk. 5,000/- per katha from the members of the respondent-Society who applied for allotment,

14. In their affidavit-in-reply the petitioners of the first group stated that in reality, a large area has been requisitioned to sell those to people in small plots after developing and constructing houses, thereby enabling the Executive Committee of the respondent-society to make huge profits for themselves. Members of the Executive Committee are High Government officials and influential persons owning houses at Dacca City. The respondent-society was formed to make commercial gains and not to help solve housing problems of low-income group people. Mr. Abdul Momen Khan, Minister for Food is the Chairman, Mr. Khan-e-Alam Khan, Commissioner, Dacca Division, is the Vice-Chairman and .Mr. Quddus, Deputy Secretary, Islamic Foundation is the Secretary of the respondent-Society. The petitioners of the other groups have reiterated their objections to the requisition in their affidavits-in-reply.

15. The first point urged by Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 5 of 1980 of the first group is that the impugned requisition has not been made for a public purpose. The submission has three branches. First, the respondent-Society is a private enterprise, notwithstanding its co-operative character and requisition has been made for a private society to serve its private interests for commercial gain. Secondly, in view of the general embargo on the acquisition of private land for Co-operative Housing Societies contained in the Government's Memo dated 5.7.79 (Annexure 'C' to the petitions of the first group), the actual order of requisition dated 7.9.79 passed by the Authorised Officer and, Land Acquisition Officer, Dacca runs counter to a declared Government policy. Thirdly, there were no materials before the Authorised Officer and Land Acquisition Officer, Dacca, who actually passed the order of requisition on 7-9-79, in coming to the conclusion that the requisition was being made for a public purpose.

16. Mr. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate for the petitioners of the other writ petitions of the first group, Mr. S. R. Pal, learned Advocate for the petitioners of the writ petitions of the second group and Mr. Md. Abdur Rouf, learned Advocate for the petitioner of the third group have adopted the arguments of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed.

We shall take up the first branch of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed's arguments first.

<u>17. When the Government acquires land for its own purpose or for the purpose of a statutory body, then the scope of enquiry into public purpose is limited. Cooperative ownership, however is not state ownership nor is it a public enterprise. Article 13 of our Constitution recognises cooperative ownership as a form of ownership separate and distinct from State ownership and private ownership. When land is acquired by the Government for a Co-operative Society, it is an acquisition is favour of co-operative ownership, as distinct from state ownership and private ownership. Acquisition for a co-operative society is not per se an acquisition for a public purpose. Land, for example, is a scarce and very costly commodity at Dacca. Taking advantage of an acute housing problem and a still more acute problem of lack of available and suitable building sites any group of influential land speculators may combine themselves into a co-operative housing society and embark upon a profitable scheme of land reclamation, land development and housing primarily with the purpose of enriching themselves. To use the coercive powers and machinery of the State in aid of such profit-making entrepreneurs will clearly not be a public purpose.</u>

<u>18. Again, construction of dwelling houses cannot be Considered necessarily or per se to be a public purpose. Construction of houses in an area where there is already an excess of dwelling houses or where there is heavy concentration of population in existing houses cannot serve a public purpose. When land is acquired for a co-operative housing society it is therefore legitimate, nay, necessary to consider the kind of area that is being acquired, the purpose of the housing scheme, the public good that will come out of it, the conditions under which the Society has been allotted the land, etc. The list is not exhaustive. Other relevant considerations may crop up which will vary from case to case.</u>

19. The bye-laws of the respondent-Society are not a part of the voluminous affidavits filed in these writ petitions except a part of it in Writ Petition No. 96 of 1980 of the second group, but a copy of the same has nevertheless been made available to us for our perusal. The objects of the Society have been stated to be to promote the interest of the anglers and all persons associated with its activity and interested in agricultural operation and improved method of cultivation and in bonafide need of housing accommodation for residence. More particularly the objects of the Society are directed to:

"(a) acquire agricultural lands or obtain on lease pond, tank, fishery and for the purpose of angling and to practice improved methods and technique of angling and farming.

(b) to develop pisciculture in the matter of fish farming and rearing for promoting and protecting the interest of the anglers, persons interested in or associated with farming.

(c) encourage thrift, self-help and mutual aid among the members:

(d) to provide for housing and recreational facilities for the members by setting up houses as per a common plan and campus and providing other community facilities as shay be necessary;

(e)

20. As for qualification of membership it is provided in the bye-laws that any person above 18 years of age engaged and interested in angling and development of pisciculture and in bonafide need of housing accommodation for residence "having faith in the collective ownership and management of the property of the Society" shall be eligible to be a member of the Society.

<u>21. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed has submitted that the housing scheme is a secondary venture of the respondent-society. Its main activity is farming and pisciculture. From a reading of the bye-laws it comes quite clear that building up of houses as per common plan and campus is not an incidental object of the respondent-Society. We do not see why construction of houses as per common plan and campus for those members of the Society who have no land or house in Dacca city will not serve a public purpose. The beneficiaries under the scheme will be limited in number, but it is not the number of beneficiaries which determines public purpose. It is the good that accrues to the community at large that determines public purpose. If 600 allotted are accommodated in a planned manner with common facilities like school, recreation centre, playground, etc. it adds to the planned development of the city and relieves the problem of housing, however slightly.</u>

22. It has been argued that the real object of the housing scheme is to earn profits for the Society for eventual distribution to its members. It has been allege that land acquired for the Society will be divided into small plots which will be sold to the allotted after development keeping huge profits. We have no hesitation in holding that if this allegation is true, the requisition and acquisition will fail on this ground alone, because the coercive power of acquisition cannot be utilised to facilitate primarily the profit-making aims of an agency, be it a private party or a co-operative Society.

23. Unfortunately, no material has been furnished by the petitioners in support of their allegations. A bare avocation and a mere apprehension cannot tail the Court into concluding that the respondent Society will primarily indulge into profit-making out of the scheme. The respondent-Society has stated in its supplementary affidavit-in-opposition that it has not embarked upon the scheme with a profit-making motive. In fact its costs will be at actuals without keeping any profit for the Society. The requisitioning authority has averred in its supplementary affidavit-in-opposition that the ownership of the acquired land will remain with the requiring body. The members of the respondent-Society, its bye-laws says, must have "faith in the collective ownership and management of the property of the Society". If the land remains the property of the Society the houses built thereon will also be the property of the Society. The allotted will apply for and obtain allotment only if they have faith in the collective ownership and management of the property of the Society, i.e., the land acquired and the houses to be built thereon. Thus on the materials on record we cannot hold that the respondent-Society has been allowed to sell the plots or that if has been allowed to divest itself of the ownership of the land after it is acquired for the Society. The requisitioning authority is bound by its statement that the ownership of the land acquired for the Society will remain with the Society.

24. It has also been argued that although the avowed purpose of the housing scheme is to provide housing accommodation to those members of the respondent-society who have no land or house in Dacca city, yet most of its member are influential high officials who already own houses in the city. The respondent-Society has not denied that some of its members are high Government officials nor has it denied that certain highly placed Government officials are its office-bearers It, however, states that the officials have not applied for allotment of any residential plot and they have no Personnel interest in the housing scheme. We are unable to conclude from these materials that those member of the respondent-Society who have already land or house in Dacca city will, in fact, be given allotment in the acquired land as well.

25. We have noticed the two conditions under which the lands in question has been allowed to be acquired in favour of the respondent-Society. The conditions are that the respondent-Society is to allot acquired land only to those of its members who have no land or house in the capital city of Dacca. Secondly, persons having lands in the area may also be allotted plot if they agree to be members of the respondent-Society and act in accordance with its bye-laws. These two conditions have been incorporated in clause (5) of the Agreement (Annexure 'X9' to the supplementary affidavit in-opposition of the respondent-Society) between the Government and the respondent-Society. Clause (6) of the Agreement provides that the Government will examine the question of acquisition of the land for the aforesaid purpose and if as a result of the examination the Government decides that land shall not be acquired for the said purposes, then the Society shall surrender the land to the Government for release and restoration under section 8 of the Act. Clause (6) means, in our opinion that before the Government makes a decision about the acquisition of the requisitioned property under section 5(6) of the Act, after receiving the report of the Deputy Commissioner together with the case records under section 5(5) of the Act, at before publishing its decision to acquire the property under section 5(7), the Government shall examine the allotment list of the respondent-Society and shall be satisfied that the respondent-Society has made the allotment in terms of clause (5) of the Agreement. Even after such satisfaction the Government may decide that it shall not acquire land for the aforesaid purposes. Sufficient safeguard has been provided, therefore, to see that plots are not allotted to those who have already land or a house in Dacca city. Moreover, the respondent-Society has impliedly agreed in the Agreement that the ownership of the land will remain with it.

26. It has not been denied that the land under requisition falls in an 'unzoned area' in the master plan. For most part of the year the major part of the requisitioned land remains under water. Housing in this area will necessitate land reclamation and land development. If a co-operative housing society embarks upon a planned scheme of land reclamation, land development and housing in such an area it will add to the development and expansion of the city and will not be any unwarranted interference with an already developed area.

The first branch of the submissions of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, therefore, fails.

27. Next comes the second branch of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed's submission. The order of requisition was passed by the Authorised Officer and I and Acquisition Officer, Dacca on 7.9.79 Prior to this date, on 5.7.79, the Government had already decided that no private land will be acquired in favour of a co-operative housing society. The relevant Government memo is contained in Annexure 'C' to the Writ petitions of the first group and in the writ petitions of the other groups as well and runs as follows:—

"Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Dev, and Co-operatives, Section XIII

No. S-XIII/1M-15/78/681(21) dated 5.7.79. To: (1) The Registrar of Co-operative Societies, Bangladesh, Dacca.

Sub: Acquisition of land under L.A. Act for Housing Co-operative Societies.

The undersigned is directed to say that the question of acquisition of private properties of individuals for the Housing Co-operative Societies has been examined by the Govt. and it has been decided that no petition for such acquisition should be entertained.

It is, therefore, requested that no petition from any Housing Co-operative Societies for acquisition of land of private individuals should be entertained by him.

Sd/-R.U. Chowdhury 5/7/79

R U. (Chowdhury)

Section Officer.

28. From the above Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed argues that the Government approval given to the scheme on 28.8.79 is subsequent to the policy decision and the order of requisition is also subsequent to the policy decision. The order of requisition has been passed in clear violation of a declared Government policy and cannot be said to serve a public purpose.

29. Both Mr. M.M. Hoque, le4rned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the requisition authority and Mr. Syed Eshtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate for the responded Society have vehemently argued that the embargo placed by the memo in question does not affect the present requisition and acquisition proceedings, because, firstly, it is an embargo upon entertaining any future petition, and secondly, it does not say that earlier petitions which have already been entertained should not he proceeded with Indeed, from tilt wordings of the memo in question we do not find any embargo upon carrying into effect those petitions which have already been entertained. Although the actual order of requisition in the instant L.A case has been passed on 7.9.79, the petition of the respondent-Society had been entertained, approved and processed by the District Land Allocation Committee from long before. The history of the development has been recounted in the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent-Society, and we need not repeat the same. Besides the impugned requisition and acquisition have the approval of two Ministries of the Government. So much for the second branch of the submissions of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed.

30. Coming now to the third branch of submission of Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, it is contended that there were no materials before the Authorised Officer and Land Acquisition Officer, Dacca for his satisfaction that the lands were being acquired for a public purpose, The respondent-Society furnished no materials before the , requisitioning authority about itself. No bye-laws of the respondent-Society, no annual budget for the year in question, no resolution of the Boad of Directors of the respondent-Society in favour of the housing scheme, no statement or undertaking that the land acquired would remain the property of the respondent-Society or that the, respondent-Society would administer the housing scheme on a non-profit-making basis were there before the requisitioning authority. It is only before this court that these vital information have been furnished. Therefore, at the time the order of requisition was passed there were no materials for coming to the conclusion that the lands were being acquired for a public purpose.

<u>31. The records of L. A. Case No. 54/77-78 were made available to us by Mr. M. M. Hoque, learned Assistant Attorney General. On perusal we find that the officer who actually passed the order of requisition had before him the resolution of the District Land Allocation Committee allocating 45'10 acres of land to the respondent-Society, the clearance given by the Dacca Improvement Trust and the Urban Development Directorate, the administrative approval given by the Ministry concerned and the consent of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to start the requisition and acquisition proceedings. It cannot, therefore, be said that there were no materials at all for his satisfaction that the lands were being acquired for a public purpose. It is, however, true that those materials, which Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed has specifically pointed out to be missing from the consideration of the requisitioning authority, were not there before it at the time the order of requisition was passed. We feel that the considerations advanced by Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed are the most relevant considerations for the purpose of coming to the conclusion that the requisition and acquisition for a particular co-operative housing society would serve a public purpose. If later enquiry showed that the respondent-Society had no sizeable number of members who have no land or house in the Dacca city, that it had embarked upon the housing scheme on a purely profit-making motive, that housing is only an incidental object of the Society, that it would sell small plots after developing them at a huge profit, that it had or has no capacity to embark upon such an ambitious scheme, all the clearance from various agencies would have been of no avail. It is essential, therefore, that the requisitioning authority must apply its mind to the facts and circumstance of each case and particularly direct its searching eyes on the requirements, bonafide and modus operandi of the respondent-Society and its housing scheme. Unfortunately for the petitioners however, no materials have been produced to show that if the requisitioning authority had directed its mind along the lines indicated, the result would have been otherwise i.e it would have come to a conclusion that the acquisition was not for a public purpose. On all points the materials that have come before this Court do suggest that had an inquiry been made by the requisitioning authority on those points, the result would have been the same. Allegation of lack of relevant materials is actually an allegation of lack of relevant enquiries. We do not think the allegation in this particular case can carry the petitioners too far. As held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Province of East Pakistan vs. Abdus Sowdagar 16 D.L.R. (S.C.) 38:</u>

<u>“the order of requisition would be valid even though there was insufficient inquiry if in fact property was required for a public purpose. The want of inquiry in such a case could not be a ground for objection for the inquiry if made would have revealed only the true state of affairs. The order would be valid because the actual existence of requirement for a public purpose would by itself attract the application of section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act."</u>

32. Next, it has been argued by Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, which has been adopted by the other learned Advocates for the petitioners of the other groups, that after the passage of Town Improvement Act, 1953, the Dacca Improvement Trust remains the only authority to whom the task of land development and housing can be entrusted. No private agency or co-operative agency can be allowed, under the said statute the task of land reclamation, land development and housing, Our attention was drawn to the preamble and to sections 38, 39 and 40 of the said Act. We are unable to read into the provision of the said Act any, exclusive jurisdiction of the Dacca Improvement Trust into the area of activities mentioned there in. A more positive language in the statute is required for coming to the conclusion that it is the Dacca Improvement Trust alone which is authorised to embark upon those activities. The Dacca Municipal Corporation has also been conferred the power of town planning including preparation of master plan, site development scheme entailing division of sites into plots, building control etc. under  sections 95 and 96 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. These powers and functions are therefore permissive in nature and are subject to the prior approval of the Government.  It is ultimately for the Government to decide which areas will be developed by which agency. The Dacca Improvement Trust has given its own clearance for the housing scheme in question, and there is no question of a competing claim between a statutory body and a co-operative Society.

<u>33. It has also been, argued that recourse to East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 could not be made, because the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 specifically provides for acquisition of land for a co-operative Society. The answer to this submission is provided in the following passage of the decision in the case of Moosa Haji Vs. Province of East Pakistan, 12 DLR (Dacca) 236:-</u>

<u>"When the Legislature confers upon the Government two modes of acquisition, on under the ordinary Act and the other under the Emergency Act, and the authority chooses on one which makes it possible to acquire the property immediately, it cannot be said that this mode of acquisition is unlawful, because the other one is more beneficial to the citizen. To uphold the contention of the learned Counsel would mean defeating the very object of the Emergency Act."</u>

<u>Their Lordships also held that Government is the sole judge about the existence of urgency in taking possession of the land. If the question of urgency can be agitated, or, in other words, made justifiable in a Court of law, the very object of the Emergency Act will be frustrated.</u>

<u>34. Moreover, in assessing compensation for acquisition of land under both the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 it cannot be said any longer that compensation can be had for a bigger amount on a more liberal provision under the former Act than under the latter. The matters to be considered in determining compensation, matters to be, neglected in determining compensation and the rate at which properties are to be valued are the same in both the two Acts.</u>

35. Mr. M. M. Hoque has relied upon the cases of Mohammad Mansur Rahman Vs., Province of East Pakistan, 14 D.L.R. (Dacca) 604; Tej Ram Jag Ram Vs. Union of India, AIR 1959 Punjab 478 and several other decisions from the Indian jurisdiction in support of his contention that requisition and acquisition of land for co-operative housing Society have been held to be for a public purpose. We have considered the present L. A. case on its own merits, in the light, of the facts and circumstances of these petitions. We hold the present requisition and acquisition to be for a public purpose on the strength of its own peculiar circumstances.

36. Regarding the Writ Petition of the third group it has been alleged by both the requisitioning authority and the respondent-Society in their respective affidavits-in-opposition that the petitioner. Panthoshala Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. is not the owner of the plots in question. Requisition notices have been served upon other persons having title to the lands as per available records. The petition is, therefore, not maintainable. In its affidavit-in-reply the petitioner-Society has annexed a kabala deed (Annexure 'J') to show that a certain land was purchased by one Firoz Ahmed Chowdhury who described himself as a member of the petitioner-Society. That does not make the purchase a purchase by the petitioner-Society itself. Two other documents of purchase were shown to us at the time of the hearing. These purchases were made by the petitioner-Society itself, but after the order of requisition was passed. The petitioner-Society has failed to show that it is the owner of the lands in respect of which the impugned order of requisition was passed. The writ petition of the third group is therefore not maintainable at all.

<u>37. The petitioners have been served with notices of acquisition under section 5(3) of the Act simultaneously with notices under section 3 of the Act bearing the same date. Section 5(1) of the Act says that the Government may, if it thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property on the proposal of the Deputy Commissioner in the manner provided in that section. It has been argued that even where the requisitioning authority want to acquire the property immediately, they have first to requisition the property and then they have to take steps under section 5 of the Act for acquiring it. The notices under section 5(3) are, therefore, illegal. In the present Writ petitions, however, this court is concerned only with the notices of requisition and not of acquisition and therefore, this question does not call for an opinion in these cases.</u>

In the result, all the Rules in all the writ petitions are discharged without any order as to costs.

38. It is submitted by Mr. Mohammad Ali learned Advocate that he has instruction to prefer special leave to appeal to the Appellate Division against this decision of this Court. In this view of the matter, he prays that the operation of the impugned order of requisition may be stayed for ten weeks. The prayer is allowed and the operation of the impugned order of requisition is stayed till 21st October 1981 from date.

Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J. I agree.

End.

B.B. Roy Chowdhury, Assistant Attorney-General, instructed by the S.S. Hoda, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondents.
