case_source: From the judgment and order dated 3-2-71 passed by the Dacca High Court in petition No. 124 of 1970.
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J. - This appeal is against a judgment of a bench of the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan, dismissing a writ application made by Mr. M.H. Khandker, the appellant, who happens to be a lessee of a residential plot of land under the Government at Dhanmandi Residential Area in the, city of Dacca, by which the validity of a notice calling upon the appellant to pay certain taxes in addition to annual rent payable in respect of his lease-hold property was challenged. Mr. M.H. Khandker, a senior advocate of this Court has appeared in person and had addressed the Court in support of his appeal.

<u>2. The appellant obtained the lease of a plot of land at the Dhanmandi Residential Area of the City from the Govt. of East Pakistan for a period of 99 years commencing from the 29th day of January, 1957 in consideration of the payment of 7,980/- as salami and annual rent of Rs. 36/- which is liable to be revised, according to the terms of the deed of lease, after a period of 30 years. The appellant was called upon by a notice dated 20-3-70, issued by the Sub-Divisional Manager (Sadar) South, Dacca, who is Respondent No.2 in this appeal, to pay by 30-3-70 sum of Rs.545/70 on account of land revenue which, it was stated in the notice, he had not been making payment of or to show cause by the said date why legal action should not be taken against him under Public Demands Recovery Act for “willfully defaulting payment". The appellant showed cause against the said notice by a letter dated 28-3-70 addressed to Respondent No.2, stating that all rents till 1969 has been deposited and asked for withdrawal of the said notice. On an enquiry made by the appellant he was informed that the amount of the demand consisted of Development and Relief Tax at the rate of 25% of the rent with effect from 1367 B.S. under the East Pakistan Finance (3rd) Ordinance, 1958 (Ordinance No. LXXXII of 1958), a local rate of 12% with effect from 1367 B.S, under Article 59 of the Basic Democracies Order 1958 and also an Additional Development and Relief Tax at the rate of 50 paisa per acre under The East Pakistan Finance Act 1967 (Act No.XVII of 1967) with effect from 1374 B.S. Respondent No.2, in reply to the appellant's letter asked the appellant to get all the payments of rent as claimed by him noted by Tahshilder on production of Chalans and to pay the subsequent dues upto 14-4-70 (i.e. upto current Bengali year 1376 B.S.) amounting to Rs. 82-26 paisa by the said date of 14-4-70, which included, as the appellant was informed on further enquiry, Development and Relief Tax, local rate and additional Development and Relief Tax. In spite of demands however according to the appellant, he was not supplied with the breakup of the said amount of the demand of Rs. 82/26 paisa.</u>

3. The appellant, thereafter, moved High Court of East Pakistan under Article 6(B) of the Provisional Constitutional Order, 1969 read with Article 98 of the late Constitution of Pakistan for a declaration that the notice asking the appellant to make payment of Rs. 82/26 was without any lawful authority and also for a direction restraining Respondent No. 2 from realising amount in excess Rs. 36/- per year payable under the deed of lease dated 29-6-57. The appellant contended in the said application that the lease in his favour was not a tenancy under any of the provisions of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that the terms and conditions were exclusively controlled by the deed of lease under which he held the land and that according to the said terms the rent being payable according to the Gregorian Calendar the attempt to realise rent according to Bengli Calender year was absolutely without any lawful authority.

4. The claim of the appellant was contested by the respondent on the ground that according to the terms of appellant's lease the appellant was bound to pay all rates and taxes whichever bad already been levied or whatever might have been thereafter levied and that as, such the appellant should pay all Development and Relief Taxes, the local Rates and the Additional Development and Relief Taxes which having been imposed after the lease under subsequent legislations were obligatory upon the appellant.

5. The High Court on a consideration of the contentions raised before it came to the view that the appellant was a tenant within the meaning of the East Pakistan Finance (3rd) Order of 1958 and East Pakistan Act XVII of 1967 and was assessable under the said two enactments and that all lands assessable to under Article 59 of the Basic Democracies Order, 19J9 being subject to the local rate$ the land of the appellant being assessable to rent within the meaning of the said Article were also liable to be assessed to local, rate as demanded by the Respondents.

6. Special leave to Appeal was granted by the Appellant Division of the Supreme Court for deciding the question as to the legality of the imposition of the Development and Relief Tax under the East Pakistan Ordinance No. LXXXII of 1958 only. But on a perusal of the judgment of the High Court and hearing, the learned Counsel of both the parties it appears that the question as to the legality of the imposition of the Additional Development and Relief Tax under East Pakistan Act XVI of 1967 and of the Local Rate under Article 59 of the Basic Democracies Order also merits consideration. The appellant was, therefore, allowed by this Court to address it on the said question as well.

7. Mr. M.H. Khandker, the appellant, who has appeared in person, has submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court were wrong in taking the view that he was a tenant under the Govt. in respect of the residential plot of land, leased out to him on the basis of the Indenture of lease dated 29-6-57 by the Governor of East Pakistan for the purpose of assessment of the Development and Relief Tax and Additional Development and Relief Tax under the two East Pakistan enactments referred to above. His contention is that he is a lessee of piece of Govt. Khas land within the meaning of the Transfer of Property Act on the terms and conditions as laid down in the Indenture of lease and that he cannot be taken to be a tenant, as contemplated in the said two Taxing Statutes, which means, according to the appellant, a holder of agricultural land. The appellant has also contended that the term 'tenant' has got a specific connotation in the context of the land law system of the country and generally refers to a holder of agricultural land, as has been contemplated in the definition clause, section 2(17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, which has been bodily incorporated in section 2(27) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the latter Act having ultimately been repealed and replaced by the Bengal Tenancy Act, and that inasmuch as ordinarily a holder of agricultural land under another person is known as tenant & that of the non-agricultural land is known as lessee, the appellant, who in a lessee of some non-agricultural Govt. Khas land, cannot be brought within the purview of Taxing Statutes in question, which refer to a tenant and not to a lessee. It has been further submitted by Mr. Khandker that the basis of the decision of the learned Judges of the High Court that the appellant is a tenant within the meaning of Taxing Statutes being that he has been described as such in the very Indenture of lease by which lease was created and that the appellant's lease is in effect a lease in perpetuity is absolutely erroneous, as misdescription of the status of a person in a private document cannot alter has legal position and that the lease of the appellant having been created specifically for a term of 99 years cannot be taken to be a lease in perpetuity.

8. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the Respondents, has, on the other hand, submitted that the term 'tenant' as has been used in the Taxing Statutes in question, is a general expression meaning a holder of land under another person on condition of payment of rent to such person, irrespective of the nature of the land and that there is absolutely no warrant for restricting the meaning of the said expression by confining it to the holder of agricultural land only.

9. In order to appreciate the respective contentions of the parties, let us first look into the relevant terms and conditions under the Indenture of lease creating the appellant's title, a copy which has been placed before us-The relevant terms and conditions of the said Indenture are to the following effect:—

"This Indenture of lease made this 29th day of June one thousand nine hundred and fifty seven, BETWEEN the Governor of East Pakistan hereinafter called ''the lessor"* * * of one part

And

Mofazzal Hossain Khandker * * * hereinafter referred to as ''the Tenant" * * * of the other part.

Where the lessor is the 16 annas owner and in exclusive possession of the piece or parcel of land measuring one bigha, more or less fully described in schedule I annexed hereto, hereinafter called "the demised property."

And whereas the Tenant has proposed to take and lessor has agreed to give, lease of the demised property on the terms and conditions hereinafter following. Now This Indenture Witness that in consideration of the payment of Rs.7980 (Seven thousand nine hundred and eighty) salami * * * and the rent, covenants and conditions hereinafter reserved and contained and on the part of the tenant to be paid, performed and observed, the lessor both hereby demise upto the Tenant the demised property for the purpose of erecting thereon by the Tenant buildings for residential purposes for the period of 99 (ninety nine) years commencing from the 29th day of June, 1957 on the terms, covenants and conditions hereinafter contained, that is to say, the Tenant's covenants with the lessor.

1. That the Tenant has paid Rs. 2250/-(Rupees two thousand two hundred and fifty) only in part payment of the premium for the demised property and shall pay to the lessor rent and balance of the premium of Rs. 5730/-(Rupees five thousand seven hundred and thirty) only according to the terms mentioned in Schedule II annexed hereto.

2. That the Tenant shall promptly and regularly pay to the lessor or to such other person as the lessor may authorise or to the local authorities all rates, taxes, charges, duties, assessments, impositions, levies and any other outgoings whatsoever that are now levied or may hereafter be levied under any law for the time being in force upon the demised property and/or upon any building or structure that may be erected thereon in respect thereof including rates and taxes for essential services and shall comply with and carry out all municipal or local requirements as to drains, sewers and sanitary arrangements of the premises and keep the same in good repair and in a proper and sanitary condition.

19. That the Tenant shall not sell, charge, mortgage, exchange, gift away or otherwise assign, subject, encumber or in any way part with or dispose of the demised property or any part thereof before the construction of the buildings, out houses and appurtenances hereby covenanted to be erected.

20. That subject to the provision of clause 19 the Tenant shall be at liberty to transfer or sublet subject to the conditions of these presents the whole of the demised property subject to the obligation that the transfer shall be registered in the office of such authority as may be appointed by the lessor, and unless this is done, the lessor will not be bound to recognise or accept any person as Tenant of the demised property in place of the transferor:

Provided that without prior written sanction of the lessor no transfer of a portion of the demised property shall be valid, binding or effective.

25. It is hereby further mutually agreed and settled between the parties as follows:-

(I) The lessor reserves the right to revise the rent of the demised property after period of 30 (thirty) years and to determine the rent payable by the Tenant thereafter subject to an enhancement upto 12% per cent. His decision as to what is the fair rent shall be final and binding upon the parties.

* * *

Schedule II

<u>* * * *</u>

3. The annual rent of Rs. 36 (thirty six) at the rate of Rs.36 per bigha is payable by the Tenant in two equal half-yearly of April and on the 1st day of October each year.

10. In addition to the annual rent which is payable in two equal half-yearly installments, as has been one of the terms of the Indenture of lease, the Government has sought to impose two taxes, namely, Development and Relief Tax and Additional Development and Relief Tax under the provisions of East Pakistan Ordinance No.LXXXII of 1958 and East Pakistan Act XVI of 1967 respectively, the relevant provisions of which may be quoted below:

The East Pakistan

Finance (3rd) Ordinance, 1985

. . . 2.(1) There shall be levied and collected by the provincial Government development relief tax from every tenant at the rate of four annas on each rupee of rent payable by him in respect of the land comprised in his tenancy with effect from the 1st day of Baishakh, 1362. Provided that when such land is held free of rent, such development and relief tax shall be levied and collected at the rate of four annas on each rupee of rent that would be assessable on such land on the principles laid down in section 26 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act,1950.

(2) The development and relief tax levied under sub-section (1) shall be realized in the manner in which rent is realized by the provincial Government."

East Pakistan

Finance Act, 1957

(Act XVII of 1967)

"2.(1) There shall be levied and Finance Act, collected by the provincial Government an additional development and relief tax from every tenant at the rate of fifty paisa per acre in respect of the land comprised in his tenancy with effect from the 1st day of Baishakh, 1374.

(2) The additional relief and development tax levied under sub-section (1) shall be realised in the manner in which rent, is realised by the Provincial Government.

11. Both the taxes were sought to be levied and collected under the terms of the two taxing statutes from "every tenant" at a certain rate on the payable by him or on the area "in respect of the lands comprised in his tenancy". From the manner of the levy and the method of collection of the taxes, as have been provided in the said statutes, it is clear that such a tenant would be one of the lands held under the Government. Tenant has not been defined in any of the said two statutes. According to the well-established rule of statutory construction, every word is to be understood in its plain and natural meaning. If, however, such a word has received a distinctive or technical meaning in the statutes in pari materia i.e., statutes dealing with the same person or thing or class, the aid of such a meaning may be taken for interpreting the word as used in the statute under consideration.

In the legal literature, the word "tenant" has acquired a meaning which is substantially definite and precise. The legislative history in respect of the Tenancy Laws of the country also provides a dependable guideline for the proper appreciation of the word. It is also a well-settled rule of construction that the legislative language will be interpreted on the assumption that the legislature, while enacting a particular statute, was aware of the course of legislation and of the existing statutes, where a particular word or words had been given a specific definition or meaning. The rule of construction in this connection has been stated in Craies on Statute law, 6th Edition, at page 141, after referring to the observation made by Lord Shaw of Dunfermline in the case of Lennon Vs. Gibson & Howes Ltd. (1919) A.C. 709 in the following words:

".........where the legislative has given to words a statutory definition in one statute, and has used the same words in a similar connection in a later statute dealing with the same subject matter, it may be presumed in the absence of any context indicating a contrary intention that the same meaning attaches to the words in the later as in given to them in the earlier statute."

12. The English term 'tenant' ordinarily means an occupier of immovable property having a kind of relationship respecting the said property with another person who is generally called the 'landlord'. The relationship of landlord and tenant generally arises when the owner of the property confers by a demise a right of exclusive possession of that property upon another person on condition of periodical payment of what is called rent. This relationship may also arise out of a contract between two persons when one of them inducted into the occupation of the property by the other person having a dominion over the said property by virtue of ownership or otherwise on condition of payment of rent for such occupation. According to the terms of the demise or contract, this right of occupation may be created permanently or for a fixed period or from period to period (i.e., from year to year or month to month). As used in English, this term 'tenant’ had never been confined in its application to a particular kind of immovable property, agricultural or non-agricultural, or rural or urban. The general principles relating to landlord and tenant have been stated in Halsbury's laws of England (3rd Edition) Vol. 23 paragraph 985 at page 407 in the following words—

"985. General principles. The relation of landlord and tenant was originally one of contract only, but from early times the contract conferred an estate in the land on the tenant without losing all its contractual characteristics. The relation arises as a rule when one party confers on another the right to the exclusive possession of land, mines or buildings, for a time which is either subject to a definite limit originally, as in the case of a lease for terms of years or which, though originally indefinite, can be made subject to a definite limit by either party as in the case of a tenancy from year to year. The interest in the property which remains in the landlord is called the reversion, and, as a rule, there is, incident to it, the right to receive from the tenant payment for the use of the property in the shape of rent."

13. Mr. Khandker has sought to argue that a tenant is to be distinguished from a lessee and that whatever general connotation the term 'tenant' may have had in the context of the laws relating to English real property, it has been always understood, when used in relation to the land laws in force in the eastern part of the Indian subcontinent, in the restricted sense of being applicable only in case of agricultural holding. This contention of Mr. Khandker does not bear scrutiny, when the provisions of different legislations relating to land, which had been operative in this part of the country, are brought under examination. A tenant of agricultural holding has had a specific designation, namely, 'raiyat’ in India since the days of the Muslim rule. This is an Arabic word meaning tenant and this word and other connected words, viz 'korfa raiyat' or 'under raiyat’ have been invariably used in this country in all legislations relating to land to denote tenants of agricultural land while the general expression 'tenant’ has been used in such legislations in connection with lands of every description 'agricultural or non-agricultural'.

14. It is true that having regard to the historical and socio-political conditions of this country, the laws relating to the lease of agricultural and non-agricultural property have developed here differently. Because of the fact that at the advent of the East India Company in this country towards the middle of the 18th century, when the entire territory which came under their control was agrarian in its nature, the laws which were enacted regarding landlord and tenant were mainly in respect of agricultural lands and until 1882 it does not appear that there were any codified law relating to leases of non-agricultural land. As we have indicated above the tenancy laws connected with agricultural holding have developed stage by stage and the rights and liabilities of the lessors and the lessees of such holding have undergone changes with the changing pattern of the society. There have been charges also in the laws relating to the leases of non-agricultural lands with the increase in the pressure of population in the urban areas of the country.

15. It should be borne in mind that the earliest legislative measures, experimented by the East India Company in the eastern region of the Indian sub-continent, such as Permanent Settlement Regulation (Regulation No. 1 of 1973) or Patni Taluk Regulations (Regulation No. VIII of 1819), generally dealt with the interest of the Zamindars, including other holders of Estate, and Talukders and others tenure holders, and were not much concerned with the rights and conditions of the tenants of agricultural holdings who were the actual tillers of the soil. Nevertheless there has been some reference in these legislations as well to such tenants as have been generally referred therein as 'raiyats' and cultivators of soil.

16. In 1859 Rent Act (Central Act X of 1859) re-enacted, with certain modifications, the provisions of the existing law relating to the rights of the raiyats and this Act appears to be the earliest of the comprehensive tenancy legislations to safeguard the interests of the tenants of agricultural land. In the said Act the tenants of agricultural land have been referred mainly as 'raiyats' and in certain provisions they have been referred also as 'under tenants or raiyat'. The next important legislation was the Rent Act (Bengal Act VI of 1862) which was enacted to amend the law relating to the recovery of rent in the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal as contained in Rent Act of 1859. The next Act was also a Bengal Act being Landlord and Tenant Procedure Act (Act VIII of 1869) which was to amend the procedure in suits between the Landlord and Tenants. Although in the title of the Act the general term 'tenant' had been used, the 'tenant' contemplated in the said title was really the raiyat and he had been referred to as to such in the different provisions of the Act.

17. It is also interesting to notice that the settlement by which the right of a raiyat was created in agricultural land was also referred as 'lease' in section 2 of two of the above mentioned enactments, viz. Rent Act, 1859 and Landlords and Tenant Procedure Act, 1859 in identical language, as quoted below:—

''Every raiyat is entitled to receive from the person to whom the rent of the land held or cultivated by him is payable, a patta containing the following particulars:—

The quantity of land; and where fields have been numbered in a Govt. survey, the number of each filed; the amount of annual rent; the installments in which the same is to be paid; and every special conditions of the lease; if the rent is payable in kind the proportion of produce to be delivered and the time and manner of delivery."

18. In 1885, the Bengal Tenancy was enacted to amend and consolidate certain enactments relating to law of landlord and tenant within the territories under the administration of the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal, and by the said Act all those Acts referred to above, namely, Rent Act, 1859 (Central Act X of 1859), Rent Act, 1862 (Bengal Act VI of 1862) and the Landlord and Tenant Procedure Act, 1869 (Bengal Act VIII of 1869) were repealed. In the district of Sylhet, however, the said Acts remained in force until the enactment in 1936 of the Sylhet Tenancy Act-whereby the provisions similar to those in the Bengal Tenancy Act were brought into force in the said district, which was at that time a part of the province of Assam.

19. Although the Bengal Tenancy Act was stated in the preamble to be an amending and consolidating Act relating to landlord and tenant, the provisions of the Act were made applicable only to the case of lease-hold, interest in agricultural land only. The definitions of 'tenant' and 'landlord' as were given in section 3 of the Act were expressed in general terms and it does not appear that they were to be understood in the restricted sense of being applicable only to the holders of agricultural land. The definitions of landlord, rent and tenant as given in clauses (6), (13) and (17) of section 3 are quoted below:—

"3. (6) "landlord" means a person immediately under whom a tenant holds, and includes the Government.

(13) "rent" means whatever is lawfully payable or deliverable in money or kind by a tenant to his landlord on account of the use or occupation of the land held by the tenant..............."

(17) "tenant" means a person who holds land under another person and is, or but for a special contract would be liable to pay rent for that land to that person<u>* * * *</u>

20. These definitions are in very general language irrespective of the nature of the land in relation to which the said terms were defined. It may be mentioned that in 1929 a proviso was added by an amendment of the Act, to the definition of tenant in section 3 (17), by which a class of share-croppers of agricultural land was sought to be excluded from the category of tenant. This proviso did not in any way detract from the generality of the expressions of the main provision.

21. Section 4 of the Act, however, purports to confine the operation if the Act to the particular classes of tenants namely, tenants connected with agricultural holdings. The following provisions of the Act clearly indicate the scope of the operation of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Section 4:

"There shall be for the purpose of this Act, the following classes of tenants (namely):—

(1) tenure-holders, including under-tenure holders;

(2) raiyats, and

(3) under-raiyats, that is to say, tenants holding, whether immediately or mediately, under raiyats; * * Section 5 (1) "tenure-holder" means primarily a person who has acquired from a proprietor or from another tenure-holder a right to hold land for the purpose of collecting rents or bringing it under cultivation by establishing tenants on it, and includes also the successor in interest of persons who have acquired such a right;

(2) "Raiyat" means primarily a person who has acquired a right to hold land for the purpose of cultivating it by himself, or by members of his family or by servants or labourers or with the aid of partners, and includes also the successors in interest of persons who have acquired such a right.

22. It will thus appear that Mr. Khandker was not correct in his initial assumption on the basis of which he built up the subsequent part of his argument that in the Bengal Tenancy Act the terms "tenant” has been used in the sense of holder of agricultural land. The framers of the Act were very clear in their mind as to the general connotation of the term leant and, therefore, deliberately categorised the tenants connected with agricultural holding as tenure-holder, raiyat or under raiyat for the purpose of application of the provisions of the Act to them.

23. Before we deal with the subsequent development of the tenancy laws of the country we shall have to consider another law, namely The Transfer of Property Act which was enacted about 3 years before the enactment of the Bengal Tenancy Act and has some relevance to our present discussion. The Transfer of Property Act (Act IV of 1882) and the provision of Chapter V of the said Act comprising sections 105 to 117 dealing with leases of immovable property have some bearing upon the present question. In these provisions the term 'lease' and other connected terms have been statutorily defined and the rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee have also been clearly laid down. By section 117 of the Act, however, leases of agricultural land have been kept outside the purview of the provisions of this Chapter. But that does not modify or restrict the meaning of the general expressions as have been used in the said chapter. In this context, the provisions of section 105 of the Act, by which "lease" has been defined, section 106, which deals with duration of various leases, and section 117, by which leases of agricultural land have been kept outside the scope of the Act, may be referred to. Lease has been defined in section 105 of the Act in the following manner:—

"A lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property made for a certain time, express or imputed or in perpetuity in consideration of a price paid or promised or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specified occasions to the transferor by the transferee who accepts the transfer on such terms.

The transferor is called lessor, the transferee is called the lessee, the price is called the premium, and the money, share, service or other thing to be so rendered is called the rent."

24. This definition indicates that by a lease a subordinate interest is created by a person in favour of another person in respect of some immovable property on condition on payment of premium and/or rent. The fact that the nature of the immovable property, the subject matter of lease, has not been spe-cified indicates that it may be any kind of immovable property, agricultural or non-agricultural. It is true that in this definition section the transferor has not been termed as landlord nor the transferee has been named as tenant but that this relationship, as is created by lease, is the relationship of a landlord and tenant as is evident from the provisions of section 106 in which the manner of termination of various kinds of leases by service of notice at the instance of the lessor hat been prescribed, providing that the notice wilt be, subject to any contract to the contrary, 15 days or 6 months expiring with the end of a month or year of the tenancy as the case may be. This provision clearly indicates that the right which is created by the lease is the right of tenancy. Section 117 by which agricultural tenancy has been kept outside the purview of the Act Hat also been referred as "leases for agricultural purpose."

<u>25. From the aforesaid provision of the Act it is clear that the terms, 'lease' and 'tenancy' are cognate terms, implying the same kind of jural relationship. There appears to be absolutely no basis for imagining that 'lease' is a kind of relationship peculiar to non-agricultural land and that the terms 'tenancy' is a kind of expression which is exclusively applicable to only agricultural land.</u>

<u>26. It is the contention of Mr. Khandker that by the Indenture of lease a lease of some non-agricultural Govt. Khas land was granted to him by the Provincial Government in consequence whereof he became a lessee under the Government, the lessor, and that the description of his status as a tenant in the said Indenture was misconceived. In support of his contention, that a transaction of lease is to be distinguished from that of tenancy, Mr. Khandker has referred with a good deal of persistence to the definition clauses of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the Transfer of Property Act and have also cited certain decisions which, in our opinion, have rather demonstrated that the distinction between the said two terms, which Mr. Khandker has so strenuously tried to impress upon us, is without any difference. A lessee is, in its ordinary acception, no other then a tenant and the lessor, the landlord, and when such terms have been given any statutory definitions in any enactment they have not departed from meanings.</u>

27. The decisions which have been cited by Mr. Khandker also re-inforce the said proposition. Reference maybe made to the case of Kally Das Ahiri Vs. Man Mohon Das LLR. 24 Cal 440: I C.W.N. 321 where the question was whether the legal effect of a perpetual lease and a conveyance was similar and whether there could be, in such a lease, forfeiture of the lessee's right because of his denial of lessor's right. Jenkin, J, in delivering the judgment in the case, explained the nature of the transaction of a lease at page 447 of the Report in the following words:

"Because at the present day, a conveyance in fee simple leaves nothing in the grantor, it does not follow that a lease in perpetuity here has any such result. As a matter of fact, this effect of an English grant dates from the Statute of Westminster III, known as Quia Emptores, which, for reasons stated in the preamble, forbade the system of sub infeudation that upto that time had prevailed; for at common law a feeoffment made by A to B of a portion of the lands would create the relation of lord and tenant with all the incidents attaching to the relation including the right of forfeiture.

* * *

A man, who being owner of land grant? a lease in perpetuity, carves a sub-ordinate interest out of his own and does not annihilate his own interest. This result is to be inferred by the use of the word, 'lease' which implies an interest still remaining in the lessor. Before the lease the owner had the right to enjoy the possession of the land, and by the lease he excluded himself during its currency from the right, but the determination of the lease is a removal of that barrier and there is nothing to prevent the enjoyment from which he had been excluded by the leasse."

This view of Jenkins, J was approved by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Abhirain Goswami Vs. Shyama Charan Nandi, 36 IA 148; 36 Cal 1003; 14 CWN 1; Raja Kumar Thankur Vs. Mogblal Pandey, LR 44 IA 246; ILR 45 Cal 87; 22 CWN 201 and also Raghu Nath Roy Marwari Vs. Raja Durga Prasad Singh LR 46 IA 158; 23 CWN 914. The view expressed in these judicial authorities as to the characteristics of a lease is in conformity to the definition of the term as has been given in section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. In such a transaction the relationship which is created between the transferor and the transferee of certain immovable property in consideration of periodical payment of what is called rent is essentially that of landlord and tenant and this relationship of landlord and tenant arises independently of the nature of the immovable property, the subject matter of the lease.

<u>28. It is pertinent to mention that the provisions of Chapter V of the Transfer of Property Act, which reserve a large scope for settlement of terms by mutual agreement, were for a long time the only legal provisions regulating the rights and liabilities arising out of the leases other than for agricultural purposes. With the gradual change in the socio-economic conditions of the country, there was a consequent increase in the pressure of population in urban and other areas resulting in larger demand for land and houses for purposes other than agriculture. By the time the Second Great War broke out, the necessity for some legislations for regulating the leases of residential houses and non-agricultural land was felt and in consequence certain legislative measures were promulgated for control of rent of certain premises and non-agricultural land and for safeguarding the interests of the tenants of such premises and land. Since the partition of the country, these legislations have gradually taken more comprehensive shape. Now, the leases of premises for residential and non-residential purposes solely on payment of rent are controlled by the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and the Transfer of Property Act, 1892. So far as the leases of non-agricultural land were concerned, the ultimate specific legislation was the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, which was enacted "to make better provisions relating to the law of landlord and tenant of certain non-agricultural tenancies in East Bengal." Sub-section (2) of section 85 of the Act, however, excludes the non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government from the operation of the said Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.</u>

29. It should be noticed that the lessees of the premises, as contemplated in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, as well as the lessees of non-agricultural land, as have been dealt in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, have been defined as "tenants" for the purposes of the respective enactment. By such definition of the term in the said Ordinance and Act, it has been given a restricted meaning for the purposes of the said Ordinance and Act.

In 1951 a comprehensive legislation was promulgated in East Bengal, which is now Bangladesh, in the shape of The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

30. This Act may be divided into two main divisions in accordance with the subject matter dealt therein: (1) the first one containing parts II and IV of the Act relates to the acquisition of the interests of all rent-receivers and the lands in excess of the maximum limit set down by the Act and (2) the second one comprising part V, of the Act relates to the tenancy laws which are to be operative after the process of acquisition as provided in the earlier parts of the Act has been completed.

<u>31. The peculiar feature of the tenancy laws prevalent in this part of the country since the ancient days was a kind to successive sub-infeudation and creation of interests of various grades superimposed upon one and the same piece of land. The main object of the Act, as contained in parts II and IV, was to eliminate all those interests Intervening between the Government and the tenant in actual occupation of the land and to create, throughout the country, one class of tenants directly under the Government, which would be the sole receiver of rent payable by the tenants in respect of the lands comprised in their tenancy, and their rights and liabilities would be regulated by uniform Code of laws. The definition of tenant, as has been given in section 2 (27) of the Act, is in the same language as in the Bengal Tenancy Act and, by providing a definition of land in the Act, it has been made clear that the land comprised in his tenancy may be agricultural or non-agricultural. As we see, 'land' has been defined in section 2(16) of the Act as meaning land cultivated, uncultivated or covered with water at any time of the year and includes benefits to arise out of land, houses or building and all things attached, to the earth of permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth and this definition does not leave any room for doubt that the term "tenant" within the meaning of the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a generic expression of which tenant of agricultural holding is a species. This view is reinforced by the definition of "Khas land" or "land in Khas possession" as provided in clause (15) of section 2 of the Act which "includes any land let out together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity". That the scope of parts II and IV of the Act relating to acquisition of all rent-receiving interests is wide enough to include such interests connected with non-agricultural land as well as borne out also by the definition of rent-receiver, as provided in clause (23) of Section 2 of the Act which runs thus:</u>

<u>''rent-receiver" means a proprietor or a tenure-holder and includes a raiyat, an under-raiyat or a non-agricultural tenant whose land has been let out and also the immediate landlord of a person who holds any land free of rent in consideration of some service to be rendered, but does not include a person in respect of such of his lands, as has been let out, together with any buildings standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity."</u>

<u>32. The interests of the rent-receivers in respect of non-agricultural land also were to be acquired under the provisions of the said parts of the Act, and the non-agricultural tenants having lands in their khas possession within the meaning of clause (15) of section 2 of the Act would be tenants directly under the Government. The definitions of "rent-receiver" and ''khas Land" keep the interests of the landlords letting out land together with building and necessary adjuncts thereto otherwise than in perpetuity, outside the mischief of acquisition.</u>

<u>33. Part V of the Act incorporating the tenancy laws has come into force on different dates in different areas of the country on repeal of a number of enactments including The Bengal Tenancy Act and The Sylhet Tenancy Act in the respective areas and the rights and liabilities of the tenants which were formerly determined under the relevant repealed enactments are now regulated by the provisions of the said part of the Act. Most of the repealed enactments, no doubt, relate to the rights connected with agricultural land, but the scope of this new Act in respect of the class of tenants dealt therein is manifestly wider than those of the earlier legislations so repealed. This Act, unlike the Bengal Tenancy Actor the Sylhet Tenancy Act, is not confined in its application to the tenancies for agricultural or horticultural purposes only. Both of the main divisions of the Act, dealing with acquisition of superior interests and tenancy rights, as referred to above, purport to cover interests in all kinds or properties, agricultural or non-agricultural.</u>

<u>34. Mr. Khandker appears to have accepted the position that the assessee under the two taxing statutes for the purpose of levy of. Development and Relief Tax and Additional Development and Relief Tax are the tenants within the meaning of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but contends that such tenants, as contemplated in State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, are necessarily-tenants of agricultural holding and that the appellant does not belong to the said category. Mr. Khandker is undoubtedly correct in the first part of his contention that the assessee must necessarily be a tenant within the meaning of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. because the said Act was the existing general law dealing with the rights and liabilities of tenants at the time of the enactment of the two taxing statutes and the said statutes which purport to fasten a liability upon the tenants to be assessed to certain taxes do not lay down any special definition of tenant. It may also be noted in this connection that the proviso to Section 2(1) of the Finance Ordinance, 1958, in particular, which makes the principles laid down in Section 26 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act applicable for the assessment of rent-free land of a tenant for the purpose of levy of the tax imposed by the said Ordinance makes it abundantly clear that the tenant contemplated in the Ordinance is no other than the tenant within the meaning of the said Act. The second part of the contention of the appellant seeking to exclude himself from the said category, however, appears to have no reasonable basis.</u>

<u>35. Now, the definition of tenant, as has been given in section 2(27) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act/is in the same language as in the definition of tenant in the Bengal Tenancy Act, which, as we have already noticed, is a kind of general definition without specifying the nature of the land held by such a tenant, agricultural or non-agricultural. If the provisions of the Act are carefully examined, it will be seen that the terms, "tenant" and "raiyat" have been used in the Act for distinct purposes, the former implying the holder of any kind of land and the latter implying the holder of agricultural land only.</u>

36. A bare reading will show that some of the provisions of part V are applicable only to the case of a tenant of an agricultural holding, whereas the other provisions are applicable to the cases of tenants, irrespective of the nature of their holding. The provisions sections 81 and 81(A) of the Act which are quoted below will clearly elucidate the position:

"81. On and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this part in any area, there shall, within that area, be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely; maliks and the rights and liabilities of every such land holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this part:

Provided that nothing in this section shall confer on any such malik any right to any interest in the sub-soil including rights to minerals in his holding:

Provided further that when the Provincial Government lease out any land for any particular period, the rights and liabilities of such a lessee shall be governed by such terms and conditions as may be set forth in the lease."

"81A. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this part, the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under Provincial Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act.

(2). The rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants shall-except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882:

Provided that, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non agricultural tenant shall sublet the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms and conditions whatsoever and, if any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sublet in contravention of this provision, the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Provincial Government from the date of such sub-letting free from all encumbrances."

<u>37. In section 82, clauses (1) and (2) new definitions of 'bona fide-cultivator' and 'raiyat' have been given for the purposes of the tenancy part of the Act and it has been provided in clause (8) of the said section that the word ‘malik’ should be deemed to have been subs-muted for the word 'raiyat' or 'tenant', wherever they occur in part V in relation to agricultural land. The provisions which have been quoted above clearly contemplate two categories of holders of land, one in case of a lease for agricultural purposes and the other is a general expression without such limitation as to the nature of land. When the Act itself envisages a tenant of a holding without any limitation as to its nature and a raiyat meaning thereby a tenant of agricultural holding, there seems to be no valid reason for taking the view that the tenant as has been mentioned in the taxing statutes under consideration shall be deemed to refer to only tenants of an agricultural holding.</u>

<u>38. After part V of the Act has come into force, all raiyats, that is, tenants of agricultural land, have been styled as maliks and their rights and liabilities are regulated, as has been provided in section 81 of the Act, by the provisions of part V of the Act subject to the condition that in case of a lease of any land by the Government for a particular period the rights and liabilities of such a lease to be governed by the terms of the lease. The position of the tenants of non-agricultural lands under the Government has been dealt with in section 81A of the Act, as has been quoted above. According to the said section such tenants have been divided into two categories, namely, (1) those who have become tenants under the Government because of the acquisition of the superior interest of their landlords by the government under the Act and were governed by the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act at the time of the acquisition of the superior rights over the said land, and (2) other non-agricultural tenants. The rights and liabilities of the tenants of the first category would be regulated by the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and those of the second category would be controlled by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act except in the matters relating to determination, enhancement or reduction of rent or sub-letting, which would necessarily be governed by the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

39. It is necessary to refer at this stage to the definition of "non-agricultural tenant" as has been provided in section 2 (17) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which is as follows:

"2.(17) 'non-agricultural tenant' means a tenant who holds land for purposes not connected with agricultural or horticultural but does not include a person holding land together with any building standing thereon with any necessary adjuncts thereto under a lease other than a lease in perpetuity."

<u>40. Learned Judges of the High Court appear to have made some confusion in interpreting the said definition clause and in holding the appellant to be a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of that clause on the view that he was a holder of a lease in perpetuity. The appellant is obviously not a holder of a lease in perpetuity, as the preamble of the Indenture of the lease clearly provides that it is a lease for the specified period of 99 years. Term no 23 (3) (a) of the Indenture does no doubt reserve the right of option for the lessee for the renewal of the lease after the expiry of the specified period of 99 years and in case of exercise of such option the lessor shall have to renew the lease but on such terms, covenants and conditions and for such period as the lessor may determine. There is no doubt that this is not a lease in perpetuity but is one for a fixed period, though a lease in perpetuity is unlike in England, sanctioned under the law of the country, as provided in section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. Although there seems to have been some misapprehension in the said observation of the learned Judges of the High Court in respect of the meaning of non-agricultural tenant, their conclusion that the appellant is a non-agricultural tenant cannot be taken exception to in view of the fact that he having held lands for purposes other than agriculture or horticulture comes under the first part of the said definition clause and being the owner of the buildings standing on such land does not come under the second part of the said clause. According to the said definition, a person who is a tenant in respect of the land as well as the building standing thereon on the basis of a lease which is not perpetual is not a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of the said definition clause and he may be a tenant coming within the purview of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. According to the definition clause quoted above, only such a person will be a non-agricultural tenant as has constructed the building, if any, in his own right on the land leased out to him by the owner of such land. It is, therefore, abundantly clear that the appellant is a tenant as well as a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of sub-section (2) of section 81A of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and his rights and liabilities are, according to the said provision, to be governed by the terms of the Indenture of his lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act except in regard to his powers of sub-letting and in matters relating to determination, enhancement and reduction of rent, which shall be regulated according to the provisions, of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, notwithstanding anything contrary thereto in the terms of the lease or elsewhere. There is, therefore, no difficulty in holding that the learned Judges of the High Court were correct in taking the view that the appellant is assessee under the provisions of the two taxing Statutes as have been referred to above.</u>

41. The next question is with regard to the applicability of the provision of Article 59 of the Basic Democracies Order, 1959 to the appellant. The said article reads as follows:

''59. Local rate.- (1) All lands assessable to rent or land revenue shall be subject to the payment of a rate to be known as the local rate.

(2) The local rate in each District shall bear such proportion to the rent or land revenue in the District as the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, from time to time fix:

Provided that the local rate shall not exceed fifty percentum of the rent or land revenue as the case may be.

(3) The local rate shall be collected in the prescribed manner along with the rent or land revenue by the village revenue officials responsible for its collection and the proceeds thereof shall be credited to the local firms of the District Council and the Union Councils in the District in such proportion as may be fixed by the Government from time to time."

<u>42. Rent has been defined in Article 3(37) of the Basic Democracies Order in the following words:</u>

<u>"3. (37) 'rent' means whatever is by law payable in money or kind by a tenant or lessee to the Government on account of the occupation or use of any land in East Pakistan held by the tenant or lessee."</u>

<u>According to article 59, as quoted above, the local rate is to be imposed on all lands which are assessable to rent or land revenue and from the definition of rent, which also has been set out above, it is clear that all kinds of lands lying in East Pakistan, which is now Bangladesh, as held by the tenant or lessee, may be assessable to rent. There is hardly any scope for doubt that the lease-hold land held by the appellant under the Government by virtue of the Indenture of lease, whether as a tenant or a lessee, is assessable to rent and as such, such land is also amenable to the levy of the local rate as contemplated in Article 59 of the order.</u>

<u>43. Mr. Khandker has contended, despite the clear words of the articles considered above, that the provisions of the Basic Democracies Order, 1959 are applicable only to the lands administered by the Union Council and are outside the jurisdiction of the Municipal Administration. Having regard to the provisions of the said order, we do not think that this contention of Mr. Khandker has any substance. The Basic Democracies Order, 1959 purported to cover the entire area of the then Pakistan including the whole of the territory which is now Bangladesh. The question of applicability of the provisions of this Order to the Municipal areas was considered by the Appellate Division in the case of M/S. Amin Jute Mills Ltd. Vs. Bangladesh and another in 29 DLR, (SC) 85 and it has been held at page 96 of the Report:</u>

<u>"The object of this Order was to provide for the constitution of basic democratic institutions and to consolidate and amend certain laws relating to local government. Under this Order, basic democratic institutions were set up throughout the country, in municipal as well as in non-municipal areas. But at that time the function of local Government was given to such institutions as were newly constituted in the villages only, which replaced the Union Boards and came to be known as Union Councils. In municipal areas, these institutions came to be known as Town Committees or Union Committees but they did not replace the already existing Municipal bodies, which now co-existed with the, said basic democratic committees after the said order has come into force. According to Article 31 such Committees had to perform functions relating to national reconstruction, social uplift etc. In addition to those which were specifically assigned to them. Municipal bodies or Cantonment Boards also could delegate some of their functions to these Committees."</u>

<u>Further observations in this regard have been made at pages 99-100 of the Report:</u>

<u>"It is no doubt true that the Basic Democracies Order covered the entire area of Pakistan, but we have already pointed out that it repealed the village self-Government Acts but did not repeal the Municipal Acts, with the result that the self-Governing institutions functioning in the village outside the Municipal and Cantonment areas were completely supplanted by the Basic Democratic institutions, namely, Union Councils in the villages. But in areas within the limits of a Municipality or Cantonment, the relevant Municipal body or Cantonment Board continued to function along side with the Union or Town Committee which was a newly created basic democratic institution under the Order. Their functions being different and complementary, as it appears from Article 31 of the Order, there appears to have been little conflict between them or between the provisions of the respective enactments so as to invite the operation of Article 6 of the Order <u>* * * *</u></u>

<u>* * * *</u>

<u>It is clear that so far as municipal areas were concerned, the underlying concept of the Basic Democracies Order was a kind of harmonions operation of its provisions along with those of the relevant Municipal law and the Order does not appear to have introduced any conflict between them."</u>

<u>44. The provision of clause (1) of Article 59 of the Order is sufficiently clear to indicate that all lands assessable to rent shall be subject to the payment of local rate, and the lands within municipal areas are certainly assessable to rent as has been defined in clause (37) of article 3 of the Order. Clause (2) of article 59 prescribes that the local rate shall bear a certain proportion to the rent in each district, which shall, subject to the maximum of fifty percentum, be fixed by the Government. There is nothing in this clause as well, which may suggest that such a rate is leviable only within the jurisdiction of a Union Council. In clause (3) of the article there is no doubt the provision to the effect that the local rate shall be collected along with rent or land revenue by the village revenue officials responsible for the collection and the Local Rate (Assessment, Collection and Distribution) Rules, 1960 framed under clause (2) of article 19 of the Basic Democracies Order is primarily concerned with the collection of local rate within the limits of Union Councils but having regard to the provisions of article 59 as a whole, it is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Khandker that such rate shall be collected only from the rural areas. It will appear that the proceeds of the collection shall have to be credited to the local funds of the District Council and the Union Council in the district in such proportion as may be fixed by the Government from time to time. The amount of the local rate collected from areas outside the jurisdiction of the Union Councils and a proportion of the local rate collected within the Union Councils are necessarily to be credited to the local fund of the District Council for the purpose of discharging the functions of the District Council as enumerated in the Fourth Schedule to the Order, which may involve works within municipal areas also. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the learned Judges of the High Court were correct in their view in respect of the liability of the appellant regarding payment of the local rate as well.</u>

<u>45. There appears to be, however, one irregularity in respect of the demand under challenge. It is to be noticed that the method of payment of rent as has been settled in the a terms of the Indenture of lease is by two half yearly installments payable according to English Calendar year but according to the rules; framed read with section 135 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, rent is payable, according to the Bengali Calendar year. Having regard to the provision of section 81 A, which has been already considered and section 135, which also protects the terms of agreement as contained in the Indenture, the appellant's liability to pay according to the English Calendar year has not been affected. From the provisions of the East Pakistan Ordinance No.LXXXII of 1958 and the East Pakistan Finance Act, 1967 it is clear that the taxes under the said two enactments were to be levied and collected with effect from the first day of the Bengali year whereas the local rate under Article 59 of the Basic Democracies Order is to collected along with the rent of the land, which is payable by the appellant in accordance with the terms of the lease, according to English Calendar Year. The break up of the demand as stated by the respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition shows that annual rent payable by the appellant was split up, for the purpose of showing his liability from the beginning of the Bengali Year. This being contrary to the terms of the Indenture of lease is not permissible. The annual rent as well as the local rate, so far as the appellant is concerned are to be collected according to the English Calendar year. The demand of the annual rent and local rate contrary to the said time schedule was not therefore lawful.</u>

The result, therefore, is that subject to the observation made above, the appeal is dismissed. There shall, however, be no order as to costs.

End.
