full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury, J.: This is a petition by Khapan Bittahin Co-operative Society Limited for review of the judgment and order dated 7.5.91 passed by this Court making the Rule absolute in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990.

2. The case of the petitioner (respondent No. 4 in the said Writ Petition) is as follows:

The review petitioner was granted settlement of Sarai Beel Fishery for 1397 BS to 1399 BS at the rent of Tk. 4,200.00 per year by an order dated 19.6.90 passed by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer. Balaganj Upazila, Sylhet, and a lease deed was executed in its favour on 25.6.90 (Annexure-A to the petition). It was given delivery of the fishery on 30.6.90 vide writ of delivery of possession dated 30.6.90 by the Upazila Fishery Officer, Balaganj, on receipt of rent (Annexures-B and C respectively). The review petitioner undertook development as per approved scheme dated 17.6.90 of the Government and invested large sums of money. A copy of the scheme is annexed as Annexure-D.

3. While in possession of the fishery the review petitioner was served with a notice of summons of Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Balaganj, Sylhet filed by Nijkurua Matsyajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd. Respondent No. 1 of this review petition as plaintiff against the Government and review petitioner challenging the grant of lease in favour of their petitioner society by the order dated 19.6.90. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff also filed a petition for temporary injunction and the petitioner appeared in the suit and prayed for time to file written statement and the Assistant Judge on consideration of the plaint came to a finding that the plaintiff had failed to make out any case about his subsisting interest after 1396 BS in the suit fishery and there being no cause of action rejected the plaint by his judgment and order dated 31.10.90. A photocopy of the certified copy of the said order dated 31.10.90 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure- 'E'.

4. After respondent No. I's plaint was rejected in the said Title Suit, the respondent filed Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 before this Court and swore affidavit on 22.11.90. The respondent No. 1 obtained a Rule on 26.11.90 directing the proforma defendants and this petitioner why the said order dated 18.6.90 and 19.6.90 passed by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer annexed to the writ petition as Annexures-T and ''J'' respectively should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. A copy of the Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 with annexures is annexed to this petition and marked as Annexure - 'F'.

5. In paragraph 18 of the said writ petition the respondent No. 1 as petitioner had stated that on 31.10.90 its prayer for temporary injunction in the said Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 which was then pending, but as a matter of fact the respondent No. 1 in the writ petition completely suppressed the fact that on 31.10.90 the plaint of the said Title Suit was rejected by the civil Court and the suit was not pending on 22.11.90 when the affidavit in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 was sworn for respondent No. 1 on 26.11.90 when the Rule in the writ petition was obtained, and thereby the respondent played fraud on this Court and obtained the said Rule. After obtaining the Rule, the respondent No.1 preferred Title Appeal No. 1 of 1991 before the District Judge, Sylhet against the judgment and order dated 31.10.90 passed by the Court of Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 and afterwards filed an application on 28.4.91 stating that he did not want to proceed with the appeal and accordingly the District Judge dismissed the appeal for non-prosecution by his order dated 28.4.91. The information slip No. 65 dated 18.5.91 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-'G'.

6. The petitioner has stated that although it was made respondent No.4 in the said writ petition and notice was served, upon it, its local lawyer advised that since the government was the main respondent in the writ, the government would take necessary steps on behalf of its lessee, that is the review petitioner, and further since there was a decree of the civil Court in Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 rejecting the plaint there was no chance of any order being passed that would prejudice the petitioner and as such in good faith took no steps in the said writ petition. But the Government as proforma respondent took no step in the matter and the Rule was made absolute ex parte. The petitioner came to learn from Respondent No.1 on 5.6.91 that the Rule was made absolute and obtained a certified copy of the judgment and order dated 7.5.91 in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 and being aggrieved by the said judgment and order passed by this Bench, the petitioner Co-operative Society has filed this review petition.

7. An affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of Nijkurua Matsyajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd., Respondent No. 1 that is the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 has been filed stating, inter alia, that the grant of Sarai Beel Fishery for 1397 BS to 1399 BS in favour of the petitioner was illegal and without jurisdiction as the government had already leased out the said fishery in favour of the respondent No. 1 for a period of 6 years from 1394 BS to 1396 BS and from 1397 BS to 1399 BS under a development scheme and a lease deed was executed between the government and the respondent on 9.12.87. The respondent's right to continue as lessee upto 1399 BS could not be arbitrarily taken away as it had spent large sums of money in the development of the fishery.

8. The respondent No. 1 in its affidavit-in- opposition has not denied that as plaintiff it had filed the said Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 against the government and the petitioner society, challenging both the order dated 18.6.90 passed by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Balaganj whereby its lease of the fishery was cancelled and the order dated 19.6.90 passed by the same officer granting lease in favour of the petitioner. The respondent also does not deny having filed a petition for temporary injunction and that the petitioner appeared in the suit and prayed for time and that the Assistant Judge on consideration of the plaint came to a finding that the plaintiff (Respondent No.1) failed to make out any case about its subsisting interest after 1396 BS in the suit fishery and there was no cause of action of the suit and accordingly rejected the plaint by his judgment and order dated 31.10.90 but the respondent, has stated that the Assistant Judge by the said order dated 31.10.90 allowed time to the petitioner for filing written statement on 27.11.90 and while disposing of the application for temporary injunction filed by the respondent No. 1 in the suit suo motu rejected the plaint of the suit as he did not find any cause of action, but, on the other hand, allowed time to the petitioner for filing written statement fixing 27.11.90. The respondent No. 1 also has not denied the statement made by the review petitioner in paragraph 7 of this petition that respondent No. 1 having failed to establish its title to the suit fishery for the period after the expiry of 1396 BS and in not getting the said orders dated 18.6.90 and 19.6.90 passed by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Balaganj as illegal and without authority by the civil Court, it had filed the Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 before this Court and obtained this Rule on 26.11.90 directing the petitioner and the proforma respondents why the orders dated 8.6.90 and 19.6.90 annexed to the writ petition as Annexures-'I' and 'L', but has stated that it was compelled to file the writ petition, and bonafide thought that the order of the learned Assistant Judge dated 31.10.90 rejecting the plaint being an improper and erroneous order, it would be "cured before the learned Assistant Judge by filing an application" and that is why the respondent No. 1 in the writ petition undertook that it would not proceed with Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 and accordingly filed an application before the Assistant Judge on 28.11.90 for setting aside the order dated 31.10.90 on review but the learned Assistant Judge by his order dated 28.11.90 rejected the application. The respondent has also not denied that it withdrew Title Appeal No.1 of 1991 before the District Judge, Sylhet against the order dated 31.10.90 passed by the Assistant Judge which was dismissed for non-prosecution. However the respondent has submitted that the petitioner which was respondent No.4 in the writ petition in spite of receiving the notice of the Rule and also the notice of injunction granted by this Court not to catch fish, sat idle and did not appear, and thereby gave up the right to controvert the statement in the writ petition and to contest the Rule. The petitioner was therefore estopped and barred in law from raising any objection by way of a Review.

9. We have heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the respondent No. 1 who have argued and made submissions on their respective stands taken in the petition and the affidavit-in-opposition.

10. Mr. Subrata Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1, has raised the preliminary objection that in writ jurisdiction there is no power of this Court to review a decision once given. He contends that as orders were passed on 7.5.91, this Court is functus officio and cannot change them on any ground whatsoever. He further submits that as the petitioner did not appear to contest the Rule and controvert the facts stated in the writ petition, he cannot now come with the application for review of the orders passed by this Court. He has also submitted that the petition is barred by limitation.

<u>11. The right to claim review of any decision of a Court of law, like the right to appeal, is a substantive right and not a mere matter of procedure, and as such, neither of them is available unless it has been conferred by law. Under Article 105 of the Constitution of Bangladesh the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to review its judgment and orders. There is no corresponding provision in the Constitution with regard to High Court Division's jurisdiction to review its decision. However, section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure confers jurisdiction on the Courts of Civil Judicature to review judgments pronounced by them, and Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code prescribes the grounds on which such review can be claimed apart from the Court's limited inherent power of review, this is the only legal provision which confers power of review on civil Courts, that is, Courts of civil jurisdiction. There appears to be no rule, making the provisions of section 114 of the Code inapplicable to the High Court Division in the exercise of its Original Civil jurisdiction. The Code envisages exercise of two kinds of jurisdiction by the High Court Division, namely Civil Appellate jurisdiction and original civil jurisdiction. Hence; the power of review under section 114 of the Code is available to .the High Court in the exercise of these jurisdictions. The writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution is an original jurisdiction. The question then arises as to whether the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure other than the provisions expressly excepted shall apply in the exercise of the writ jurisdiction by the High Court under the said Article.</u>

<u>12. This question was exhaustively dealt with by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Hussain Bakhsh Vs. Settlement Commissioner Rawalpindi reported in 1970 PLD (SC) 1. When the question was whether the High Court had power to review an order made by it in exercise of its power under Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan (1962), the Supreme Court held that apart from the High Court's power to .correct errors apparent on the face of the record in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction, the High Court has power under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to review its own order made in writ jurisdiction in a civil matter. A proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution concerning a civil matter being a civil proceeding relating to the High Court's original civil jurisdiction and section 114 of the Code conferring power of review not having been made inapplicable to the High Court in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction, the power to review an order made by the High Court in its writ jurisdiction will be available to it Under the said section 114. The Civil Procedure Code regulates civil proceedings. The nature of the proceeding does not necessarily depend on the nature of the jurisdiction of the Court invoked In order to determine whether a proceeding is a civil proceeding or not, it is necessary to see what are the questions raised and decided in the proceeding. If the proceeding involves the assertion or enforcement of a civil right, it is a civil proceeding. The provisions of the Code, other than the specially excepted ories, shall apply in the exercise of the High Court's jurisdiction in a civil matter, whatever may be the nature of that jurisdiction [Sabitri Takurani Vs. Savi 1921 AIR (PC) 80 ref:]. In this connection section 141 CPC and the decisions in the cases of Thakur Prasad Vs. Fakirulla, LLR 17 Allahabad 106 and Neeralil Tea Estate Vs. Govt. 41 DLR 90 may be seen. 'Civil proceeding' is a process for recovery of individual right or redress of individual wrong, inclusive, in its proper legal sense, of suits by the Crown. Whether a proceeding is civil or not depends on the nature of subject-matter of the proceeding and its object, and not on the mode adopted or the forum provided for the enforcement of the right. A proceeding which deals with a right of a civil nature does not cease to be so merely because the right is sought to be enforced by having recourse to the writ jurisdiction. Judged from these aspects, it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that a proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution relating to a civil matter is a civil proceeding, although the High Court's jurisdiction in such a proceeding is constitutional jurisdiction of an original kind. A civil proceeding in a Court of Civil jurisdiction is governed by the provisions of the Code other than the provisions which are specially excepted 1970(PW) (SC) 1.</u>

13. Section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads.as follows:

"Subject as aforesaid, any person considering himself aggrieved-

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal has been preferred,

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed by this Code, or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order, and the Court may make such order thereon as it thinks fit."

14. In dealing with the submissions made by the counsel for the respondent No. 2 in Hussain Bakhsh's case that an order made by the High Court in the exercise of writ jurisdiction does not come under any of the clauses (a), (b) and (c) of section 114 of the Code, the power of review under that section is not available to the High Court, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held:

"Clause (a) applies in a case where the decree or order sought to be reviewed is one from which an appeal is allowed by the Code itself. Since the commencement of the 1962- Constitution, an appeal from the judgment, decree or order of a High Court in a civil matter is competent only in the circumstances mentioned in Article 58 thereof, and not otherwise, Hence, clause (a) is no mere applicable to a decree or order made by the High Court. It then remains to be seen if an order of a High Court made in its writ jurisdiction in a civil matter is liable to be reviewed under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code. The power to issue certain prerogative writs was conferred on the High Courts, first section 223-A of the Government of India Act, 1935. Later on, the same power was successively available to the High Courts under Article 170 of the 1956- Constitution and the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958. For so long as the Government of India Act, 1935 was in operation, appeals from the High Courts' decisions in civil matters including orders made in writ jurisdiction were governed by the provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure. After the coming into force of the 1956-Constitution, such appeals came to be governed by both the Article 158 of that Constitution and the provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the Code. Although the said Article 158 substantially adopted the provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the Code, those sections were not rendered inoperative inasmuch as appeals from the High Court's decisions in civil matters including orders made in writ jurisdiction were competent on the grant of certificates of fitness by the High Courts under clause (c) of section 109 of the Code. Thus the Code allowed such appeals until the commencement of the 1962 Constitution. With the coming into force of the said Constitution, sections 109 and 110 of the Code became completely inoperative because of provisions of Article 58 of that Constitution according to which civil appeals including appeals from orders made in writ jurisdiction in civil matters are competent only in the circumstances mentioned in that Article. The result, therefore, is that such appeals which were hitherto competent under sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure are no more allowed by the Code. That being so, the requirement of clause (b) of section 114 of the Code is satisfied in the case of an Order made by a High Court in its writ jurisdiction in a civil matter. A review of such an order is therefore competent under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If this view be not correct, then the High Court will be completely bereft of the power of review even in respect of a decree or order made under the provisions of the Code for the simple reason that, for the purpose of appeal, such a decree or order and an order made by a High Court in its writ jurisdiction in a civil matter, in view of Article 58 of the Constitution, stand exactly on the same footing. Thus, any view contrary to the view held as above will give rise to an absurd situation. The view taken by me as regards power of review also finds support from the dictum laid down by the House of Lords in the case of National Telephone Company Ltd. Vs. Postmaster- General (1). The dictum laid down in that case, in the words of Viscount Haldane, is as follows:

"When a question is stated to be referred to an established Court without more, it, in my opinion, imports that the ordinary incidents of the procedure of that Court are to attach, and also that any general right to appeal from its decisions likewise attaches."

As the High Court has been found to have power under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure to review an order made in its writ jurisdiction in a civil matter, the appeal succeeds. I would, therefore, allow this appeal, set aside the judgment and order of the High Court and declare that, apart from the High Court's power to correct errors apparent on the face of the record in the exercise of its inherent jurisdiction, it has power under the Code of Civil Procedure to review its own order made in writ jurisdiction in a civil matter. The High Court will now hear the application for review according to law."

15. Article 103 of the Constitution of Bangladesh reads thus:

"103(1). The Appellate Division shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals from judgments, decrees, orders or sentences of the High Court Division.

(2) An appeal to the Appellate Division from a judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division shall lie as of right where the High Court Division-

(a) certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this constitution; or

(b) has sentenced a person to death or to transportation for life; or

(c) has imposed punishment on a person for contempt of that division;

and in such other cases as may be provided for by Act of Parliament.

(3) An appeal to the Appellate Division from a judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division in a case to which clause (2) does not apply shall lie only if the Appellate Division grants leave to appeal".

16. With these provisions of Article 103 in the Constitution according to which civil appeals including orders made in writ jurisdiction in civil matter are competent are only in the circumstances mentioned in that Article, as such appeals under sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure are no more allowed by the Code in respect to appeals from the High Court Division to the Appellate Division. That being the position, the requirement of clause (b) of section 114 of the Code is satisfied in the case of an order made by the High Court Division in its writ jurisdiction in a civil matter. A review of such an order is, therefore, available under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

17. On the question of limitation, we find that it has been stated by the petitioner that he came to know of the judgment dated 7.5.91 in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 when he came to Dhaka on 6.6.91 and obtained a certified copy on the same day. It was then that he found that respondent No. 1 by suppressing material facts and practising fraud upon this Court he got the Rule made absolute. Accordingly he filed this review petition and swore affidavit on 9.6.91 that is 3 days after he found that fraud had been committed on the Court.

<u>18. If fraud is proved, then there is no question, of limitation and it will run from the date when fraud was detected. This view was held by the Appellate Division in the case of Abul Khair Mia Vs. Abdul Latif Sardar reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167. Relianee may be placed on the cases of Abdul Rou] Vs. Abdul Hamid Khan 17 DLR (SC) 515=1965 PLD (SC) 671 and Sailur Rahman Vs. Haider Shah, 19 DLR (SC) 433, In the instant case the petitioner had discovered on 6.6.91 that fraud had been committed on this Court and filed his review petition on 9.6.91 that is, three days after the discovery of fraud. Therefore there has been no delay in filing the review petition and is not barred by limitation. Turning to the question of suppression of facts by respondent No. 1 it appears from Annexure 'F' to the Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 that the affidavit to the writ petition was sworn on behalf of respondent No. 1 that is the petitioner of the writ petition on 22.11.90 and a Rule Nisi was issued on 26.11.90. It is admitted that the respondent No. 1 as plaintiff had filed the Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 before the Assistant Judge, Balagunj challenging the order under Memo. No. Matsya/ Bala/125/1(2) dated 18.6.90 passed by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Balaganj cancelling the lease of the respondent No. 1 and the order of lease granted in favour of the petitioner by the said Upazila Nirbahi Officer under Memo No. 1 Matsya Bala/84/ 90/ 127/ 1(2) dated 19.6.90 in respect of Sarai Beel Jalmahal which were impugned by the respondent No.1 in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 as, Annexures-'I' and 'L' respectively. It is also admitted that the Assistant Judge by his order dated 31.10.90 rejected the plaint of respondent No. 1 in Title Suit No. 12 of 1990 on the ground that there was no cause of action, and the said respondent in its affidavit-in-opposition has not stated that it had no knowledge of the order of the Assistant Judge and therefore had full knowledge of the said order dated 31.10.90 rejecting the plaint when the affidavit of the writ petition was sworn on 22.11.90 and on 26.11.90 when the Rule Nisi was obtained. This deliberate suppression of material fact of the rejection of plaint by the civil Court and the false statement to the effect that the suit was pending and that the suit would be withdrawn by the respondent, is a fraud committed on this Court by the respondent No. 1. It further appears that after suppressing the fact of rejection of the plaint by the Assistant Judge and obtaining a Rule Nisi from this Court, the respondent No. 1 filed a review petition before the said Assistant Judge for review of his order dated 31.10.90 which -was rejected by the Assistant Judge on 28.11.90, and against that order the respondent filed Title Appeal No.1 of 1991 before the District Judge, Sylhet, All these facts were also suppressed after obtaining the Rule Nisi, and thereby the respondent continued to deceive and mislead this Court. The contention of the respondent that the order dated 31.10.90 passed by the Assistant Judge was improper and erroneous and "would be cured before the learned Assistant Judge by filing an application" was not followed up until the Rule Nisi and injunction order was obtained from this Court. The respondent by suppressing facts was obviously seeking remedy simultaneously in two forums for the same cause of action which it cannot do under law. The judgment pronounced by this Court is normally final and should not be readily disturbed or interfered with by way of review. This Court would be most hesitant to review its judgment when such application is made by a defaulting respondent who failed to appear and controvert the facts stated by the petitioners in the writ petition, but where fraud is alleged to have been committed upon this Court the Court has a duty to review as fraud vitiates all proceedings. In the case of Grindlays Bank Limited Vs. Murree Brewery Company Limited reported in 8 PLR (Lahore) III it was held by a judgment delivered by Muhammad Munir CJ, as he then was, that a judgment or an order, however high or independent the tribunal delivering or making it and however exclusive its jurisdiction, is a nullity if it be proved that it was obtained by fraud. It was further held that a lower Court in a suit properly constituted, is certainly competent to set aside a judgment of a higher tribunal if it be proved that such judgment was obtained by fraud; it must a fortiori follow that a Judge of the High Court, sitting singly, has jurisdiction under section 151, Code of Civil Procedure, to vacate an order passed by a Division Bench, of which he was one member, provided the issue whether the order was obtained by fraud, properly comes up before him. In appropriate cases, it is the duty of the Court that has seisin of the case to recall suo motu an order procured by fraud.</u>

19. In Najmul Huq Vs. Panchanan Poddar reported in 21 DLR (Dac) 78 it was held that a fraudulent contrivance was enough to make an auction purchase invalid. If the auction sale is brought about by fraudulent contrivance on the part of decree holder, then it cannot be said that the auction-purchaser, even though he is not involved in the fraud itself, should be allowed 10 be protected.

20. Since fraud vitiates all proceedings it has been held that even contravention of law is no ground for allowing an order obtained by fraud, to stand. In the case of Muhammad ldtis Khan Vs. Haji Erfanuddin reported in 9 DLR 601 it was held that the fact that an application for review of an ex parte order granting the landlord permission to sue the tenant for eviction was made beyond 30 days from the date of the order or that in contravention of the provision of section 29(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act the application was made to a Rent Controller other than the one who passed the order will not make any difference where the order has been fraudulently obtained from the Court by suppressing summons and in such a case the Rent Controller has inherent jurisdiction to set aside such order and restore the case to file.

<u>21. In the case of Abul Khair Mia Vs. Abdul Latif Sarder reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167 it was held by the Appellate Division that a decree obtained by fraud is a nullity in the eye of law and it must be set aside.</u>

22. From the review of these authorities it is clear that if this Court is misled into passing certain order by suppressing material facts which constitute fraud on this Court, then this Court is entitled to review its own judgment and order and set aside any order passed on a fraudulent and false representation.

23. Therefore, the submission by the respondent No. 1 that the petitioner did not avail of the opportunity to appear and point out the fraud at the time when the Rule was taken up for hearing, cannot be a ground to reject the petition as that would be overlooking the fraud committed by the respondent on this Court, and in no circumstances a party should feel encouraged or be allowed to commit such fraud.

24. We find that the whole proceeding of the Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 is vitiated by fraud by suppressing the order of rejection of plaint by the Assistant Judge, Balaganj in Title Suit No. 12 of 1990.

In the above circumstances and in the light of our discussion this, review petition is allowed. The judgment and order dated 7.5.91 passed by this Bench in Writ Petition No. 2551 of 1990 is set aside and consequently the Rule in the said Writ Petition is discharged. There is no order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for special leave to Appeal No. 160 of 1977.
lawyer:
K.A. Bakr, Sr. Advocate, with Serajuddin Ahmed, Advocate, instructed by B.C. Panday, Advocate-on-Record. ------- For the petitioner. 
Not represented ------- Respondents.
parties:
Ambia Khatun and anr. ------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Syed Altaf Hossain and another  ------- Respondents.
case_source: From the Judgment dated 31st August, 1976 passed by the High Court in S.A. No. 1126 of 1962.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This petition for special leave to appeal is against a judgment of a Single Judge of the High Court, dismissing a Second Appeal, arising out of a suit for specific performance of contract brought by the petitioners as plaintiffs.

2. The petitioners alleged in the said suit that there was a contract for sale between them and Respondent No. 1 for a consideration of Tk. 7055/-, whereby the said Respondent agreed to execute a deed of permanent lease in respect of certain property in part of which the petitioners were put into possession. The suit was contested by the respondents on the contention that there was a lease of 1/3rd share of the property only but there had been no final contract with regard to the rest of the property.

3. The Trial Court found that there had been no contract for lease of the entire premises as alleged in the plaint but that there had been a contract for lease of a portion of the building which had been duly implemented. The plaintiff's suit was dismissed on the basis of the said finding.

4. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge modified the decree of the trial Court en the finding that there had been, as a matter of fact, a contract for lease of the entire premises for a consideration of Tk. 7055/- but the contract for permanent lease, having contravened the provision of section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the petitioners claim for specific performance of the said contract was not sustainable. The learned Subordinate Judge maintained the decree for dismissal of the suit for specific performance of contract but passed a decree for the refund of Tk. 2755/- which was found to have been paid by the petitioners in respect of the said contract.

It may be mentioned that the respondents also preferred a Second Appeal to the High Court from the same judgment and decree, which was heard analogously with the Second Appeal preferred by the petitioners.

5. The learned Single Judge who heard the appeals has dismissed both the Second Appeals on the view that the Court of the Subordinate Judge had come to a correct finding as to the disputed contract for permanent lease and rightly construed the provision of section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

6. Mr. K.A. Bakr, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners, has submitted that the learned Single Judge of the High Court erred in construing the provisions of Section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and in holding that the agreement for permanent lease of the premises in question was 'subletting' within the meaning of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. According to the learned Counsel, the provisions of section 75A of the Act are attracted only in the case of an agricultural and horticultural holding and as the disputed property was a residential home the aforesaid provisions have no application to the instant case. If the said provision were attracted to the case of a lease of a residential premises, it has been further submitted, the creation of a monthly tenancy of such premises, as is sanctioned under The Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 would also be brought within the mischief of this prohibitory provision and the legislative intent behind the said provision was, therefore, learned Counsel has argued, to exclude 'premises' within the meaning of the said Ordinance from the purview of section 75A of the Act.

<u>7. We do not think that there is any substance in the contentions of the learned Counsel. Section 75A of the Act provides [hat on and from the date of publication of a notification under sub-section (3) of section 17 or under sub-section (1) of section 31, no person shall sublet any land in his khas possession in [he area to which such notification relates and that any subletting, made in contravention of sub-section (I), shall be null and void. What has been prohibited under section 75A of the Act is the subletting of any land in one's khas possession. The definitions of "land" and "land in khas possession", as given in clauses (15) and (16) of section 2 of the Act, are relevant for ,the purpose of construing the above section, and they are to the following effect;</u>

<u>"2 (15) "khas land" or "land in khas possession", in relation 10 any person, includes any land let out together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity ;</u>

<u>(16) "land means land which is cultivated, uncultivated or covered with water at any time of the year, and includes houses or buildings and also things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth."</u>

<u>From the definitions it is clear that the term "land" or" land in khas possession" is not confined to agricultural or horticultural land, but is wide enough to include all kinds of land and any non-agricultural land covered by any building is contemplated within the said definition clauses. The provisions of section 75A appear to be clearly attracted in respect of the disputed property.</u>

<u>8. It does not appear also that there is any inconsistency between the provision of section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1963 which provides for letting out of premises on monthly basis.</u>

<u>9. The main object of the State Acquisition Act 1950 was to eliminate all kinds of rent-receiving interests and make the Government the sole landlord and create only one class of tenants, who would be styled as "maliks", Section 75A of the Act, which was enacted in 1954, purported to prevent, after some steps had been taken for the purpose of the preparation of the compensation assessment roll, the creation of any rent receiving interest other than those which were already existing. All rent receiving interests as well as all non-retainable lands of the rent receivers were acquired under a notification under section 3 of the Act with effect from 14-4-56 and thereafter the excess khas lands as well as the non-retainable khas land of non-rent receivers were acquired on the publication of the compensation assessment roll made under Chapter V of Part IV of the Act. Part V of the Act, which contains provisions relating to the rights and liabilities of the tenants under the Government after the elimination of all kinds of rent-receivers, came into force in different areas on different dates. Proviso to section 8lA of the said Part also provides a provision similar to that contained in section 75A. Section 81A is to the following effect:</u>

<u>"81A(1) Except. as otherwise provided in this part, the rights and Liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the provincial Government In respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provision of this Act shall where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of this Act.</u>

<u>(2) The rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenant shall, except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; Provided that notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or, in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant .shall sublet the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms and conditions whatsoever and, if any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sublet in contravention of this provision, the interest of the non-agricultural tenant In the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Provincial Government from the date of such subletting free from all encumbrances".</u>

10. What is prohibited under section 75A is the sub-letting of the land in one's khas possession and that under section 81A is the subletting of the whole or any part of a non-agricultural tenancy. The definition of the expression, "land in khas possession" as has been used in section 75A, has been given in section 2(15) of the Act and has already been quoted. The definition of "non-agricultural tenant" as given in section 2(17) and that of "rent receiver" as given in section 2(23) are relevant for our present consideration and they are to the following effect:

"2(17) 	"non-agricultural tenant" means a tenant who holds land for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture, but does not include a person holding land together with any building standing thereon and any necessary adjuncts thereto under a lease other than a lease in perpetuity;

(23) "rent receiver" means a proprietor or a tenure-holder, and includes a raiyat, and under-raiyat or a non-agricultural tenant whose land has been let out and also the immediate landlord of a person who holds any land free of rent in consideration of some service to be rendered, but does not include a person in respect of such of his lands, as has been let out, together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts there to, otherwise than in perpetuity;"

<u>11. From these definitions it appears that the Legislature sought to keep any letting out of land along with a building standing thereon on a temporary or periodical basis outside the scope of sub-letting prohibited under section 75A of the Act. The letting out of some land along with building standing thereon otherwise than in perpetuity does not operate to take away the said land out of the khas possession of the lessor. Despite such letting out, the land continues to be the land in the khas possession of the lessor and, as such, the lessor does not become a rent receiver nor the lessee a non-agricultural tenant. What has been sought to be prohibited under section 75A or section 81A of the Act, as has been already observed, is the creation of any rent receiving interest and since any letting out of land with a building standing thereon otherwise than in perpetuity does not make the landlord a rent receiver within the meaning of the Act, such letting out does not appear to be within the mischief of the aforesaid prohibitory provisions, As a matter of fact, the legislature which enacted the State Acquisition anti, Tenancy Act also enacted legislations for the control of the rent of the premises let cut on monthly basis. The East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 which has been continued in force in Bangladesh with necessary charge is the present law for regulating the relationship of landlord and tenant in respect of the premises let out on a periodical basis. It is obvious that although the provisions of section 75A or section 81A, as the case may be, are applicable to non-agricultural land, letting cut such premises on monthly basis, consistently with the provision of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, does not come within the mischief of either of the said provisions.</u>

<u>We do not find any merit in this petition which is dismissed.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree passed in the High Court of East Pakistan, Dacca dated 27th April, 1969, in Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 181 of 1954)
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim J. - This civil appeal arises from the judgment and decree of the Dacca High Court passed in P.M.A. No.181 of 1954 on April 27, 1965. 2. The plaintiff-appellant which is a registered partnership firm and carrying on business at Chittagong imported from Karachi 175 bales and 200 bales of cotton yarn both of Camel Brand count 20/1 (China origin) with leading mark "ARAG" and 25 cases of cotton piece goods with leading marks "H.T. ARAG MARKS CHITTAGONG" per "S.S. FIRDAUSA" belonging to defendant-respondent No.1. After its arrival at Chittagong on February 28, 1951 the ship discharged goods on and from March 3, 1951 to March 5, 1951. The aforesaid goods were found in a damaged condition and the appellants went to the Jetty on March 4, 1951 to take delivery. The defendant respondent No.2 which is the local agent of the respondent No.1 was requested by the appellant, both verbally and writing, to make steamer survey of the goods. On their failure to make any arrangement for the survey the appellant had the goods surveyed by the Lloyd's agents on various dates beginning from March 4 to March 13, 1951. The survey by the Lloyd's was made both at the Jettyshed and at the appellant's premises. Re-survey of 200 bales was made at the request of the Lloyd's agents on March 13, 1951 and the survey report was signed by one Mr. Percy of Steel Brothers and Company Ltd. Chittagong. On the survey of the aforesaid 175 bales of cotton yearn, 148 bales were found to be damaged to the extent of 10 per cent and out of 200 bales 170 bales were found damaged to the extent of 20 per cent and 30 bales were found damaged to the extent of 10 per cent. The damage was caused by coal and/or coal sweepings and out of 25 cases of cotton piece goods 8 pieces from one case was found missing. The appellant demanded compensation for goods damaged and loss but with no result. The appellant served notice on the respondent No.3, the Federation of Pakistan as it then was. On the expiry of the period of notice the appellant instituted Money Suit No.23 of 1952 in the Court of Subordinate Judge Third Court, Chittagong for recovery of Rs. 82, 307-15-9 on account of damage to and loss of the goods imported and also for loss of profit as a result of the negligence of the respondent. The breakup of the total claim under different heads was shown in the schedule to the plaint as follows:—

3. The respondents Nos.1 and 2 by filing a joint statement contended that the plaintiff appellant had no cause of action against them that the suit was barred by limitation under the provisions of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, that as the plaintiff appellant gave no notice of claim to them within the period stipulated in the bill of lading the appellant is not entitled to get any relief and that no damage was caused to the appellant's goods so long as they were in the custody of these respondents. The damage, if any, caused to the appellant's goods occurred after the goods left the ship's tackle and while they were under the custody of the jetty authorities and of the appellant. Further, as the bales were packed with single gunny cover damage, if any, caused due to handling was ascribed to the shippers. It was, however, admitted by these respondents that the ship carried coal in addition to general cargo but the general cargo, it was contended did not come in contact, with the coal in the ship. The goods were carried with proper care and caution and there was no negligence by the carrier ship. 4. The respondents Nos.3 and 4 filed a separate joint written statement in which they denied the allegations made by the appellant against them. They contended that the suit was barred tinder Section 69 of the Partnership Act and also that the suit was bad for want of notice under section 80 C.P.C. As the appellant received goods in full from the Jetty shed under clear receipt and without any protest, these defendants were not liable for any of the claims made against them. 5. The Trial Court framed seven issues and after taking evidence, both oral and documentary, decided the case in favour of the appellant and decreed the same for Rs. 77, 659/-. On an appeal against the judgment of the Trial Court, the High Court in interpreting the clause in the bill of lading that "in all causes and under all circumstances the Company's liability shall absolutely cease when the goods are free of the ships tackle and thereupon the goods shall be at the risk for all purposes and in every respect of shippers and consignee" dismissed the suit. 6. It was observed by the High Court that "so far as the responsibility of the ship is concerned, according to the clause already quoted, it would appear to us to have ceased at the time that the general goods were disembarked at the outer anchorage from the ship on to lighter vessel. The liability of loss or damage after the goods left the ship was clearly that of the plaintiff in accordance with provisions of the aforesaid clause of bill of lading". The learned Judges of the High Court differed from the decision in Adam Limited Vs. East West Steamship Company, PLD 1962 Karachi 715 which had held that the word "vessels" in the second part of the clause included any lighter vessels to which the transhipment may be made. Reasons for arriving at this conclusion were that the definite Article "The" preceding the word "vessel" makes the word referable only to the ship in which the goods are being shipped. "Accordingly, it was held that "the whole purpose of the clause is to the effect that if necessary the goods will be transhipped to other vessels and the cost of conveyance will be borne by the shipping Company but the risk would be that of the shipper from the moment the goods leave the side of the original vessel." Further, the High Court observed that "according to this clause, whatever the claim, the damage must be referable to a period before the goods left the ship's side." 7. The plaintiff-appellant moved the Supreme Court of Pakistan against the judgment of the Dacca High Court, the point raised being as to what would be the legal effect of the incorporation of such a clause in the bill of lading upon which a difference of opinion occurred between the two High Courts. 8. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, Counsel for the appellant, contended that the decision of the High Court of East Pakistan was wrong inasmuch as it did not correctly interpret the special clause in the bill of lading which aimed at protecting the shipowners in the circumstances mentioned therein. The clause in the bill of lading which has raised the controversy is as follows:— "The Company is to be at liberty to carry the goods to their part of destination by the above, or any other steamer or steamers, ship or ships, motor vessel or vessels either belonging to the Company or to other persons, and to tranship or land and store the goods either on shore or afloat to re-ship and forward same at the Company's expense but at shipper's or consignee's risk; at the like risk to deviate as above mentioned. In all cases and under all circumstances, the Company's liability shall absolutely cease when the goods are free of the vessel's tackle and thereupon the goods shall be at the risk for all purposes and in every respect of shippers or consignee." The learned Counsel mentioned that the question raised in this appeal is now covered by a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan namely, East and West Steamship Company Vs. Husain Brothers (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 530=PLD 1968 SC 15. 9. In that case though the agreed facts were that there was no damage caused to the goods either during the time they were in the ship's hold or at the time of their discharge at the outer anchorage and that the goods were actually damaged by rain water when they were in the lighter the question whether the ship owners were completely protected by a similar clause in the bill of lading as above-mentioned was answered in the negative. In arriving at this conclusion the Supreme Court of Pakistan considered. The Hague Rules which have been incorporated in the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925. As in the present case, there was a paramount clause in the bill of lading whose opening words were; "all the terms, provisions and conditions of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, and the Schedule thereto are to apply to the contract contained in this bill of lading." 10. Also as in the present case there was similar provision in the bill of lading as follows; "the said goods to be carried and delivered subject to the terms and conditions of this bill of lading in the like good order and condition at the port of Chittagong unto order or his or their assignees." The relevant provisions of The Hague Rules which were considered by the Supreme Court of Pakistan are as follows:— Rules (b) and (e) of Article I: ‘‘(b) 'Contract of carriage' applies only to contracts of carriage covered by a bill of lading or any similar document of title, insofar as such document relates to the carriage of goods by sea including any bill of lading or any similar document as aforesaid issued under or pursuant to a charter party from the moment at which such bill of lading or similar document of title regulates the regulations between a carrier and a holder of the same." "(e) 'Carriage of goods' covers the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time when they are discharged from the ship." Article IT. "Risks.—Subject to the provisions of Article VI, under every contract of carriage of goods by sea the carrier in relation to the loading, handling, stowage, carriage, custody, care and dis-charges of such goods shall be subject to the responsibilities and liabilities, and entitled to the rights and immunities hereinafter set forth." Rules 2 and 8 of Article III; "2. Subject to the provisions of Article IV, the carrier shall properly and carefully load, handle stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods carried.' "8. Any clause, covenant or agreement in a contract of carriage relieving the carrier or the ship from liability for loss or damage to or in connection with goods arising from negligence, fault or failure in the duties and obligations provided in this Article or lessening such liability otherwise than as provided in these Rules, shall be null and void and of no effect. A benefit of insurance or similar clause shall be deemed to be a clause relieving the carrier from liability." 11. Mr. Hafizullah, Counsel for the respondent Nos.1 and 2 advanced similar arguments as were made on behalf of the shipowners in the case. He drew our attention to the expression "carriage of goods" which occur in Rule (e) of Article 1 and submitted that the respondent's obligations under the bill of lading were fulfilled as soon as the goods in question were discharged from the ship and cannot be held liable for any damage to the goods that might have been caused after the goods were put into lighter vessels. The contract to carry the goods continued only during the period when the goods were loaded till the time they were discharged from the ship. As the time for the performance of the contract of carriage of goods lapsed with the discharge of the goods from the ship, the liability of the shipowners also ceased with it. In Pyren Company Ltd. Vs. Scindia Company Ltd. (1954) 2 QBD 402, Devlin, J. when repelling similar contention that the right and liabilities under the aforesaid rule attached to a period of time, observed that it attached to a contract or part of a contract. In elaborating this view Devlin J. observed as follow:— "It is not intended to specify a precise moment of time. Of course, if the operation of the rules began and ended with a period of time a precise specification would be necessary. But they do not. It is legitimate in England to look at section 1 of the Act, which applies the rules not to a period of time but "in relation to and in connection with the carriage of goods by sea." The rules themselves show the same things. The obligations in Article 3, rule 1, for ex-ample, to use due diligence to make the ship seaworthy and man and equip her properly are independent of time. The operation of the rules is determined by the limits of the contract of carriage by sea and not by any limits of time." The views are, in our opinion, unassailable and they offer a complete answer to the contention of the learned Counsel for the respondents. 12. Referring to the exemption clause in the bill of lading which says that "Company's liability shall absolutely cease when the goods are free of the vessel's tackle." Mr. Hafizullah, submitted that the clause provides absolute exemption to the ship-owner from the moment the goods are discharged from the ship. Left alone, the exemption as provided in the afore-said clause might appear to be very comprehensive and even wide enough to absolve the shipping company from responsibility after the goods have been discharged from the ship. But, as was observed in Sze Hai Teng Bank Limited Vs. Rambler Cycle Co. Ltd. (1959) 3 All. E.R. 182 (PC), "if such an extreme width were given to the exemption clause", it would run counter to the main object and intent of the contract." Since the proper delivery of the goods by the shipping company, 'unto order or his or their assignee' is one of the main ob-jects, such contention, if accepted, would, as their Lordships felt, defeat this object entirely. 13. In view of the obligations imposed upon the carrier in rule 2 of Article 3 of The Hague Rules to "properly and carefully discharge the goods carried'', if appears that one of the main object of the contract would be frustrated if the goods are not delivered by the shipowners in the same condition it was received by them. There is no scope for violation of the aforesaid rule which by incorporation in the bill of lading constitute one of the main objects of the contract. 14. Mr. Hafizullah, Counsel for the respondents Nos.1 and 2 while drawing our attention to that part of the evidence which dealt with the manner and time in which damage was caused to the goods, submitted that there was no evidence to show that the goods were damaged before they were delivered from the ship. He submitted that the ship was carrying the goods in question as general cargo and also coal. Since the ship did not get the berth at the Chittagong port and was detained at the anchorage the goods in question was damaged at the outer anchorage and then the discharge of coal took place. A portion of the coal was discharged at the outer anchorage to lighten the ship and the rest of the coal was discharged when the ship anchored at B.O.C. Moorings. He submitted that the shipowner’s responsibility ceased when the general cargo including the goods in question was disembarked from the ship at the outer anchorage and ultimately from the lighters to the jetty premises unto the care and custody of the Chittagong Port Trust. 15. It may be mentioned that the lighters in which the appellant's goods were discharged at the outer anchorage were engaged by and at the disposal of the respondent No.2, M/s. James Finlay and Co. Ltd. the local agent of the respondent No.1. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, the appellant's Counsel submitted that the importers had no control over these lighters and had no means of supervision of the delivery of the cargo into the lighters which took place at the outer anchorage. 16. Mr. Hafizullah, Counsel for the respondents No.1 and 2 referred to the evidence and submitted that the appellant had not succeeded in establishing the fact that the goods were damaged before they were delivered into the lighters. It appears from the judgment of the Trial Court that there is full discussion of evidence, both oral and documentary, as to the condition in which the goods were shipped. The relevant passages from the judgment quo-ted below:— "The bill of lading Ext. 3 shows that 175 bales of cotton yarn, 200 bales of cotton yarn and 25 cases of cotton piece goods with clear leading (?) marks were shipped in apparent good order and condition. Ext. "B(1) series ate landing tally slips produced by defendants No.1 and 2 and Ext. B(2) series are those filed by defendants No.3 and 4. These tally slips are prepared jointly by the jetty staff and the staff of the steamer agents. They show the condition of the goods at the time they were landed to the jetty. It will be seen from these tally slips that almost all the bales of cotton yarn and a case of C.P. goods were landed from the steamer in a damaged condition. The word 'T' in the right hand column of the tally slips indicates packages landed slightly damaged, such as band broken, defective planks, nails missing' etc. vide jetty circular Ext. C(2). According to D.W.4 Sheikh Ahmed, who is a tally clerk of the steamer agents, ‘T' is used to indicate damage upto 20% Ext.1, 1(a) and 1(b) are survey reports. These reports show damages upto 10% and 20% and the plaintiffs have based their claim on these survey reports. These reports show that the affected bales which had gunny covering torn at ends exposing contents were carefully examined especially where hanks were exposed at both ends and in the opinion of the surveyor Mr. D' Cruze who is Lloyds' surveyor the cause of damage is coming in contact of exposed contents with coal and/or coal sweeping. According to the ship manifest, she carried 8487 tons of coal from Karachi in addition to general cargo. Carrying capacity of the ship was 9300 tons dead weight. Neither the defendants No.1 and 2 nor defendants No.3 and 4 challenged the survey reports in the written statement, though in the plaint every important particular thereof was mentioned. But at the time of trial the learned lawyer for defendants No.1 and 2 halfheartedly put some questions to the witnesses of these reports. Mr. Kidd who is the Manager of the steamer department of Mesrs. James Finlay and Co. (defendant No.2) was examined by the plaintiffs as P.W.2. Mr. Kidd has attested the survey reports. Of course, he stated in his deposition that he has got nothing to do with the survey business of Lloyd's Department except attesting survey reports in the absence of the senior member of the firm. He is of the idea that to certify a survey report is to certify the qualification of surveyor appointed by Lloyd's and that the routine requirements as laid down by the Corporation of Lloyds according to the book of instruction has been carried out. Messrs James Finlay are the Lloyds' agents. They are also the shipping agents of the steamer company as stated above, though they worked at water tight compartments. The surveyors are appointed by Messrs. James Finlay and Co., from the trained surveyors. According to Mr. Kidd the surveyor Mr. D. Cruze who submitted the survey reports Ext.1 series is considered to be a fully qualified surveyor. When signed the survey reports in question he had no reason to doubt the propriety of survey reports. Mr. Kidd further said that as this case was considered to be important the senior surveyor was appointed by the Lloyds otherwise a junior might have been appointed by them. This Mr. Kidd signed the written statement and verification thereof in this case for defendants No.1 and 2. He also gave instruction for the written statement in his capacity as the Manager. In these circumstances the defendant No.1 and 2 cannot be heard to say that the survey report is not correct and that no importance should be attached to it. Having regard to what has been stated by Mr. Kidd and having regard to the fact that none of the defendant has challenged the survey reports in the written statement and on the contrary they having been in a way relied on by defendant No.1 and 2 in para 7 of their written statement, I find that the survey report must be taken as correct and that it represents actual state of things. Now the surveyor recommended 10% and 20% damages and also has stated in his report that 8 pieces of C.P. goods were missing. 17. Apart from the survey report which shows the extent of the damage caused to the appellant's goods, the Trial Court, while considering the question whether the carrier or the Jetty caused the damage to the appellant's goods, considered the evidence as to whether the appellant's goods were damaged by coming in contact with coal or coal sweepings after they had been landed at the Jetty. The passage, containing the evidence of the witnesses for the appellant and the respondent is quoted-below:— "P.W.3 Md. Saleh, who is the Assistant Manager of the plaintiff's firm stated in his deposition that goods were discharged in crafts and trawlers from 3-3-51. From the beginning he was watching the landing and he saw bales being landed in a damaged condition. He saw no coal in the jetty shed. Then and there he complained against defendants No.1 and 2. Under clear receipts the plaintiffs received delivery of the goods from the jetty. He has further stated that no question of a complaint arose against the jetty. Mr. Kidd (P.W.2) admitted in his cross-examination that no coal is ever discharged at the jetty unless it is specially requested. D.W.6 M.A. Sharif who is the jetty Inspector stated that since 1949 no coal is landed from any ship at the jetty. Coal is landed at coal dump at Pateoga and Maheskhal. When S.S. 'Firdausa' came to Chittagong Port there was no coal at the jetty yard. According to him there is no coal or dirt in the jetty sheds. Sweeper sweeps the yard, platform and the sheds three times daily According to D.W.3 Abdus Sobban who is a Jetty clerk of defendants No.1 and 2 the jetty platforms remain very dirty when goods are landed there But by 'dirty' he means full of dust, sand and scrap of papers." As to whether the appellant's goods came in contact with coal sweepings at the time of shipment of coal at Karachi oral the time of delivery of the goods into the lighter the following evidence was considered by Trial Court: "D.W.1 Augustin Arabinda Sarkar who is an employee of Messers A.K. Khan & Co. who were coal lighterage contractors for EB Rly in I951 and who has been examined by defendants No.1 and 2 stated that coal cargo was discharged at outer anchorage to country boats and barges which took it direct to the coal dump at Patenga. Therefore no liability attaches at all to defendants No.3 and 4. On behalf of defendants No.1 and 2 several witnesses including D.W.5 Cowasjee R.F. Cowasjee, who is one of the partners of the Steamer Co. has been examined to show how goods were stowed at Karachi in the ship and how there was no possibility of the general cargo coming in contact with coal in view of the fact that coal was loaded in the lower holds and tween decks. It is an admitted position that the ship carried a huge quantity of coal and a small quantity of general cargo. There are 3 decks in S S "Firdausa", the lower hold, the shelter deck and the tween deck. The tween deck comes in between the shelter deck and the lower hold Coal was stowed in all the "tween decks". Over the tween deck is the shelter deck, Cotton piece goods and cotton yarn are general cargo. The coal cargo was shipped by the Coal Commissioner on behalf of the E.B. Rly." 18. From the discussion of the aforesaid evidence the Trial Court concluded that coal sweepings could not come in contact with, the general cargo at the time of shipment at Karachi. As there was no evidence to show whether the general cargo came in contact with the coal in the process of shipment or discharge at Colombo the Trial Court came to no finding. 19. The trial Court could not, in view of the evidence, both oral and documentary, accept the case that since at the Chittagong port general cargo was discharged first and then discharge of coal began, the appellant's goods could not come in contact with the coal or coal sweepings on board the ship. The evidence as discussed by the Trial Court on this point is contained in the following passage:— "According to D.W.2 Mohammad Ali who is a Cargo Supervisor under the Clan Line Steamer Co. of whom Messers. James Fin lay and Co are the agents, S.S. "Firdausa" arrived at outer anchorage (Chittagong) on 23-2-51 and completed discharge of all the general cargo before noon of 25-2-51 and according to D.W.1 Augustin Arabinda Sarkar discharge at outer anchorage of coal cargo began at 11 A. M of 25-2-51 to country boats and barge. Discharge of coal cargo these according to him continued upto 28-2-51. After the discharge of some coal at outer anchorage the vessel became lighter and was brought to the B.O.C. Moorirg. The remaining coal cargo was taken in barges and country boats to the dump at Patenga. Discharge at the B.O. C. Mooring continued upto 7-3-51 (But no tally for landing of the cargo from the Steamer to the crafts have been filed by 7-3 51. This is also evidenced by Ext. Al series which are the statements of coal discharge According to D.W. 2 after 25-2-51 there was no discharge of general cargo. He further stated that if any barge had discharged cargo at the jetty after 25-2-51 she must have waited in mid-stream for berth all this time. But tally slips Ext B (2) series would show that some general cargo was landed at the jetty on 3rd, 4th and 5th March also. Tally sheet Ext. B (2) (7) shows some landing of general cargo at the jetty at night of 23-2-51. So it cannot be said that general cargo was allowed to be in mid-stream for (7/8) days. Boat notes maintained in the office of the steamer agents would clearly show the position. But they have not been filed. Non production of boat notes is very significant”. 20. The Trial Court therefore, concluded that there was simultaneous landing of coal cargo and general merchandise from the ship and, therefore, there was every possibility of the general cargo coming in contact with the coal. The Trial Court also mentioned that there was no evidence to show that the lighters into which the general cargo was discharged were clean and not dirty with coal sweepings. The correctness of the evidence as discussed by the Trial Court was verified by us referring ourselves to the evidence concerned. 21. It appears, therefore, that the evidence has established that the damage to the appellant's goods occurred before they were landed at the Jetty. 22. The conclusion would be that the shipowners did not perform the duty of carriage and discharge “properly and carefully" as is enjoined by the contract. When the ship was carrying coal in a large bulk from the port of Karachi, it was certainly their duty to ensure that the appellant's goods did not come into contact with the coal which the ship was carrying from there to Chittagong and also while discharged the same into the Lighter. It was also this duty to be satisfied that the lighter did not simultaneously carry coal and the appellant's goods. The respondents have not, it appears, taken ordinary care and caution in carrying and discharging the goods in the condition they were received, thus leading to breach of the obligation imposed upon the shop owner by rule 2 of Article 3 of the Hague Rules as incorporated in the bill of lading. The very fact that the damage was caused to the appellant's goods while in the ship-owner's custody shows that there has been negligence on the part of the respondents which shows they cannot escape by relying on the exemption clause Farther the expression "Free of the vessel's tackle" cannot be construed as exempting the respondents from their liability until the goods in question were delivered to the Jetty authority for the appellants. 23. We express agreement with the views of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case cited above as to the effect of The Hague Rules which, as quoted earlier, were incorporated in the bill of lading. Fazle Akbar J. as he then was, of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, thus observed: "I may also point out that if there was a clause in the bill of lading exempting the shipowners from liability for loss or damage resulting from negligence in discharging cargo even then it would not have helped them because the same would be null and void by reason of Article III of The Hague Rules. Rule 2 of Article III imposes on the carrier certain obligations in relations to those matters which the shipowner agrees to perform under the contract of affreightment. Further, the obligations set out therein must be carefully carried out by the shipowner. Article IV gives him certain rights and immunity in relation to those obligations which are mentioned in Article III, Rule 2, rule 8 of Article III invalidates any provisions in the bill of lading by which the carrier seeks to relieve himself from liability for loss or damage to or in connection with goods otherwise than as provided in Article IV. Once the goods are loaded on the ship, the shipowner can free himself from the obligation by bringing himself within the exception mentioned in Article IV. Rule 2 of Article III has already been cited. It is directed to the manner in which the obligations entered into are to be carried out. No doubt, rule 2 of Article III is subject to Article IV. But exceptions mentioned in Article IV do not cover a case of failure to discharge the goods "Properly and carefully.” For the reasons stated above the appeal is allowed with costs, the judgment of the High Court of East Pakistan is set aside and the judgment and decree of the Trial Court are restored. End.
