parties:
Habibur Rahman
Vs.
State
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J:- These two appeals by special leave arise from the judgment of the High Court Division dated December 4, 1979 refusing to interfere with the order dated January 14, 1977 passed by the Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal, Kushtia vacating the order, allowing withdrawal of the criminal case against the appellant on August 5, 1975 on the prayer of the Public Prosecutor and sending the case record to the Chief Martial Law Administrator, Dacca for necessary action. Leave was granted to examine the question as to whether the Session Judge and Special Tribunal was competent to pass the order vacating the previous order allowing withdrawal of the case and sending the case records to the Chief Martial Law Administrator for action.

2. Two criminal proceedings were initiated against the appellant along with others who had been charge-sheeted in one case under section 364 of the Penal Code read with President's Order No. 50 of 1972, and in another case the appellant along with others had been charge-sheeted under sections 364/ 302 of the Penal Code read with President's Order No. 50 of 1972. Both the cases were received by the Sessions Judge and Ex-Officio Special Tribunal, Kushtia from the Court of Special Magistrate where the cases were pending, for trial on April, 1974, and were numbered as Special Tribunal Case Nos. 1 and 2 of 1974 and the cases were fixed for trial on 11th June, 1975 and 14th August, 1975. On an application filed by the Public Prosecutor the Special Tribunal by its order dated 1-8-75 allowed the cases to be withdrawn under section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and discharged the accused. Thereafter the case records were sent to the District Control Centre on the prayer of the Public Prosecutor and subsequently again on the prayer of the Public Prosecutor the Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal vacated its earlier orders dated 1-8-75, allowing withdrawal of the case, and sent the case records to the Chief Martial Law Administrator from where the records again received back by the Tribunal on 22-6-77. The cases remained pending for quite some time and ultimately the Special Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1974 was fixed for trial on 12-3-79, and the Special Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1974 was fixed for trial on 19-3-79. In Special Case No. 1 of 1974 P.W. 1 of the prosecution witness was examined and cross-examined on 15.3.79, and the case was adjourned till 21.3.79 for further P.Ws. On the following day further proceedings of the case was stayed by an order of the High Court Division. Similarly in Special Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1974, P.Ws. 1 and 2 were examined on 20.3.79 and 21.3.79 and were cross-examined, and further proceedings of the case was stayed on the following day. Further proceedings of both the cases were stayed by the High Court Division on the applications filed by the appellant for quashing the proceedings. The High Court Division dismissed both the applications on taking the view that Regulation 7B of the Martial Law Regulation No. 1 of 1975 was applicable to ordinary Criminal Courts and Tribunals other than Martial Law Courts constituted under the Martial Law Regulations, and as such the learned Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal had the power to vacate the orders allowing withdrawal of the cases for retrial in exercising the power under Regulation 7B.

<u>3. Mr. Aminul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submitted that in the absence of the phrase criminal court mentioned in Regulation 7B, the said Regulation as not applicable to a criminal case pending in a Criminal Court or Tribunal. The impugned orders do not indicate that the learned Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal while vacating the order allowing withdrawal of the cases exercised the power provided under Regulation 7B. However, it may be presumed that while vacating the order allowing withdrawal of the cases Regulation 7B was in mind. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State argued that Regulation 7B is not limited to Martial Law cases or Martial Law Courts but it is equally applicable to the criminal cases pending in ordinary criminal courts or special tribunals. Now it should be examined whether Regulation 7B is wide enough to apply to criminal cases pending in ordinary Criminal Courts and Special Tribunals. Regulation 713 reads as under:-</u>

<u>"7B Fresh trial of withdrawn cases Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code or in any other law for the time being in force any case which was withdrawn at any time before the commencement of these Regulations, whether or not the withdrawal was made before or after the framing of a charge or whether or not any charge was required to be framed, and whether the accused was discharged or acquitted upon such withdrawal, may be tried afresh."</u>

<u>4. The Martial Law Regulations, 1975 (Regulations No. 1 of 1975) provided that the Chief Martial Law Administrator may by notification in the official Gazette constitute Special Martial Law Courts and Summary Martial Law Courts for such areas as may be specified in the notification. The Martial Law Courts were given the jurisdiction to try any offence punishable under the Martial Law Regulation or Order or under any other law. That is to say, a Martial Law Court was empowered to try an offence under any penal law. Clause (5) of Regulation 3 provides that a Martial Law Court trying an offence under any of the Regulations shall follow the procedure laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, for summary trial of summons cases. Regulation 8 provides that the provisions of the Criminal Procedure, so far only as they are applicable and not inconsistent with the provisions of any Martial Law Regulations or Order shall apply to the proceedings of Martial Law Courts and Tribunals constituted under these Regulations. From the above provisions it is clear that the Regulations are applicable to Martial Law Courts and Tribunals constituted under these Regulations. Whenever there was any necessity for the Chief Martial Law Administrator to exercise his power with regard to a criminal case pending in an ordinary Criminal Court, the Regulation in clear language provided that power. For instance clause (2) of Regulation 3 empowers the Chief Martial Law Administrator to transfer a case from one Martial Law Court to another Martial Law Court or from a Criminal Court or Special Tribunal to a Martial Law Court. The Explanation to clause (2) provides that a case tribal by a court of Sessions pending before the Magistrate for inquiry may also be transferred to the Martial Law Court for trial. In this Regulation ordinary Criminal Court and Special Tribunal have been specifically mentioned while empowering the Chief Martial Law Administrator to transfer a criminal case to a Martial Law Court. If the intention was to make Regulation 7B applicable to criminal cases pending before the Criminal Courts and Special-Tribunals, the intention would have been made clear by providing the necessary language therein. In our opinion Regulation 7B is applicable only to Martial Law cases pending before the Martial Law Courts and a criminal case pending in a Criminal Court or Special Tribunal does not come within the ambit of Regulation 7B. In that view of the matter we find that the learned Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal acted wholly without jurisdiction in vacating the order of withdrawal of the cases made on the prayer of the Public Prosecutor. The impugned orders also suffer from impropriety, because, the orders do not show any application of mind by the Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal, and the orders indicate that he acted practically at the behest of the Public Prosecutor.</u>

5. Effect of withdrawal of Criminal case under section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in the instant cases after trial started, that is, after examination of the accused under section 242 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, amounts to acquittal and fresh trial on the self-same charge, as per section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is barred.

6. The learned Judges of the High Court Division were not correct in taking the view that Regulation 7B is an enabling provision and it does not exclude the ordinary Criminal Courts and Tribunals. The learned Judges expressed their opinion in the following terms:

"We, therefore, find no reason why the Regulation which is an enabling provision conferring certain powers on all courts could exclude the ordinary criminal courts and the Tribunals."

The observation made by the learned Judges does not get support from the language of Regulation 7B itself; and there is nothing in the Regulation that it was intended to confer this powers on all courts including the Martial Law Courts. Had there been any such indication in the Regulation the question of excluding the ordinary Criminal Courts and the Tribunals would not arise. Language of Regulation 7B does not warrant the view taken by the learned Judges of the High Court Division. Regulation 7B does not automatically include ordinary Criminal Courts and Tribunals it being a special ado measure must, be construed strictly. Therefore, the learned Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal obviously passed the impugned orders without jurisdiction, and as such the impugned orders cannot be sustained and are to be quashed.

7. In that view of the matter both the appeals are allowed. The order of the High Court Division is set aside. The minuend orders are quashed and the appellant discharged from his bail bonds.

SHAHABUDDIN AHMED, .J:- I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Ruhul Islam, J. While I agree that the two appeals should be allowed and the accused petitioner in both the cases be acquitted; I would give my own reasons which are rather different in respect of one point from those of my learned brother. My view is that the Special Tribunal was quite competent and had got jurisdiction under Martial Law Regulation 7B to hold fresh trial of these cases by vacating the earlier order allowing the withdrawal of those cases, but that the impugned order for fresh trial is not sustainable in law as it is found to have been passed without due application of mind.

<u>8. The question is whether Martial Law Regulation 7B applies to criminal cases pending in ordinary Criminal Courts, such as Courts of Sessions, Special Tribunals or Magistrate's Courts. This Regulation has been already quoted in the judgment of my learned brother and as such it need not be quoted again. It provides for "fresh trial of withdrawn cases", that is, cases which were withdrawn before the commencement of Martial Law Regulation No. 1 of 1975. It provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the Criminal Procedure Code or in any other law for the time being in force "any case which was withdrawn at any time before the commencement" of' the Martial Law Regulations, 1975, whether the withdrawal resulted in acquittal or discharge of the accused "may be tried afresh". According to the interpretation sought to be put to this Regulation 'any case' means only Martial Law case and not any ordinary case pending in ordinary criminal court. I am afraid, this interpretation runs counter to the letter and spirit of this Regulation which obviously aims at only ordinary cases which were withdrawn in the pre-martial law period or in the period proceeding these Martial Law Regulations. Mr. Aminul Huq argues that "in the absence of criminal courts mentioned in this Regulation, 7B, this Regulation is not applicable to criminal cases pending in the ordinary criminal courts". It is true that this Regulation does not mention any criminal case or any case pending in ordinary criminal courts which may be retried. But, in the same way, this Regulation does not mention any Martial Law case pending in any Martial Law Court either. In fact this Regulation neither mentions the nature of "any case" nor the court from which the case was withdrawn. But nevertheless both the nature of the case and the court from which it was withdrawn have been clearly and with utmost precision indicated by referring to the period during which the case was withdrawn. This Regulation shows that only those cases may be tried afresh which were withdrawn "at any time before the commencement of these Regulations". These cases cannot be Martial law cases withdrawn while pending in Martial law courts simply because the commencement of these Regulations there was neither any Martial law case pending nor any Martial Law court in existence. These Regulations called the Martial Law Regulations, 1975, (Regulation’s No. 1 of 1975) came into force with effect from the 22nd day of August. 1975. Regulation 7B, though promulgated on 2nd October, 1975 by Martial Law (Second Amendment Regulation 1975), was given retrospective effect from the 22nd day of August, 1975, in the words "they shall be deemed to have come into force on the 22nd day of August, 1975." Both Martial law courts and Martial law offences are creations of these Martial Law Regulations. They therefore cannot precede these Regulations. As such there is no scope for any Martial law case having been "withdrawn at any time before the commencement of these Regulations." Any case withdrawn before the commencement of these Regulations necessarily means Non-Martial law cases that is ordinary cases withdrawn by or under the order of ordinary criminal courts. For, before these Regulations came into force there were only ordinary criminal courts in the country trying cases under ordinary criminal law in fact Regulation 7B has totally excluded Martial law cases from its ambit. The two cases in question having been withdrawn before the commencement of these Martial law Regulation by the order of the Special Tribunal, it is the Special Tribunal which is competent to try them afresh.</u>

9. Next question is, whether the order of the Special Tribunal for holding fresh trial of these two cases by vacating its earlier order allowing withdrawal thereof is sustainable in law. Regulation 7B, though it provides for fresh, trial or retrial of a withdrawn case, does not provide that the order of withdrawal would be vacated as a matter of course for the purpose of fresh trial. This Regulation simply enables a court to try a case afresh which was earlier with brawn. The words "may he tried afresh" clearly slow that a withdrawn case may be retried if the court deemed it fit for retrial. In other words, a fresh trial may be held at the discretion of the court, and this discretion being a judicial discretion must be exercised properly applying the court's mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The offence involved in the two cases are serious in nature and the Public Prosecutor had withdrawn from prosecution of those cases earlier and consequently the accused petitioner was acquitted under section 494, Criminal Procedure Code. But when the new law, Regulation 7B came in, providing for retrial, the Public Prosecutor changed his mind without assigning any reason and prayed for retrial by reviving them. The offences in question were committed about six years before the retrial was to be held. In such circumstances the Special Tribunal ought to have given due consideration as to whether it is necessary in the interest of justice to revive the cases and retry the accused. The impugned order reviving the cases is found to be an order passed mechanically, just on the application of the Public Prosecutor. This order, therefore, is not sustainable in law.

<u>10. The appeals are allowed, the impugned order for retrial is set aside and the order of the Special Tribunal dated 1-8-1975, allowing the withdrawal is restored. Consequently the petitioner stands acquitted under section 494 Cr.P.C.</u>

End.

parties:
Fariduddin Ahmed
Vs.
Secretary Bangladesh Bar Council & Another
full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J:- This appeal under Article 36 of Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order, 1972 (hereinafter called the Order) arises out of an order passed by a Tribunal of the Bangladesh Bar Council rejecting the appellant-advocate's prayer for stay of the case pending before it till the decision in a money suit and directing the appellant to show cause why his Sanad should not be suspended in view of the allegations made against him.

2. Facts leading to this appeal, in brief, are that upon a complaint lodged by respondent No. 2 before the Bar Council making various allegations against the appellant, the natter was transferred to Tribunal No. 1 for enquiry and trial. The appellant on receipt of notice from the Tribunal duly appeared before it. On 30.1.81 an application was filed by the appellant before the Tribunal under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 151 of the Code for stay of the case pending before the Tribunal against him on the ground that a money suit between the "appellant and the complainant was pending before the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca, wherein on the prayer of the appellant, the complainant has been restrained by an order of temporary injunction by the Court from proceeding further with his complaint before the Bangladesh Bar Council till the disposal of the suit. The Tribunal after hearing the parties on 30:1.81 passed the following order:

“30.1.81. Complainant and opposite party are present. Mr. B. Hossain, A.A.G. is present on behalf of A.G. Opposite party submits that complainant has filed a Civil Suit (Vide M.S. No. 15/79) in the court of 3rd Sub-Judge, Dacca and the opposite party has got temporary injunction order restraining the complainant to proceed with his complaint before the Tribunal. There are two allegations in the complaint. The Tribunal is not inclined with the matter regarding non-payment of money to the opposite party. But the other allegation involves serious professional misconduct. Opposite Party is directed to show cause why his 'Sanad' be not suspended in view of the allegations made on the complaint. The hearing is adjourned to 27.3.81 at 10-30 A.M. Inform the parties".

Hence the present appeal at the instance of the Advocate concerned.

3. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Counsel for the appellant has argued that in view of the order of temporary in, junction passed by a competent court, the Tribunal ought to have stayed the matter till the disposal of the money suit between the complainant and the Advocate concerned. This was the sum and substance of all the grounds taken in the memorandum of appeal befogs this Court.

4. In reply, Mr. A.K.M. Shaftqur Rahman, the learned Counsel for the Bangladesh Bar Council has assailed the Maintainability of the appeal itself under Article 36 of the Order on the ground that the impugned order not being an order passed under Article 34 of the Order, no appealed. He has further argued that the order of temporary injunction only restrained the complainant from proceeding with the complaint but the said order did not in any way restrain the Bar Council or the Attorney General who was the prosecutor of the delinquent Advocate. Since the Bar Council was not a party in the proceeding before the Civil Court and under the Order the Bar Council was competent to proceed with the complaint on its own without the complainant, there was no reason for the Bar Council to stay its hand.

5. For the sake of convenience we shall first take up the question of maintainability of the appeal. The impugned order has been quoted in full above. We have also perused the order of temporary injunction passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, a certified copy of which was produced before us.

6. It appears that although the learned Subordinate Judge found that the two proceedings were of different kind and nature, one relating to disciplinary matter and the other relating to recovery of money, nevertheless passed the order of temporary injunction restraining the complainant who was the plaintiff in the money suit, from proceeding with his complaint before the Bar Council From the impugned order it appears that the Tribunal decided not to proceed with that part of the complaint which related to the issue directly involved in the money suit but to proceed with the other part of the complaint relating to professional misconduct against the delinquent Advocate and accordingly directed the appellant to show cause why his 'Sanad' should not be suspended in view of the allegations made against him. Article 36 of the Order reads as follows:-

"36.(1) Any person aggrieved by an order of Tribunal under Article 34 may, within ninety days from the date of the communication of the order to him, prefer an appeal to the High Court.

(2) Every such appeal shall be heard by a Division Bench of the High Court which may pass such order thereon as it may deem fit and the order of the High Court shall be final."

Article 34 of the Order reads as follows:-

"34. (1) In enquiries relating to conduct of Advocates, a Tribunal shall follow such procedure as may be proscribed.

(2) The Tribunal shall fix a date for hearing of the case and shall cause notice of the day so fixed to be given to the advocate concerned and to the Attorney General for Bangladesh and shall afford the advocate concerned and the Attorney General an opportunity of leading evidence, if any, and of being heard before orders are passed in the case.

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in this order of any other law for the time being in force, the Chairman the Tribunal may empower one of the Members of the Tribunal to consider and decide preliminary issues and to record evidence.

(4) On completion of the enquiry the Tribunal may either dismiss the complaint or, where reference to the Tribunal was made at the motion of the Bar Council, direct that the proceedings be filed; or it may make an order imposing any of the penalties referred to in clause (1) of Article 32.

(5) Where the Tribunal makes an order for the suspension of an advocate from practice, it shall specify the period of suspension, and for that period the advocate shall be debarred from practicing in any court or before any authority or person in Bangladesh.

(6) The Tribunal may make such order as to the costs of proceedings before it as it may deem fit; and where the Tribunal is of the opinion that a complaint made against advocate is false and vexatious, it may, in addition, and without prejudice to any other remedy available to the advocate, impose deterrent costs not exceeding a sum of five hundred rupees upon the complainant, which shall be paid to the advocate as compensation,

(7) Every order of the Tribunal as to costs or deterrent costs shall be executable as an order of the High Court:

(8) The Tribunal may, of its own motion .or on application made to it iii this behalf, review any order passed under clause (4) or (6) and maintain, vary or rescind the same, as it thinks fit.

(9) When any advocate is reprimanded or suspended under this Order, a record of the punishment shall be entered against his name in the roll and when an advocate is removed from practice his name shall forthwith be struck off the roll; and the certificate of any advocate so suspended or removed shall be re-called".

7. Article 36 of the Order clearly lays down that an appeal can be preferred by an aggrieved person against any order passed under Article 34 only. The impugned order as is evident comprises of two parts—one is the decision to proceed with the complaint on the allegations of professional  misconduct and the second part relates to the notice to show cause why his Sanad should not be suspended. It is pertinent to recall that the application for stay of the proceeding’s before the Tribunal was filed under section 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure Section 10 of the Code lays down as follows:-

"10. Stay of suit No Court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties; or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title where such suit is pending in the same or any other court in Bangladesh having jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed, or in any court beyond the limits of Bangladesh established or continued by the Government and having like jurisdiction, or before the Supreme Court".

The principle underlying section 10 of the Code is to prevent multiplicity of proceedings and conflict of decisions in respect of the same subject matter involved in two different suits between the same party. In order to attract the provision of section 10 of the Code, the matter in issue in both the suits must be substantially the same between the same parties. One of the essential test for the application of section 10 was whether the decision in the earlier suit will operate as res judicata in the suit instituted subsequently. In the light of those principles it was abundantly clear that the application for stay must be filed before a court. Although, under the Order the Bar Council may be deemed to be a Civil Court and some of the provisions of the Code have been made applicable to it, nevertheless it was not a Civil Court in the legal sense of the term. It would be further evident from the fact that an appeal against an order passed by the Tribunal or the Bar Council has been provided for under the Order itself by a specific provision and not under the Code of Civil Procedure as in the case of a Civil Court.

8. Under Article 35 of the Order it has been laid down that a Tribunal shall have the same powers as are vested in a court under the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of enforcing the attendance of any person, compelling the production of documents and issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses Clause (2) of Article 35 further lays down that an enquiry under the order shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding with the meaning of sections 193 and 288 of the Bangladesh Penal Code and a Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for the purposes of sections 280 and 382 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It was, therefore, evident that the Tribunal would be deemed to be a Civil Court only for certain specific purposes as laid down under the order.

<u>9. The use of the word "deemed" under Article 35(2) of the Order clearly indicates that the Tribunal is not a Civil Court for all purposes but it shall be considered so for some specific purposes as discussed above. The Tribunal has been constituted under a special statute for discharging some specified functions. Although such a body may have the trappings of a court, it is not really a court of law which a Civil Court is.</u>

<u>10. In the instant case, there was neither any suit pending before the Tribunal nor was the Tribunal Court nor were the issues in both the matters substantially the same nor could it be said that decision in the case of one would operate as res judicata in the other. Applying all the tests, we are clearly of the view that the application under section 10 of the Code before the Tribunal itself was misconceived and was not maintainable.</u>

<u>11. Now, coming to the question of maintainability of the appeal we find that none of the two parts of the order impugned before us come within purview of Article 34 of the Order. The delinquent Advocate has only been asked to show cause as to why his Sanad should not be suspended pending disposal of the case against him. This notice evidently comes within the purview of Rule 51 of the Order which says that the Tribunal shall have the power to suspend the advocate concerned, pending enquiry against him, and to vary or rescind such order. This suspension under Rule 51 pending disposal of the case is not a punishment as envisaged under Article 32 of the Order. Furthermore, under Article 32(2) of the Order the Bar Council may of its own motion refer any case to the Tribunal in which it has reason to believe that any advocate is guilty of misconduct and under Rule 50 the Bar Council may suo moto start a proceeding against an advocate. Under Rule 44 of the Order it has been laid down that the proceedings before the Tribunal against an advocate shall be conducted by the Attorney General or by an Advocate appearing on his behalf and the Attorney General shall have a prior right to conduct the proceedings against the advocate. All these provisions clearly show that once a complaint is lodged, before the Bar Council it may on its own proceed with the enquiry and trial, whether or not the complement chooses to prosecute the case subsequently. We, therefore, do not find any illegality in the impugned order directing the delinquent advocate to show cause why his Sanad should not be suspended. It is only after an order is passed one way or the other that the, appellant may have a cause of action but we do not see how he could feel aggrieved by a mere notice to show cause.</u>

<u>12. Having regard to these facts and circumstances we bold that the impugned order does not come within the purview of Article 34 of the Order and as such the appeal preferred under Article 36 of the Order is not maintainable in law.</u>

The appeal is accordingly dismissed but in the facts and circumstances we make on order as to costs.

End.
