case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 17-1-1974 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case No. 582 of 1973).
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division, discharging a Rule issued on an application made by the appellants under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order or the Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali, recording abatement of a suit, instituted by the appellants, under section 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972.

2. The appellants instituted the suit being Title Suit No. 30 of 1 948 in the Second Court of the Subordinate Judge, Barisal, for a declaration of the plaintiffs right, title and interest in the disputed lands as Karsha tenants and for confirmation of their possession in the said lands as well as for a permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with their said possession in any manner. This suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 59 of 1954, when it was transferred to the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal and thereafter the Sub-Division of Patuakhali having been constituted as a District, it was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali and registered as Title Suit No. 146 of 1969.  This suit was, however, withdrawn on 3.8.71 with permission to institute a fresh suit on the same cause of action and Title Suit No. 3 of 1972 was thereafter filed on 24.1.72 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge of Patuakhali in pursuance of the aforesaid permission.

3. According to the plaintiff's case, as made out in the plaint, the disputed lends appertained to the Estate of Bishweshwar Roy Choudhury, which were diluviated and after the said lands had reappeared as reformation in stu and had become fit for possession. Babu Rajeswar Choudhury, the then executor of the -10/- annas share of the Estate of late Bishweshwar Roy Choudhury settled the said lands with the predecessors of plaintiffs 1 to 42 and plaintiff No. 45 at an annual rent of Tk. 250/- on the basis of a Karsha Kabuliyat dated 1st Jaistha, 1331 B.S. corresponding to May, 1924.  The proprietors of 6/- annas share of the said Estate settled their 6/- annas share of the said lands with some of the defendants at an annual rent of 7k. 75/- on the basis of another Kabuliyat of the sane date, namely, 1st Jaistha, 1331 B.S. which were ultimately sold, and purchased in auction by the landlords, in execution of a decree for rent obtained by them and were then settled in 1344-45 13.S. with the predecessors of some of the plaintiffs on the basis of a Kabuliyat at a rental of Tk. 75. After the rent receiving interests of the previous landlords had been acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the Government has stepped into the shoes of the previous landlords and the plaintiffs have become tenants directly under the Government, in respect of the said lands, some of which had been wrongly recorded in the name of the Government. The Government, however, have had no right, title and interest in the said lands nor any right to dispossess the plaintiffs from any part thereof, which are the lands of their tenancy.

4. The suit was contested by defendant's No. 1, 19, 34, 44 and 58. Who filed a joint written statement, as well as by Defendants No. 144 and 146, on the contentions, inter alia, that the disputed lands were accretion to Government lands and that the Government had settled the lands with them.

5. After the amendment of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 the contesting defendants filed an application for abatement of the suit under the said amended provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. While disposing of the said application by his order dated 24.3.73. the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have gone into the question of the truth or otherwise of the allegations made in the plaint and having held, on the basis of certain papers, that the story of reformation in situ and the induction of the plaintiffs as tenants could not be believed, recorded an order of abatement of the suit in respect of the lands in suit on The basis of the amended provisions of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

6. It may be mentioned that some of the plots of lands of which the plaintiff are alleged to have taken settlement from the previous landlords, bad been, according to the plaint, correctly recorded in the names of the plaintiffs, who have been recognized as tenants by the Government in respect of the said lands and the plaintiffs also have been paying rent, in respect thereof and as a matter of fact, no prayer was made by the plaintiffs in respect of the said lands in the present suit but the learned Subordinate Judge by a subsequent order dated 5.4.72, passed a decree, under a misapprehension of the plaintiffs claim in respect of the lands, for which there was no dispute and as such there was no prayer in the suit.

7. The High Court Division was moved under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure on behalf of the plaintiffs against the order of abatement made by the learned Subordinate Judge but the learned Judges of the High Court Division affirmed the decision of the Subordinate Judge on holding that the suit had been rightly held to have abated in view of President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 amending the provisions of Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

8. Special Leave to appeal was granted by the Appellant Division to consider whether the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by the Presidential Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 could be applied in respect of the lands in the instant suit. This appeal, thus, raises an important question as to the interpretation of the amended provisions of the aforesaid two sections of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

9. The decision of the High Court Di-vision dismissing the revisional application of the appellants, was also based up, n the view that the order of abatement of the suit having had the effete of a decree within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lay to the High Court Division from the said order of abatement and that as such the revisional application was not maintainable. No special leave was granted on this question of maintainability of the revisional application presumably be-cause the said view of the High Court Division was prima facie correct, but in view of the great importance of the question relating to the interpretation of the amending provisions of President's Order Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972, the decision of the High Court Division required further consideration and if the said decision was found, on an examination by this Court, to be wrong, there would be no difficulty in correcting the same by treating the revisional application to be the Memorandum of appeal.

<u>10. It should be pointed out at the out-set that the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division were not correct in going into the question as to the truth of the allegations made in the plaint before any evidence had been adduced in deciding the question of abatement of the suit as a preliminary issue. To decide the question of abatement of the suit in the light of the provisions of the newly enacted sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act., the proper procedure which should have been followed was to take the allegations made in the plaint as such and then to see if the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act were attracted to them.</u>

11. The plaint of the suit, out of which the appeal arises, if properly read, would show that the claim of the plaintiffs is based upon an allegation of settlement of the tenancy right in respect of the disputed lauds in their favour by the former proprietors of the estate to which the disputed lands appertained. The said proprietors are alleged to have acquired right to the said lands when they reappeared after division by virtue of their right to reformation in situ and there appears to be no allegation in the plaint relating to accrual of any right of accretion at any stage, requiring the application of section 87 as amended by President's Order Nos. 72 and 137 of 1972 but as the trial Court held that the suit abated in view of the amended section 87, and the learned Judges of the High Court expressed the view that the suit had abated in view of the provisions of both the sections, namely sections 86 and 87, as amended the Appellate Division granted special leave to consider the meaning and scope of both the said two sections amended by the relevant Presidential Orders.

<u>12. For the proper understanding of the said provision is necessary to appreciate that the right to reformation in situ and the right of accretion are two distinct rights of different nature and it will be appropriate for the said purpose to follow the develop meat of the law relating to the said two rights in the light of their legislative history.</u>

<u>13. There has been no positive legislation creating or defining the right to reformation in situ but it is a right incidental to one's title to a tangible property. The principle underlying this right is that a person's right to any property is not destroyed or affected in any way if it merely goes under, or is covered by, the waters of a' Sea or a River. He is deemed to be in constructive possession of his property throughout the period of its sub emergence and he can claim back the said property in his own right whenever it, if it can be so identified, reappears out of the waters. A classic exposition of this principle had been given by Lord Justice James in the celebrated case of Felix Lopez Vs. Muddun Mohan Thakoor, 13 Moor's I.A. 467 where, after referring to the analogous rule of English law as expounded in a work of great authority, the noble Lord stated the principle in the following words at page 473 of the Report:</u>

<u>"The principle is one not merely of English Law, not a principal peculiar to any system of 	Municipal law, but it is a principle founded in universal law and justice : that is to say, 	that whoever has land, where ever it is, whatever may be the accident to which it has been exposed whether it be a Vineyard which is covered by lava or ashes from a Volcano, or a field covered by the Sea or by a River the ground, the site, the property remains in the original owner."</u>

14. The enunciation of this rule of universal law, which emphasizes that the title of a person to his property is not destroyed nor affected in any way by the mere fact of its submergence under water or any other thing, was however made subject to the following observation at page 468 of the Report :

Their Lordships, however, desire it to be understood that they do not hold that the property absorbed by a Sea or a River is, under all circumstances and after any lapse of time, to be recovered by the owner. It may well be that it may have been so complete y abandoned as to merge again, like any other derelict land, into the public domain, as part of the Sea or River of the State and so liable to the written law as to accretion and annexation".

<u>15. The right of accretion in respect of a property, which was a part of the public domain and to which a riparian owner had previously no right, was however, a creature, originally, of usage and subsequently, of positive law. This rule was given legislative shape for the first time in Alluvium and Dilution Regulation (Bengal Rag XI of 1825) which was promulgated in the Presidency of Bengal which included the territory which is now 'Bangladesh. The main purpose of the legislation was to resolve certain disputes which used to arise frequently because of the peculiar physical features of the soil in the region, which was formed by the deposit of alluvial sands, with the Sea in the South and intersected by numerous rivers and streams, which often shifted their courses. The aim and object of the said legislation was very lucidly described in an unusually long preamble of the Regulation, which was to the following effect:-</u>

<u>"In consequence of the frequent changes which take place in the channel of the principal 	rivers that intersect the territories immediately subject to the Presidency of Fort William and the shifting of the sands which lie in the beds of those rivers, chars or small islands are often thrown up by allusions in the midst of the stream, or near one of the banks, and large portions of land are carried away by an encroachment of the river on one side, whilst accessions of land are at the same time, or in subsequent years, gained by	dereliction  of the water on the opposite side; similar instances of alluvium, encroachment and dereliction also sometimes occur on the seacoast which borders the southern and southeastern limits of Bengal.</u>

<u>The lands gained from the river is or sea by the means above mentioned are a frequent source of contention and affray, and although the law and custom of the country have established rules applicable to such cases, these rules not being generally known, the Court of Justice have sometimes found it default to determine the rights of litigant parties claiming chars or other lands gained in the manner above described.</u>

<u>The Court of Sadar Diwani Adalat, with a view to ascertain the legal provisions of the 	Muhammadan and Hindu laws on this subject, called for reports from their law officers of each persuasion and on consideration of the reports furnished by the law officers in consequence as well as of the decisions which have been passed by the Court of Sadar Diwani Adalat in cases brought before them in appeal which involved the rights of claimants to lands gained by alluvium or by declaration of rivers or the sea, the 	Governor-General-in-Council has deemed it proper to enact the following rules for the general information of individuals as well as for the guidance of Courts of judicature ; to be in force as soon as promulgated throughout the whole of the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort William".</u>

16. The first clause affection 4 of Regulation X1 of 1825 has stated the law of accretion the following words:

"When land may be gained by gradual accession, whether from the recess of a river or of the sea, it shall be considered an increment to the tenure of the person to whose land or estate it is thus annexed, whether such lands or estate be held immediately from Government by a Zmaindar or other superior land-holder, or as a sub-ordinate tenure, by any description of under tenant whatever:

Provided that the increment of land thus obtained shall not entitle to which the land may be annexed to a right of property or permanent interest therein beyond that possessed by him in the estate or tenure to which the land may be annexed, and shall not in any case be understood to exempt the holder of it from the payment to Government of any assessment for the public revenue to which it may be liable under the provisions of 	Regulation 11, 1819 or of any other Regulation in force.

Nor, if annexed to a subordinate tenure held under a superior landholder, shall the under-tenant, whether a khudkas raiyat, holding a mourusi is tamari tenure at a fixed rate of rent per-bigha, or any other description of under-tenant liable by his engagements or by established usage, to an increase of rent for the land annexed to his tenure by alluvion, be considered exempt from the payment of any increase of rent to which he may be justly  liable".

This provision is clear enough to show that the accrual of the right of a riparian owner to the lands gained by the recess of a river or the sea is not dependent upon the recognition of the said right, or settlement of any rent in respect of the lands, so gained, by any authority. There is no postponement of the accrual of the right, which arises as and when the accretion takes place. The only conditions attaching to the recrual of such right, as has been stated in the proviso to the main provision, are that the owner cannot claim a better right in the added lands than what he has in the lands to which added lands have been annexed nor be can claim any exemption from the liability to pay rent in respect of such added land.

17. The principle underlying the law of accretion as was stated in the aforesaid provisions of Regulation X of 1825 has also been explained by Lord Justice James in the case of Felix Lopez Vs. Muddun Mohan Thakoor at page 473 in the following words:

"There is, however, another principle recognized in the English Law derived  from the Civil Law, which is thus-that where there is an acquisition of land from the Sea or River, by gradual, slow and Imperceptible means, there, from the supposed necessity of the case, and the difficulty of basing to determine, year by year, to whom an inch or foot or a yard belongs the accretion by allusion is belt to belong to' the owner of the adjoining land".

<u>18. The reason behind the legislation relating to the right of accretion has been very correctly, though very briefly, stated in the above quoted passage. The acquisition of land having been by a gradual, slow and imperceptible process, it is very often extremely difficult to measure and demarcate the additional lands with any amount of precision and to allocate the same to somebody else for the useful tutor such lands If the accreted lands are not of sizeable area and generally it is, not so except after a lapse of considerable time and have no proper approach, nobody else than the riparian holder, to whose lands the additional lands have been annexed, can faithfully use the said land. The reference to the supposed necessity and the difficulty respecting recurrent measurement of the additional land every year as was made by Lord James in the case of Felix. Lopez, is to be understood in the context of the natural features of the soil and the beheavier of the Rivers of the region. It is to be noticed that the right of accretion could be claimed by a riparian owner of lands in respect of some lands, which did not belong to any individual owner but appertained to public domain, that is, the property of the State, and was liable to pay a proportionately increased rent in respect of the additional lands gained by alluvion. If the land so added by alluvion was the reformed land belonging to another individual could claim back the said land in his own right because his right to the said land bad not been affected in any manors by the fact of its submergence under water and also because the right of accretion to which the repairing owner to whose land this newly appearing land was joined by recess of water, was entitled, was not in derogation of anybody' else's right. This right could not be claimed in defeasance of an owner's right to reformation in situ.</u>

19. The former tenancy law, as incorporated in sections 17 and 18 of the Rent Act 1859, recognized the principle that a tenant was liable to enhancement of rent in case of increment of the area of the land of his tenancy by allusion or otherwise and that similarly a tenant was entitled to abatement of rent in case of diminution of the area of the land of his tenancy by dilution or otherwise. On diluvion a tenant was entitled to reduction of rent in respect of the diluviated property under section 17 of the Act but his title to such property was not affected in any way by such dilution and whenever they said property reappeared he could take back the property in his own right, however long the period of submergence might be. On the repeal of the Rent Act 1859, by the enactment of Bengal Tenancy Act 1885, similar provisions as to abatement and enhancement of rent were made in section 52 of the Act. There were no specific provisions relating to the right of accretion or right to reformation in sue either in the Rent Act of 1889 or The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885. Such matters were regulated by e provisions of Alluvion and diluvion Regulation of 1825 and the principles laid down by the judicial authorities. Some change was effected in 1929 when section 86A was inserted in the Bengal Act by an amendment introduced by Bengal Act IV of 1928, which provided that the tenants' right in the diluviated lands, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, would be deemed to have been surrendered and would be extinguished, if the tenant obtained any abatement in respect of such dilution. This extinction of the right in respect of reformation in situ was dependent on the tenant's obtaining an abatement of rent of such land which was to be deemed, according to the amendment, an act or surrender on his part. It was, however, clearly provided in sub section (2) of this newly inserted section that such extinction of right would not affect the accrual of his right of accretion in respect of the said land if it was available to him under any other law. In 1938 a new section 86A was substituted in place of the aforesaid provision, enlarging the rights of the tenants in certain respects. This new provision provided for automatic abatement of rent in case of the loss of land by delusion, and also ensured the subsistence of the right title and interest of the tenant in the lands lost by such diluvion for a period of 20 years, notwithstanding the abatement of rent of such lands.

<u>20. After the partition of the country a big change was effected in 1951 in the land tenure system of the country by the enactment of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 where under all grades of rent-receivers intervening between the Government and the actual occupants of the soil were abolished and such occupants became tenants directly under the Government, subject to a ceiling as to the maximum area of land which a tenant can hold. No substantial change in regard to the law as to accretion or reformation in situ was, however, brought about by this enactment excepting that a specific provision incorporating the law of accretion, which was so long regulated by the provisions of Bengal Regulation XXI of 1825 was made in section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The provisions relating to abatement of rent due to diluvion of some land of the tenancy and subsistence of the tenants' title in respect o such land, similar to those contained in section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act, were incorporated in section 86 of the new Act, Part V of the Act which contains sections 86 and 87 came into force on different dates in different areas of the country on the publication of the Notifications as prescribed under section 79 of the Act and, according to the provisions of section 80 of the Act, on and from the date of coming into force of the said Part in a particular area the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed in the said area.</u>

<u>21. On June 28, 1972 the riparian owner's right of accretion which was recognized by the usage and custom of the country, as referred to in the preamble of the Bengal Regulation XI of 1815 and which had enjoyed the sanction of positive legislation for about a century and a half was abrogated by President's Order No. 72 of 1972, which substituted, in place of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, a new Section 87 which is to the following effect;</u>

<u>"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being enforce, when any land has been gained by gradual accession, whether from the recess of a river or of the sea, it shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy to which it may be thus annexed, but shall vest absolutely in the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and shall be at their disposal."</u>

22. The aim and object of this amending legislation has not been spelt out in the Presidential Order nor there do any reference in the order to any possible mischief which this legislation intended to remedy. It has been stated in a very brief preamble, as is usual in modern legislation, that "it is expedient to amend the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950" "for the purposes appearing" in the enacting provisions. When the law of accretion was given a legislative shape in Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 the law-making authority explained in a very detailed and comprehensive preamble, which may have been prolix in certain respects but sufficiently expressive of the considerations which weighed with the said authority in making the said legislation. This preamble has been quoted above for the proper appreciation of the nature and background of the right created by the said regulation and the principle underlying it.

23. The provisions of this new section 87 are obviously prospective and became operative only from the date of the enactment of the Order i.e. 2th June, 1972. According to the terms of the said provisions they are applicable only to those lands which accreted to the land of a riparian owner after the date of the promulgation of the said President's Order. There seems to be no difficulty in the construction of these provisions. On the 4th November, 1972, however, another President's Order being President's Order No. 137 of 1972 was promulgated making further amendment of the law of accretion by re-numbering the aforesaid provision of section 87 as sub-section (1) and by adding two other sub-secretions to the following effect:

"(2) The provision of sub-section (1) shall apply to all land so gained whether before or after the 28th June, 1972, but shall not apply to any land so gained before the said date if the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Sixth Amendment) Order 1972 	(P.O. No. 137 of 1972), under the law then in force.

"(3)All suits, applications, appeals or other proceedings for the assertion of any claims to hold, as an increment to any holding, any land gained or alleged to have been gained from the recess of a river or of the sea, pending before any Court or authority on the date of commencement of the said Order shall not be further proceeded with and shall abate and no Court shall entertain any suit, application or other legal proceedings in respect of any such claim".

24. Sub-section (2) purports to give a kind of retrospective effect to the provision of sub-section (1), and sub-section (3) purports to enact a very wide barring provision in respect of suits, applications, appeals and other proceedings, in which any claim of right of accretion has been or may be made. It is these two sub-sections of section 87, which have given rise to the controversy as to their correct import. It has been urged by the learned Attorney-General as well as by Mr. S. R. Pal. learned Counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent No. 7, and by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of respondents No. 1 and 6, that the expression, "whether before or after 28-6-72" as contained in the above quoted sub-section (2), does not contain any limiting words as to the point of time beyond which the retrospective operation of the said sub-section cannot be extended and the plain meaning of such an expression is that the right of accretion cannot be claimed by a person in respect of any lands which may have accreted to his lands at any time before 28-5-72 or may accrate at any time after the said date. According to them, the only limitation the abrogation of the right of accretion, in respect of the lands which were gained before 28-6-72, as provided in sub-section (2), is contained in the later part of the said sub-section which is recognition or declaration of such right by a competent authority or the Court before the date of the commencement of the President's Order No. 137 of 1972 i.e., 4th November, 1972.

25. Mr. T.H. Khan, learned Counsel for appellants, has on the other hand, contended that the effect of making the provision of sub-section (1) retrospective by virtue of the provision of sub-section (2) is the divestment of the title of a riparian owner to the accreted lands which had already been acquired by him under the law of the country and the provision of sub-section (2) is to be therefore strictly construed in such a way as will affect the vested right as little as possible.

<u>26. It is a well-settled rule of interpretations that statutes are to be interpreted prospectively, unless the language of the Statutes makes them retrospective, heiter expressly or by necessary intendment. The statement of this role has been made in Craies on Statute Law (6th Edition, 1963) at pp 388-389 in the following words;</u>

<u>"And perhaps no rule of construction is more firmly established than this-that a retrospective operation is not to be given to a statute so as to impair an existing right or obligation otherwise than as regards matter of procedure unless that effect cannot be avoided without doing violence to the language of the enactment. If the enactment is expressed in language which is fairly capable of either interpretation, it ought to be construed as prospective only.</u>

<u>27. The effect of making the provision of sub-section (1) of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act applicable to any land which may have been gained by accession by the recess of a river or the sea before 28.6.72, as it purported to have been done under President's Order No. 137 of 1972 appears to do away with, in the literal sense of the words used in the amending Presidential Order/ the right which had been acquired by the riparian owner under Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 and, if such accession took place after Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act had come into force, also under section 87 of the Act, as it stood before the enactment of the President's Order No. 72 of 1972.</u>

28. The Endeavour of the Court shall be to interpret the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act in such a manner as will not affect, or, will affect as little as possible, the said right without doing any violence to the language used and if the language used in the said provision is capable of being interpreted both ways, that is prospectively as well as retrospectively, the former is to be preferred.

<u>29. In considering the rules of interpretation in respect of a statutory provision having retrospective operation, the following statutory rule of English law as laid down by Lindey L.J. in delivering the judgment of the Court of Appeals in the case of Lauri vs. Renad, (1892) 3 Ch. 402 at page 421, may be usefully referred to:</u>

<u>"It is a fundamental rule of English Law that no statute shall be construed so as to have a retrospective operation unless its language is such as plainly to require such a construction; and the same rule involves another and a sub-ordinance rule to the effect that a statute is not to be construed so as to have a greater retrospective effect than its language renders necessary."</u>

30. No doubt, the expression, 'whether before or after 28-6-72' , as contained in sub-section (2) of section 87, purports to make the provision of sub-section (1), which has, in effect, abrogated the law of accretion, applicable also to the case of land which appeared before 28-6-72 and such application having had the effect of extinguishing an existing right of the tenant in respect of the land which had been added to his land as accretion, there seems to be no difficulty in holding that some retrospective effect was sought to be given to the said provision. If, however, we road the said provision in the context of the provisions of the Act as a whole, it will be evident that notwithstanding the use of very general terms in sub-section (2), much limited retrospectively is to be given to the said expression so as to make it meaningful and consistent with the rest of the provisions of the Act.

31. The provision of sub-section (1) of section 87 that the land gained by accession shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy makes it abundantly clear that the said provision is applicable only to the land which has been added to the land of a raiyat or any other tenant and it is not attracted to the case of the land which has been added to the khas land of a proprietor or a tenure-holder. If for the applicability of the aforesaid provision the Legislature conceived of a situation where there were the lands of a tenant as well as those of a proprietor or a tenure-holder, there appears to be absolutely no good reason to exclude the khas land of a proprietor or a tenure-holder from the operation of the said provision and thus to discriminate against those who were not so. The inference seems to be irresistible that, for the application of the said provision, the Legislature was conceiving of a situation where there were no proprietors nor tenure holders but were only tenants and such a situation arose when all the rent receiving interests were acquired by the Government under the provisions of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

32. The provisions of section 3 of the Act which incorporate special provisions for acquisition of the interest of the rent-receivers are very significant in this connection. According to sub-section (4) of section 3, on and from the date specified in the notifications issued under Section 3(1), all interests of rent receivers in the estate, taluks holdings or tenancies including their interests in their khas lands, as covered by the said notifications, vested absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and the consequences, as adumbrated in clauses (e) and (f) of sub-section (4), followed. The relevant parts of the said clauses are quoted below:

33. Section 3(4) : On and from the date specified in the notification under sub-section (1)-

(e) all tenants holdings lands in such estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies directly under the rent-receiver specified in the notification under subsection (1) shall become tenants directly under the Provincial Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent paying lands so held by them, to the Provincial Government and not to anybody else :

(f) all such rent-receivers shall be entitled to hold as tenants directly under the Provincial Government such of their khas lands as has not been acquired under subsection (2) and shall be liable to pay to the Provincial Government, the rent determined for such lands under section 5."

<u>24. According to the aforesaid provisions on and from the date specified in the notifications all tenants in respect of the lands of their tenancies, and the rent receivers in respect of their khas lands, became tenants directly under the Government in respect of the said lands. If any land had accreted to the land of the tenants or the khas land of the rent-receivers before the date specified in the said notifications, the said accreted land became a part of their tenancies or khas land, as the case may be, under the law then in force and they became tenants, by virtue of the provisions of clauses (e) and (f) of sub-section (4) of Section 3 of the Act, directly under the Government in respect of the said lands. The right of accretion accruing to the tenants or the rent-receivers in respect of the lands, accreting to the lands of their tenancies of khas lands, was given a new statutory force by the said legislative & provisions and the right so acquired became indefeasible in the sense that it was not dependent for its enforceability on any further recognition or declaration by any authority or court. Since the State Acquisition an Tenancy Act had come into force on 16.5.51, the notifications under section 3 of the Act were issued in respect of certain big rent receivers from time to time as a special measure for acquisition of their interests on or about the 2nd April, 1956 several omnibus notifications under section 3 of the Act purporting to acquire the entire interest of the whole body of the rent-receivers within the province of East Bengle with effect from 14.4.56 were issued, and since 14th April, 1956 all accreted lands, if any, adjoining those of the tenants or rent receivers became parts of their tenancies by virtue of the aforesaid provisions of The State Acquisition on and Tenancy Act. Having regard to the legal consequences flowing from the notifications under section 3 of the Act, as referred to above, no retrospective effect can be given to the provision of sub-section (2) of Section 87 of the Act, in any view of the matter, in most of the cases beyond 14.4.56, as the said provision read with that of sub-section (1) does not purport to extinguish or nullify any right which has been created under the provision of this very statute, of which this newly enacted section 87 is a part. It is significant that in the introductory clause of sub-section (1) of section 87, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force" there is reference only to ''any other law", but there is no reference to the law as contained in the present Act. It is, therefore, reasonable to conclude that there was never any intention on the part of the legislative authority to extend the retrospectively of section 87 beyond 14.4.56 or such other date as may have been specified in any earlier notifications under section 3(1) of the Act.</u>

35. Further statutory cover has been given to the rights of rent-receivers as well as agricultural and non-agricultural tenants to hold the lands of their tenancies as tenants under the Government under items No. (1) and (4) of Section 44 of the Act. After the interests of all the rent receivers as well as all non-retainable lands belonging to such rent-receivers had been acquired under the special provisions of Chapter II, as contained in section 3 of the Act, Compensation Assessment rolls in respect of all the acquired interests as well as other acquirable interests, which were not acquired under the special provisions, were prepared and finally published under section 42 of the Act. As has been provided under section 44 of the Act, on the publication of a notification in the Official Gazette under sub-section (2) of section 43, declaring that a compensation Assessment Roll has been finally published, certain consequences as mentioned in items (1) to (8) of section 44 ensued, of which items (2) and (4) are relevant for our purpose, and the said items are to the following effect :

(2) Each proprietor, tenure holder and other rent receiver, whose interests in any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy or in any part of any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy as the case may be, within the area to which such roll relates, are acquired under this Act, shall with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the Official Gazette, be entitled to retain possession of this Act, as a tenant. under the Provincial Government all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession of and holy, subject to the provision of this to, as a to cant, under Provincial Government all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession under Chapter IV and he hall.; to pay rent for such lands to the Provincial Government ;

(4) all cultivating radiates, cultivating under radiates and other tenants holding lands within the area to which such roll relates immediately before the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of such publication of such notification, shall with effect from the first day of the said agricultural year, if they have not already become tenants directly under the Provincial Government under any other provision of this Act, become tenants directly under the Provincial Government and shall have the right to continue to hold, subject to the provisions of this Act, as tenants under the Provincial Government, such of those lands as have not vested in the Provincial government under item (3) or under any other provision of this Act and shall be liable to pay rent to the Provincial Government in respect of the lands so continued to be held;

<u>36. Under the aforesaid provisions of section 44, on the publication of a notification under section 43(2) that a Compensation Assessment roll had been finally published for a certain local area, all rent receivers, including the proprietors and tenure holders, all cultivating radiates and underraiyats and other tenants within the said area, to which such roll related, acquired the right to hold the lands which had not been acquired by and vested in the Provincial Government with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the publication of the said notification. All holders of land within the area in respect of which the Compensation Assessment roll had been published became tenants, under the aforesaid statutory provision, under the Provincial Government in respect of the lands held by them, and if there had been any land gained by accession from the recess of river of the sea, they became tenants liable to pay rent to the Government in respect of the said land as well, under the provision of Section 44. Statutory right also does not appear to have been set at naught by the legislature by enacting sub-section (2) of section 87. The retrospectively of the said provision cannot therefore be extended beyond the first day of the agricultural year next following the publication of the notification under section 43(2) of the Act evidencing the final publication of the Compensation Assessment Rolls.</u>

37. There appears to be another limitation to the retrospectively of section 87 of the Act. This section is contained in Part V of the Act, which includes sections 9 to 152 of the Act. We have already noticed that section 79 provides for commencement of the provisions contained in Part V of the Act in different areas on different dates and section 80 provides for repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act along with some other Statutes in the said areas on the commencement of the sad Part therein. It is pertinent to quote section 79 in this connection, which is as follows;

"79 This Part or any portion thereof shall comment force in such areas, on such dates and to such extent as the Provincial Government may by notification direct and when any portion of this Part comes into force in any area the provisions of such portion shall have effect in such area notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force."

<u>38. According to the above quoted provision, section 87 could have no effect before the provisions of Part V were brought into operation by the Government by issuing appropriate notifications under section 79 of the Act, the first of which appears to have been issued on 5.8.54 in the Sub-Division of Patuakhali in the district of Bakerganj and the last of which appears to have been issued on 5.8.65 in the District of Faridpur. Now, we are as to find out the intention of the Law maker as to the extent of retrospectively of section 87, from the use of the words "whether before or after 28.6.72" instead of so gained" in sub-section (2), It may also very well be argued that had it been the intention of the Law maker to give the widest possible retrospective effect to the provision of sub-section ('), it could have been very well expressed in sub-section (1) itself, instead of enacting sub-section (2). by inserting the words "nor shall be deemed to have been considered'' in sub-section (1) after the words "it shall not be considered" and the words and shall be deemed to have vested" after the words "shall vest" and by adding at the end of the said subsection, the words of the later part of sub-section (2) in the following manner:</u>

<u>"unless (Sic) the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (6th Amendment) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 137 of 1972) under the law then in force.</u>

<u>39. By the use of such phraseology, the expression of the legislative intent, if such intent was to give the full retrospective effect would have been less ambiguous and more certain, and there would have been also more economy of words. But the manner in which sub-section (1) and subsection (2) have been drafted, it is manifest that it was no legislative intent to give such a wide retrospective operation to the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87. The past rights which have already accrued have not been sought to be affected by President's Order No. 137 of 1972 retrospectively, but such rights were purported to be affected only prospectively. That is to say, the right of accretion which the riparian owner had acquired in respect of the lands added to his holding before 28-6-72 using the more specific provision "whenever ceased to be operative and to remain in force only since 4-11-72, the date of the coming into force of the President's Order No. 137 of 1972. In that sense also it would no doubt, be destructive of some vested rights, though in a prospective sense.</u>

<u>40. The use of the term 'Malik" in sub section (2) is also significant. Such term can be used in place of the term 'raiyat' or tenant only after Part V of the Act has come into operation. Section 81 (1) of the Act provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of Part V in any area, there shall be within that area one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, Maliks' and the rights and liabilities of every such land holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part, and clause (8) of section 82, which is an interpretation section also provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this Part in any area, the word 'Malik' shall be deemed to have been substituted for the word 'rayiat' or 'tenant'. The use of the word malik in place of the word 'raiyat' or tenant' in sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act to denote a person whose right to hold the newly added land as accretion to his holding or tenancy might be recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the commencement of President's Order No. 137 of 1972 unmistakably points out that the legislative authority was contemplating a situation in subsection (I) and sub-section (2) of Section 87 Which could arise only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act in the area in which the accreting lands are situated. The retrospectively of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act cannot therefore be pushed beyond the date of the commencement of Part V of Act in the area where the accretion in question had taken place and it is only such accretion as took place after the coming into force of Part V of the Act to which sub-section (1) read with sub-section (2) of section 87, may apply. The date of the commencement of Part V of the Act in any area must necessarily be a date later than that of the publication of the notification under Section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act in that area.</u>

41. Now we are faced with the question as to the interpretation and true import of subsection (3) of section 87 of the Act. This subsection, if read in isolation from the rest of the section and independently of the remaining provisions of the Act, would lead to some absurd result. All the three sub-section of section 87 must be read together and all of them must be given a coherent and consistent meaning. The provisions of sub section(1) and (2) of the section have provided for non-accrual, and, in certain cases, extinction, of the right of accretion, and the barring provision contain d in sub-section (3) is to be related necessarily to such non-accrual or extinction.

<u>42. We have seen that, because of the limited retrospectively of the provision of sub-section (2) there may have been accretions to the lands of a tenant, after the publication of a notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act but before the commencement of Part V of the Act, which have not been affected by the retrospective operation given to sub-section (1) by sub-section (2) and, as we have held, only such accretions as took place after Part V of the Act had come into force in the area where the accreted lands are situated, have been brought under the purview of subsection (I) and (2) of section 87 of the Act. It is natural that subsection (3) will have operation only in respect of such accretions as have been contemplated in sub-section (1) and (2) of section 87 of the Act.</u>

43. The plain meaning of sub-section (3) in literal sense, appears to be that all pending suits, applications, appeals and other legal proceedings in which there is any assertion of a claim of the right of accretion in respect of any land shall abate and no court shall entertain any suit, application, appeal or other legal proceeding in respect of any such claim, but such a meaning is clearly in-consistent with the true import of sub-section (1) and (2) of section 87, as has been indicated above.

<u>44. We have noticed that all accretions, which took place before the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act, have been statutorily recognized to be the lands appertaining to the tenancies of the riparian owners and the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of Sections 3(4) or items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act have clearly conferred the right of tenancy upon the riparian owner in respect of such accredited lands. Any suit etc. which may be brought in respect of such land is not obviously a suit in which the assertion of the claim of right is on the basis of the riparian owner's right of accretion. Such a suit is really on the basis of the statutory right as has been conferred by clauses (e) and (0 of sections 3 (4) or items (2) and (4) of sect ion 44 of the Act and is, there-fore, clearly outside the purview of sub-section (3) of section 37 of the Act. As regards the accretions, which took place after the publication of the notifications under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act but before the coming into force of Part V of the Act, they are also, we have noticed above, beyond the scope of sub-sections (1) and (2) of sections 87 and as such, the rights which accrued to the riparian owners in respect of such accretions have not been affected in any way by the said provisions of section 87. There seems to be no conceivable reason why the legislative authority, while preserving the right of a riparian owner in respect of such accretions under sub-section (1) and (2) would deprive, by sub-section (3) the said owner of the remedy to enforce the said right. Such reading of sub-section (3) would undoubtedly lead to injustice and some absurd consequences, which cannot be the intention of the legislative authority. Sub-section (3) should be read harmoniously with sub-sections (1) and (2) and the land gained or alleged to have been gained from the recess of a river or the sea, as have been contemplated in subsection (3) must be such lands as are within the purview of sub sections (1) and (2) of section 87. It will necessarily be those accredited lands which have appeared as hard soil only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act and the provision as to the and abatement of suits etc. as made in sub-section (3) are attracted in case of those suits etc. where a claim of the right is asserted in respect of such lands.</u>

45. Let us now try to find out the meaning and scope of section 86 of the Act which was substituted on the 4th November, 1972 by President's Order No. 135 of 1972, replacing the old section 86 of the Act, the relevant provisions of which are to the following effect: Section 86(1) If the land of a hold in or a portion of such lands are lost by dilution, the rent of the holding shall be abated by such amount as may be considered by the Revenue Officer to be fair and equitable in accordance with the rules made in this behalf by the Government."

(2) "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors in interest shall be extinguished in such lands or a portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by dilution took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972 lands or portion thereof within twenty years of their loss by dilution, and be liable to pay the arrears of rent without interest or damage in respect of the land, which has re-appeared, for the period during which it was lost or four years whichever is less;

Provided that when the lands or portion thereof which have so reappeared added to the total area of land already in the possession of such tenant or his successors-in interest exceed the area of land which the tenant was allowed to retain in his possession under section 20, or the limit laid down in section 90 whichever be greater such tenant or his successors-in-interest shall not have the right to re-possession of such excess area of lard ; and such excess area shall vest in and be at the disposal of the Provincial Government ; (3) All lands, so lost by dilution under sub-section ( 2 ) which re-appeared -before the date of commencement of the said Order, but in respect of which the right of the tenant, whose land was so lost or his successors-in-interest, to repossession was not finally recognized or declared by a competent a authority or Court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands. So lost by dilution under the said ubsection which may reappear on or after the said date shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and shall be at its disposal.

(4)

(5) All suits, applications, appeals or other proceedings in respect of any claim to the re-possession of any land lost by dilution which has re-appeared or is alleged to have reappeared, pending before any Court or authority on the date of commencement of the said Order, shall not be further proceeded with and shall abate and no court shall entertain any suit, application or other legal proceedings in respect of any such claim.

Explanation:-For the purpose of this section, the word "family" shall have the same meaning as in clause (a) of section 151 J, as amended by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order 1972".

46. It will appear that the provision of subsection (1) of this new section, which latest to abatement of rent in respect of the land lost by dilution did not bring about any great charge in the law then in force, as this provision is similar to sub-section (I) of the old section as amended by East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXI of 1969 which dispensed with the filing of an application by the tenant to the Revenue Officer for abatement of rent, as was required under the former provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act. This provision is clearly prospective and refers to land which is still subject to delusion. The provision of sub-section (2) which purports to extinguish the title of the tenant to the land which has been lost by delusion, whether before or after the commencement of the President's Order No. 135 of 1972, is also clearly prospective and there is no difficulty as to the construction of the said provision. But the construction of subsection (3) which purports to confer title upon the Government in respect of the lands which were lost by delusion under sub-section (2) but re-appeared before the date of commencement of the Order seems to be fraught with some difficulty, in so far as its real import is concerned. The plain meaning of the said provision seems to be that the lands which were lost by diluvion but have reappeared before the commencement of the Order and also the lands so lost by diluvion which may re-appear on or after the said date shall vest in the Government and shall be at the disposal. So far as the second part of the subsection is concerned, there is no difficulty, but the first part of the sub-section which provides for accrual of right in favour of the Government in respect of the lands which were lost by diluvion but have re appeared before the commencement of the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 does not appear to be consistent with the provision of subsection (2) of the section, which purports to extinguished the title of the tenant to such land as has been lost by diluvion. Subsection (2) does not appear to contemplate a case where the lands which were lost by diluvion before the commencement of the order but have also re-appeared before such commencement does on the other hand, mean that the title of the tenant to the land which is lost to him by diluvion at the time of the commencement of the Order shall be extinguished on such commencement, although the diluvion took place before such commencement. If the diluvion and the loss in consequence thereof have ceased, and the land reappeared before the commencement of the Order there was no discontinuance of his right and it subsisted with all its force. But the first part of subsection (3) which purports to vest such lands on the Government seems to be incongruous to a certain extent, because, by such vesting, the tenant is also correspondingly divested of all his rights by necessary implication, although under sub-section (2) which provides for the extinguishment of the tenants' right, such divestment is not contemplated. However, if sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 86 are read together, it appears that the legislative authority wanted to give a kind of retrospective effect to the provision of subsection (2) although such intention has not been properly expressed in the language used in the said subsection (3) is clear so far as it Oaks to divest, though in-directly a tenant of his title to the land which was once lost by diluvion but reappeared before the commencement of the Order, unless his right to repos session was recognized or declared by a competent authority or court. But the question is, as it was the case of sub-sections (I) and (2) of section 87 whether the lawmaker intended to give the full or limited retrospective effect to the provision of sub-section (3) of section 85 of the Act.

<u>47. For the consideration discussed in connection with the interpretation of section 87 of the Act, we are of the opinion that the provisions of subsection (2) and (3) of section 86 of the Act cannot be given any retrospective effect beyond the date of coming into force of Part V of the Act in the area in which the diluviated land is situated.</u>

48. Subsection (5) of section 86 creates a bar in respect of certain kind of suits, applications, appeals and other proceedings and provides for abatement of such suits, applications, appeals and proceedings, if pending at the commencement of the Order. The barring provisions, as contained in sub-section (f) of section 86 are in terms similar to those in sub-section (3) of section 87 of the Act and, in a similar way, the provisions of sub-section (5) of section 86 shall have to be read, for the proper application of their import, along with subsection (2) and (3) of the said section. Such reading will show that the said provision is applicable in respect of those suits, applications, appeals and other legal proceedings, the subject-matter of which is a claim to the repossession of the land contemplated in sub sections (2) and (3) of section 86 and that such suits etc. if pending on the commencement of the Order, shall abate.

49. We have already noticed that sub-section (2) of section 86 is applicable to the land which was lost by diluvion before commencement of President's Order No. 135 of the 1972 and was still under water on the commencement of the said Order, as well as those lands which are lost after commencement of the said Order and that sub-section (3) of the section attracted to the land which was lost by diluvion but has re-appeared before the commencement of the Order, but after coming into force of Part V of the Act, as well as the lands which were lost by diluvion but have re-appeared on or after the commencement of the Order. The suits, applications appeals and other legal proceedings ferried to in sub-section (5) must necessarily involve claims which come within the mischief of sub sections (2) and (3) of the section 86 and relate to lands which are lost by diluvion after the commencement of the Order as well as lands which were lost by diluvion before the commencement of the Order, but have reappeared after coming into force of Part V of the Act.

<u>50. Now, the provisions of sections 86 and 87 as have been enacted by President's Order Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 are clearly inapplicable to the facts of the suit out of which this appeal arises, inasmuch as there is no assertion in the plaint of the suit of a claim of the right of accretion or reformation in situ in respect of the lands in suit. The allegations made in the plaint are that the lands in suit which formerly appertained to the estate of Bishweswar Roy Chowdhury were lost by diluvion, that the said lands having re-appeared as firm land and become fit for cultivation, the 10/-annas share of the said lands was settled with the predecessors of plaintiffs No. 1 to 42 and plaintiff No. 45 by the proprietors of the said share on the 1st Jaistha, 1331 B S. that is, middle of May, 1924 and the remaining 6/4 as share in the said lands was also settled with some of the plaintiffs and the predecessors of some other plaintiffs in 1345 B.S. i.e. 1938/39. The basis of some of plaintiffs' claim in respect of the 10/- as share of the lands is the settlement granted by the landlords of the said share in May, 1924 and that of some other plaintiffs in respect of the remaining 6/- as share is the settlement granted to the said plaintiff by the landlords of the 6/- as share in 1938/39. There is no recital in the plaint as to accretion in respect of any part of the lands in suit. There are, no doubt, some allegations in the plaint as to diluvion of the land in suit aid subsequent reformation of the said lands but they happened, according to the said allegations, long ago i.e., prior to May 1924. The plaintiffs have prayed in the suit for a declaration of their title which accrued, according to the averment made in the plaints, from the settlement granted by the proprietors, partly in May 1924 and partly in 193 8/39. After the promulgation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in 1961 the rent receiving interests of the plaintiffs' landlords were acquired by the Government on publication of the notification under section 3 and section 43(2) of the Act and the plaintiffs have become tenants directly under the Government by virtue of the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of sub-section (4) of section (3) and items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act slur then. The immediate basis of the plaintiffs' claim in the suit, therefore, is the statutory right conferred upon them by section 3(4)(e) and (f) and there-after, under items (2) and (4) of section 44 and the remote basis of the claim may be said to be the settlement granted by the superior land-lords partly in 1924 and partly in 1938-39. But the basis of the plaintiffs' in respect of the lands  in their site after they had been lost by diluvion, and, as such, the present suit cannot be said, in any view of the matter, to be a suit for a claim to repossession of any land lost by diluvion which has re-appeared or is alleged to have reappeared.</u>

51. It has already been pointed out that the reformation of the dituviated lands as recited in the plaint, took place before 1924 and on such reformation the lands were restored to the possession of the proprietors in full right under the law then in force and the said proprietors, by granting settlement transferred certain right, title and interest in respect of the said lands to the plaintiffs or their predecessors, who acquired the said right, title and interest by virtue of the said settlement. There having been no recitals in the plaint to the effect that the lands in suit were under water as a result of diluvion on or after the commencement of the Order or that they re-appeared before the commencement of the Order, after they previously lost by diluvion. Sub-section (3) of section 87 has no manner of application to the facts of the case. Similarly, we have seen that there having been no allegation of accretion with respect to lands in suit, sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 86 of the Act are clearly inapplicable to the facts of the instant suit. The learned Judges of the High Court were therefore not correct in holding that the suit was hit by the provisions of sections 86 and 87 as amended by President's Orders No. 72 of 1972, 135 of 1972, and 137 of 1972.

52. The result, therefore, is that the appeal is allowed with no order as to costs. Let the revisional application filed before the High Court Division be treated as a Memorandum of Appeal and the appeal before the High Court Division, so treated is allowed with costs against the contesting respondents and the order of abatement as made by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge and affirmed by the High Court Division is set aside, subject to the payment of deficit court fees payable on the Memorandum of Appeal so treated within six months from the date of the arrival of the records in the High Courts.

End.
