parties:
Sher Ali Mia --------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Special Tribunal No. IV, Dacca and others. ----------Respondents.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, C.J.—In this application the petitioner prays for a declaration that the order dated 8.4.75 passed by the Special Tribunal No. IV of Dacca in Special Tribunal Case No. 66 of 1975 to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Facts in short which laid to the filing of the writ petition in this Court are like this. The petitioner and 27 other members of the Putiya Weavers Co-operative Society lodged a First Information Report on 9.3.74 with the Shibpur Police station alleging various criminal activities against the Secretary of the Society Khandker Gulzar Hossain. In the First Information Report it was alleged, inter alia, that the Secretary misappropriated a few lakhs of takas of the Society by illegally disposing of allotted quota of yarn; and that the Secretary misappropriated a sum of Taka 50,000/- which he realised from the Society members as share money; and that the Secretary possesses illegal arms and threatens the members whenever there is any protest from them.

3. After police investigation charge sheet was submitted on 20.12.74 against Khandker Gulzar Hossain and 5 others under sections 406/467/420 of the Bangladesh Penal Code and section 25 of the Special Powers Act and under section 9 of the Essential Commodities Act (Act I of 1956). The Special Tribunal took cognizance of the case under Special Powers Act, and when the case was pending for trial, the Special Public Prosecutor submitted an application on 8.4.75 for according consent for withdrawal of the case under section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the ground that the prosecutor had been given the instruction by the Ministry of lime Affairs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Vide Memo No. 160/E (Home), Dated 8-4-75) to withdraw the case. The Special Tribunal passed the impugned order allowing the prayer of the Special Public Prosecutor for withdrawal of the ease.

The petitioner challenged the legality of the impugned order.

4. Mr. Sirajul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the Special Tribunal acted illegally and without jurisdiction in according the consent for withdrawal of the case, although the power contained in section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not available to the Special Tribunal. It is further contended that the impugned order cannot be sustained also on the ground that the Special Tribunal accorded consent to the prayer for withdrawal mechanically and without proper application of mind.

5. In elaborating the first point the learned Advocate submits that the Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act, 1974 is not a criminal Court as contemplated under the Code of Criminal Procedure and as such, such a Tribunal is not competent to exercise the power as contained in section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. With reference to sections 1 (2), 5(2), 6 and 29 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the learned Advocate submits that the legislature never contemplated a Court of the nature of Special Tribunal. This is a Tribunal created under special statute for trial of special type of cases. Such Tribunal is competent to exercise only those powers which have been specifically conferred upon the Tribunal. According to the learned Advocate, Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act is not a Criminal Court as enumerated in the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this context the learned Advocate submits that the Special. Tribunal judge is not competent to exercise any power under the Code of Criminal Procedure which has not been included in the powers of Special Tribunal as conferred under sections 27(4), 28 and 29 of the Special Powers Act. According to the learned Advocate section 29 of the Special Powers Act clearly provides that the Special Tribunal will exercise only those provisions of the Code, so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act; and while exercising the power the Special Tribunal shall exercise all the powers conferred by the Code on a Court of Sessions exercising original jurisdiction.

According to the learned Advocate the matter of withdrawal as provided in section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure not being a part of the trial the Special Tribunal, on the authority as contained in section 29, is not competent to accord consent to the prayer of withdrawal of the case made by the Special Public Prosecutor.

6. Fakir Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the Respondent No. 2 submits that the Special Tribunal as constituted under Special statute, is a Criminal Court as contemplated under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Advocate also refers to sections 1(2), 5(2), 6 and 29 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to show that a Criminal Court constituted under special statute has been indicated in the Criminal Procedure Code  itself. According to the learned Advocate under sections 27(4), 28 and 29 of the Special Powers Act the Special Tribunal is with all the powers of a Court of Sessions exercising original jurisdiction. The Special Tribunal being a Criminal. Court as contemplated under the Code of Criminal Procedure, is competent to exercise the powers conferred in Section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In support of the argument the learned Advocate refers to the case of Govinda Shed Jamadar and others Vs. The State 27 D.L.R. 67, wherein permission of withdrawal of prosecution under sec; ion 494 of the Code in connection with a proceeding under Article 8(1) of the Bangladesh Collaborators (Special Tribunal) Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 8 of 1972), has been found to have passed in accordance with law.

<u>7. On examination of the relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, namely, sections 1(2), 5(2), 6 and 29 of the Code it appears that a Criminal Court constituted under special statute is contemplated in the Code of Criminal Procedure. It further appears that such a criminal court is competent to exercise only those powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure as specifically conferred upon it under the special statute. Section 5(2) of the Code provides as under:</u>

<u>"All offences, under any other law shall be investigated, inquired into, tried, and otherwise dealt with according to the same provisions, but subject to any enactment for the time being in force regulating the manner or place of investigating, inquiring into, trying or otherwise dealing with such offences."</u>

<u>Section 29(1) of the Code reads as under "Subject to the other provisions of this Code, any offence under any other law shall, when any court is mentioned in this behalf in such law, be tried by such Court."</u>

<u>There cannot be any doubt that the Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act, or for that matter any court constituted under any special statute, is a criminal Court as contemplated in section 29(1). Such a court is to exercise its powers as are specifically conferred under the statute. In this Special Powers Act the Special Tribunal as constituted therein under section 26, has been empowered to try an offence under the Act and while trying offence the Special Tribunal is to try summarily and shall follow the procedure laid down in the Code of summary trial in summons cases. Section 28 of the Special Powers Act empowers the Special Tribunal to pass any sentence authorised by the law against any person convicted in the case. Section 29 of Special Powers Act provides as to the application of the Code of Criminal Procedure to the proceedings before the Special Tribunal. This section reads as under:</u>

<u>"The provisions of the Code, so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, shall apply to the proceedings of Special Tribunals and such Special Tribunals shall have all the powers conferred by the Code on a Court of Session exercising original jurisdiction, and a person conducting prosecution before such Special Tribunals shall be deemed to a public prosecutor."</u>

<u>8. From the above noted provision it appears that the Special Tribunal have all the powers conferred under the Code exercising criminal jurisdiction. The power as conferred under section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is one of such powers as conferred under the Code on a Court of Sessions. Therefore the Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act it competent to entertain an application filed by the Special Public Prosecutor, to accord consent to the prayer for withdrawal of the case. Section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure containing the power and procedure, provides a mode of disposal of a case. The section provides that if withdrawal is permitted before a charge has been framed the accused shall be discharged in respect of such offence or offences; and if it is made after a charge has been framed, or when under this Code no charge is required, the accused shall be acquitted in respect of such offence or offences. Therefore, an application under section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is very much part of the trial of the case, and as such the Special Tribunal exercising all the powers of a Court of sessions, is no doubt competent to allow disposal of the case as provided under section 474 of the Code.</u>

<u>9. With regard to the second contention of the petitioner that the Special. Tribunal passed the order mechanically and without application of its mind as to whether it was fit and proper to accord consent to the prayer for withdrawal of the case, it would be sufficient to say that such grievance cannot be entertained in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. Apart from that from the impugned order it appears that the learned Special Tribunal passed the order on perusal of the letter containing instruction from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh for withdrawal of the case. This order was passed after hearing the learned Special Public Prosecutor.</u>

We do not find any substance in any of the contentions raised in this application.

Therefore, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

M. H. Rahman J.—I agree.

End.

lawyer:
Ahmed Sobhan with M. Fazlul Karim, Advocates ---------For the Petitioner. 
Md. Shafiqur Rahman, Advocate ----------For Respondent No. 2.
parties:
A. Gafur---------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Election Tribunal and Munsif 2nd Court, Feni, Noakhali and another --------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam C. J.—In this application the order dated 1-3-77 passed by the Election Tribunal and Munsif, Second Court, Feni, Noakhali, granting ad-interim injunction against the petitioner restraining him from acting as. Chairman of No. 4 Fulgazi Union Parishad and taking over charge of the office of Chairman from respondent No. 2 pending the final disposal of the application for injunction has been impugned as illegal and without any lawful authority.

2. Petitioner's contention is that the Election Tribunal acted without jurisdiction in granting injunction ( ad-interim ) inasmuch as, the relevant election laws do not confer all the powers of a Civil Court, upon the Election Tribunal in other words, the Election Tribunal not being a Civil Court within the meaning of the Code of Civil. Procedure, acted without jurisdiction in slanting in junction under order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

3. From the application it appears that the petitioner was declared elected as Chair-man in the election held on. 18.1.77 for electing Chairman of No. 4 Fulgazi Union Parishad. Respondent No. 2, a defeated candidate, filed an election petition before the Election Tribunal for setting aside the election of the Chairman on various allegations. After filing the election petition respondent No. 2 filed an application praying for an order of injunction restraining the petitioner not to function as the Chairman and from taking charge from respondent No. 2 till the disposal of the case. The Election Tribunal while registering the election case issued notice upon the petitioner and others to show cause within 10 days from the date of service of the notice, as to why the petitioner should not be restrained from acting as Chairman of the said Union Parishad and from taking charge of Chairmanship from respondent No. 2 till the disposal of the case. Pending final disposal of the application an order of ad-interim injunction was made which has been impugned in this application.

4. Respondent No. 2 has entered appearance but no cause has been shown by filing any affidavit in opposition. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2 frankly concedes that the impugned order is bad in law, but he submits that the application is premature, because, the petitioner has impugned the ad interim order of injunction without waiting for the order to be passed by the Tribunal on the date fixed for hearing of the injunction matter when the petitioner could have raised all the objections.

5. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the parties and examined the relevant provisions of Local Government Ordinance, 1976 and the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1976. On examining the relevant provisions of the Election Law, it appears that the Election Tribunal acted totally without jurisdiction in entertaining an application under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with rule 49 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1976. Since the impugned order suffers from want of jurisdiction, we do not accept the submission of the learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 2 that the application is premature because, the petitioner should have raised this objection before the Tribunal at the final hearing of the application for injunction.

<u>6. We are rather surprised to find that the Election Tribunals have started exercising the power of a Civil Court as conferred under the Code of Civil Procedure, and in many cases granted injunction by exercising the Civil Court's power under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Such orders have been passed in total disregard of the decisions of this Court even though some of the decisions have been reported in the Dacca Law Reports. The person constituting the Election Tribunal should not suffer from any doubt as to the power conferred under Local Government Ordinance, 1976 and the Union Parishad. (Election) Rules, 1976. This question has been very clearly settled by this Court that Election Tribunal is a creature under the Election Laws alone. There is no scope for exercising all the powers of the Civil Court at the trial of the election petition, the question as to whether the Election Tribunal is a "Civil Court" was considered in several decisions of this Court. Two of the reported decisions in the Dacca Law Reports are discussed here. In the case of Shamsul Huq Sikder versus. Election Tribunal and others, 27 D.L.R. 388 precisely the question for consideration was as to whether the Election Tribunal had the jurisdiction to grant temporary injunction under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the report it appears that a Division Bench of this Court by an elaborate judgment answered the question in the negative. The learned Judges held as follows :—</u>

<u>“On question of applicability of the provisions of order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a proceeding before an Election Tribunal, there is no gainsaying the fact that the said provisions have no application in terms to an election dispute tried by an Election Tribunal."</u>

7. In a subsequent decision, in the case of Muzahiduddin Ahmed-Vs-Munsif, Sunamganj, Sylhet and others, 28 D. L. R. 189, the question for consideration was to whether the Election Tribunal was competent to entertain an application under order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this case the view taken in the case reported in 27 D. L. R. 388 has been followed. In this decision, to which one of us was a party the Division Bench after examining the relevant provisions of the Election Laws held as follows :—

"These Rules, in our opinion, clearly show that the Tribunal is neither a full-fledged Civil Court nor has it been invested with all the powers available under the Code of Civil Procedure. The only relief which can be granted to a party is laid down in rule 60 and the Election Tribunal is not competent to travel beyond the said rule."

8. The decisions noted above are still relevant for the purpose of the present consideration of the question as to whether the Election Tribunal is competent to act as a Civil Court and grant temporary injunction pending decision of the election petition, under the Local Govt. Ordinance, 1976 and the Union Parishad ( Election ) Rules, 1976. Section 26 of the Ordinance provides that no election under this Ordinance shall be called in question except by an election petition. Sub-section (2) provides that any candidate may make an election petition challenging the election at which he was a candidate. Sub-section (3) provided that an election petition shall be presented, in such manner as may be prescribed, to the Election Tribunal appointed under section 27. Section 27 of the Ordinance provides the power of the government to appoint the Election Tribunal by a Notification in the official gazette. It further provides that for this purpose a judicial officer is to be appointed as a Election Tribunal. Section 29 of the Ordinance empowers the government to transfer the election petition from one Election Tribunal to another. Section 29 of the Ordinance provides the method of trial of an election petition. Sub-section (3) of section 29 provides that the decision of the Election Tribunal shall be final and shall not called in question in or before any Court. Relevant rules for election dispute and trial thereof are rules 45, 48, 49 and 50 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules 1976. Rule 45 provides the manner of filing the election petition. Rule 48 provides the procedure to be followed by the Tribunal.

It reads as under :

"Subject to the provisions of these rules every election petition shall be tried, as nearly as may be, in accordance with the Procedure for the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 ( V of 1908)."

Rule 40 provides the power of the Tribunal. It reads as under:

"The Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 ( V of 1908), and shall be deemed to  be a Civil Court within the meaning of Sections 480 and 482 of the Code or Criminal Procedure, 189 8 (V of 1 898)."

9. The provisions of the rules quoted above are similar to the corresponding rules as contained in the Union Parishads and Pourashava (Election) Rules, 1973. Rule 48 is identical to Rule 61A of the Rules of 1973 and Rule 49 is identical to Rule 61 B.

<u>10. Rule 48 only empowers the Election Tribunal to try the election petition "as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure of the trial of a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure." Rule 49 provides that the Tribunal "shall have all the powers of the Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure." It further provides that it shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of Section 4 80 and 482 of the Cede of Criminal Procedure. From a reading of the rules 48 and 49 it leaves no doubt that the Election Tribunal is not Civil Court but it has been given the power to try the election petition as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure for the trial of a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure". That it is not a Civil Court is evident from rule 49 itself which provides that the Election Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Election Tribunal constituted under the special statute for the specific purpose, namely, to try the election petition as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure of the trial of a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, and further empowered to exercise all the powers of civil court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, is not clothed with all the powers of a Civil Court. If the intention of the legislature was to clothed the Tribunal with all the powers of a Civil Court and to treat it as a Civil Court, then there would not have been any necessity for providing by way of clarification, that the Tribunal shall be deemed to be a civil court within the meaning of Sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The last clause of rule 49 makes it clear beyond any doubt that the Election Tribunal, although empowered specifically to exercise the powers of the Civil Court in trying election petition, is not empowered to exercise all the powers of the Civil Court constituted under the East Bengal Civil Court Act, 1887. Election Tribunal is empowered to exercise only those powers which are necessary for trial of the election petition.</u>

<u>11. Injunction not being a part of the trial of election petition, Election Tribunal constituted under the Local Government Ordinance, 1976 is not competent to exercise any of the powers conferred under Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Election Tribunal exercising any power under order 39 of the Code of Civil procedure acts without jurisdiction.</u>

12. In view of what has been stated above the impugned order granting ad-interim injunction against the petitioner, the elected Chairman, from functioning as the Chairman pending disposal of the election petition is declared illegal and to have been passed without any lawful authority.

Therefore, the Rule is made absolute and the order dated 1-3-77 made in Election Tribunal Case No. 3 of 1977, granting ad-interim injunction, is quashed. We make no order as to costs.

M. H. Rahman, J.—I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
This rule at the instance of the pre-emptor is directed against a judgment of affirmance in a proceeding for pre-emption.

2. The petitioner, claiming to be a tenant holding land contiguous to the land sold in auction on 3-3-56 at a certificate sale, prayed for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The subject-matter of the pre-emption relates to the land recorded in R.S. Khatian 797 of Mouza Shahajira within police station Gournadi.

The certificate sale was held on 3-3-56. The property was purchased by the opposite party for a sum of Tk. 125/-. The sale was confirmed on 5-5-56 and the auction purchaser took delivery of possession 5-6-56. The certificate debtor, in spite of the sale and delivery of possession, continued in possession and the auction purchaser could not take physical possession. The petitioner claims to be the owner of a contiguous holding and as such applied for pre-emption. He learnt about the auction sale for the first time on 1-4-63 from Alauddin and Abdus Sobhan who came to know about the sale in a criminal case filed by Jamini Kanta Roy. The petitioner, thereafter, on obtaining necessary particulars and depositing the requisite amount, filed the application for pre-emption on 26-4-63. The entire land under the certificate sale is cultivable land. The land already in possession of the petitioner together with the land sought to be pre-empted will not exceed 100 bighas.

3. The auction purchaser opposite party contested the case traversing the material allegations and contending inter alia that the petitioner has no locus standi to pre-empt and as such his claim is not maintainable. According to the opposite party, he took delivery of possession through Court and is in possession of the land. He claims to have made improvement at a cost of about Tk. 8,000'00 within the knowledge of the petitioner. According to him the petitioner had knowledge of the auction sale from before and that the alleged date of his knowledge was not true and correct. The application was barred by limitation. It is further contended by the opposite party that he took delivery of possession through Court pursuant to the decree in title suit No. 388 of 1961 on 8-11-62 and that he has been enjoying usufructs through bargadars by cultivating the nal and bhiti land and also enjoying the fruits of fruit-bearing trees and the tanks by catching fish. According to the opposite party many persons holding contiguous land were not impleaded and as such the application was bad for defect of parties. It was further contended that the land in mainly a homestead, garden and tank and as such section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not applicable.

4. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record rejected the clam of pre-emption holding inter alia that application was barred by limitation. The learned Munsif, however, found that the petitioner was a contiguous owner and as such had locus standi to maintain the application for pre-emption. The learned Munsif held that the application was bad for defect of parties.

5. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the decision of the learned Munsif and rejected the pre-emption application. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the application was barred by limitation. The learned Subordinate Judge did not believe the evidence of the P.Ws. Alauddin and A. Sobhan. According, to him these P.Ws. are not disinterested witnesses. The learned Subordinate Judge found that “it is the admitted case of the petitioner that the opposite tarty cut away trees from auction sold land, filed Title Suit No. 288 of 1961 against okhroit Bijoy Kumar and the latter filed criminal case against the opposite party so on and so forth. On the face of it, the case of the petitioner that he learnt about sale on 1-4-63 cannot be believed. It seems that the petitioner as owner to the contiguous holding had knowledge of the sale from the very beginning. "The learned Subordinate Judge on a consideration of the materials on record held that "the petitioner had no locus standi to file the case and that the case is not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In reaching this conclusion the learned Subordinate Judge found that the case was one under the Bengal Tenancy Act but since the petitioner was not a co-sharer, he had no right to pre-empt under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act.

<u>6. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule contends that the pre-emptor had locus standi to apply for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred and accordingly the application was maintainable. That the sale was held on 3-3-56 and was confirmed on 5-5-56 and that the auction purchaser took delivery of possession on 5-6-66 are not disputed. According to the learned Advocate the right of pre-emption accrued not on the transfer but on the date of the pre-emptor's knowledge. That Part V of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in operation in the part of the district where the suit land situates is not in dispute. According to the learned Advocate since Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was in operation when the pre-emptor had knowledge of the transfer 'namely, the auction sale, the right of pre-emption as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred was available to the petitioner by operation of law. It is not disputed that Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in force on 2-1-58 in that locality. According to the learned Advocate the whole period can be divided into two parts, one from 3-3-56 to 1-1-58 and the other from 2-1-58 onwards. During the period from 3-3-56 till before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was made applicable to the district, obviously, the petitioner had no right of pre-emption since he was not a co-sharer to the holding and during this period the candle of the Bengal Tenancy Act was burning. Thus, the right of pre-emption if any did not accrue in favour of the petitioner from the date of auction sale as contended by Mr. Rahim. He does not dispute that the auction purchaser's title to the land in question accrued on the date of sale i.e. on 3-3-56. If this branch of argument of the learned Advocate is accepted, the position comes to this that a right of pre-emption does not accrue with the transfer. Such an interpretation is not possible without violence to the language of the statute which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"If a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may within four months of the service of notice given under section 89, or if no notice has been served under section 89; within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves and if a holding or a portion or a share of a holding is transferred, the tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may, within 4 months from the date of the knowledge of such transfer, apply to the Court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves."</u>

<u>Thus, on a construction of the statutory provision quoted above, it is evident that the right of pre-emption does not accrue on the date of knowledge but on and from the date of the transfer. The period of 4 months referred to in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is the limitation prescribed for exercising the right by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred from the date of the knowledge of such transfer. Therefore, the petitioner had no right of pre-emption before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation. The right of pre-emption in respect of a transfer after Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation was available to co-sharers as well as tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred. A transfer before Part V came in force was open to pre-emption under the Bengal Tenancy Act although the application was made after Part V came into operation. In the circumstances there is no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate The petitioner had no locus standi to file an application for pre-emption as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred in respect of a transfer which took place some two years before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in force. Accordingly the application under section 96(1) at the instance of the petitioner was not maintainable. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge correctly decided the question on consideration of the materials on record and upon application of the law correctly to the facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

<u>7. It was next contended by Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, that the application was not barred by limitation. According to him the petitioner derived the knowledge of the transfer from Alauddin and Abdus Sobhan on 1-4-63. The learned Advocate contends that since the opposite party contended that the petitioner had prior knowledge, it was for the opposite party to prove positively that the pre-emptor had such knowledge in order to knock out the claim of the petitioner on the ground of limitation. I do not think 'there is any substance in this contention. The petitioner came to court to enforce a right. A period of limitation is prescribed by the statute for the purpose. The burden lies with him to prove the date of his alleged knowledge and that it is within the period of limitation. The pre-emptor is to succeed on the strength and proof of his own case. The learned Munsif, on consideration of the evidence on record made a clear finding that the petitioner was aware of the auction sale since before November, 1962 '" Reading the judgment as a whole, the irresistible conclusion is that the petitioner had knowledge of the auction sale since before November, 1962. The learned Subordinate Judge while concurring with the learned Munsif clearly found that: the petitioner as owner to the contiguous holding had knowledge of the sale from very beginning. In reaching the above finding the learned courts below considered the evidence of P.Ws. Alauddin and Sobhan. The learned Munsif disbelieved the evidence of Abdus Sobhan since he was over-zealous in support of the petitioner and went to the extent of saying what was "unusual". As regards Alauddin, the learned Munsif was of the view that he clearly stated in his evidence that he informed the petitioner after the acquittal of the criminal case which was on 12.8.63. The learned Munsif found that the story that the petitioner came to know of the sale for the first time on 1.4.63 from Abdus Sobhan and Alauddin is false." The learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the evidence of these two persons since they were not disinterested witnesses. 'As quoted earlier the learned Subordinate Judge observed Pit is the admitted case of the petitioner that opposite party cut away trees from auction sold land, filed T. S. No. 388 of 1961 against Okhrait Bijoy Kumar and the latter filed criminal case against the opposite party, so on and so forth. On the face of it, the case of the petitioner that 'he learnt about sale on 1.4.63 cannot be believed." Thus in view of the findings of the courts below on the question of the pre-emptor's alleged knowledge, the application is clearly barred by limitation.</u>

<u>8. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman next contends that the courts below acted with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in not correctly appreciating import of the term "knowledge". According to him, knowledge means a clear and definite knowledge on perception of necessary facts. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to the case of Kumud Nath Roy Chowdhury Vs. Rai Jatindra Nath Chowdhury 15 C.W.N. 399. This appeal arose out of an order of refusal to set aside an ex-parte decree. "Knowledge of the decree" within the meaning of Schedule II, Article 164 of the Limitation Act, was held to mean "knowledge not of a decree but of the particular decree which is sought to be set aside". In the case of Pundalick Vs. Vasanta Rao, II Bombay Law Reports, 1296 it was held that "knowledge" in article 164 of Limitation Act means "a certain and clear perception of a fact, the fact being the decree in the suit." In the case of Bapurao Sakharam Vs. Sadhu Bhivba, AIR 1923 Bombay 183 the import of the term "knowledge" within the meaning of article 164 of the Limitation Act came up for consideration and the learned Judges expressed themselves in the following terms :</u>

<u>"We think the words of the article mean something more than mere knowledge that the decree has been passed in some suit in some Court against the appellant. We think it means that the applicant must have knowledge not merely that the applicant had been passed by some Court against him but that a particular decree has been .passed against him in a particular Court in favour of a particular person for a particular sum."</u>

<u>In the case of Mst. Johora Begum Vs. Rafiqul Kader, 25 D.L.R. 91, Ruhul Islam J, as his Lordship then was, observed:</u>

<u>"Knowledge is something more than mere knowledge that a decree has been passed against him in a particular Court in favour of a particular person for a particular sum (or in respect of particular property) and not merely the knowledge that decree has been passed by some court against him."</u>

<u>In the case of Biman Chandra Datta Vs. Pra-matha Nath Ghose, 36 Calcutta Law Journal 295, the term knowledge occurring in Section 18 of the Limitation Act was subjected to scrutiny. This Letters Patent appeal arose out of a suit for recovery of money misappropriated by the defendant Mokerjee J. dealt with the question of knowledge in the context of Section 18 in the following terms:</u>

<u>"The true position then is that where a suit is on the face of it barred, it is for the plaintiff to prove in the first instance the circumstances which would prevent the statute from having its ordinary effect. A person who, in such circumstances, desires to invoke-the .aid of section 18, must establish that there has been fraud and that by means of such, fraud he has been kept from the knowledge of his right to sue or of the title whereon it is founded. Once this is established, the burden is shifted on the other side to show that the plaintiff had knowledge of the transaction beyond the period of limitation. Such knowledge must be clear and definite knowledge of the facts constituting the particular fraud; as Lord Hobhouse points out, it is not sufficient for the defendant to show that the plaintiff had some clues and hints which, perhaps, if vigorously and actually followed up, might have led to a complete knowledge of the fraud."</u>

<u>The facts of the case of Biman Chandra Datta (Supra) are clearly distinguishable. The petitioner, in the instance case, did not set up a case of fraud. His case is that on 1.4.63 he came to know about the auction sale from Alauddin and Abdus Sobhan and thereafter, on obtaining necessary particulars and depositing the requisite amount, he filed the application for pre-emption on 26.4.63, As observed earlier, the learned courts below, did not accept the evidence of the petitioner, Alauddin and Abdus Sobhan to the effect that the petitioner came to know of the transfer for the first time on 1.4.63. Therefore, the burden that the petitioner is "to prove in the first instance the circumstances which would prevent the statute from having its ordinary effect" remained with him. He failed to prove that he had clear and definite knowledge of the fact of the transfer on or after the date alleged by him. In other work the petitioner failed to prove that he had a clear and definite perception of the necessary particulars of the fact of transfer on or after 1.4.63 so as to constitute his knowledge of the transfer sought to be pre-empted. Thus the decisions referred to by the learned Advocate do not assist him.</u>

<u>9. On a consideration of the language used in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it further appears that the definite article "the" has been used to qualify “knowledge" occurring twice in the section. It, therefore, indicates that “the knowledge" must be definite knowledge. A precise or exact perception of the necessary particulars of a fact is the determinant of "the knowledge" which is essentially a question of fact. For the reasons stated above there is no substance in this application.</u>

The result, therefore, is that the Rule is discharged with costs assessed at 5 G. M.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptor is directed against a judgment of affirmance in a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

2. The disputed land compromising a tank on plot No. 131 and recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 1 belonged to petitioner and others in Taluki Right appertaining Touzi No. 358. The tank in question was taken away by the Comilla Municipality for management. The opposite party No. 1 took lease of the tank under the Comilla Municipality for a term of 12 years commencing from January, 1955 "and executed an agreement on 3-2-55. The opposite party No. 1 was in possession of the tank as a lessee under the Municipality and filed Title Suit No. 109 of 1967 for partition of the said tank. The petitioner and other co-sharers were impleaded in the said partition suit. The petitioner on receipt of summons along with a copy of the plaint came to know that one Taiyabun nessa, wife of O.P. No. 1 took a kabala dated 10-8-55 from Atul Chandra Das who took settlement of the land from one Shabmhu Charan by a kabuliya dated 5-9-46. Shambhu Charan took lease under the Talukdars Bardhans in the berami of Debendra Nath Chattarjee in the year 1943 or 1944. The petitioner thus came to know of the transfer made by Atul Chandra Das in favour of Taiyabunnessa on 8-41-67. The petitioner contends that he had no prior knowledge of the transfer. No notice of the said transfer was served upon him. Since the tank was in possession of the O.P. No. 1 as a lessee of the Municipality, he had no occasion to know about the alleged transfer. According to the petitioner, Taiyabunnessa was a stranger to the land. Taiyabunnessa died leaving O.P. Nos. 1 to 7 as heirs. On these allegations the application for pre-emption has been filed upon necessary statutory deposit.

3. The O.P. No. 1 traversing the material allegations made in the application contested the claim of the petition contending, inter alia, that the petitioner was fully aware of the sale when it took place. The application is eventually barred by limitation. It was further contended that the petitioner is not a co-sharer of the holding of the land and be Las no locus stand to make this application for preemption. The petitioner was a co-sharer of the superior Taluk. The other co-sharers created tenancy in favour of Shambhu Charan Misir in Mirash right and Shambhu Charan in his turn settled the suit land with Atul Chandra Das in raiyati interest and Atul was in possession of the disputed land as a raiyat under Shambhu Charan when he transferred his interest to Taiyabunnessa. The superior interest has already been acquired by State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The petitioner has no interest in the disputed land and the application filed by him is misconceived and not maintainable.

4. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record rejected the petitioner's claim holding inter alia that the petitioner was not a co-sharer in the raiyati held by Atul Chandra Das and as such had no right to apply for pre-emption. The learned Munsif further found that the application was barred by limitation.

5. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the decision of the learned Munsif on both the counts. The learned Subordinate Judge clearly found that "the present petitioner is not a co-sharer of the tenancy held by Atul Chandra Das as a raiyati holding. As such the petitioner has no locus stand to file this application for pre-emption and this application for pre-emption is not maintainable under the law." The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the application was barred by limitation. According to the learned Subordinate Judge "the petitioner was aware of the transfer made to Taiyabunncssa by Atul Chandra Das when it took place. So, I decide this point also against the petitioner and I find that the case is absolutely barred by limitation."

<u>6. Mr. Salam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the land. According to him after the acquisition of superior interest, the petitioner become a tenant in respect of the disputed lard along with other tenants including Atul Chandra Das. The learned Advocate submits that the property in suit being a tank is impartible in nature and as such the pre-emptor become a co-sharer in joint ownership and possession with ether tenants. Mr. Salary has Prefaced his contention by referring to the decision in the case of, Anwara Begunm Chowdhurani and Shamsul Huda Chowdhury Vs. Nur Jahan Begum and others reported in 27 DLR (Appellate Division) 109. There is no dispute with the proposition that after the notification issued under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the status of an under raiyat was upgraded to that of a tenant. There is also no dispute that with the acquisition of rent-receiving interests by the Government, all the intermediary interests disappeared and a person holding land under the landlord became a tenant holding land directly under the Government. These aspects of law have no direct reference to the question raised by the learned Advocate. The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not contemplate the merger of all the existing tenancies into one common tenancy and all the tenants under the different tenancies become co-sharers in such a tenancy. The facts of the instant case clearly indicate that the petitioner was a co-sharer of the Touzi No. 358 recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 1. There is no dispute that Hemanga Mohan Bardhan was a co-sharer in the said Khatian. No. 1. This Bardhan settled some land of the disputed tank in favour of Shambhu Charan Misir. The settlement obtained by Shambhu Charan constituted a tenancy distinct and separate from the holding recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 1. It further appears that Shambhu Charan settled the suit land in favour of Atul Chandra Das by a registered Kabuliyat Exhibit B dated 5. 9. 46 in raiyati right. Thus the raiyati right of Atul Chandra Das constituted a holding which was different from the holding of Shambhu Charan and the holding recorded C. S. Khatian No. 1. On an analysis of these facts, it transpires that the contention of Mr. Salain, leads to an absurd proposition of law. By no stretch of imagination it can be conceived that with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act coming into force, all these three holdings merged into one holding and all the tenants in respect of these different holdings became co-sharers to one common holding, in other words a co-tenancy emerged. The effect of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is that the intermediary interests ceased to exist and the tenants who were holding as under-tenants became tenants directly under the Government. Mr. Salam, however, could not cite any authority in support of his proposition. He has, however, referred to the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury and another Vs. Musammat Rezia Begum and another 16 DLR 77 to contend that Atul Chandra Das, Shambhu Charan and Bardhan became co-sharers with the petitioner. The principle laid down in the said case does not extend any Support to the view Mr. Salim has advanced. He has relied upon the following passage from the case of Brindaban Chandra:</u>

<u>"If a share or portion of a non-agricultural land is sold, then a person can be a co-sharer tenant, even if he is not a co-possessor (physical speaking) of the specified land, provided a co-tenancy is established in respect of land itself. The sharing of the tenancy in respect of land is the gist of the Section. The co-tenancy itself must appertain to the disputed land and not to any other land. This is the plain meaning of the words "co-sharer tenants of such land." The passage referred to and relied upon by Mr. Salam is of no assistance to him unless he succeeds in proving "that a co-tenancy is established in respect of the land itself" as observed earlier. The different holdings standing in the name of Atul, Shambhu Charan and the Bardhans with the petitioner did never constitute a co-tenancy. In the circumstances this decision is of no assistance of Mr. Salam.</u>

7. Further, on the date of the transfer namely, 10-8-55 the petitioner was not a co-sharer in a tenancy in respect of the land. Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act cud not come in operation to invest a person with a right which was not available to him on the date of transfer. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act makes no reference to any retrospective operation of the right of pre-emption. Thus, in any view of the matter whether the properly is partible or not, whether or not the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act made the petitioner a tenant in respect of the land held by him under khatian No. 1, the petitioner was not a co-sharer having a right of pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

8. Mr. Salam next contends that the learned Subordinate judge acted with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in holding that the application was barred by limitation. According to Mr. Salam the petitioner came to know of the transfer on 8.11.67 when he received the summons of Partition Suit No. 109 of 1967 along with a copy of the plaint. Mr. Salam has drawn my attention to the evidence of the petitioner to the effect that after the service of summons along with the copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 109 of 1967, he obtained a certified copy of the impugned deed of transfer and thereafter filed the application on 16.1.68. Mr. Salam submits that the application was filed within four months from the date of knowledge of the transfer and as such the application was not barred by limitation.

9. The learned. Munsif on consideration of the materials on record reached a clear finding in the following terms:

"From my discussion of the evidence both documentary and oral, and the circumstances of the case, I find that the petitioner knew about the sale from before the alleged date of knowledge."

The learned Subordinate Judge held that the petitioner was "aware of the transfer made to Taiyabunnessa by Atul Chandra Das when it took place."

<u>10. Mr. Salam referring to a decision in the case of Mrs. Zohura Begum Vs. Rafiqul Kader 25 DLR 91 contended that "knowledge is something more than mere knowledge that a decree had been passed against him in a particular court in favour of particular person for a particular sum (or in respect of particular property) and not merely the knowledge, that decree has been passed by some Court against him." This reference does not help Mr. Salam to get over the hurdle of limitation. Knowledge is a fact and is referable to certain state of things representing a fact. Knowledge is not a mere information but something more. Knowledge pre-supposes a knower and a known. Knowledge is a knower-known relation, a product of interaction between the knowing self or subject and the object to be known. It is not a mere subjective state of mind or a simple objective representation but a conscious relation between the subjective mind and the objective phenomenon. A clear and definite perception of necessary particulars of a fact may be said to constitute "knowledge" which is in essence a question of fact to be determined in the facts and circumstances of each case. The information about the transfer by Atul Chandra Das in favour of Taiyabunnessa received from the plaint of Title Suit No. 109 of 1967 did not represent the material particulars to establish a relationship between the object namely the transfer and the knower namely, the petitioner. The particulars disclosed by the said plaint were not sufficient to enable the petitioner to make the application upon compliance of the requirements of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. More material particulars were necessary for the purpose. But the Courts below did not accept on evidence, the petitioner's alleged, facts constituting his knowledge. The learned courts below took into consideration the evidence adduced by the contending parties and on assessment of evidence concurrently found that the petitioner had knowledge of the transfer when it took place. On a careful consideration of the judgments of the courts below, it transpires that the finding as regards the knowledge of the transfer does not suffer form any imperfection. Further, the fact of possession, according to the courts below, indicated the knowledge of the petitioner.</u>

<u>Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 contends that an inference on a question of fact is also a finding of fact.</u>

11. On a consideration of the materials on record, it is evident that the learned courts below reached the finding on the question of limitation upon due consideration, assessment and appreciation of the evidence. Hence the question of limitation is concluded by the concurrent finding of fact.

For the reasons stated above, the contentions raised by Mr. Salam are of no substance and must consequently fail.

In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs.

End.
